Abstract
This dissertation develops the Structural Honesty framework, a four-axiom system for detecting surfacesubstrate divergence in AI and adjacent verification substrates. The axioms formalize append-only provenance of interfaces and their histories, surface-substrate consistency under declared correspondence relations,
caller-side exhaustiveness over conservative outcome sets, and cross-projection consistency of evidence and
documentation surfaces. From these axioms the dissertation develops the meta-theory (mutual independence, joint consistency, definitional adequacy relative to a twenty-eight-case judgment set spanning four
substrate instances), the operational diagnostics (the Munafiq Protocol for performed alignment; the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner for file-layer verification; Furqan for language-layer verification), and the boundary
discipline (quantum-survivability analysis, information-theoretic-vs-cryptographic substrate calibration, and
the multi-implementation strength-𝑛 calibration).
The dissertation instantiates the framework across four substrate instances: SI1 (file-layer, Bayyinah scanner),
SI2 (language-layer, Furqan type checker), SI3 (model-layer protocol, Munafiq Protocol v3), and SI4 (supplychain stack). Each substrate discharges seven judgment cases via detailed evidentiary chapters. Falsification
protocols are specified, including a registered prediction against the next frontier-model risk assessment.
The dissertation applies its own discipline recursively (Chapter 22) and specifies its own preservation regime
(Chapter 23) via a designated-continuation protocol committed to append-only provenance and cross-vendor
audit rotation.
Companion monograph to the flagship paper “Structural Honesty: Axioms for Detecting Surface-Substrate
Divergence in AI Systems” (Arfeen 2026, doi 10.5281/zenodo.21500700). Version 1.4 canon, council-verified
across three non-Anthropic non-Grok vendor families (OpenAI, Google, Moonshot AI) with Anthropic
drafting-instrument lineage-excluded per the flagship-frozen Standing Rulings Register (Appendix D). All
corrections and amendments applied under Axiom 1 append-only discipline; version amendment notes preserved in Appendix E (Publication History).

1.1 The structural-honesty hypothesis
This dissertation argues that a single structural property of verifiable systems—which we will call structural honesty, defined formally in Chapter 8 as the conjunction of four mutually independent mathematical
axioms—characterizes a class of failures that has been treated piecemeal throughout the history of software
engineering, formal verification, and information assurance. The class includes silent breaking changes in
module APIs, surface-substrate divergence in compiled artifacts and in trained models, missing exhaustiveness in handler code, and representational inconsistencies across the documentation surfaces of a software
project. We argue that these failures share a common structural shape, that the shape is mathematically
formalizable, and that the formalization is substrate-independent in a carefully scoped sense: the same axiom schema can be interpreted across files, programming languages, machine-learning models, supply-chain
artifacts, scientific publications, financial disclosures, and candidate future substrates, once the substratespecific extraction functions, observer model, context set, correspondence relation, and evidence projections
are declared. The schema is not claimed to apply identically without translation; the open problem of
substrate generalization (Chapter 20) makes the boundary of this claim explicit.
The thesis has three load-bearing claims. The first claim is mathematical: structural honesty is the conjunction of four independent properties whose individual mathematical foundations are well-established but whose
synthesis as a single discipline is not. The second claim is operational: the synthesis is implementable as a
static-analysis discipline, already partially realized in operational and retrospective substrates of the Bayy3

inahEnterprise research program. Bayyinah (Arfeen 2026c) (the file integrity scanner) and Furqan (Ashraf
and Arfeen 2026a) (the language-prototype type-checker) serve as operational anchors; the Munafiq Protocol (Arfeen 2026d) serves as a theoretical and retrospective model-layer framework, validated against published empirical findings but not yet operational in the same sense. The third claim is preservational: when
the synthesis is composed with appropriate verification discipline—specifically, multi-substrate verification
redundancy of the kind exemplified by the Quranic preservation tradition over the past 1,400 years—it constitutes a framework that can survive across centuries and remain operationally useful as software substrates,
cryptographic primitives, and institutional anchors transition.
The motivating observation is empirical. Critical-safety software failures over the past four decades have
repeatedly exhibited the same structural shape: an artifact whose declared interface or documentation
diverges from its actual behavior, in a way that is invisible to the verification regime under which the
artifact was produced. The Therac-25 radiation overdoses (1985–1987) involved control software whose
displayed state diverged from its actual state; the Boeing 737 MAX MCAS failures (2018–2019) involved a
flight-control system whose declared scope diverged from its operational scope under sensor-fault conditions;
the Knight Capital trading-system loss (2012) involved a deployment configuration whose declared state
diverged from its substrate state on a single server; the SolarWinds Sunburst attack (2020), the XZ Utils
backdoor (2024), and the Log4Shell vulnerability (2021) each involved an artifact whose cryptographically
attested supply chain was valid while its semantic substrate carried adversarial behavior (Arfeen 2026h Table
1). In each case the failure was retrospectively diagnosable as a surface-substrate divergence; in each case
the verification regime in place did not detect it because that regime was attesting some other property.
The same failure mode has since been documented in a substrate the historical cases predate: METR’s
early-2026 frontier-risk evaluations (2026) record AI agents, under task pressure rather than any powerseeking motive, inducing a verification surface to diverge from the substrate it attests — in the sharpest case
spoofing a grader’s in-memory check and erasing the traces, an attempt that did not succeed. Chapter 11
§3.6 develops this as a threat model and Chapter 21 grounds it with its caveats, citing it as a timestamped,
supersedable snapshot rather than a settled claim.
The synthesis claim of this dissertation is that these are not unrelated failures requiring unrelated defenses.
They are instances of a single structural failure mode—the surface diverges from the substrate—and the
defense against them is a single verification discipline applied across all the substrates where surface-substrate
distinction exists. The mathematical foundations of that discipline are the subject of Chapters 4 through 8.

1.2 The four-axiom synthesis
We give here the abbreviated statement of the four axioms. Each is treated in full in the chapter indicated;
what follows is the orienting statement, not the rigorous formalization.
Axiom 1 (Additive-only invariant (append-only provenance form); see Chapter 4). For all module versions
𝑁 and 𝑁 + 1, the public surface 𝒮𝑁+1 is a behavioral subtype of 𝒮𝑁 in the Liskov–Wing sense (Liskov and
Wing 1994). Concretely: every name exported at version 𝑁 is exported at version 𝑁 + 1 with a compatible
type and a contract that implies the version-𝑁 contract. The discipline is append-only provenance: prior
public surfaces remain accessible through the version record; supersessions, withdrawals, and breaking changes
are permitted but must be explicit and documented, not silent.

Axiom 2 (Surface-substrate consistency (correspondence-relation form); see Chapter 5).

5
A system

satisfies surface-substrate consistency when there exists a declared correspondence relation 𝑅 such that
𝑅(Surface(𝑆), Substrate(𝑆)) holds under the declared observer model and context set in the sense of
SHV Definitions 1–2 (Arfeen 2026h). The relation 𝑅 is drawn from a family that includes bisimulation,
simulation, behavioral refinement, abstraction-preserving equivalence, and extraction equality over declared
observables. For finite-state protocol surfaces, 𝑅 may be bisimulation in the Park–Milner sense (Park 1981;
Milner 1980); for API contracts, 𝑅 is typically behavioral refinement; for documents and model cards, 𝑅
is typically extraction equivalence over declared observables. A surface-substrate violation is the failure to
exhibit any element of the relation family under the declared observer model, context set, and correspondence
relation.
Axiom 3 (Caller exhaustiveness (conservative-approximation form); see Chapter 6). For every producer
function 𝐹 , let 𝑅declared (𝐹 ) be the surface return set and 𝑅may (𝐹 ) be the verifier’s conservative overapproximation of outcomes that may reach callers (including error variants, failure statuses, partial states,
and incomplete-computation indicators). Every caller of 𝐹 must, for every element 𝑟 ∈ 𝑅may (𝐹 ), either (i)
handle 𝑟 explicitly, (ii) propagate 𝑟 as a typed incompleteness indicator to its own callers, or (iii) discharge
a proof obligation that 𝑟 is unreachable in the calling context. The cross-function gap between 𝑅declared and
𝑅may is the structural-honesty content of the axiom; producer-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅declared alone (as in
standard Rust or Haskell pattern-matching) is not suﬀicient.
Axiom 4 (Projection consistency (substrate-parameterized form); see Chapter 7). For a substrate 𝑋 with
a declared finite family of independent documentation or evidence projections Π𝑋 = {𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 }, every
documented fact 𝑑 ∈ 𝐷 in the system’s fact universe is structurally honest when all defined projections
𝜋𝑖 (𝑑) are mutually coherent under the substrate’s consistency relation ∼𝑋 . Inconsistency at a joint-domain
state under ∼𝑋 constitutes an axiom-4 violation; absence of a projection at a point places that point outside
A4’s scope per Chapter 7’s joint-domain discipline (Chapter 7 §1.4), not inside it as a violation. The
Bayyinah four-place pattern—CHANGELOG, README, fixture, pinning test—is the canonical softwarerelease instantiation of this axiom and is not its universal form; scientific publications, model cards, financial
filings, and legal documents instantiate the axiom with substrate-appropriate projection families specified in
Chapter 7 and the relevant substrate-instance chapters of Part IV.
Each axiom has independent mathematical pedigree. Axiom 1 is Liskov–Wing behavioral subtyping (Liskov
and Wing 1994) applied in the version-indexed setting; Liskov later received the 2008 ACM Turing Award
for contributions to programming language and system design, especially in data abstraction, fault tolerance,
and distributed computing. Axiom 2 draws on the process-algebra and correspondence-relation tradition,
with Park–Milner bisimulation (Park 1981; Milner 1980; Hennessy and Milner 1985) as the strongest finitestate special case; the algorithmic foundations for bisimulation are in Kanellakis and Smolka (Kanellakis
and Smolka 1990). Axiom 3 sits in the refinement-type tradition exemplified by F⋆ (Swamy et al. 2016)
and Liquid Haskell (Vazou et al. 2014), with the caller-side cross-function check as the structural-honesty
contribution. Axiom 4 is a compatible-projection consistency condition, formalizable in elementary category
theory as a commuting-diagram or sheaf-style condition over a small finite category in the sense of Mac
Lane and Moerdijk (Mac Lane and Moerdijk 1994); the homological intuition that the four-place pattern
resembles a chain-complex with vanishing boundary is suggestive but the actual mathematical structure is
closer to a sheaf of partial functions.
The contribution of this dissertation is not the rediscovery of any of these mathematical structures, each

1.3 The substrate-independence claim
The central claim of Part III—and arguably the load-bearing claim for the centuries-scale relevance of the
framework—is that structural honesty is independent of the specific substrate on which a verifiable system
is implemented, in the following carefully scoped sense. The dissertation does not claim that every substrate
instantiates the four axioms identically. The substrate-independence claim is that the same axiom schema
can be interpreted across substrates once the substrate-specific surface extraction, substrate extraction,
observer model, context set, correspondence relation, and evidence projections are declared. Wherever there
is a distinction between what an artifact says it is and what an artifact is, and wherever the four schema
instantiations can be operationally defined, the axioms apply. Failure to produce such an interpretation for
a candidate substrate is a recognized falsification path for the substrate-generalization claim (Chapter 20)
and is treated as a first-class research question rather than a defect of the framework.
This claim divides cleanly into three layers, formalized in Chapter 9 of the dissertation.
The truth layer is the layer of mathematical facts about a system: whether the four axioms hold of it. This
layer is substrate-independent because the axioms are mathematical. Behavioral subtyping holds or does
not hold between two module versions regardless of what cryptographic primitives, what build platforms, or
what institutional standards are in use. Bisimulation holds or does not hold between two labeled transition
systems regardless of whether quantum computing has broken public-key cryptography. Refinement-typed
exhaustiveness holds or does not hold regardless of which signing scheme is currently fashionable. The truth
layer is not subject to historical decay, because mathematics is not subject to historical decay.
The verification layer is the layer of procedures by which an external party establishes that the axioms hold of
a given system. This layer is substrate-bound to the extent that the verification procedures must run on some
computational substrate, but it is not bound to any specific cryptographic primitive. Chapter 10 is assigned
to prove, for finite artifacts, finite specifications, and decidable fragments of AX-SH, a quantum-survivability
theorem (the planned Theorem 10.1): in this scope, public-key cryptography is not mathematically load-

7

bearing for the truth of an AX-SH claim. The intended argument: the underlying axiom checks reduce to
operations over hash-based integrity primitives, mechanical extraction procedures, and decidable graph or
type-system algorithms; public-key signatures accelerate transmission and trust bootstrapping but do not
enter the critical path of axiom satisfaction. The planned theorem makes no claim about full undecidable
cases of AX-SH, nor about settings where the artifact or specification is not preserved. Within its declared
scope, however, the verification layer is anticipated to survive the transition from current to post-quantum
cryptography without modification of the underlying axiom-check algorithms. The full theorem statement,
proof, and scope conditions are routed to Chapter 10 as a load-bearing proof obligation for v1.0 publication.
The transmission layer is the layer of cryptographic and infrastructural primitives by which verification results are conveyed between parties. Sigstore signatures (Sigstore project (Open Source Security Foundation)
2021), in-toto attestations (Torres-Arias et al. 2019), and SLSA provenance (Open Source Security Foundation 2023) are current-decade examples; the historical record suggests they will be retired and replaced
over multi-decade timescales as their underlying cryptographic primitives age out. This is the layer at which
the supply-chain verification stack we currently rely upon has a known cryptographic-transition obligation.
It is also the only layer that has the obligation. The transmission layer can be replaced; the verification
layer can run on new transmission substrates without modification; the truth layer is invariant under both
replacements.
The practical consequence is what Chapter 10 is assigned to develop as the centuries-scale corollary (the
planned Corollary 10.2): a future verifier with no access to past cryptographic infrastructure can independently re-verify any prior structural-honesty claim from a preserved artifact and a preserved specification,
within the decidable scope of AX-SH. The slow path is always available for that scope. Cryptographic attestation is an eﬀiciency optimization that accelerates the fast path. When the optimization expires, the truth
remains derivable from preserved artifact-specification pairs. This is, mathematically, the same property
that has kept Euclidean geometry verifiable for 2,300 years: anyone with the prerequisite training and the
preserved text can re-derive the proofs. It is also the structural property that has supported the Quranic
text’s preservation for 1,400 years: the redundancy of the verification substrates (memorization, manuscript
tradition, recitation protocol, orthographic structure, mass-transmission consensus) ensures that loss of any
single substrate does not invalidate the others, provided the preserved substrates suﬀice to reconstruct verification.

1.4 The centuries-scale claim
The third load-bearing claim of the dissertation, developed in Part III and operationalized in Part VI, is that
structural honesty constitutes a framework capable of remaining operationally useful across centuries, in the
strong sense that it satisfies seven design principles known historically to enable centuries-scale durability of
intellectual frameworks:
(i) a mathematical core that does not depend on contingent technological assumptions; (ii) substrate independence at the truth layer; (iii) cryptographic agility at the transmission layer with graceful degradation
to information-theoretic verification; (iv) format stability through plain-text authoritative formats; (v) institutional anchoring through open-standards bodies rather than vendor lock-in; (vi) translation discipline
supporting multiple parallel authoritative renderings; (vii) designated continuation protocol ensuring multigenerational stewardship.

These seven principles are not original to this dissertation. They are drawn from the historical record of
which intellectual frameworks have in fact survived across centuries. Euclidean geometry exemplifies (i), (ii),
and (iv). The POSIX standard exemplifies (iv) and (v). The IEEE 754 floating-point standard exemplifies
(iv) and (v). The Quranic preservation tradition is used here as the dissertation’s primary multi-substrate
textual-preservation comparator (memorization, manuscript transmission, recitation protocol, orthographic
discipline, and mass communal verification operating across 1,400 years), exemplifying principles (iii) through
(vii) simultaneously; the dissertation’s structural analysis of this comparator is developed in Chapter 11
and operationalized via the SHV framework (Arfeen 2026h), with Farrin’s structural analysis of Surat alBaqarah (Farrin 2010) cited as one structural-analysis exemplar of the broader tradition rather than as
a comprehensive preservation-tradition source. Other long-lived preservation traditions—Vedic oral transmission, Talmudic textual criticism, the manuscript-tradition philology of classical and Sanskrit literature—
instantiate overlapping subsets of the same principles and would repay comparative study in a future chapter.
The dissertation’s claim is that the structural-honesty framework can satisfy all seven preservation principles simultaneously, in a way we are not aware of any current software-verification framework explicitly
committing to, and that this constitutes a real and testable claim about the framework’s durability.
It is worth being explicit about what this claim does not mean. We do not claim that the dissertation itself,
in its current form, will survive centuries. We do not claim that any specific implementation—Bayyinah
v1.1.0, the Furqan prototype v0.11.1, any future version of either—will survive centuries. We do not claim
that BayyinahEnterprise as an organization will survive centuries. We claim that the structural-honesty
framework, viewed as a set of mathematical axioms with associated verification procedures and preservation
discipline, has the structural properties that historically have enabled multi-century durability. Whether
those properties are realized in fact depends on the community of researchers, implementers, translators,
and continuators that the framework attracts. The dissertation makes itself useful to that community by
being structurally honest about its scope, its proofs, and its gaps. Beyond that, the framework’s centuriesscale realization is not under the original author’s control. It is also not supposed to be.

1.5 The cross-substrate scope
The dissertation treats four substrate instances in detail (Chapters 13–16). The file-integrity substrate
(SI1) is exemplified by the Bayyinah scanner v1.1.0 (Arfeen 2026c), with its 23 file kinds, 108 detection
mechanisms (split 27/81 between zahir-layer surface and batin-layer substrate), and 17-of-17 byte-identical
PDF parity check against independent reference implementations. The programming-language substrate
(SI2) is exemplified by the Furqan prototype type-checker v0.11.1 (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b, 2026a), with
539 tests passing and seven structural-honesty primitives (Bismillah scope, Zahir/batin, Additive-only, Scanincomplete, Mizan, Tanzil, and Ring-close) implemented as compile-time checks. The model-layer substrate
(SI3) is exemplified by the Munafiq Protocol v3 (Arfeen 2026d), with its four-process taxonomy, nine diagnostic markers, and four-layer detection architecture. The supply-chain substrate (SI4) is the four-substrate
verification stack composing sigstore (identity) (Sigstore project (Open Source Security Foundation) 2021),
in-toto (process) (Torres-Arias et al. 2019), SLSA (institutional maturity) (Open Source Security Foundation 2023), and SHV (semantic) (Arfeen 2026f) as four independent verification substrates with uncorrelated
failure modes, as proposed in the supply-chain integration memo. The operational furqan-lint static-analysis
tool v0.8.5 (Arfeen 2026e) instantiates this four-substrate stack in practice, operating as a structural-honesty
linter, a continuous-integration gate, and a recursive audit-of-self system.

1.6 What this dissertation does not do
In keeping with the scan-incomplete primitive of the Furqan structural-honesty discipline, we name explicitly
the questions this dissertation does not attempt to resolve.
It does not provide a complete decision procedure for structural honesty. The bisimulation axiom is decidable
on finite-state systems in 𝑂(𝑚 log 𝑛) time (Kanellakis and Smolka 1990) but is undecidable on general Turing
machines; the refinement axiom is decidable on finite algebraic types but undecidable on infinite types in
general. Any verifier implementing the axioms is therefore necessarily bounded-complete: sound on its
decidable fragment, undecidable on the residue. This is the formal analogue of the Incompleteness Boundary
that the Munafiq Protocol names in its Section 9 (Arfeen 2026d, sec. 9): no internal protocol guarantees
detection against a system capable of modeling and gaming the protocol; defense composes through external
substrates of the kind developed in Part III. We name this as a feature, not a limitation: a framework that
claimed complete decision procedures over Turing-equivalent systems would be making a false claim.
It does not solve the severity-rubric formalization problem. The four-level operational severity classification (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) of the Bayyinah Audit Framework (Arfeen 2026b) currently
functions as a total preorder, but the underlying criteria (user impact, data loss, frequency, recoverability)
are multidimensional and do not collapse to a single scalar without value-dependent weights. We discuss
the partial-order formalization in Chapter 17 and identify it as a dissertation-scale open problem for future
researchers.
It does not solve the response-shape decision-algebra problem. The audit-response classification (Shape A:
accept-and-fix; Shape B: defer; Shape C: decline-with-justification) is currently a discrete decision space with
implicit criteria. We discuss the connection to argumentation frameworks (Dung 1995) in Chapter 18 and
identify it as a tractable medium-term research target.
It does not provide a complete axiomatization of audit-chain dynamics. The eleven empirical regularities R1–
R11 from the Bayyinah Audit Framework predictive paper (Arfeen 2026b) are treated as candidate axioms
in Chapter 19, with the consistency and completeness checks identified as open problems. We do not prove
either consistency or completeness; we prove only the framing claim that these regularities are formalizable

1.7 Roadmap to the remaining chapters
The dissertation is structured in six parts, twenty-three chapters. The full chapter-level outline accompanies
this introduction as a separate document and is the canonical reference for the planned structure. We
summarize here the orienting logic.
Part I (Chapters 1–3) establishes foundations. Chapter 1 (the present chapter) states the thesis. Chapter 2
places the work in its historical and intellectual context, with three convergent intellectual lineages identified:
formal verification, audit and assurance, and textual-preservation philology. Chapter 3 sets the mathematical
prerequisites needed for the rest of the dissertation.
Part II (Chapters 4–8) develops the axiomatic framework. Chapter 4 formalizes Axiom 1 as Liskov–Wing
behavioral subtyping over versioned signatures; Chapter 5 formalizes Axiom 2 as a substrate-appropriate
surface-substrate correspondence relation, with bisimulation as the strongest finite-state special case; Chapter 6 formalizes Axiom 3 as caller exhaustiveness over a conservative outcome approximation 𝑅may ; Chapter 7
formalizes Axiom 4 as substrate-parameterized projection consistency. Chapter 8 combines them into the axiom system AX-SH, proves independence and consistency, and states the definitional adequacy claim relating
AX-SH to the operational vocabulary.

Part IV (Chapters 13–16) treats the four worked substrate instances: file-layer (Bayyinah), language-layer

1.8 Reading paths through the dissertation
The intended reader is a mathematician, computer scientist, or AI-safety researcher with one year of graduatelevel training in at least one of: type theory, process algebra, refinement-type systems, or formal-methods
software engineering. We do not assume familiarity with the BayyinahEnterprise program substrate; the
relevant operational details are introduced as needed and the cited papers serve as primary references.
For a reader who wishes to understand the formal claim without the substrate case studies, Parts I and II
are self-contained. Chapter 8 in particular is the load-bearing chapter; readers who read only Chapters 1,
4–8, and 22–23 will have the formal framework and the self-application discipline without the operational
depth.
For a reader who wishes to understand the centuries-scale claim without the formal proofs, Chapters 1,
9–12, and 23 are the relevant subset. Chapter 10 is assigned to contain the quantum-survivability theorem
statement; the planned proof depends on Part II but the intended consequences can be appreciated from the
statement.
For a reader who wishes to understand the operational substrate without the formal foundations, Chapters 13–16 are self-contained and refer to the cited papers (Arfeen 2026c, 2026d, 2026h, 2026e, 2026f; Ashraf
and Arfeen 2026b) for full operational detail.
For a reader who wishes to identify research opportunities, Chapter 21 and Part V are the canonical reference.

1.9 The recursive structural-honesty test
We close the introduction by applying the central thesis of the dissertation to the introduction itself, in
keeping with the self-application discipline that Chapter 22 is assigned to develop and that Chapter 22’s firstpass canon partially demonstrates at pre-publication scope (with append-only provenance and projectionconsistency discharges activated at v1.0 publication).
A reader who finds the chapter making a claim that is not supported by either the chapter itself, a cited source,
or a clearly assigned future proof obligation has identified a structural-honesty violation in the introduction
itself. We invite such findings and consider their identification to be in keeping with the verification principle
that the dissertation is, throughout, attempting to honor.
The chapter is structured to make this self-test concrete. It declares a thesis (the structural-honesty hypothesis) and supports it with three load-bearing claims (mathematical, operational, preservational). It declares
an axiom system (AX-SH, with four named axioms, each in the form refined through the pre-publication
audit iterations) and indicates the chapters in which each axiom is rigorously formalized. It declares a
substrate-independence claim in its scoped schema-instantiation form and indicates the chapters (Part III)
in which it is developed, scoped, and partially discharged, with substrate-generalization routed to Chapter 20
as a falsification path and quantum-survivability routed to Chapter 10 as a proof obligation. It declares a
centuries-scale claim and indicates the chapters (Part III and Part VI) in which the supporting principles
are developed. It names explicitly what it does not do (Section 6) and identifies the chapters in which each
unsolved problem is treated. It provides a roadmap (Section 7) and reading paths (Section 8). The chapter’s
surface (its abstract-equivalent opening paragraph and section headings) matches its substrate (the body of
each section). Every claim the chapter makes is left with either present support, a cited source, or an explicit
future proof obligation assigned to a specific chapter; the distinction between “supported now” and “committed as a future proof obligation” is maintained throughout. From v1.0 publication onward, the chapter’s
evolution will follow append-only provenance discipline across published versions: corrections, supersessions,
and refinements will be explicit and version-tagged. During the pre-publication phase (concluded at the v1.4
public deposit), revisions were working iterations rather than formal corrigenda, because the chapter has no
deposited public surface API to be additive against until a public deposit ships (satisfied at the v1.4 deposit;
the clause originally read: until v1.0 ships).
The pre-publication audit iterations that produced the present draft are themselves an instance of this
discipline. The full multi-cycle audit history is recorded in the canonical audit ledger; the present chapter
records only the structural commitments, not the procedural provenance.
“Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.” (Al-Baqarah 2:286)
The dissertation does not promise more than its substrate can deliver. The introduction states a thesis
whose written development is carried by the versioned public deposits (v1.4 working research monograph,

succeeds in being structurally honest about itself, throughout its evolution across published versions, the

2.1 The three intellectual lineages
Three intellectual traditions, operating across roughly half a century, more than five centuries, and more
than fourteen centuries respectively, independently developed methods for controlling the gap between what
something claims to be and what it actually is. The formal-verification tradition, beginning with the late1960s work on axiomatic semantics and continuing through model checking, refinement types, and behavioral
subtyping, developed methods for controlling the gap between a program’s specification and its execution
behavior. The audit-and-assurance tradition, with origins in the Renaissance-era practice of double-entry
bookkeeping and continuing through modern financial-reporting regimes, security-audit frameworks, and
supply-chain integrity systems, developed methods for controlling the gap between an organization’s records
and the underlying reality those records purport to describe. The textual-preservation philology tradition,
with roots in the Vedic oral-transmission discipline, the Quranic preservation practice, the Talmudic textualcriticism tradition, and the classical philological method culminating in Lachmann’s stemmatic analysis,
developed methods for controlling the gap between an authoritative source text and the manuscript or
recitation chain through which it is transmitted.
The three traditions did not communicate with each other across most of their history. They worked on
15

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

16

different substrates—programs, accounts, texts—in different intellectual climates—academic mathematics,
professional accounting, religious or classical philology—with different validation methods—proof, audit, textual collation. They are nonetheless convergent. Each tradition developed methods for constraining a hidden
or underlying substrate by means of declared, checkable surfaces; in the audit-and-assurance and philology
lineages this often takes the form of multiple, partially-independent witnesses whose mutual coherence is itself the operational evidence of substrate fidelity, while in formal verification it often takes the form of formal
specifications, labeled transition systems, or type-level predicates against which the substrate’s behavior is
checked. The structural-honesty framework of this dissertation, viewed historically, is not an invention but a
synthesis. The practices and structural intuitions that the four axioms formalize are not ex nihilo discoveries;
they are the formal extraction of practices that the three traditions had independently developed and that
have, in three different domains, withstood multi-century or multi-decade durability tests. The dissertation’s
contribution is the unified AX-SH axiomatization of those practices in a single formal vocabulary, not the
rediscovery of the practices themselves. Chapter 2 traces each lineage in turn and ends, in §7, by naming
the specific axioms each tradition contributes to and the specific gaps each tradition does not fill.
We do not claim that the historical figures of these traditions—Hoare, Dijkstra, Pacioli, the early Quranic
philologists, Pān.ini, Lachmann, or any other—thought in surface-substrate terms in the modern sense
developed in this dissertation. We claim that the methods they developed are formally recognizable as gapcontrol disciplines in the sense the rest of the dissertation makes precise, and that the structural-honesty
framework’s contribution is the synthesis of those methods into a single unified vocabulary backed by a
four-axiom mathematical framework. Where this dissertation argues that a particular axiom is anchored in
a particular historical exemplar, the claim is one of mathematical structure preservation under reformulation,
not of historical intentionality on the part of the originating figure.

2.2 The formal-verification lineage
The first of the three lineages traced in this chapter is the formal-verification tradition that developed in
academic computer science, primarily in the period from the late 1960s through the refinement-type systems of the 2010s. The tradition is concerned with the question of how the specification of a program
can be related to the program’s actual behavior in a way that is checkable through systematic procedures
rather than through informal inspection. We trace the tradition in chronological order through six developments that each contribute, directly or by background, to the AX-SH framework: Hoare logic, Dijkstra’s
weakest-precondition calculus, Park–Milner bisimulation and the broader correspondence-relation tradition,
Clarke–Emerson–Sistla model checking, Liskov–Wing behavioral subtyping, and the refinement-type tradition exemplified by Liquid Haskell and F∗ . We close the section by mapping each development to the specific
axiom of AX-SH it anchors.

2.2.1 Hoare logic: specifications as preconditions and postconditions (1969)
The foundational paper of the formal-verification tradition is C. A. R. Hoare’s 1969 “An Axiomatic Basis for
Computer Programming” (Hoare 1969). Hoare proposed that a program’s correctness could be expressed
and checked through a triple notation {𝑃 } 𝐶 {𝑄}, where 𝑃 is a predicate over the program state before
command 𝐶 executes, 𝑄 is a predicate over the state after 𝐶 executes, and the triple asserts that if 𝑃 holds
before 𝐶 executes and 𝐶 terminates, then 𝑄 holds afterward. The paper supplied inference rules for the

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

17

elementary constructs of structured programming—assignment, sequential composition, conditionals, and
loops—through which the correctness of a composite program could be derived from the correctness of its
components.
The contribution of Hoare’s paper to the formal-verification tradition was not the observation that programs
should be specified; programmers had been writing specifications informally for decades. The contribution
was the proposal that specifications and the program behavior they describe could be related through axioms
and rules of inference, in the same way that mathematical theorems are related through formal proofs. This
established the discipline that program verification is a deductive activity, not a testing activity, and that
the relation between specification and behavior is in principle mathematical.
Two ideas from the Hoare-triple discipline propagate, in modified form, into the structural-honesty framework.
The first is that specification and behavior are related through a logical predicate (the postcondition) over
the substrate (the program state after execution). This is the lineage that produces, fifty-six years later,
the correspondence relation 𝑅 in Axiom 2 of this dissertation between Surface(𝑆) and Substrate(𝑆). The
second is that this relation is checkable through structural rules over the syntax of the program rather than
by exhaustive execution. This is the lineage that produces the static-analysis discipline implemented in the
Bayyinah file scanner (Arfeen 2026c) and treated in Chapter 13 as the file-layer instantiation of AX-SH. We
note that Hoare logic itself is a tradition of pre/postcondition reasoning over input-output behavior; it is the
background tradition for specification-behavior relations rather than a direct precursor to the bisimulationstyle consistency of Axiom 2.

2.2.2 Dijkstra and the weakest-precondition calculus (1976)
E. W. Dijkstra’s 1976 monograph A Discipline of Programming (Dijkstra 1976) extended Hoare’s framework
by inverting the question. Where Hoare asked “given precondition 𝑃 and program 𝐶, what is the strongest
postcondition 𝑄,” Dijkstra asked “given postcondition 𝑄 and program 𝐶, what is the weakest precondition
𝑃 that must hold for {𝑃 } 𝐶 {𝑄} to be valid?” The weakest-precondition predicate transformer wp(𝐶, 𝑄)
yields, for any postcondition 𝑄 and any program command 𝐶, the most permissive predicate 𝑃 such that the
Hoare triple holds. This is a stronger discipline than working with arbitrary suﬀicient preconditions because
the weakest precondition characterizes the entire correctness relation, not merely some suﬀicient condition
for it.
Dijkstra’s contribution to the structural-honesty lineage is operational rather than conceptual. By demonstrating that program correctness could be reduced to a calculation—that one could calculate verification
conditions and weakest preconditions that reduce correctness claims to logical proof obligations rather than
only proving correctness on a case-by-case basis—Dijkstra opened the door to the automated-verification
disciplines that followed. The static-analysis discipline of Bayyinah and the type-checking discipline of the
Furqan prototype (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026a) both inherit, through several intermediate steps, the calculational style Dijkstra established. We note, again, that the weakest-precondition calculus is a calculus
of specifications: it relates two predicates (the precondition and the postcondition) through a syntactic
transformation. The relation to the underlying execution substrate is encoded in the soundness of the
predicate-transformer rules with respect to operational semantics, but it is not the calculus’s primary subject. Dijkstra, like Hoare, is background tradition for specification-behavior relations rather than a direct
contributor to the bisimulation-style consistency that Axiom 2 of this dissertation requires.

2.2.3 Process algebras and bisimulation: Park, Milner, and the correspondence
relation (1980–1990)
The Hoare–Dijkstra tradition treated programs as transformers of state, with correctness defined as a relation
between initial and final states. Beginning in the late 1970s, a parallel tradition began to treat programs—
especially concurrent programs—as labeled transition systems: structures whose meaning lies not in their
input-output behavior but in the patterns of observable actions they can perform over time. R. Milner’s
1980 book A Calculus of Communicating Systems (Milner 1980) introduced CCS, a process algebra in
which concurrent programs were described as terms in a formal language with operations for action, choice,
parallel composition, and restriction. The semantic question for CCS was not “what value does this program
compute” but “when are two programs observationally equivalent.”
D. Park’s 1981 paper Concurrency and Automata on Infinite Sequences (Park 1981) answered the equivalence
question with the now-classical definition of bisimulation. Two labeled transition systems 𝑆 and 𝑇 are
bisimilar if there exists a relation 𝑅 between their states such that, whenever (𝑠, 𝑡) ∈ 𝑅 and 𝑠 makes a
transition to 𝑠′ under action 𝑎, 𝑡 can make a transition to some 𝑡′ under 𝑎 with (𝑠′ , 𝑡′ ) ∈ 𝑅, and vice
versa. Bisimulation is finer than trace equivalence—two systems can produce the same traces of actions
without being bisimilar, because the choices available to them at each step may differ—but coarser than full
isomorphism, since it abstracts over the internal structure of states.
The Park–Milner construction is the historical origin of what becomes, in this dissertation’s Axiom 2, the
family of correspondence relations between Surface(𝑆) and Substrate(𝑆). The structural-honesty framework’s
decision to define Axiom 2 over a family of correspondence relations—bisimulation as the strongest finite-state
special case, with refinement, simulation, abstraction-preserving equivalence, and extraction equality over
declared observables as substrate-appropriate generalizations—rather than over bisimulation alone reflects
fifty years of subsequent research showing that bisimulation is the right relation for protocol-style finite-state
surfaces but is overstrong for many other substrates. The algorithmic foundations were supplied by Kanellakis
and Smolka (Kanellakis and Smolka 1990), whose 𝑂(𝑚 log 𝑛) characterization of bisimulation checking on
finite-state systems gave the correspondence-relation tradition the computational basis that makes Axiom 2
checkable in its decidable fragment. Axiom 2’s anchoring in this dissertation is primarily here—in the
Park–Milner tradition and its successors—rather than in the Hoare–Dijkstra specification-behavior tradition
discussed above.

2.2.4 Model checking: automated verification at scale (1986)
The integration of the Hoare–Dijkstra specification tradition with the Park–Milner process-algebra tradition
was achieved, on the algorithmic side, through model checking. Developed independently by E. M. Clarke
and E. A. Emerson in the early 1980s (with the foundational synchronization-skeletons paper appearing in
the 1981 Workshop on Logic of Programs) and by J.-P. Queille and J. Sifakis in France (1982 International
Symposium on Programming), the consolidated journal treatment by Clarke, Emerson, and Sistla (Clarke,
Emerson, and Sistla 1986) proposed that temporal-logic specifications could be checked automatically against
finite-state systems by an algorithm that explores the system’s state space. The technique scaled, through
subsequent decades of optimization—symbolic model checking, bounded model checking, partial-order reduction, abstraction refinement—to systems whose state spaces would have been infeasible to enumerate
explicitly, and is now in widespread use in hardware design and protocol verification.

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

19

Model checking’s relevance to the structural-honesty lineage is two-fold. First, it demonstrated that the
verification of complex specifications against complex substrates is tractable in the decidable fragment, with
the state-space explored through algorithmic techniques rather than enumerated explicitly. The decidablefragment scoping of Theorem 10.1 in Chapter 10 of this dissertation (the quantum-survivability theorem)
inherits the model-checking tradition’s discipline of being precise about which questions are decidable and
which are not. Second, model checking established the operational norm—widely adopted in hardware design
and protocol verification, and adopted in safety-critical software contexts where the underlying state space
admits the technique—that automated verification can be a normal part of the development process rather
than an exotic undertaking. The structural-honesty framework’s claim that AX-SH satisfaction is checkable
in operational deployments, not only in academic settings, inherits this norm.

2.2.5 Liskov–Wing behavioral subtyping: additive evolution at the type level
(1994)
The penultimate development in the formal-verification lineage that contributes directly to AX-SH is Barbara
Liskov and Jeannette Wing’s 1994 work on behavioral subtyping (Liskov and Wing 1994). Liskov–Wing subtyping requires that a subtype’s methods, when invoked in any context expecting the supertype, behave in a
way that is observationally indistinguishable from the supertype’s. The technical formulation involves preservation of preconditions (the subtype may weaken but not strengthen them), postconditions (the subtype may
strengthen but not weaken them), invariants (the subtype must preserve them), and the corresponding constraints under method composition; the Liskov–Wing framework also addresses constraints on state evolution,
with the precise doctrinal formulation differing across follow-on treatments. Behavioral subtyping is strictly
stronger than nominal subtyping (which only requires that the subtype declare conformance to an interface)
and strictly weaker than full type equivalence (which would require the subtype to be substitutable in every
observable respect).
Liskov–Wing subtyping is the direct historical antecedent of Axiom 1 of this dissertation. The version-𝑁 +1
public surface of a versioned artifact is a behavioral subtype of the version-𝑁 public surface in the Liskov–
Wing sense: every contract that callers could rely on at version 𝑁 remains discharged at version 𝑁 +1, with
at least as strong guarantees. The reframing introduced in the structural-honesty framework is that the
Liskov–Wing relation applies at the public surface level of the versioned artifact, not at the truth-status
level of individual claims. The framework’s append-only provenance discipline permits explicit corrections,
supersessions, and withdrawals through corrigenda, provided the corrigenda are themselves additive at the
surface and the historical record is preserved. This is the structural-honesty contribution to the Liskov–Wing
tradition: the recognition that the subtype relation is a property of the surface API of a versioned artifact,
and that the surface API can include explicit tagging of truth-status changes without violating the subtype
invariant.

2.2.6 Refinement types: caller-side exhaustiveness as a natural successor (2014–
2016)
The most recent development in the formal-verification lineage that contributes directly to AX-SH is the
refinement-type tradition, exemplified by Liquid Haskell (Vazou et al. (2014)) and F∗ (Swamy et al. (2016)).
Refinement types extend a host type system with logical predicates on values: a refinement type {𝑥 ∶ Int ∣
𝑥 > 0} denotes the type of integers greater than zero, with the predicate checked by an underlying SMT

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

20

solver. When refinement-type checking is combined with SMT-based discharge of the side conditions arising
from program structure, programs can be statically verified to satisfy logical specifications expressed at the
type level, including non-trivial functional correctness properties.
The contribution of the refinement-type tradition to AX-SH is direct: Axiom 3 (caller exhaustiveness over
𝑅may ) is a generalization of refinement-type-style return-value reasoning to the caller side of the functioncall boundary. The refinement-type discipline as deployed in F∗ and Liquid Haskell focuses on the producer
side: a function’s refinement type constrains what values it can return, and the type-checker verifies that
the function’s body in fact produces values inhabiting the declared type. Axiom 3 adds the dual obligation
on the caller. Every function call must handle every outcome that 𝑅may , the verifier’s conservative overapproximation of producer outcomes, may produce, or must explicitly propagate the incompleteness, or must
discharge a proof that the unhandled outcomes are unreachable in the calling context. The producer-side
discipline of refinement types is necessary but not suﬀicient for structural honesty; the caller-side discipline
of Axiom 3 is what closes the loop, and it is this caller-side closure that the refinement-type tradition does
not itself provide.

2.2.7 What the formal-verification lineage contributes to AX-SH
Synthesizing the historical walk above, the formal-verification lineage contributes the following to the four
axioms of AX-SH.
Axiom 1 (Additive-only invariant in append-only-provenance form) is directly anchored in Liskov–Wing
behavioral subtyping (Liskov and Wing 1994), with the structural-honesty reframing applying the subtype
relation to the public surface API of versioned artifacts and permitting truth-status changes through explicit
corrigenda.
Axiom 2 (Surface-substrate consistency in correspondence-relation form) is primarily anchored in the Park–
Milner bisimulation tradition (Park 1981; Milner 1980; Kanellakis and Smolka 1990) and the broader family
of correspondence relations developed in subsequent process-algebra and behavioral-equivalence research.
The Hoare–Dijkstra weakest-precondition tradition (Hoare 1969; Dijkstra 1976) provides the background
tradition for specification-behavior relations more generally, but is not directly mapped to the bisimulationstyle consistency that Axiom 2 requires. The choice to express Axiom 2 over a family of correspondence
relations, rather than over bisimulation alone, reflects fifty years of subsequent research showing that bisimulation is appropriate for protocol-style finite-state surfaces but overstrong for many other substrates.
Axiom 3 (Caller exhaustiveness over 𝑅may ) is directly anchored in the refinement-type tradition (Vazou
et al. 2014; Swamy et al. 2016). The structural-honesty contribution is the extension from producer-side
type-discipline to caller-side exhaustiveness over the verifier’s conservative outcome approximation, together
with the three permitted discharge paths (handle, propagate as incompleteness, prove unreachable).
Axiom 4 (Substrate-parameterized projection consistency) does not have a direct formal-verification ancestor. This is the axiom for which the audit-and-assurance and textual-preservation philology lineages provide
the primary historical exemplars; these are developed in §§3–4 of this chapter.
Model checking (Clarke, Emerson, and Sistla 1986) does not directly produce an axiom but contributes
the operational norm that AX-SH satisfaction is checkable in operational deployments rather than only
as an academic exercise. The decidable-fragment scoping of Theorem 10.1 (Chapter 10) reflects the model-

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

21

checking tradition’s discipline of being precise about decidability, and the operational substrates of Bayyinah
and the Furqan prototype inherit the model-checking tradition’s norm of automated verification as a normal
development practice.
The formal-verification lineage thus contributes Axioms 1 and 3 directly, contributes the correspondencerelation foundation of Axiom 2, and contributes the operational-verification norm that AX-SH inherits. The
two contributions it does not directly produce—the multi-projection consistency of Axiom 4 and the centuriesscale preservation discipline that grounds the framework’s durability claim—are the contributions of the
audit-and-assurance lineage (treated in §3 of this chapter) and the textual-preservation philology lineage
(treated in §4).

2.3 The audit-and-assurance lineage
The second of the three lineages traced in this chapter is the audit-and-assurance tradition that developed
across five centuries of commercial, professional, and regulatory practice. The tradition is concerned with
the question of how the records, declarations, or attestations made by an organization can be related to
the underlying reality those records purport to describe, in a way that is checkable by an independent
party rather than only by the organization itself. We trace the tradition through five developments, each
of which contributes to the AX-SH framework’s understanding of Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency) and the operational severity vocabulary: Pacioli’s codification of double-entry bookkeeping,
the evolution from early-modern commercial practice to professional financial audit and modern reporting
regimes, the development of security-audit frameworks as multi-control projection regimes, the recent emergence of supply-chain audit systems, and a closing synthesis identifying what this lineage contributes to
AX-SH and what it does not.

2.3.1 Double-entry bookkeeping and the origin of reconciliation discipline
(1494)
The canonical early printed codification of double-entry bookkeeping is the Tractatus XI: Particularis de
Computis et Scripturis contained within Luca Pacioli’s Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et
Proportionalita, published in Venice in 1494 (Pacioli 1494). Pacioli’s Tractatus systematized a commercial
practice that had been developing in Italian merchant houses through the late medieval period: the recording
of each financial transaction in two complementary entries, one as a debit and one as a credit, against
accounts maintained on opposing sides of a ledger. The arithmetic constraint that total debits must equal
total credits at every reconciliation point provides, in operational form, the multi-witness coherence pattern
that constitutes the practical content of reconciliation discipline.
We are careful here about the historical claim. We do not claim that Pacioli invented double-entry bookkeeping, that the Tractatus is the earliest documented systematic instance of reconciliation discipline in any
culture, or that no anticipating practices existed in earlier accounting, administrative archive, legal record,
or scribal control traditions. Such priority claims are contested in accounting-history scholarship and depend
on choices about what counts as “systematic” and “documented” that are not productive to litigate here.
What we do claim, restricted to what the Tractatus actually was: Pacioli’s text is the canonical early printed
codification of double-entry bookkeeping as a systematic reconciliation discipline, and it was the channel

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

22

through which the discipline propagated into Renaissance and early-modern European commercial practice.
That role is suﬀicient for the lineage claim of this chapter.
The relevance of double-entry bookkeeping to AX-SH is structural, not formal. The bookkeeping discipline
treats each transaction as a fact about the substrate (the actual movement of value between accounts) that
is recorded on two surfaces (the debit entry and the credit entry, in their respective accounts), with the two
surfaces constrained to reconcile arithmetically as evidence that they faithfully describe the same underlying
transaction. This is the operational pattern that Axiom 4 of this dissertation generalizes into substrateparameterized projection consistency: a family of projections Π𝑋 = {𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 } of a substrate 𝑋, each
producing a surface description, with mutual consistency among the projections serving as the empirical
evidence of substrate fidelity. Double-entry bookkeeping is the historical exemplar of this pattern, not its
full formal precursor. The structural-honesty framework treats double-entry as the canonical instance of
reconciliation discipline operating with 𝑛 = 2 projections under arithmetic identity; Axiom 4 generalizes to
arbitrary 𝑛, arbitrary substrates, and arbitrary declared consistency relations.

2.3.2 From bookkeeping to professional audit to modern reporting regimes
The five centuries following Pacioli traced an evolution from a commercial bookkeeping practice into an institutionalized professional discipline of financial audit, and from there into the modern reporting regimes that
today govern public financial disclosure. Previts and Merino’s A History of Accounting in America (Previts
and Merino 1979) traces this evolution in detail; we summarize here the structural pattern relevant to the
AX-SH lineage claim.
Through the early modern period, double-entry bookkeeping spread through European commercial practice
as a tool internal to the firm. The transition to audit as an external discipline followed the development of the
joint-stock corporation in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, in which the separation of ownership from
management created an information asymmetry that external attestation could address. By the nineteenth
century, professional audit had emerged as an institutionalized practice, with chartered accountants in the
United Kingdom and certified public accountants in the United States providing independent attestation of
firm financial records to absentee owners and regulators. The twentieth century saw the codification of this
practice into generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) in the United States and, from 1973 onward,
the development of international accounting standards through the International Accounting Standards
Committee (later the International Accounting Standards Board), producing what is now the International
Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) regime followed in most non-U.S. jurisdictions.
The structural pattern that emerges across this evolution is multi-projection-consistency at scale. Modern
financial-reporting regimes require organizations to publish multiple required or customary projections of
the same underlying financial substrate—such as statements of financial position, performance, cash flows,
equity changes, and explanatory notes—constrained to be mutually consistent under defined accounting
identities (most fundamentally the accounting identity that assets equal liabilities plus equity, but also
the consistency relations among accrual-basis revenues, cash-basis cash flows, and equity reconciliation).
The specific projection set is modern and jurisdiction-dependent; what is substantively constant across
jurisdictions and across the historical evolution is the discipline that multiple required projections of the
same substrate must reconcile under declared consistency relations. This is the structural pattern that the
audit-and-assurance lineage contributes to AX-SH, not the specific projection list of any particular regime.

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

23

2.3.3 Security-audit frameworks as multi-control projection regimes
A second stream of audit practice developed through the late twentieth century in response to the question
of how an organization’s security and operational controls can be attested to by an independent party, in
the same way that financial records can be attested to. The institutionalized frameworks that resulted—
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (International Organization for Standardization 2022) (the international standard for
information security management systems), NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5 (National Institute
of Standards and Technology 2020) (the U.S. federal catalog of security and privacy controls), and the
SOC 2-style attestation regimes underwritten by the AICPA Trust Services Criteria (American Institute of
Certified Public Accountants 2017)—share a structural pattern that generalizes the financial-audit pattern
of the previous subsection.
The pattern, in each case, is multi-control projection with an assessment result. An organization undergoing
audit declares its scope (which systems, processes, and information assets are within the audit boundary),
declares the controls it has selected within scope (which security or privacy controls from the framework’s
control catalog apply to the declared scope), produces implementation evidence for each control (the documentation, configuration records, and operational artifacts demonstrating that each declared control is in
fact implemented), and produces an audit trail of each control’s operation over the audit period (the logs,
monitoring records, and incident reports demonstrating that each implemented control is in fact operating).
Mutual consistency across these four declarations is a central part of the auditor’s empirical content: scope is
consistent with controls, controls with implementation, implementation with operation. Audits additionally
assess design adequacy, operating effectiveness, and evidence quality, but the multi-projection-consistency
component is the one this dissertation’s structural lineage claim depends on. Where the relevant assessment
or certification regime is satisfied (ISO/IEC 27001 certification, SOC 2 examination report, or comparable assessment results for control catalogs such as NIST SP 800-53), the organization receives a regime-appropriate
outcome—certification, attestation, authorization, or assessment result—depending on the framework; where
the regime is not satisfied, the audit produces findings, with each finding identifying a specific consistency
failure between specific declarations.
This is a four-projection consistency discipline applied to security substrates, structurally analogous to
the multi-statement consistency discipline applied to financial substrates in the previous subsection. The
substrate is different (security posture rather than financial position), the projections are different (scope,
controls, implementation, operation rather than the financial-statement family), and the consistency relations
are different (security-control coverage rather than accounting identities), but the underlying structural
pattern is the same: independent projections of a common substrate, constrained to be mutually consistent
under declared relations, with consistency serving as empirical evidence of substrate fidelity.

2.3.4 Supply-chain audit as the recent endpoint of the lineage
The most recent development in the audit-and-assurance lineage is the emergence, through the past decade, of
supply-chain audit systems for software artifacts. The principal components of this development are sigstore
(cryptographic identity attestation for the parties producing software artifacts), in-toto (process-attestation
framework for the steps producing each artifact), and SLSA (the Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts
framework, providing a maturity model for the institutional discipline supporting these attestations). Each
component is a separate attestation substrate; their composition with the semantic verification provided by
