SHV is the four-substrate verification stack proposed in the supply-chain integration memo (Arfeen 2026f).
The present subsection notes only that supply-chain audit is the recent endpoint of the audit-and-assurance
lineage; the full development of the four-substrate composition, its operational requirements, and its instantiation as the supply-chain layer of the dissertation’s worked substrate instances is reserved for Chapter 16.
This restriction is deliberate: §3 of the present chapter is the historical-lineage section, not the supply-chain
case-study chapter, and treating the four-substrate composition in detail here would conflate the lineage
claim of Chapter 2 with the substrate-instance claim of Chapter 16.

2.3.5 What the audit-and-assurance lineage contributes to AX-SH
Synthesizing the four developments traced above, the audit-and-assurance lineage contributes the following
to AX-SH.
The lineage contributes the practical discipline behind Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency). The structural pattern that runs from double-entry bookkeeping through financial audit through
modern reporting regimes through security-audit frameworks through supply-chain audit is the same: independent projections of a common substrate, constrained to be mutually consistent under declared consistency
relations, with consistency serving as empirical evidence of substrate fidelity. Double-entry bookkeeping is
the canonical historical exemplar of this discipline operating at 𝑛 = 2 under arithmetic identity; modern audit regimes operate at larger 𝑛 under jurisdiction-dependent consistency relations; security and supply-chain
audit operate at larger 𝑛 still over qualitatively different substrates. Axiom 4 is the formal abstraction of
this pattern to arbitrary projection families over arbitrary substrates under arbitrary declared consistency
relations. Double-entry bookkeeping is the historical exemplar of reconciliation discipline, not a full formal
precursor to Axiom 4 in its substrate-parameterized form.
The lineage contributes the operational severity vocabulary (CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW),
which is shared with the security vulnerability-management and incident-response practices of security audit
(notably, the qualitative severity ratings that the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) translates
numerical scores into) and was later formalized in the Bayyinah Audit Framework (Arfeen 2026b). The
severity rubric currently operates as a total preorder; its formalization as a partial order capturing the
multidimensional nature of severity (user impact, data loss, frequency, recoverability) is identified as an
open problem in Chapter 17. The lineage’s contribution at the level of AX-SH is the practical vocabulary;
the formalization is dissertation-internal work.
The lineage does not contribute Axioms 1, 2, or 3. Those are formal-verification contributions, treated in §2
above. It also does not contribute the centuries-scale preservation discipline that grounds the framework’s
durability claim; that is the contribution of the textual-preservation philology lineage, treated in the next
section.

2.4 The textual-preservation philology lineage
The third of the three lineages traced in this chapter is the textual-preservation philology tradition that
developed across more than two millennia in multiple cultures. The tradition is concerned with the question
of how a text treated as authoritative within a transmission community can be preserved across centuries of
transmission through manuscript copying, oral recitation, or both, in the face of inevitable transmission noise,

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

25

the loss of individual transmission channels, and the gradual transformation of the cultural infrastructure
in which the text is read. We trace the tradition through five developments—Vedic oral transmission and
the Sanskrit philological tradition, Quranic preservation as a multi-substrate verification practice, Talmudic
and Masoretic textual-criticism traditions, classical philology culminating in Lachmann’s stemmatic method,
and a closing synthesis—and identify what this lineage contributes to AX-SH that the previous two lineages
do not.
A boundary discipline applies throughout this section, and we name it explicitly before beginning. The
structural-honesty framework treats each of these preservation traditions as a verification substrate exhibiting
specific gap-control disciplines. The framework does not adjudicate the theological content, religious truth
claims, scriptural status, or comparative ranking of any of these traditions. The Quranic preservation
tradition, the Vedic oral-transmission tradition, the Talmudic and Masoretic traditions, and the classical
philological tradition are all treated here as historical instances of multi-substrate textual preservation; the
framework’s mathematical structure depends on the operational disciplines these traditions developed, not
on the religious or scholarly content of the texts those disciplines preserved. This is the §4 analogue of the
“no retroactive attribution” discipline of §1, but applied to a more contested domain where overclaim risk is
higher; we therefore anchor the boundary discipline repeatedly across the section: here at the opening of §4,
again at the opening and closing of §4.2 (the highest-risk subsection), again at the closing of §4.3, and again
in the synthesis at §4.5. The redundancy is deliberate.

2.4.1 Vedic oral transmission and Sanskrit philological traditions
The Vedic oral-transmission tradition is an ancient and extensively studied practice of disciplined textual
preservation. Practiced over millennia in the Indian subcontinent, the tradition developed multiple parallel memorization patterns—samhitā-pāt.ha (the continuous-text recitation), pada-pāt.ha (the word-by-word
recitation, isolating each word from its phonetic neighbors), krama-pāt.ha (the step recitation, in which
adjacent word-pairs are recited in overlapping sequence), jat.ā-pāt.ha (the braided recitation, in which wordpairs are recited forward and backward), and ghana-pāt.ha (the dense recitation, applying further permutations) (Staal 1986). The proliferation of memorization patterns is not redundant in the everyday sense;
it serves a verification function. A transmission error in the samhitā-pāt.ha may not be detectable in that
pattern alone, but is detectable when the same text is recited under the pada-pāt.ha or krama-pāt.ha pattern,
because the error will manifest differently against the different phonetic and syntactic constraints of each
pattern. The patterns collectively constitute multiple, partially-independent verification substrates over the
same source text, with mutual coherence across patterns serving as the operational evidence of transmission
fidelity.
A second and distinct strand of the Sanskrit tradition is the grammatical formalization developed in Pān.ini’s
As.t.ādhyāyı̄, dated conventionally to the mid-first-millennium BCE. Pān.ini’s grammar provided a rule-based
formal anchor that constrained well-formed Sanskrit linguistic forms with precision suﬀicient to permit
derivation of correct forms from a small set of underlying constituents. The structural-honesty framework
treats Vedic oral transmission and Pān.inian grammar as distinct traditions: the first is a preservation
practice operating over a specific corpus of texts, the second is a formal grammatical anchor operating over
the language in which those texts are composed. They share an intellectual climate but address different
problems. Conflating them, which an earlier draft of this chapter risked doing, would misdescribe both.
Staal’s 1986 analysis is the canonical scholarly source for the relationship between the two and for the

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

26

verification-substrate character of Vedic transmission.

2.4.2 Quranic preservation as multi-substrate verification
This subsection treats Quranic preservation as a verification substrate, not as an adjudication of theological
truth, scriptural status, or religious authority. The structural claim that follows is about the operational
discipline of multi-substrate preservation; it is not a claim about the religious content, religious truth, or
comparative status of the tradition. The framework’s boundary discipline (§4 opening) is named again
here, at the opening of the highest-risk subsection within §4, and a third time in the closing paragraph of
this subsection, because the structural-honesty framework’s exposure to drift is greatest precisely where the
operational discipline being described is religiously significant to a substantial community.
The Quranic preservation tradition has operated continuously across approximately 1,400 years and constitutes, as discussed structurally in the SHV synthesis paper (Arfeen 2026h), one of the most extensively
studied historical instances of multi-substrate textual preservation; Farrin’s structural analysis of Surat alBaqarah (Farrin 2010) is cited here as one structural-analysis exemplar of the broader tradition rather than
as a comprehensive preservation-tradition source. The tradition combines several independent verification
substrates that operate over the same source text in mutually constraining ways.
The first substrate is h.ifz.: the memorization of the complete Quranic text by individuals trained in the discipline of recitation. H.ifz. is practiced across large communities of reciters distributed across geography and
generation. A community of memorizers operating as an aggregate constitutes a verification substrate whose
redundancy makes single-point transmission failure extremely diﬀicult; the formal information-theoreticstyle analysis of mass-transmission redundancy is deferred to Chapter 11 of this dissertation, where the
tawatur-style framework is developed.
The second substrate is manuscript transmission under explicit orthographic discipline.

The Quranic

manuscript tradition operates under documented rules governing letter forms, consonantal skeleton (rasm),
and the placement of diacritical marks added in the early Islamic centuries to support disambiguation.
Manuscript copies are produced under the orthographic discipline; copies that fail to conform are identified
as such rather than treated as alternative readings.
The third substrate is recitation protocol, the discipline of tajwı̄d, which prescribes the phonetic realization of
the text in recitation. Tajwı̄d is itself transmitted through chains of teacher-to-student authorization (ijāza),
and the chains that meet the criterion of mass transmission (mutawātir) provide a redundancy structure
over the recitation discipline itself.
The fourth substrate is the riwāyāt tradition of canonical variant transmissions. The major recognized
riwāyāt are recorded explicitly, with documented chains of transmission, providing a controlled variant space
rather than an uncontrolled drift over textual readings.
The fifth substrate is mass communal verification, in which congregational practice of recitation across
geographically distributed communities provides ongoing cross-checking against any single substrate’s drift.
A reciter in one community whose memorization or recitation diverges from the cross-community pattern is
identified through ordinary practice rather than through specialized audit.
The structural-honesty framework treats these five substrates as partially-independent projections of the
same source text, with mutual coherence across substrates serving as the operational evidence of preservation

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

27

fidelity over the 1,400-year transmission window. This is the structural claim of §4.2, and it is restricted to
that claim. The framework does not adjudicate the theological content of the Quranic text, the religious truth
or falsity of any claim made by or about the text, the scriptural status of the text within or outside Islam, or
the comparative religious ranking of the Quranic preservation tradition against any other tradition. These
adjudications are outside the framework’s scope; the structural-preservation claim and the religious-content
claim are independent and the framework speaks only to the first.

2.4.3 Talmudic and Masoretic textual-criticism traditions
A third strand of the textual-preservation philology lineage is the development of systematic textual-criticism
practices within the Jewish scholarly tradition, principally through the Masoretic discipline applied to the
Hebrew Bible and the Talmudic discipline applied to the corpus of rabbinic dialectical and legal commentary.
The Masoretic tradition, developing across roughly the seventh through tenth centuries of the common
era, produced explicit textual-criticism instruments: the systematic distinction between the consonantal
text (ketiv) and the vocalized reading (qere), the marginal note systems of Masorah parva and Masorah
magna that catalog textual variants and unusual forms, and the documented qere/ketiv variant catalogs
that preserve variant readings alongside the preferred text (Tov 2012). The Talmudic tradition developed
parallel attributional and dialectical practices that preserve named authorities, variant readings, and the
argumentative contexts in which positions were articulated (Strack and Stemberger 1996), providing a multiwitness substrate over the corpus of rabbinic commentary.
The structural pattern across these traditions is the preservation of variants alongside the preferred text
rather than the suppression of variants in favor of a single authoritative reading. Cross-witness comparison—
across manuscript copies, across recensions, across attribution chains—provides the empirical basis for textual
decisions and for the construction of authoritative editions. The Talmudic and Masoretic traditions illustrate,
within a Jewish-tradition specialization of the broader textual-preservation philology lineage, the discipline
of treating variants as data rather than as noise to be discarded. The same boundary discipline applies as
in §4.2: the framework describes the operational textual-criticism practices and the verification-substrate
character of variant preservation, without adjudicating the religious content or scriptural status of the texts
those practices preserve.

2.4.4 Classical philology and Lachmann’s stemmatic method
The classical philological tradition, working across the corpus of Greek and Latin literature transmitted
through medieval manuscript copying, culminated in the nineteenth-century formalization of the stemmatic
method conventionally associated with Karl Lachmann—though Timpanaro, in the work translated and
introduced by Glenn Most (Timpanaro 2005), argues that the method was substantively developed by Lachmann’s predecessors and contemporaries (notably Karl Gottlob Zumpt, Friedrich Madvig, and others) and
that the unified “Lachmann’s method” is in part a historiographical construct. Granting that complication,
the method as it is now received formalized the practice of reconstructing an archetypal source text from a
corpus of derivative manuscripts by tracing the genealogical relationships among manuscripts through patterns of shared errors. Two manuscripts that share an error not present in the broader manuscript tradition
are likely to share a common ancestor in which the error was introduced; the systematic application of this
principle permits the construction of a stemma, or family tree of manuscripts, from which the readings of
the archetype can be inferred even when no copy of the archetype itself survives.

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

28

The structural pattern in Lachmann’s method is similar to the pattern of the previous subsections, with
one important inversion. Each surviving manuscript is treated as a projection of the archetype, mediated
by a chain of intervening copies each of which may have introduced its own errors. The empirical basis for
archetype reconstruction is cross-manuscript collation: where multiple independent manuscript lines agree,
the agreement is evidence of an archetype reading; where lines disagree, the pattern of disagreement reveals
the genealogical structure. Reynolds and Wilson’s Scribes and Scholars (Reynolds and Wilson 2013) treats
this lineage comprehensively, with attention to the social and institutional infrastructure of the manuscript
tradition (the scriptoria, the libraries, the patterns of textual recovery during the Carolingian and Italian
Renaissances) within which the method developed. The inversion relative to the previous traditions is that
Lachmann’s method operates on a corpus in which the archetype is in fact lost—no surviving manuscript is
the original—rather than on a tradition in which the source text is preserved through redundant substrates.
The structural pattern of multi-witness cross-collation as the empirical basis for textual claims is nonetheless
the same.

2.4.5 What the textual-preservation philology lineage contributes to AX-SH
Synthesizing the four traditions traced above, the textual-preservation philology lineage contributes the
following to AX-SH.
The lineage contributes the centuries-scale preservation discipline that grounds the framework’s durability claim. The seven durability principles stated in Chapter 1, §4—mathematical core, substrate independence, cryptographic agility, format stability, institutional anchoring, translation discipline, and designated
continuation—are not original to this dissertation; they are the formal extraction of practices that the
textual-preservation philology lineage has historically used to achieve multi-century durability of intellectual
frameworks. At the level of historical analogy developed here, and subject to the more careful justification of
the mapping deferred to Chapter 12, the Quranic preservation tradition exemplifies principles (iii) through
(vii) simultaneously over a 1,400-year transmission window; Vedic oral transmission exemplifies (ii) and (iv)
over a longer window using purely oral substrates; the Masoretic tradition exemplifies (iv), (v), and the
discipline of variant preservation; Lachmann’s method illustrates the recovery of authoritative readings even
when individual transmission channels have failed.
The lineage contributes the multi-substrate redundancy intuition that underlies the framework’s treatment of cross-substrate verification. The pattern of multiple, partially-independent verification substrates operating over a common source—memorization plus manuscript plus recitation protocol plus variant tradition
plus communal verification, in the Quranic case; multiple memorization patterns plus grammatical anchor, in
the Vedic case; multiple manuscript lines plus marginal-note variant cataloging, in the Masoretic case; crossmanuscript collation, in Lachmann’s method—is the operational discipline that the framework’s preservation
strategy (Chapter 12) adopts and that grounds the dissertation’s structural-honesty claim against substrate
failure.
The lineage does not supply the dissertation’s primary mathematical anchors for Axioms 1, 2, or 3; those
are formal-verification contributions, treated in §2 above. Philological and grammatical traditions including
Pān.inian formalism do contribute mathematical structure of their own, with non-trivial formal-grammatical
and information-structural content, but not the specific formal-methods structure used for Axioms 1–3 in
this dissertation. The lineage’s principal contribution to AX-SH is the operational preservation discipline
that the framework adopts, not the formal-methods machinery of the lower axioms.

The boundary discipline of §4.2 holds throughout this synthesis: the structural-honesty framework treats
the textual-preservation philology lineage as a set of verification substrates exhibiting specific gap-control
disciplines, with the religious or scholarly content of the texts those substrates preserve held separately.
Where the lineage’s traditions are religiously authoritative within their respective communities, that authority is not under the framework’s purview, is not endorsed or denied by the framework, and is not what
the framework’s preservation claim depends upon. The framework’s contribution is structural: it extracts
the operational disciplines that historically enabled multi-century durability and proposes that the same
disciplines can ground the dissertation’s own preservation strategy. The religious and scholarly content of
the preserved traditions is what those traditions are about; the structural-preservation discipline is what the
framework borrows.

2.5 Synthesis: what AX-SH unifies
The three lineages traced in §§2–4 have been described in their own terms: the formal-verification lineage
as the academic-computer-science tradition for reasoning about programs, the audit-and-assurance lineage
as the professional-practice tradition for reasoning about organizational records, the textual-preservation
philology tradition as the cross-cultural practice for preserving authoritative texts across centuries. The
structural question that the remainder of this chapter takes up is what to make of the three lineages together.
§5 states the synthesis claim that the dissertation pursues; §6 maps the four axioms of AX-SH onto specific
historical exemplars within the three lineages; §7 identifies, for each lineage, what it did not develop that
AX-SH does. The result positions the dissertation’s axiomatic framework not as the invention of a wholly
new discipline, but as the formal unification of structures that the three lineages independently developed
without ever unifying.

2.5.1 Three lineages, complementary rather than interchangeable
The first claim of the synthesis is that the three lineages are complementary rather than interchangeable.
Each lineage developed verification discipline for a different aspect of the structural-honesty problem, and
the discipline developed in each lineage cannot substitute for what was developed in the others. The formalverification lineage contributes mathematical specification-and-behavior machinery: precise specification languages, correspondence relations relating specifications to behaviors, type-theoretic compositional reasoning,
automated model checking, and the extension of type discipline from producer-side correctness to caller-side
exhaustiveness. The audit-and-assurance lineage contributes reconciliation discipline over multiple records
or projections: the requirement that independent declarations of the same underlying fact remain mutually
coherent under explicit consistency relations, the scaling of that requirement across substrates of increasing complexity, and the operationalization of the discipline as professional practice with named severity
vocabulary. The textual-preservation philology lineage contributes long-horizon preservation discipline and
multi-substrate redundancy: the maintenance of authoritative texts across centuries of transmission through
manuscript copying, oral recitation, or both, with multiple partially-independent verification substrates so
that the loss or corruption of any single substrate does not destroy the textual record. None of these three
sets of contributions reduces to or substitutes for the others. The complementarity is the structural ground
for the synthesis claim that follows.

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

30

2.5.2 No single lineage supplies all four axioms
The second claim is that no single lineage individually supplies all four AX-SH axioms. The formal-verification
lineage supplies the primary mathematical anchors for Axioms 1, 2, and 3, as developed in §2 and as
the axiom-to-exemplar mapping of §6 specifies; it does not supply Axiom 4, and it does not supply the
centuries-scale preservation discipline that the dissertation’s seven durability principles encode. The auditand-assurance lineage supplies the practical reconciliation discipline behind Axiom 4 and the operational
severity vocabulary that the structural-honesty framework uses for classifying findings; it does not supply
the formal axiomatic machinery of Axioms 1, 2, or 3, and its operational discipline is not packaged as a
unified axiom system. The textual-preservation philology lineage supplies the centuries-scale preservation
discipline and the multi-substrate redundancy intuition that grounds the framework’s durability claim; it
does not supply the mechanized static verification of any of the four axioms, and its operational practices are
not formalized as axiomatic systems in the formal-methods sense. Each lineage supplies a partial structural
contribution; none supplies the whole. The synthesis claim is that the partial contributions, taken together,
are jointly suﬀicient to ground a single unified axiomatic framework, which is what AX-SH proposes.

2.5.3 Synthesis under AX-SH, not invention
The third claim concerns what the dissertation’s contribution is, and what it is not. The dissertation’s contribution is synthesis under AX-SH, not the invention of the underlying mathematical structures or historical
practices. The “no retroactive attribution” boundary discipline of §1 is restated explicitly at the synthesis
level: AX-SH is the dissertation’s formalization of structures the three lineages independently developed;
the historical figures whose contributions §§2–4 traced—Pacioli, Park, Milner, Liskov, Wing, Hennessy,
Kanellakis, Smolka, Clarke, Emerson, Sistla, Lachmann, the Vedic transmitters, the masoretes, the riwayat
scholars, the rabbinic authorities preserved in the Talmudic tradition, and others—are not attributed AX-SH
terminology or AX-SH-equivalent intent. None of them was working toward this dissertation’s axiomatic
framework; each was working on a specific verification problem within their own intellectual context. The
dissertation reads their contributions, in retrospect and from the dissertation’s perspective, as historically
situated work that supplies structural materials for a unification that none of them undertook. The synthesis
claim is the dissertation’s; the underlying materials are the lineages’.

2.5.4 Three lineages as partial projections of a broader verification problem
From the dissertation’s perspective, the three lineages can be read as partial projections of a broader verification problem: whether declared surfaces, underlying substrates, caller obligations, and documentary projections of the substrate remain mutually consistent across time. Each lineage developed verification discipline
for a different facet of this problem. The formal-verification lineage worked on the surface-substrate consistency facet (the bisimulation-style relation between a program’s claimed semantics and its actual behavior),
the producer-caller-obligation facet (the type-theoretic discipline of how caller-side and producer-side obligations compose), and the additive-evolution facet (how successive versions of a public surface relate to earlier
ones). The audit-and-assurance lineage worked on the documentary-projection-consistency facet (how multiple independent records of the same substrate constrain each other under declared consistency relations). The
textual-preservation philology lineage worked on the time-durability facet (how the projection-consistency
discipline can be sustained across centuries through multiple verification substrates). The reading of the
lineages as partial projections of one structural problem is the dissertation’s interpretive framing, not a

claim about how the lineages understood themselves. The lineages are real intellectual traditions with their
own self-descriptions, methods, and concerns; the projection reading is what AX-SH proposes as a unifying
perspective on them, with the formal adequacy of that proposed unification to be established in subsequent
chapters.

2.5.5 The synthesis claim is preliminary at Chapter 2
The synthesis claim is preliminary at Chapter 2. Its formal adequacy is established only by the development
that the dissertation’s mathematical work pursues across Chapters 3–8. Chapter 3 introduces the categoricalequivalence machinery (Mac Lane 1998), correspondence-relation families, refinement-type machinery, and
projection-consistency machinery generalizing the accounting-identity pattern needed to formalize the four
axioms. Chapters 4–7 develop the axioms themselves against the operational vocabulary of the Bayyinah
file-layer scanner (Arfeen 2026c), the Furqan language-layer type-checker (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b, 2026a),
the Munafiq Protocol (Arfeen 2026d), and the supply-chain four-substrate stack composing sigstore, in-toto,
SLSA, and SHV (Sigstore project (Open Source Security Foundation) 2021; Torres-Arias et al. 2019; Open
Source Security Foundation 2023; Arfeen 2026f) substrates (the four worked substrate instances SI1–SI4).
Chapter 8 establishes definitional adequacy through Theorem 8.3: that AX-SH captures the operational
Bayyinah/Furqan/Munafiq/supply-chain vocabulary that the dissertation defines using structures abstracted
from the three lineages, relative to the twenty-eight-case judgment set 𝐽 . Chapter 2 motivates the synthesis
historically; Chapter 8 establishes whether the historical motivation succeeds at the formal level. The status
at the end of Chapter 2 is that the synthesis is motivated; the status after Chapter 8 is whether the motivation
is borne out. Both statuses are necessary; neither alone is suﬀicient.

2.6 Axiom-to-exemplar mapping
Having stated the synthesis claim in §5, the next step is to map each of the four AX-SH axioms onto
its primary historical anchor within the three lineages. The mapping is many-to-one (multiple historical
exemplars per axiom), partial (each exemplar motivates one structural property but does not exhaust the
axiom’s final mathematical definition), and heuristic (the mapping captures structural correspondence at the
motivational level, with the formal axiom developed against the operational SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary
rather than reconstructed from the historical exemplar). The pattern across all four axiom subsections is
that each historical exemplar is the primary motivating structure for its axiom, but the final mathematical
axiom is developed in Chapters 4–8 against the operational substrates rather than against the exemplar
itself.

2.6.1 Axiom 1 from Liskov–Wing behavioral subtyping
Axiom 1 (additive-only invariant in append-only-provenance form) is the AX-SH axiom that governs how
versioned public surfaces evolve over time. Its primary historical anchor is Liskov–Wing behavioral subtyping (Liskov and Wing 1994). The reframing introduced by AX-SH is that the Liskov–Wing relation applies
at the public surface level of the versioned artifact, not at the truth-status level of individual claims. The
framework’s append-only-provenance discipline permits explicit corrections, supersessions, and withdrawals
through corrigenda, provided the corrigenda are themselves additive at the surface and the historical record
is preserved. Liskov–Wing behavioral subtyping is the primary historical anchor and motivating structure

for Axiom 1, but the final mathematical axiom (specified in Chapter 4) is developed against the operational
SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary, not by reconstruction from the Liskov–Wing original. The historical anchor lies entirely within the formal-verification lineage; no audit or philology exemplar contributes to Axiom 1
in primary form.

2.6.2 Axiom 2 from the Park–Milner correspondence-relation tradition
Axiom 2 (surface-substrate consistency in correspondence-relation form) is the AX-SH axiom that governs how
a substrate’s declared surface relates to its actual behavior. Its primary historical anchor is the Park–Milner
correspondence-relation tradition: Park’s bisimulation work (Park 1981), Milner’s Calculus of Communicating Systems (Milner 1980), the Hennessy–Milner modal logic for bisimulation equivalence introduced
in their 1980 ICALP paper (Hennessy and Milner 1980) with subsequent algebraic-laws work (Hennessy
and Milner 1985), and the Kanellakis–Smolka algorithmic foundation for bisimulation checking (Kanellakis
and Smolka 1990). The choice to express Axiom 2 over a family of correspondence relations, rather than
over bisimulation alone, reflects fifty years of subsequent research showing that bisimulation is appropriate for protocol-style finite-state surfaces but overstrong for many other substrates. The Hoare–Dijkstra
weakest-precondition tradition (Hoare 1969; Dijkstra 1976) provides background reasoning for specificationbehavior relations more generally but is not the direct bisimulation-style anchor that Axiom 2 requires. The
Park–Milner correspondence-relation tradition is the primary historical anchor and motivating structure for
Axiom 2, but the final mathematical axiom (specified in Chapter 5) is developed against the operational
SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary as a family of correspondence relations indexed by substrate, not by reconstruction from any single classical correspondence relation.

2.6.3 Axiom 3 from refinement-type reasoning
Axiom 3 (caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may , the verifier’s conservative over-approximation of possible
producer outcomes) is the AX-SH axiom that governs how callers reason about producers’ possible behaviors.
Its primary historical anchor is refinement-type reasoning as developed in F∗ (Swamy et al. 2016) and Liquid
Haskell (Vazou et al. 2014). The reframing introduced by AX-SH extends the refinement-type discipline
from producer-side type discipline to caller-side exhaustiveness: where the original refinement-type tradition
required producers to satisfy refinements declared in their signatures, AX-SH additionally requires callers
to handle every outcome the verifier’s conservative over-approximation 𝑅may permits. Refinement-type
reasoning is the primary historical anchor and motivating structure for Axiom 3, but the final mathematical
axiom (specified in Chapter 6) is developed against the operational SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary, with
the 𝑅may construction itself being substrate-specific and developed in Chapter 6 rather than borrowed from
any specific refinement-type system.

2.6.4 Axiom 4 from audit reconciliation and textual-preservation crosswitnessing
Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency under a declared consistency relation over a
substrate-specific projection family) is the AX-SH axiom that governs how multiple independent records or
projections of the same substrate remain mutually coherent on a declared joint domain; inconsistency at a
joint-domain state under ∼𝑋 constitutes an axiom-4 violation, while absence of a projection at a point places
that point outside A4’s scope per Chapter 7’s joint-domain discipline (Chapter 7 §1.4) rather than inside it

2.6.5 The mapping is many-to-one and partial
The axiom-to-exemplar mapping is many-to-one and partial. Each historical exemplar motivates one structural property that the corresponding AX-SH axiom formalizes, but no exemplar exhausts the axiom’s final
mathematical definition. The formal axioms are developed in Chapters 4–7 against the operational vocabulary of Bayyinah, Furqan, Munafiq Protocol, and the supply-chain four-substrate stack (the four worked
substrate instances SI1–SI4), with Chapter 8 establishing definitional adequacy; the development is not a reconstruction from the historical exemplars. The mapping in §6 is heuristic and motivational: it identifies the
historical structure each axiom most directly generalizes, so that a reader who knows the historical exemplar
can recognize what each axiom is doing structurally, without misreading the historical exemplar as already
containing the axiom. The relationship between exemplar and axiom is one of motivated generalization, not
extension by reconstruction.

2.7 What each lineage did not develop
§5 and §6 have stated what the three lineages, taken together, supply to AX-SH. §7 turns to the complementary question: for each lineage, what did it not develop that AX-SH does? The framing is important.
The question is what each lineage did not develop in the specific form that AX-SH requires, not what each
lineage failed at as an intellectual tradition. Each lineage developed sophisticated discipline within its own
scope; the gaps relative to AX-SH are not failures but absences of work that each lineage did not undertake,
and that another lineage or the dissertation’s own synthesis must supply. Each subsection states what the
lineage did develop before specifying the gap, both to avoid caricaturing the lineage’s strengths and to make
precise what the AX-SH synthesis claim depends on.

2.7.1 The formal-verification lineage and centuries-scale preservation discipline
The formal-verification lineage developed rigorous specification machinery, the family of correspondence
relations relating specifications to behaviors, type-theoretic discipline for compositional reasoning, modelchecking automation, and substantial preservation-relevant infrastructure: theorem-prover proof libraries in
Coq, Isabelle, Lean, and F∗ that have been maintained across decades and through multiple revisions of
underlying theorem provers; archival proof artifacts associated with major formal-verification efforts including CompCert, seL4, and IronFleet that have been preserved through publication and ongoing maintenance;
mechanized verification infrastructure including dependency-management discipline for proof developments,
regression-testing of proofs against theorem-prover upgrades, and curation of definitional libraries within
proof communities. What the lineage did not develop, in the specific form AX-SH requires, is the dissertation’s seven-part centuries-scale preservation discipline—mathematical core, substrate independence at the
truth layer, cryptographic agility with graceful degradation, format stability, institutional anchoring, translation discipline, and designated continuation—as part of its core verification theory. The preservation work
done within the lineage operates at the timescale of decades and as community maintenance rather than as
a theoretical principle of the verification framework itself; the centuries-scale, multi-substrate, durability-aspart-of-the-axioms discipline is what the synthesis adds, with the textual-preservation lineage supplying the
operational template.

2.7.2 The audit-and-assurance lineage and unified formal axiomatization
The audit-and-assurance lineage developed sophisticated mathematical and methodological apparatus across
five centuries: the accounting identities that govern double-entry bookkeeping and modern financial reporting; statistical sampling theory adapted to audit-population analysis; quantitative risk-assessment models for
materiality determination and audit risk; standards-logic apparatus codifying when an attestation may be
issued under what control deficiencies (the qualified-opinion, adverse-opinion, and disclaimer-of-opinion taxonomy in financial audit; the control-design-effectiveness versus operating-effectiveness distinction in security
audit); and the institutional discipline of independent attestation as a profession with explicit qualification
requirements, code-of-ethics constraints, and regulatory oversight. What the lineage did not develop, in the
specific form AX-SH requires, is a unified formal axiomatic system over the reconciliation discipline that
spans all the substrates the lineage applies to. The lineage’s powerful operational vocabularies are grounded
in jurisdiction-specific standards (US GAAP, IFRS, ISO/IEC 27001, NIST SP 800-53, AICPA Trust Services
Criteria) rather than in a substrate-independent axiomatic foundation; the substrate-parameterized projection consistency that Axiom 4 formalizes is what the synthesis adds, with the formal-verification lineage
supplying the axiomatization template.

2.7.3 The textual-preservation philology lineage and mechanized verification
The textual-preservation philology lineage developed millennium-scale preservation discipline across multiple
cultures, formal structures including Pān.ini’s As.t.ādhyāyı̄ (a rule-based grammar that has been compared to
twentieth-century formal grammars in linguistics and to axiomatic systems in mathematics), and substantial
mathematical and computational apparatus: stemmatic-reconstruction algorithms developed by Lachmann
and his successors; collation methods systematized in modern critical-edition practice; the computational
stemmatics work of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries applying phylogenetic-tree algorithms
to manuscript traditions; and statistical analyses of variant distributions across manuscript witnesses. What

CHAPTER 2. HISTORICAL LINEAGES AND SYNTHESIS

35

the lineage did not develop, in the specific form AX-SH requires, is mechanized static verification of the kind
that the formal-verification lineage developed for programs and that AX-SH applies to surface-substrate consistency relations. The lineage’s verification practices operate on text as the substrate and human philological
judgment as the verification mechanism; the automated, statically-checkable, machine-mechanized verification that AX-SH requires for substrate consistency at the structural-honesty level is what the synthesis adds,
with the formal-verification lineage supplying the mechanization template.

2.7.4 Each lineage’s gap is filled by another lineage
The pattern across the three preceding subsections is that each lineage’s specific gap relative to AX-SH
is filled by another lineage’s specific strength. The formal-verification lineage’s preservation gap is filled
by the textual-preservation philology lineage’s centuries-scale operational discipline; the audit-and-assurance
lineage’s axiomatization gap is filled by the formal-verification lineage’s mathematical apparatus; the textualpreservation philology lineage’s mechanization gap is filled by the formal-verification lineage’s machinecheckable static verification. The three lineages do not jointly span every conceivable verification discipline
(there remain open problems and additional verification substrates that none of the three lineages addresses,
several of which Chapter 17 identifies), but the three lineages do jointly supply the structural components
that AX-SH requires. AX-SH is the proposed synthesis that composes these strengths into a single axiomatic
framework. The synthesis is proposed at Chapter 2; the formal proof that the synthesis succeeds is in
Chapter 8.

2.7.5 Chapter 2 closes by handing off to Chapter 3
Chapter 2 closes by handing off to Chapter 3. The historical synthesis of §§5–7 motivates the framework’s
structure: the dissertation has identified three intellectual lineages whose contributions, taken together,
supply the structural materials for a unified axiomatic framework that none of the lineages individually
developed in AX-SH’s specific form. The dissertation’s contribution is the formal unification under AX-SH,
with the historical lineages as motivating background. Chapter 3 introduces the mathematical prerequisites needed to express the four axioms formally: general categorical-equivalence machinery in the sense
of Mac Lane (Mac Lane 1998) for Axioms 1 and 2; correspondence-relation families for the bisimulationversus-simulation family that Axiom 2 ranges over; refinement-type machinery for the 𝑅may construction
that Axiom 3 ranges over; and projection-consistency machinery generalizing the accounting-identity pattern
that Axiom 4 abstracts, with sheaf-style categorical machinery in the sense of Mac Lane and Moerdijk (Mac
Lane and Moerdijk 1994) as one pedigree reference for Axiom 4. Chapters 4–7 develop the axioms themselves against these prerequisites and against the four worked substrate instances SI1–SI4 (Bayyinah, Furqan,
Munafiq Protocol, and the supply-chain four-substrate stack). Chapter 8 is assigned the definitional-adequacy
result (Theorem 8.3): whether AX-SH captures the operational structural-honesty vocabulary developed in
the dissertation’s substrate work. Chapter 2 has motivated the synthesis; the rest of the dissertation develops
it.

3.1 Mathematical objects and notation
3.1.1 Purpose of Chapter 3
Chapter 3’s role within the dissertation is to introduce the mathematical objects, notation, and conventions
that the four axiom chapters (Chapters 4–7) and the definitional-adequacy theorem chapter (Chapter 8) use
as standing foundation. Chapter 3 does not state or prove any of the four axioms of AX-SH; the axiom statements and their formal development are the work of Chapters 4–7. Chapter 3 does not establish decidability
results for the structures it introduces; the rigorous decidability claims and the quantum-survivability claim
are the work of Chapter 10. What Chapter 3 contributes is the vocabulary that those later chapters require:
typed objects for the domain entities the axioms reason about, notational conventions for the variables
that range over those domain entities, and the mathematical machinery (correspondence-relation families,
refinement-type machinery, projection families) over which the axioms express constraints.
This boundary is operationally important. Each subsequent section of Chapter 3 is to be read as introducing
machinery, never as asserting that the machinery satisfies any property; the properties are stated in Chapters 4–7 against the machinery introduced here. The discipline at the chapter level is parallel to the “no
retroactive attribution” discipline of Chapter 2 §1, but applied within the dissertation rather than across
historical lineages: introducing a mathematical object in Chapter 3 is not the same as asserting an axiom
about it in Chapters 4–7.

3.1.2 Finite-default convention
Throughout Chapter 3 and the axiom chapters that use its machinery, the working universe is by default
finite. Public surfaces are finite artifacts (finite specifications, finite APIs, finite attestation documents);
substrates are finite structures relative to a chosen observer model; correspondence relations are defined over
finite-state systems unless explicitly extended; projection families are finite collections of projections. This
convention allows Chapter 10 to formulate decidability and quantum-survivability claims over already-finite
working objects rather than arbitrary mathematical structures.
Later chapters, especially Chapter 10, identify which finite or bounded fragments support rigorous decidability and quantum-survivability claims, and which extensions remain outside v1.0 scope. The finite-default
convention is not a metaphysical claim about what exists; it is a working assumption that scopes the dissertation’s formal results to a tractable fragment. Extensions to infinite or unbounded structures are identified
as open problems in the Part V open-problem chapters (especially Chapter 20 for substrate-generalization
limits and Chapter 21 for falsification protocols) where they remain unresolved at v1.0.

3.2 Domain objects
Section 2 introduces the four domain objects on which AX-SH operates: public surfaces, substrates, observer
models, and contexts. Each is defined as a structured type with explicit components; each is illustrated
with examples drawn from the three lineages traced in Chapter 2; each carries a deferral sentence specifying
which axiom chapter will impose constraints relating the object to the others. The packaging of the four
into a unified type system is summarized in §2.5 with the explicit axiom-deferral note.

3.2.1 Public surfaces
A public surface is a formal artifact visible to callers, auditors, users, or other downstream verifiers. It is
a structured type with explicit components: the declared interface (what the surface exposes), the declared
semantics (what the surface says the substrate does), and the declared behavior expectations (what callers
may rely on). Examples include the published API specification of a software library; the visible interface of
a versioned protocol; the disclosed audit attestation of an organization undergoing SOC 2 attestation; and
a textual witness treated as authoritative within a transmission community.
A public surface carries no constraint on what behavior the underlying substrate actually exhibits. The
relation between surface declarations and substrate behavior is the work of Axiom 2 in Chapter 5; Chapter 3
supplies only the typed object.

3.2.2 Substrates
A substrate is the underlying entity that a public surface describes, implements, summarizes, or exposes.
It is a structured type with explicit components: the substrate’s actual state, its operational behavior, and
its real interface (as distinguished from the declared interface that the public surface exposes). Examples
include the program whose API is the public surface; the organization whose financial position the financialstatement family projects; the manuscript tradition whose textual content the critical edition presents; the
protocol implementation whose runtime behavior the published specification describes.
A substrate’s relationship to its public surface is parameterized by the choice of correspondence relation 𝑅
from the family introduced in §3 (Block B). The axiom that constrains 𝑅 is stated in Chapter 5; Chapter 3
supplies only the typed substrate object and the relation family over which Chapter 5’s axiom will quantify.

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

39

3.2.3 Observer models
An observer model is a formal limit on what a caller, verifier, auditor, or user can distinguish or detect when
interacting with a substrate through its public surface. It is a typed observation calculus specifying which
behaviors are observable, with what precision, and under what conditions. Examples include a refinementtype caller with the full F⋆ or Liquid Haskell type system available (Swamy et al. 2016; Vazou et al. 2014);
an audit-style auditor with sampled access to substrate state under a defined materiality threshold; a masstransmission community of reciters with limited individual access but high aggregate coverage; a static
analyzer with bounded inspection depth.
The observer model parameterizes what a verifier can observe or distinguish in a given verification regime.
Later axiom chapters will specify which observable divergences constitute structural-honesty failures under
a declared observer model. Chapter 3 supplies the observer-model typed object; the failure conditions are
stated in Chapters 5 and 6.

3.2.4 Contexts
A context is the set of operational conditions under which surface-substrate consistency claims are evaluated. It is a typed condition specification including workload range, deployment environment, audit scope,
transmission community, and any other operational parameter that determines which substrate behavior
is relevant to the claim being evaluated. Examples include the workload range under which a software
library’s API claims are evaluated; the audit scope of a SOC 2 engagement (which systems and processes
are within the audit boundary); the textual-transmission community within which a manuscript tradition’s
variants are catalogued; the protocol-deployment environment within which a network-protocol specification
is operationally meaningful.
Later chapters may evaluate the same surface/substrate pair under different contexts 𝐾1 and 𝐾2 , allowing
context-sensitive consistency claims to be stated explicitly rather than left implicit. The axiom chapters
specify how context parameterizes their respective consistency relations; Chapter 3 supplies only the typed
context object.

3.2.5 Structured-type packaging and axiom deferral
Public surfaces, substrates, observer models, and contexts are packaged as structured types used by later
chapters. The packaging is as follows. Surfaces are objects of a structured surface-type carrying declaredinterface, declared-semantics, and declared-behavior components. Substrates are objects of a structured
substrate-type carrying actual-state, operational-behavior, and real-interface components. Observer models
are typed observation calculi specifying observability conditions. Contexts are typed condition specifications.
Subsequent axiom chapters will impose constraints that relate these objects. Axiom 1 (Chapter 4) will
constrain how versioned surfaces evolve over time under the append-only-provenance discipline. Axiom 2
(Chapter 5) will constrain surface-substrate consistency under observer model 𝑂 and context 𝐾 for a chosen
correspondence relation 𝑅. Axiom 3 (Chapter 6) will constrain caller-side coverage of 𝑅may for callers
reasoning about producer outcomes. Axiom 4 (Chapter 7) will constrain projection-family consistency under
∼𝑋 for projection families Π𝑋 over substrate 𝑋.
Chapter 3 supplies the typed objects and the relation/projection machinery; the axiom chapters impose the

40

structural-honesty constraints. The vocabulary of §§1–2 is suﬀicient to state every axiom of AX-SH once the
relation and projection machinery of §§3–7 (Block B) is in place; that machinery is introduced in the next
block of Chapter 3 and is used by Chapters 4–7 to express the axioms in their final form.

3.3 Correspondence-relation families
Section 3 introduces the correspondence-relation machinery that Chapter 5 (Axiom 2) will use to state
the surface-substrate consistency requirement. The machinery is presented in six subsections: §3.1 defines
the relation family as a structured collection; §3.2 introduces the labeled-transition-system and structuraloperational-semantics foundations on which the LTS-based members are defined; §3.3–§3.5 introduce the
family members (bisimulation, simulation and refinement, abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction
equality); §3.6 introduces the relation-choice mechanism by which a substrate records which family member
it uses. Chapter 5 will state the consistency requirement over the substrate’s declared choice; Chapter 3
supplies only the machinery.

3.3.1 Correspondence-relation family as a structured collection
A correspondence-relation family is a parametric collection of binary relations between public surfaces and
substrate behaviors, indexed by structural parameters (observer model, context, finite-state-foundation
choice). Each member of the family relates the declared behavior of a public surface to the operational
behavior of the substrate it describes through a specific equivalence or refinement discipline. The family
is not assumed to satisfy any uniform consistency property at the §3.1 level: members vary in strength, in
symmetry, and in observer-sensitivity, and which member is the appropriate 𝑅 for a given substrate depends
on the substrate’s nature. The relation-strength ordering among family members is optionally representable
as a preorder or small finite category in the sense of Mac Lane (Mac Lane 1998); this categorical-equivalence
framing is the general categorical machinery on which Axioms 1 and 2 rely, with the sheaf-style machinery
of §6.5 (relevant to Axiom 4 only) treated separately in the sense of Mac Lane and Moerdijk (Mac Lane and
Moerdijk 1994).
Chapter 5 will use the relation family to state Axiom 2 by quantifying over the substrate’s declared correspondence relation 𝑅. Chapter 3 supplies the family structure (members, relationships among members,
declaration mechanism); the axiom statement is the work of Chapter 5.

3.3.2 Labeled transition systems and structural operational semantics
We adopt the standard process-algebra notation for the LTS foundations used in §§3.3–3.4. A labeled
transition system (LTS) is a triple (𝑄, 𝐴, →) consisting of a set of states 𝑄, a set of action labels 𝐴, and a
𝑎

transition relation → ⊆ 𝑄×𝐴×𝑄. We write 𝑝 −
→ 𝑝′ for (𝑝, 𝑎, 𝑝′ ) ∈ →. The LTS provides the formal substrate
over which finite-state correspondence relations are defined: bisimulation, simulation, and refinement are all
definable as conditions on the transition structure of two LTSs that are to be compared.
Structural operational semantics (SOS), introduced by Plotkin (Plotkin 2004), generates an LTS from program syntax through syntax-directed inference rules. Given a program, the SOS rules generate the LTS
whose states are program configurations and whose transitions are derived from the SOS inference rules.
The finite-default convention of MP1.2 means that we work with LTSs whose state and label sets are finite,

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

41

so that the resulting transition relation is finite and the family relations of §§3.3–3.4 are decidable in the
relevant fragment. Chapter 10 will discuss the formal decidability claims; Chapter 3 introduces only the
foundational LTS/SOS machinery.

3.3.3 Bisimulation
A bisimulation is a binary relation ℛ ⊆ 𝑄1 × 𝑄2 between two LTSs (𝑄1 , 𝐴, →1 ) and (𝑄2 , 𝐴, →2 ) such that:
𝑎
