(i) if (𝑝, 𝑞) ∈ ℛ and 𝑝 −
→1 𝑝′ , then there exists 𝑞 ′ with 𝑞 −
→2 𝑞 ′ and (𝑝′ , 𝑞 ′ ) ∈ ℛ; (ii) symmetrically, if
𝑎

𝑎

(𝑝, 𝑞) ∈ ℛ and 𝑞 −
→2 𝑞 ′ , then there exists 𝑝′ with 𝑝 −
→1 𝑝′ and (𝑝′ , 𝑞 ′ ) ∈ ℛ. Two states are bisimilar when
there exists a bisimulation that relates them.
Bisimulation was introduced by Park (Park 1981) and developed within Milner’s process-calculus tradition (Milner 1980); Hennessy and Milner introduced the modal-logical characterization in their 1980 ICALP
paper (Hennessy and Milner 1980), with subsequent algebraic-laws work (Hennessy and Milner 1985). The
Hennessy-Milner theorem establishes that, under suitable image-finite assumptions on the LTS, bisimilarity
coincides with modal equivalence in Hennessy-Milner logic: two states are bisimilar exactly when they satisfy the same modal formulas. The algorithmic foundations for deciding bisimilarity over finite-state LTSs
are due to Kanellakis and Smolka (Kanellakis and Smolka 1990); modern theoretical treatment appears in
Sangiorgi (Sangiorgi 2012).
Bisimulation is treated as the strongest standard finite-state behavioral equivalence used in this dissertation,
under the declared observer model and the relevant finite/image-finite assumptions. The qualifier “treated as”
is deliberate: stronger equivalences exist in the literature (graph isomorphism, hereditary history-preserving
equivalence in true-concurrency settings), but bisimilarity is the strongest behavioral equivalence that the
dissertation’s observer-model machinery (§2.3) is designed to express, under the finite/image-finite scoping
that the modal-characterization results require. Chapter 5 will state when bisimulation is the appropriate
𝑅 for a substrate; Chapter 3 introduces only the definition and the foundational results.

3.3.4 Simulation and refinement
A simulation is the asymmetric directional weakening of bisimulation: a relation ℛ ⊆ 𝑄1 × 𝑄2 such that
condition (i) above holds (𝑄2 can mimic 𝑄1 ’s transitions) but condition (ii) is dropped. 𝑄2 simulates 𝑄1
when there exists a simulation relating their initial states. Simulation is appropriate when the substratesurface correspondence is asymmetric: the substrate may exhibit behaviors not declared by the surface
(provided the declared behaviors are preserved), while the surface need not cover every substrate behavior.
Refinement, in the sense of Lynch and Vaandrager (Lynch and Vaandrager 1995), is a variant of simulation
used in distributed-systems and concurrency verification. A refinement is a forward simulation that additionally preserves the substrate’s externally-visible action interface: the abstract specification (the public surface
in our terminology) describes the externally-visible interface; the concrete implementation (the substrate)
may have richer internal behavior; refinement asserts that every concrete execution corresponds to some
abstract execution under the externally-visible action projection. Refinement is the natural correspondence
relation for distributed-protocol verification, where the abstract specification captures the intended protocol
behavior and the concrete implementation may include additional internal state and actions.
The relationships among bisimulation, simulation, and refinement are structural properties of the relations
themselves: every bisimulation is a simulation by definition, and in many process- and distributed-system

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

42

settings, refinement can be represented using simulation-like relations together with a preservation condition
on externally visible behavior. Chapter 5 will state when each of these is the appropriate 𝑅 for a substrate;
Chapter 3 introduces the family members without imposing a uniform choice.

3.3.5 Abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality
Not every substrate is naturally modeled as an LTS. A printed financial report, an AI model card, an
attestation document, a manuscript: these are static artifacts whose “behavior” is what an observer extracts
from them under a defined extraction procedure, not a sequence of transitions. For substrates of this form,
the correspondence-relation family extends beyond LTS-based relations to include abstraction-preserving
equivalence and extraction equality.
Abstraction-preserving equivalence is a relation ℛ between substrates defined via a designated abstraction
map 𝛼 ∶ Substrate → AbstractDomain. Two substrates are abstraction-equivalent when their 𝛼-images are
equal in the abstract domain. The relation is parameterized by the abstraction map, which captures what
aspect of the substrate the correspondence relation is sensitive to: for a financial report, 𝛼 might map a
balance sheet to the equation “assets equal liabilities plus equity”; for an attestation document, 𝛼 might
map an audit report to a control-evidence pairing; for a manuscript, 𝛼 might map a witness to its stemmatic
position and variant readings.
Extraction equality is a closely related notion in which a defined extraction procedure 𝜀 ∶ Substrate → Surface
produces a derived artifact from each substrate, and two substrates are extraction-equal when their 𝜀-outputs
are equal. The procedure 𝜀 formalizes “what the substrate is taken to mean” for the purposes of comparison:
for a manuscript, 𝜀 might be the editorial reading procedure that produces a canonical text from a witness;
for a model card, 𝜀 might be the extraction procedure that produces the model’s stated capabilities from
the card’s structured fields.
Abstraction-preserving equivalence and extraction equality are both non-LTS correspondence forms: neither requires that the substrate have a transition structure. They are appropriate for substrates including
philological texts, AI model cards, financial reports, and attestation documents. Chapter 5 will state when
these forms are the appropriate 𝑅 for a substrate; Chapter 3 introduces them as additional members of the
correspondence-relation family.

3.3.6 Relation-choice mechanism
The relation-choice mechanism is the structured field by which a substrate records which correspondence
relation 𝑅 from the family it will use. For a software-library substrate, the mechanism might be a declaration in the library’s specification document that “this library’s surface-substrate consistency is verified
under bisimilarity over the LTS generated by the library’s API surface.” For a financial-report substrate, the
mechanism might be a declaration in the audit attestation that “the report’s surface-substrate consistency is
verified under abstraction-preserving equivalence with respect to the jurisdiction-specified accounting identity.” For a manuscript substrate, the mechanism might be a declaration in the critical edition’s apparatus
that “the textual-witness correspondence is verified under extraction equality with respect to the editorial
reading procedure 𝜀.”
The declaration is itself a public-surface object (it appears on the surface where downstream verifiers can read
it) and is therefore subject to the discipline of Chapter 4 (versioned surfaces, append-only-provenance under

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

43

Axiom 1). Chapter 5 will state the Axiom 2 requirement over the declared choice. Chapter 3 introduces the
choice mechanism as the structured slot; Chapter 5 will state what it means for a substrate’s behavior to
satisfy the surface-substrate consistency condition under the declared choice.
The choice mechanism keeps the relation-family approach tractable: rather than asserting a single uniform
correspondence relation across all substrates of all types, the framework permits per-substrate declarations
recorded as structured fields. Different substrate types are likely to use different family members (LTSbased bisimulation for protocols, abstraction-preserving equivalence for financial reports, extraction equality
for manuscripts), and the declaration mechanism is what allows the same axiom statement (Axiom 2 in
Chapter 5) to apply uniformly across the substrate types without requiring a uniform correspondence relation
across them.

3.4 Versioned public surfaces and behavioral subtyping
Section 4 introduces the versioned-surface apparatus that Chapter 4 (Axiom 1) will use to state the appendonly-provenance discipline. The apparatus is presented in five subsections: §4.1 defines version-indexed
public-surface families as the typed objects over which Axiom 1 quantifies; §4.2 introduces behavioral subtyping between versions in the Liskov-Wing sense; §4.3 distinguishes compatible extension from silent breaking change at the surface level; §4.4 introduces truth-status tags as explicit surface objects; §4.5 introduces
historical-record preservation as the object-level apparatus. Chapter 4 will state Axiom 1 over this apparatus;
Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

3.4.1 Version-indexed public-surface families
A version-indexed public-surface family is a sequence 𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 of public surfaces indexed by version,
with each successive 𝑆𝑖+1 representing a published revision of 𝑆𝑖 . We use 𝑆𝑖 as §4-local notation for the
𝑖-th version of the public-surface family Surface(𝑆) associated with substrate 𝑆; the standing symbol 𝑆 from
Table 3.1 remains the substrate identifier. The version index tracks the temporal evolution of the surface:
𝑆0 is the initial published version, 𝑆1 is the first revision, and so on. The family is finite by the MP1.2
finite-default convention; the version index ranges over a finite ordinal set {0, 1, … , 𝑛} for some 𝑛.
The family is not assumed to satisfy any inheritance property between successive versions at the §4.1 level.
Chapter 4 will state Axiom 1 over the family by imposing the append-only-provenance discipline. Chapter 3
introduces the typed family as an object; the discipline that constrains evolution between adjacent versions
is the work of Chapter 4.

3.4.2 Behavioral subtyping between versions
Behavioral subtyping in the Liskov-Wing sense (Liskov and Wing 1994) is a binary relation between two
versions of a public surface at the typed-interface level: 𝑆𝑖+1 is a behavioral subtype of 𝑆𝑖 when callers whose
assumptions are valid under 𝑆𝑖 ’s declared interface continue to have those assumptions preserved under 𝑆𝑖+1 ’s
declared interface (equivalently, 𝒮𝑁+1 <∶ 𝒮𝑁 , expressing the behavioral-subtype relation that Chapter 1 §2
Axiom 1 states in Liskov-Wing prose, with Chapter 8 §1.2 Witness M1 instantiating the relation at the
type-signature level using plain 𝑆𝑡+1 -versus-𝑆𝑡 notation for the per-version contract). The relation captures
the intuition that a successor version honors the contracts of its predecessor: callers built against 𝑆𝑖 do not

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

44

break when 𝑆𝑖+1 is substituted.
Behavioral subtyping over public surfaces extends the original Liskov-Wing notion (which was stated for classinstance substitutability in object-oriented programming) to general public-surface artifacts: versioned APIs,
versioned protocol specifications, versioned audit attestations, versioned editions of textual artifacts. The
substitutability test in each case is whether a caller programmed against the predecessor surface continues
to function against the successor surface, under the caller’s declared dependencies on the predecessor.
Chapter 3 introduces the behavioral-subtyping relation as the structural relation between adjacent versions;
Chapter 4 will use it when stating the Axiom 1 append-only-provenance discipline across the version-indexed
surface family.

3.4.3 Compatible extension versus silent breaking change
A surface-level transition from 𝑆𝑖 to 𝑆𝑖+1 is a compatible extension when 𝑆𝑖+1 is a behavioral subtype of
𝑆𝑖 and any additions to 𝑆𝑖+1 are additive: new capabilities, new optional parameters, new endpoints that
do not interfere with the semantics of existing declarations. Compatible extension preserves what callers
already rely on and adds new affordances they may or may not use.
A surface-level transition is a silent breaking change when 𝑆𝑖+1 is not a behavioral subtype of 𝑆𝑖 (callers
programmed against 𝑆𝑖 break against 𝑆𝑖+1 ) and the breaking change is not accompanied by an explicit
corrigendum (truth-status tag, §4.4) marking what was changed and why. Silent breaking change is the
surface-evolution pattern that Chapter 4 will treat as the relevant structural-honesty failure mode under
Axiom 1: the surface changed, callers relying on it broke, and the change was not declared.
Chapter 3 introduces the discrimination vocabulary (compatible extension versus silent breaking change);
Chapter 4 will use this vocabulary to distinguish permitted compatible extensions from impermissible silent
breaks. The formal invariant Axiom 1 imposes over surface evolution is the work of Chapter 4.

3.4.4 Truth-status tags
A truth-status tag is an explicit surface object marking a change to previously-declared content. The
dissertation uses three tags. A correction tag indicates that a prior claim on the surface was wrong and is
revised: the predecessor surface contained an assertion the producer no longer endorses, the successor surface
replaces that assertion with a revised one, and the correction tag attaches to the change. A supersession tag
indicates that a prior claim is replaced by a newer claim that takes precedence: the predecessor’s claim was
not necessarily wrong, but the newer claim is the operative one going forward. A withdrawal tag indicates
that a prior claim is no longer maintained or defended: the producer is no longer asserting the predecessor’s
claim, but does not necessarily replace it with a substitute.
The tags are surface objects, not silent mutations. The predecessor surface remains visible in the version
history with the tag attached; the successor surface includes the revised, superseded, or withdrawn claim
along with the tag identifying which prior claim it modifies. Chapter 4 will use the tags to formalize the
corrigenda discipline that distinguishes append-only-provenance-with-corrections from silent rewriting.

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

45

3.4.5 Historical-record preservation
Historical-record preservation is the object-level apparatus that ensures the historical record across
𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 remains accessible and verifiable. The apparatus has three components: archived versions
(each 𝑆𝑖 is preserved in archived form alongside its successors, available to downstream verifiers who need
to compare versions); corrigenda registers (the truth-status tags of §4.4 are recorded in a register that lists
which tags apply to which version transitions); retention discipline (the archived versions and corrigenda
registers are retained for the period during which the surface’s claims may be relied upon).
Chapter 4 will use this apparatus to state the append-only-provenance invariant that Axiom 1 imposes.
Chapter 3 supplies the typed objects (archived versions, corrigenda registers, retention discipline) that the
invariant operates over; the invariant statement is the work of Chapter 4.

3.5 𝑅may machinery and caller-side coverage
Section 5 introduces the 𝑅may machinery that Chapter 6 (Axiom 3) will use to state the caller-coverage
obligation. The machinery is presented in five subsections: §5.1 introduces 𝑅may as the verifier’s conservative
over-approximation of producer outcomes; §5.2 distinguishes 𝑅declared from 𝑅may as standing-symbol objects;
§5.3 introduces substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines; §5.4 introduces the caller-side coverage
vocabulary; §5.5 positions the caller-side discipline as an extension of producer-side refinement-type discipline.
Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 over this machinery; Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

3.5.1 𝑅may as conservative over-approximation
𝑅may is the verifier’s typed object representing the set of possible producer outcomes that a caller must
be prepared to handle. The construction is conservative: 𝑅may includes every outcome that the verifier
cannot rule out, possibly more outcomes than the producer actually exhibits. Conservatism is what makes
the construction tractable: the verifier need only over-approximate the actual outcome set, not compute it
precisely.
For a software producer, 𝑅may might be the set of return values, exception types, and side-effect classes that
a static analyzer cannot prove to be impossible for the producer’s procedure. For an audited organization,
𝑅may might be the set of control-failure modes that an auditor cannot rule out within the engagement’s
scope. For a document extractor, 𝑅may might be the set of interpretations that an automated extractor
cannot disambiguate without further evidence. Chapter 3 introduces 𝑅may as the typed object; Chapter 6
will state Axiom 3 over it.

3.5.2 Distinguishing 𝑅declared from 𝑅may
𝑅declared and 𝑅may are both standing symbols in Table 3.1, but they play different roles. 𝑅declared is the
producer’s declared possible outcomes: what the producer says, on the surface, that the substrate can do.
𝑅may is the verifier’s conservative over-approximation: what the verifier cannot rule out, conservatively.
𝑅declared and 𝑅may are distinct standing-symbol objects that may or may not overlap; the relationship
between them is not constrained at the §5.2 level. The relationship between 𝑅declared and 𝑅may depends

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

46

on the substrate and the verification regime; Chapter 6 will state the caller-exhaustiveness obligation that
quantifies over whatever relationship between them obtains in a given verification context.
Chapter 3 introduces the distinction between 𝑅declared and 𝑅may as standing-symbol objects. The callerexhaustiveness obligation that quantifies over these objects is the work of Chapter 6.

3.5.3 Substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines
Different substrate types use different methods to compute 𝑅may . Four exemplar disciplines illustrate the
parameterization.
Type-level over-approximation uses the producer’s declared type as the over-approximation: the set of values
inhabiting the type is the set of possible producer outcomes. The refinement-type tradition—F⋆ (Swamy
et al. 2016), Liquid Haskell (Vazou et al. 2014)—extends this with refinement predicates that further
constrain the type-level over-approximation; the predicates are part of the producer’s declaration, and the
over-approximation incorporates them.
Static-analysis over-approximation uses a static analyzer to compute the set of values, exception types,
or side-effect classes that the analyzer cannot prove to be impossible for the producer. The analysis is
bounded in depth (per the MP1.2 finite-default convention) and produces a conservative over-approximation
by construction in the abstract-interpretation tradition originated by Cousot and Cousot (Cousot and Cousot
1977).
Audit-style over-approximation uses an auditor with scope-bounded access to enumerate possible controlfailure modes within a defined audit scope. The audit attestation declares which scope was examined and
what failure modes were ruled out; failure modes outside the declared scope or not ruled out remain in 𝑅may .
Document-extraction over-approximation uses an automated extractor to enumerate possible interpretations
of an ambiguous document. The extractor’s output is the set of interpretations consistent with the document;
the over-approximation is conservative because the extractor enumerates all plausible interpretations rather
than committing to one.
Chapter 3 introduces these substrate-specific disciplines as parameterizations of the 𝑅may construction; Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 over the substrate’s declared discipline.

3.5.4 Caller-side coverage vocabulary
Given 𝑅may for a producer, later chapters will frame caller use of that producer in terms of a coverage
question: what does the caller do with each outcome in 𝑅may ? The dissertation’s caller-side coverage
vocabulary supplies three discharge categories.
Handled: the caller has explicit logic for the outcome. When the outcome occurs, the caller takes a specific action—catching the exception, branching on the return value, processing the alternative document
interpretation, escalating the control-failure mode to a defined incident response.
Propagated-as-incomplete: the caller acknowledges the outcome without having explicit handling logic for
it, and propagates it to its own caller with an incompleteness annotation. The incompleteness is declared
rather than hidden: the caller’s own surface reflects that it does not handle this outcome, and the discharge
obligation transfers upward to whichever component the caller is, in turn, called by.

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

47

Proven-unreachable: the caller proves that the outcome cannot occur in its calling context. The proof
might be a refinement-type discharge (the type system rules out the outcome), a static-analysis result (the
analyzer proves unreachability), or an audit attestation (the auditor confirms the outcome is outside the
relevant scope).
Chapter 3 introduces the three-category vocabulary as caller-side discharge slots; Chapter 6 will state the
caller-exhaustiveness obligation using this vocabulary.

3.5.5 Caller obligations as extension of producer-side refinement-type discipline
The producer-side refinement-type tradition—F⋆ (Swamy et al. 2016), Liquid Haskell (Vazou et al. 2014)—
requires producers to satisfy refinements declared in their signatures: the producer’s actual behavior must
conform to the type-level refinements the producer published. This is producer-side discipline: the producer’s
obligations are stated against the producer’s own declarations.
The dissertation’s structural-honesty discipline extends this by adding caller-side obligations. Where the
producer-side tradition requires the producer to satisfy its own refinements, the dissertation additionally
addresses callers: callers face discharge obligations over 𝑅may in the three-category vocabulary of §5.4. The
caller-side discipline complements rather than replaces the producer-side discipline: the producer still must
satisfy its declarations; additionally, the caller must discharge its obligations against the verifier’s overapproximation of what the producer might do.
Chapter 3 positions the caller-side discipline as an extension of the producer-side tradition; Chapter 6 will
state Axiom 3 as the formal caller obligation that complements the producer-side refinement-type framework.

3.6 Projection families and consistency relations
Section 6 introduces the projection-family machinery that Chapter 7 (Axiom 4) will use to state the substrateparameterized projection-consistency requirement. The machinery is presented in six subsections: §6.1 defines projection families Π𝑋 as finite structured collections; §6.2 introduces projection domains and partiality;
§6.3 introduces substrate-specific consistency relations ∼𝑋 ; §6.4 catalogues the motivating projection-family
exemplars from Chapter 2’s three lineages and from contemporary computational practice; §6.5 introduces
sheaf-style and commuting-diagram vocabulary as compact descriptions; §6.6 records the deferral to Chapter 7. Chapter 7 will state Axiom 4 over this machinery; Chapter 3 supplies only the machinery.

3.6.1 Projection family Π𝑋 as a finite structured family
A projection family Π𝑋 = {𝜋1 , 𝜋2 , … , 𝜋𝑛 } over substrate 𝑋 is a finite collection of projections, each 𝜋𝑖 being
a function from substrate states (or substrate facts) to a typed view. The family is finite by the MP1.2
finite-default convention; the index set is a finite ordinal range {1, 2, … , 𝑛} for some 𝑛. Each member 𝜋𝑖 is
a typed object with explicit domain and range; the family Π𝑋 is the typed object that collects them.
The family is not assumed to satisfy any consistency property at the §6.1 level. Chapter 7 will state Axiom 4
over the family by imposing the substrate-specific consistency requirement under ∼𝑋 (§6.3). Chapter 3
introduces the typed family as an object; the consistency requirement that relates the family members is the
work of Chapter 7.

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

48

3.6.2 Projection domains and partiality
Each projection 𝜋𝑖 has an explicit domain dom(𝜋𝑖 ) ⊆ Substrate(𝑋) over which it is defined; outside the
domain, 𝜋𝑖 is partial (no projection value is produced). Different projections in the family may have different
domains: 𝜋1 may project from a strictly larger subset of substrate states than 𝜋2 , or the two domains may
overlap without one containing the other.
Partiality is structurally important. A substrate fact need not be projectable into every member of Π𝑋 ; some
substrate facts may lie in the domain of 𝜋1 and 𝜋3 but outside the domain of 𝜋2 and 𝜋4 . Later chapters will
formulate consistency checks only on regions where the relevant projections are jointly defined: the test “do
𝜋1 and 𝜋2 agree on substrate fact 𝑥” presupposes 𝑥 ∈ dom(𝜋1 ) ∩ dom(𝜋2 ). Chapter 7 will state when joint
definability implies mutual coherence under ∼𝑋 ; Chapter 3 supplies the partiality structure.

3.6.3 Substrate-specific consistency relations ∼𝑋
For each substrate 𝑋, the consistency relation ∼𝑋 is the substrate-specific relation later used to express
when two projection outputs are compatible, where both are defined on the same underlying fact. The
relation ∼𝑋 varies by substrate: arithmetic identity for double-entry bookkeeping (debit projection and credit
projection agree under arithmetic equality); jurisdiction-specified accounting identity for modern financial
reporting (balance-sheet, income-statement, and cash-flow projections agree under GAAP- or IFRS-defined
relationships); control-evidence-attestation consistency for security audit (control-design, evidence-collection,
and operational-effectiveness projections agree under the attestation framework’s consistency rules); variantrecord-comparison for textual-preservation philology (manuscript-witness projections agree when stemmatic
relationships predict their variant readings).
Chapter 3 introduces the consistency-relation parameter ∼𝑋 without yet requiring mutual coherence. Chapter 7 will state when projections in Π𝑋 are required to cohere under ∼𝑋 ; the coherence requirement is the
work of Chapter 7.

3.6.4 Motivating projection-family examples
The dissertation’s motivating projection-family examples serve as exemplars for Axiom 4’s structure, drawn
from the three lineages traced in Chapter 2 and from contemporary computational practice.
Double-entry bookkeeping (Pacioli 1494) supplies the original 𝑛 = 2 projection family: each transaction
produces a debit projection and a credit projection over the chart of accounts, with the consistency relation
being arithmetic identity (total debits equal total credits per transaction). The bookkeeping practice predates
the formal mathematical machinery by approximately five centuries.
Modern financial reporting (Previts and Merino 1979) extends the projection-family approach to multiple
statement projections: balance sheet, income statement, statement of cash flows, statement of changes in
equity. The consistency relation in this case is jurisdiction-specified (GAAP in the United States, IFRS
internationally), and the projections must agree under jurisdiction-specific accounting identities such as
retained-earnings reconciliation across statements.
Multi-control audit (International Organization for Standardization 2022; National Institute of Standards
and Technology 2020; American Institute of Certified Public Accountants 2017) supplies a projection family
of scope, control, evidence, and operational-effectiveness projections, with the consistency relation being the

CHAPTER 3. MATHEMATICAL PREREQUISITES

49

attestation framework’s defined consistency rules (for SOC 2, the AICPA Trust Services Criteria define when
scope, controls, evidence, and operations cohere).
Manuscript cross-witnessing (Timpanaro 2005; Reynolds and Wilson 2013; Tov 2012; Strack and Stemberger
1996) supplies a projection family in which each manuscript witness produces a textual-reading projection,
and the consistency relation is stemmatic: witnesses related by descent from a common ancestor are expected
to agree on inherited readings, while disagreements indicate either independent error or variant transmission.
Recitation chains for Quranic transmission supply a multi-substrate projection family in which hifz (oral
memorization), manuscript witness, tajwid (recitational ruleset), riwayat (transmission chain), and communal verification each project over the textual substrate, with the consistency relation being the multi-substrate
cross-coherence that the verification community treats as authoritative; the dissertation’s structural framing of this multi-substrate apparatus is developed in the SHV synthesis paper (Arfeen 2026h) rather than
in single-surah literary-structural analyses such as Farrin (Farrin 2010), which is cited elsewhere only as a
structural-analysis exemplar (per Chapter 1 §4 and Chapter 2 §4.2 scoping).
Software-release projection families (Arfeen 2026f) supply a contemporary example in which sigstore (cryptographic signing), in-toto (build-provenance attestation), SLSA (supply-chain integrity levels), and SHV
(structural-honesty verification) each project over a software-release substrate, with the consistency relation
being the supply-chain-consistency framework that downstream consumers rely on.
These exemplars are motivating examples, not the axiom statement. Chapter 7 abstracts the pattern to
substrate-parameterized form; Chapter 3 supplies only the exemplars.

3.6.5 Sheaf-style and commuting-diagram vocabulary
The projection-family-with-consistency-relation structure can be described using sheaf-inspired and presheafstyle restriction vocabulary in compact categorical form. Mac Lane and Moerdijk (Mac Lane and Moerdijk
1994) develop the sheaf-theoretic machinery in detail; the vocabulary relevant to the dissertation is the smallfinite-category restriction of that machinery. A projection family Π𝑋 over a substrate 𝑋 with consistency
relation ∼𝑋 can be described using sheaf-inspired / presheaf-style restriction vocabulary over a small finite
category, where each projection plays the role of a section over a local view, and restriction maps express
comparison across overlaps. Whether the consistency relation ∼𝑋 additionally satisfies the gluing condition
(that sections agreeing on overlaps extend uniquely to a global section) is not claimed here and is not required
for Chapter 3’s prerequisite role; Chapter 7 will determine which structural properties ∼𝑋 is required to
satisfy. No gluing or uniqueness condition is asserted at the Chapter 3 prerequisite level.
In compact commuting-diagram form: for projections 𝜋𝑖 , 𝜋𝑗 in Π𝑋 with overlapping domains, the consistency
relation ∼𝑋 relates the restriction 𝜋𝑖 ↾ (dom(𝜋𝑖 )∩dom(𝜋𝑗 )) to the restriction 𝜋𝑗 ↾ (dom(𝜋𝑖 )∩dom(𝜋𝑗 )), where
each side denotes the projection restricted to the joint domain.
The categorical vocabulary supplies the formal apparatus for stating Axiom 4 compactly. The analogy
with sheaves is structural and notational, not a claim that projection families are sheaves in the full topostheoretic sense; the relevant restriction is to small finite categories under the MP1.2 finite-default convention.
Chapter 3 introduces the apparatus; Chapter 7 uses it to state the axiom.

3.7 Decidable-fragment discipline and chapter handoff
Section 7 introduces the decidable-fragment discipline and identifies the candidate fragments for which
the dissertation will attempt to establish decidability in Chapter 10. The discipline is presented in five
subsections: §7.1 defines the decidable-fragment scoping discipline; §7.2 lists the candidate fragments; §7.3
distinguishes candidate from proven; §7.4 names unbounded and infinite cases as outside v1.0 scope; §7.5
closes Chapter 3 with the handoff to Chapter 4. Chapter 10 supplies the rigorous decidability and quantumsurvivability proofs. Chapter 3 supplies only the discipline and the candidate identification.

3.7.1 Decidable-fragment discipline
The dissertation’s v1.0 verification claims are scoped by declared boundedness assumptions; where no
bounded or decidable fragment is established, the relevant claim is marked as an open problem or continuation target. The decidable-fragment scoping discipline is the formal-methods analog of the scope-declaration
discipline familiar from professional audit, which states the scope of an audit engagement before stating the
audit results: the SOC 2 attestation declares what was within the audit’s scope and what was not, and the
audit opinion is meaningful only within the declared scope.
Chapter 3 introduces this scope-declaration discipline as a methodological commitment for the formal results
to follow. The actual fragments and their rigorous decidability proofs are the work of Chapter 10; Chapter 3
commits to the discipline that those proofs will be scoped explicitly.
Standing convention. Throughout this dissertation, Chapter 8 §2’s finite-witness construction (T82) operates
within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes; T82 itself does not prove general decidability
conditions. This routing convention is stated once here and is not restated at each subsequent occurrence in
Chapter 3 where decidability is referenced.

3.7.2 Candidate decidable fragments
The dissertation identifies the following candidate fragments as plausibly establishable based on standard
formal-methods results. Finite-state correspondence relations over the LTS foundations of §3.2, where standard bisimulation and simulation problems have well-studied decision procedures over finite-state systems.
Finite version histories over the version-indexed surface families of §4.1, where compatible-extension-versussilent-break determination is plausibly decidable when both versions are represented as finite-state LTS
structures and the behavioral-subtyping relation is decidable over those LTS representations—the precise decidability conditions depend on the underlying semantic model and are established in Chapter 10. Bounded
𝑅may approximations over the substrate-specific over-approximation disciplines of §5.3, where the callercoverage three-category vocabulary is plausibly decidable when 𝑅may is finitely representable. Finite pro-

Each candidate is identified as a fragment where decidability appears tractable; the rigorous decidability

3.7.3 Candidate versus proven distinction
The methodological discipline that distinguishes candidate decidable fragments from proven decidable fragments is structurally important. Chapter 3’s candidate listings (§7.2) are not commitments that the fragments are decidable; they are commitments that the dissertation will attempt to establish their decidability
in later chapters and will explicitly mark any candidate that fails to establish as an open problem in the
Part V open-problem chapters (especially Chapters 20 and 21).
The candidate-versus-proven distinction is the formal-methods analog of the conjecture-versus-theorem distinction familiar from pure mathematics: a candidate fragment is a conjecture that decidability holds within
the fragment; a proven fragment is a theorem that decidability holds within the fragment. Chapter 3 makes
only the conjectures; Chapter 10 supplies the rigorous decidability and quantum-survivability proofs.

3.7.4 Unbounded and infinite cases outside v1.0 scope
The dissertation v1.0 explicitly excludes the following cases from its rigorous decidability claims. Unbounded
𝑅may approximations (where the over-approximation is not finitely representable, for example 𝑅may over an
infinite-state probabilistic producer) are outside v1.0 scope. Infinite-state correspondence relations (where
the underlying LTS has infinitely many states) are outside v1.0 scope unless explicitly handled by a later
chapter. Infinite version histories (where the version index ranges over an infinite ordinal) are outside v1.0
scope. Infinite projection families (where |Π𝑋 | is infinite) are outside v1.0 scope.
The scope exclusion is the structural-honesty companion to the decidable-fragment discipline of §7.1: the
dissertation declares what it does not claim to prove, just as it declares what it does claim to prove. Open
problems in this excluded space are identified in the Part V open-problem chapters (especially Chapter 20
for substrate-generalization limits and Chapter 21 for falsification protocols) for the v1.0 release; future work
may address some of them in later versions of the framework.

4.1 Axiom 1: Append-Only Provenance
Section 1 states and develops Axiom 1, the first of AX-SH’s four axioms. Axiom 1 governs the temporal
evolution of public surfaces: it requires that successive versions of a public surface satisfy append-only
provenance, with compatible extensions and explicitly-tagged corrections, supersessions, and withdrawals
as the only permitted transitions, and with the historical record preserved across versions. The section is
presented in seven subsections: §1.1 supplies the formal statement; §1.2 formalizes the compatible-extension
condition; §1.3 formalizes the corrigenda-tagging discipline; §1.4 formalizes the historical-record preservation
condition; §1.5 identifies three primary failure patterns; §1.6 illustrates Axiom 1 across the four worked
substrate instances; §1.7 closes with proof obligations and the forward reference to Chapter 8’s definitionaladequacy theorem.

4.1.1 Formal statement of Axiom 1
For every substrate 𝑆 with version-indexed public-surface family 𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 (using the §4-local notation of
Chapter 3 §4.1, in which 𝑆𝑖 denotes the 𝑖-th version of the public-surface family Surface(𝑆) associated with
substrate 𝑆; the standing symbol 𝑆 from Chapter 3 Table 3.1 remains the substrate identifier), the family
satisfies append-only provenance: for every successive pair (𝑆𝑖 , 𝑆𝑖+1 ), either (i) 𝑆𝑖+1 is a behavioral subtype
of 𝑆𝑖 in the Liskov-Wing sense from Chapter 3 §4.2 (callers whose assumptions are valid under 𝑆𝑖 ’s declared
interface continue to have those assumptions preserved under 𝑆𝑖+1 ’s declared interface), in which case the

53

CHAPTER 4. AXIOM 1 (APPEND-ONLY PROVENANCE)

54

transition is a compatible extension, or (ii) 𝑆𝑖+1 is accompanied by an explicit corrigendum—a truth-status
tag from Chapter 3 §4.4’s three-tag set {correction, supersession, withdrawal}—marking what changed and
the truth-status category under which the change is published. The historical record is preserved across
𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 per the historical-record apparatus of Chapter 3 §4.5.
This is Axiom 1: append-only provenance over versioned public surfaces.
The axiom is a single requirement with three structural conditions: compatible extension (§1.2), corrigenda
discipline (§1.3), and historical-record preservation (§1.4). When all three conditions hold across the versionindexed family, Axiom 1 is satisfied; when one or more conditions fail, the failure manifests in one of three
primary failure patterns identified in §1.5.

4.1.2 Behavioral-subtyping condition for compatible extension
A version transition 𝑆𝑖 → 𝑆𝑖+1 is a compatible extension when two structural conditions hold.
(i) 𝑆𝑖+1 is a behavioral subtype of 𝑆𝑖 in the Liskov-Wing sense (Liskov and Wing 1994) as introduced in
Chapter 3 §4.2: callers whose assumptions are valid under 𝑆𝑖 ’s declared interface continue to have those
assumptions preserved under 𝑆𝑖+1 ’s declared interface.
(ii) The additions to 𝑆𝑖+1 are additive: new optional parameters with defaults; new endpoints that do not
interfere with the semantics of existing declarations; new declared semantics that preserves the assumptions
valid under 𝑆𝑖 ’s declared semantics; new components that callers programmed against 𝑆𝑖 are free to ignore.
The two conditions together capture the intuition that compatible extension is what callers programmed
against 𝑆𝑖 should be able to ignore: their existing dependencies continue to be honored (condition (i)), and
any new capabilities are opt-in rather than mandatory (condition (ii)). A version transition that satisfies
both (i) and (ii) is a compatible extension and requires no corrigendum: the transition extends the surface
without modifying any prior commitment.

4.1.3 Corrigenda discipline using correction/supersession/withdrawal tags
When a version transition is not a compatible extension—when 𝑆𝑖+1 either breaks behavioral subtyping with
𝑆𝑖 or makes a non-additive change—Axiom 1 requires an explicit corrigendum: a truth-status tag (Chapter 3
§4.4) accompanies the transition, identifying which prior surface element is modified and the truth-status
category under which the change is published.
The three truth-status categories from Chapter 3 §4.4 each classify a specific kind of non-compatible change.
A correction tag classifies a transition in which a prior claim is modified because the prior claim was wrong.
The successor surface replaces the prior claim with a revised one; the correction tag identifies the prior claim
being corrected and marks the change as a correction. The correction tag does not erase the prior claim; the
historical record (§1.4) preserves both the original incorrect claim and the corrected successor.
A supersession tag classifies a transition in which a prior claim is replaced by a newer claim that takes
precedence without the prior claim being wrong per se. The supersession tag identifies the prior claim being
superseded and marks the change as a supersession. Examples include a deprecated API endpoint replaced
by a successor endpoint with different (but not contradictory) semantics; an audit attestation replaced by a
more recent attestation that supersedes the prior period.

CHAPTER 4. AXIOM 1 (APPEND-ONLY PROVENANCE)

55

A withdrawal tag classifies a transition in which a prior claim is no longer maintained or defended, without
necessarily being replaced. The withdrawal tag identifies the prior claim being withdrawn and marks the
change as a withdrawal. Examples include an API endpoint deprecated and removed without successor; an
audit firm withdrawing a prior attestation following discovery of material misstatement.
In all three cases, the corrigendum is a public-surface object: the truth-status tag appears on the surface at
the version transition. The historical record (§1.4) preserves the predecessor surface alongside its successor;
the corrigenda register lists which tags apply to which version transitions.

4.1.4 Historical-record preservation condition
Axiom 1 requires that the historical record across 𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 remain accessible and verifiable.

The

historical-record preservation apparatus of Chapter 3 §4.5 has three components, and Axiom 1 imposes
a condition on each.
Archived versions: each 𝑆𝑖 is preserved in archived form alongside its successors 𝑆𝑖+1 , 𝑆𝑖+2 , … , 𝑆𝑛 . Preservation here is not “the current version is the only visible version”; predecessors remain visible to downstream
verifiers who need to compare versions, audit the version sequence, or verify a corrigendum’s claims about
what was modified.
Corrigenda registers: the truth-status tags of §1.3 are recorded in a register that lists which tags apply to
which version transitions. The register is a public-surface object: it appears on the surface where downstream
verifiers can read it, parallel to how the truth-status tags themselves appear on the surface. The register’s
purpose is to make the corrigenda history navigable: a verifier examining the transition 𝑆𝑖 → 𝑆𝑖+1 can look
up which tags apply.
Retention discipline: the archived versions and corrigenda registers are retained for the period during which
the surface’s claims may be relied upon. The retention period is substrate-dependent: for audit attestations,
the retention period extends through the audit-engagement scope; for software API versions, the retention
period extends through the version’s published deprecation timeline; for manuscript critical editions, the
retention period extends through the scholarly community’s expected reliance on the edition.
The three components together make the version-indexed family 𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 inspectable: a verifier can
examine the full version history, the corrigenda register, and the retained archives to determine whether
Axiom 1’s conditions are satisfied.

4.1.5 Three primary failure patterns
Chapter 4 §1.5 identifies three primary Axiom 1 failure patterns within the Chapter 4 formalization. Each
pattern is a structural failure of one or more of the conditions of §1.2 (compatible extension), the corrigendatagging requirement of §1.3, or the historical-record preservation condition of §1.4. The exhaustiveness of the
three-pattern characterization across all possible failure forms is deferred to Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy
work; Chapter 4 §1.5 identifies these three as the primary patterns the axiom treats as failures.
Silent deletion: an element of 𝑆𝑖 is removed from 𝑆𝑖+1 without a withdrawal tag in the corrigenda register.
The transition violates §1.2(i) (behavioral subtyping: callers programmed against the removed element break
against the successor) and §1.3 (no corrigendum was published for the removal). The structural-honesty

CHAPTER 4. AXIOM 1 (APPEND-ONLY PROVENANCE)

56

failure is that the surface was modified without declaration: callers who relied on the deleted element have
no recorded acknowledgment that it was deleted, and no successor pointer is available.
Silent semantic weakening: an element of 𝑆𝑖 has its declared semantics weakened in 𝑆𝑖+1 without a correction
or supersession tag. Weakening occurs when, for example, a stronger guarantee is replaced by a weaker one
(an API method that previously guaranteed sorted output now returns unsorted output; an audit attestation
that previously asserted a strong control now asserts only a weaker variant). The transition may or may
not violate §1.2(i) depending on how strictly the caller relies on the prior guarantee, but it always violates
§1.3 when no corrigendum is published. The structural-honesty failure is the same: the surface was modified
without declaration.
Untagged breaking change: any other behavioral-subtyping violation between 𝑆𝑖 and 𝑆𝑖+1 that is not accompanied by an explicit corrigendum. This pattern covers behavioral-subtyping breaks that are not categorizable
as deletion or semantic weakening but that nonetheless violate §1.2(i) without a §1.3 tag. The structuralhonesty failure is general: the surface broke its predecessor’s contract without declaring the break.
In each case, the failure pattern is a structural violation of one or more of the §1.2/§1.3/§1.4 conditions.
Whether the three patterns exhaust the failure modes of Axiom 1 within the four-substrate scope is part of
Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy proof obligation.

4.1.6 Examples across the four worked substrate instances
Axiom 1 operationalizes differently for each of the four substrate instances from Section 5 of the audit ledger.
The following examples illustrate the axiom’s application across SI1–SI4; secondary illustrative examples
(software APIs, audit attestations, textual witnesses, AI model cards) appear in subsequent chapters as
general illustrations when explicitly marked.
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner. The Bayyinah scanner (Arfeen 2026c) publishes versioned releases, each
with a public surface comprising the file-kinds list, the detection-mechanism list, the zahir-layer/batin-layer
split, the PDF byte-identical parity check, and the scan-incomplete primitive. Compatible extensions include
the addition of new file-kinds, new detection mechanisms, and new diagnostic outputs that do not interfere
with existing semantics. Breaking changes—e.g., removal of a detection mechanism, weakening of the zahirlayer/batin-layer classification—require explicit corrigenda in the release-notes register. The historical record
is preserved through the version-control system, with each release tagged and archived. Axiom 1 governs
the surface evolution of Bayyinah across release versions.
SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. The Furqan type-checker (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b, 2026a)
publishes versioned releases, each with a public surface comprising the implemented-constructs list, the
test-suite results, and the compile-time-check semantics. Compatible extensions include the addition of
new constructs, new compile-time checks, and additional test coverage that does not regress existing checks.
Breaking changes—e.g., removal of a previously-implemented construct, weakening of a compile-time check
from “must” to “should”—require explicit corrigenda. The historical record is preserved through versioned
releases with archived test-suite results. Axiom 1 governs the surface evolution of Furqan across release
versions.
SI3 — Munafiq model-layer protocol. The Munafiq Protocol document (Arfeen 2026d) publishes versioned
editions, each with a public surface comprising the four-process taxonomy, the nine diagnostic markers,

and the four-layer detection architecture. Compatible extensions include the addition of new diagnostic

The Axiom 1 proof obligations within Chapter 4 are three.
Well-formedness: Axiom 1 is well-formed as a structural condition over the version-indexed surface families
introduced in Chapter 3 §4. This is verified by the construction in §§1.1–1.4: each of the three structural
conditions (compatible extension, corrigenda discipline, historical-record preservation) is defined over typed
objects from Chapter 3 §4, and the conjunction of the three conditions is itself well-typed.
Decidability scope: Axiom 1’s compatible-extension and corrigenda-tagging conditions are candidates for

decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. Outside the finite-default fragment (infinite version histories,
infinite-state behavioral-subtyping settings), Axiom 1 remains structurally well-defined but its decidability
is not claimed for v1.0.
Exhaustiveness of the three primary failure patterns: whether the three patterns of §1.5 exhaust the failure
modes of Axiom 1 within the four-substrate scope. This is a definitional-adequacy question—whether the
three patterns are suﬀicient to classify every Axiom 1 failure observable in SI1–SI4—and the exhaustiveness
claim is deferred to Chapter 8.
The relationship to Chapter 8: Chapter 8 is assigned the definitional-adequacy proof—whether Axiom 1,
together with the other three axioms of AX-SH (Axiom 2 in Chapter 5, Axiom 3 in Chapter 6, Axiom 4

in Chapter 7), captures the operational SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary across the scoped substrate instances. Chapter 8 will evaluate whether the A1.1–A1.5 classifications are definitionally adequate for the

4.2 Axiom 1 edge cases and boundary cases
Section 2 explores Axiom 1’s behavior in edge cases that §1’s formal statement does not fully illuminate.
Each subsection identifies a structural edge case and shows how the axiom’s three conditions (§1.2 compatible
extension, §1.3 corrigenda discipline, §1.4 historical-record preservation) apply or fail in that case. The edge
cases are not a new failure taxonomy beyond §1.5’s three primary patterns; they are structurally distinct
cases of Axiom 1’s existing conditions, with their relationship to the §1.5 taxonomy deferred to Chapter 8’s
definitional-adequacy work.

4.2.1 Corrigendum-on-corrigendum
Truth-status tags are themselves public-surface objects: Chapter 3 §4.4 introduced them as surface objects,
not silent mutations. Axiom 1 therefore applies to corrigenda the same way it applies to any surface element:
a corrigendum that turns out to be wrong must itself be modified through a tagged transition, not through
silent overwrite.
When a producer publishes a correction tag, supersession tag, or withdrawal tag and later determines that
the tag itself was misapplied, the resolution is recursive: a meta-corrigendum is published that explicitly
references the prior tag, identifies the modification, and is itself recorded in the corrigenda register. The metacorrigendum carries one of the same three categories (correction/supersession/withdrawal) and is governed
by §1.3’s discipline; the historical record (§1.4) preserves both the prior tag and its meta-corrigendum so that
downstream verifiers can navigate the full corrigenda history. The recursion is bounded by the finite-default
convention that bounds the version-indexed family: corrigenda chains are finite, the corrigenda register is
finite, the meta-corrigenda are themselves entries in the register.

4.2.2 Mistaken withdrawal
A specific instance of corrigendum-on-corrigendum is mistaken withdrawal: a withdrawal tag was applied to
a claim that, on later review, should have been retained or corrected rather than withdrawn. The discovery
may come from internal review (the producer realizes the withdrawal was hasty), from external feedback (a
user or auditor identifies that the withdrawn claim was substantively correct), or from a substantive change
in the producer’s position (the claim was withdrawn pending further analysis, and the analysis subsequently
supports re-asserting the claim).
The resolution depends on the substantive situation. If the original withdrawal was wrong (the claim should
have been retained), the meta-corrigendum is a correction-of-the-withdrawal: the withdrawal tag is itself

CHAPTER 4. AXIOM 1 (APPEND-ONLY PROVENANCE)

59

corrected, the claim is restored, and the restoration is recorded. If the situation has changed (the claim is
now defensible again under new conditions), the meta-corrigendum is a supersession of the withdrawal: the
withdrawal is replaced by an updated claim. In both cases, the original withdrawal remains visible in the
historical record alongside its meta-corrigendum, so the full history (claim then withdrawal then restoration
or supersession) is navigable.

4.2.3 Supersession chains
When a claim is superseded multiple times in sequence—𝑆𝑖 ’s claim replaced in 𝑆𝑖+1 with a successor, then
𝑆𝑖+1 ’s replacement replaced again in 𝑆𝑖+2 —Axiom 1 requires each transition to carry its own supersession
tag. The chain does not collapse: 𝑆𝑖+1 ’s claim remains visible in the historical record alongside 𝑆𝑖 ’s and
𝑆𝑖+2 ’s, and the corrigenda register lists both supersession events.
The chain structure is what enables downstream verifiers to reason about the surface’s evolution. A verifier
examining 𝑆𝑖+2 ’s current claim can navigate the corrigenda register to discover that this is the second
supersession of 𝑆𝑖 ’s original claim, with 𝑆𝑖+1 ’s intermediate claim as the first supersession. The verifier can
then evaluate whether the chain reflects refinement (each supersession improving precision), correction-withsupersession (a correction tag applied first, then later refinement), or other evolution patterns. Supersession
chains do not require a maximum length or a canonical resolution; what they require is that each link in the
chain be tagged and preserved.

4.2.4 Deprecation timelines
Withdrawal tags often carry a deprecation timeline: a claim is first announced as deprecated (intent to
withdraw, but the claim remains active and supported), then enters active deprecation (the claim is no
longer recommended for new use but is still operational), then is formally withdrawn (the claim is no longer
maintained or defended).
The timeline structure is part of the withdrawal tag itself: each tag carries the dates at which the claim
transitions through the deprecation states, and the corrigenda register records the full timeline. A verifier
examining a deprecated-but-not-yet-withdrawn claim can determine, from the tag, when the formal withdrawal will take effect and what alternative claim (if any) will succeed it. The deprecation-timeline structure
does not change Axiom 1’s compatible-extension or historical-record conditions; it elaborates the withdrawal
tag’s content so that downstream verifiers can plan their reliance on the claim. The historical record (§1.4)
preserves the timeline alongside the claim, so the full deprecation history remains inspectable.

4.2.5 Archive loss as historical-record preservation failure
Archive loss is the canonical edge case for the historical-record preservation condition of §1.4. It occurs
when predecessor surfaces, corrigenda registers, or retained archives are no longer accessible for the period
during which the surface’s claims may be relied upon. The loss may be deliberate (a producer intentionally
deletes a predecessor surface), accidental (storage corruption, retention-policy misapplication), or systemic
(a substrate’s infrastructure does not preserve historical records by default).
Archive loss violates the §1.4 historical-record preservation condition directly: the preservation requirement
is that each 𝑆𝑖 remain accessible alongside its successors, that the corrigenda register list the applicable tags,

CHAPTER 4. AXIOM 1 (APPEND-ONLY PROVENANCE)

60

and that the retention discipline maintains both. When any of these fails, Axiom 1 fails on the preservation
side, regardless of whether any §1.2 or §1.3 condition was violated on the evolution side.
This is not introduced as a fourth exhaustive peer category alongside the §1.5 primary patterns. The §1.5
patterns (silent deletion, silent semantic weakening, untagged breaking change) are evolution-side failures
concerning what happens between consecutive versions; archive loss is a preservation-side failure concerning
what happens to predecessor versions in storage. The two failure-types operate on different aspects of Axiom 1
(§1.2/§1.3 conditions versus §1.4 condition), and the relationship between their respective taxonomies is part
of Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy analysis.

Axiom 1 does not specify how forked branches should be reconciled, whether one branch should be considered

4.3 Operational substrates and Chapter 5 handoff
Section 3 reviews how Axiom 1 operates across the four worked substrate instances introduced in Chapter 2
and Section 5 of the audit ledger (SI1–SI4), articulates the structural dependency that subsequent axioms
have on Axiom 1, and hands off to Chapter 5. The review in §3.1 is illustrative and preparatory rather than
a substantive substrate-adequacy finding; detailed substrate adequacy remains deferred to Chapters 13–16
and Chapter 8.

4.3.1 Substrate-by-substrate operational surface practices for SI1–SI4
Each of the four worked substrate instances has existing operational practices that can support some or
all of Axiom 1’s structural conditions. The review here identifies the support mechanisms and the places
where additional explicit surface support would be needed; substantive substrate adequacy is the work of
the case-study chapters (Chapters 13–16) and the definitional-adequacy theorem chapter (Chapter 8).
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner: existing practices that can support Axiom 1 include semantic-versioned releases (version-indexed surface family per §1.1); release notes and changelogs (corrigenda registers per §1.4);

explicit deprecation announcements (deprecation timelines per §2.4); version-control archives (historicalrecord preservation per §1.4). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for behavioral-subtyping
verification across versions, to support §1.2’s compatible-extension condition rigorously rather than informally.
SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker: existing practices that can support Axiom 1 include the versioned
test-suite results, which provide concrete evidence relevant to behavioral-subtyping preservation, especially
when successor test suites retain predecessor coverage. Release notes and changelogs serve as the corrigenda
register. Additional explicit support would be needed for truth-status tags on individual construct removals
or weakenings, currently informal in release notes rather than formally structured.
SI3 — Munafiq model-layer protocol: existing practices that can support Axiom 1 include versioned editions of
the protocol document and version-change logs. The historical record is preserved through the document’s
revision history. Additional explicit support would be needed for formal truth-status tags on diagnosticmarker changes (currently described in narrative form rather than tagged) and for behavioral-subtyping
verification of process-taxonomy refinements.
SI4 — Supply-chain four-substrate stack: each of the four layers (sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, SHV) has its own
release-management discipline. Sigstore’s identity-attestation format and in-toto’s link-attestation format
both support versioned releases with explicit deprecation. SLSA’s build-integrity-level specification has
explicit level transitions that can be read as supersession events. SHV’s structural-honesty surface itself
is the focus of this dissertation and is intended to support Axiom 1 explicitly. Additional explicit support
would be needed for cross-layer compatibility tracking, so that supersession in one layer can be related to
compatible-extension or supersession in dependent layers.
In each case, the review identifies where the substrate’s existing practices align with Axiom 1’s conditions
and where additional surface support would strengthen the alignment. Whether the existing practices are
definitionally adequate for the substrate’s structural-honesty needs is the work of Chapter 8.

4.3.2 How Axiom 1 stabilizes the target surface for Axiom 2
Axiom 1 supplies a stable, inspectable versioned public surface against which Axiom 2 (Chapter 5) can
evaluate surface-substrate consistency. Without append-only provenance, a surface may shift silently over
time, making it unclear which public commitment Axiom 2 should compare to the substrate.
The structural dependency operates as follows. Axiom 2 will state a condition relating the public surface
to the underlying substrate’s actual behavior. For this consistency check to be well-targeted, the verifier
needs to know which surface version is being checked. If the surface has been silently modified between
when the substrate’s actual behavior was observed and when Axiom 2’s check is applied, the consistency
claim becomes ambiguous: is it a claim about the substrate-behavior-versus-original-surface, or the substratebehavior-versus-current-surface? When Axiom 1 is satisfied, its append-only-provenance discipline resolves
the ambiguity by preserving the surface version at the time of observation (per §1.4) and tagging any
subsequent modifications (per §1.3), so the verifier can identify which surface version is the relevant target.
This is a structural dependency about target stability, not a statement of Axiom 2’s content. Axiom 2 itself
is stated in Chapter 5; what Chapter 4 supplies is the surface stability that makes the Axiom 2 statement
well-targeted.

5.1 Axiom 2: Surface-Substrate Consistency under Declared Observer Model and Context Set
Section 1 states and develops Axiom 2, the second of AX-SH’s four axioms. Axiom 2 governs the relationship
between a substrate’s public surface and the substrate itself: it requires that the surface be consistent with
the substrate at the level of observability that a declared observer model 𝑂 permits, within the operational
conditions specified by a declared context set 𝐾, using a declared correspondence relation 𝑅 drawn from
Chapter 3 §3’s family. Axiom 2 is a claim of relativized consistency—consistency under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅)—
not a claim of full truth or universal correspondence. The section is presented in eight subsections: §1.1
supplies the formal statement; §1.2 formalizes the observer-model declaration discipline; §1.3 formalizes the
context-set declaration discipline; §1.4 formalizes the correspondence-relation choice from Chapter 3 §3’s
family; §1.5 formalizes the satisfaction predicate evaluated under the three declarations; §1.6 identifies three
primary failure patterns; §1.7 illustrates Axiom 2 across the four worked substrate instances; §1.8 closes with
proof obligations and the forward reference to Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy theorem.

5.1.1 Formal statement of Axiom 2
For every substrate 𝑆 with public surface Surface(𝑆) and substrate object Substrate(𝑆) (using the Chapter 3
§2 notation in which Surface(𝑆) and Substrate(𝑆) are the typed surface and substrate objects associated
with substrate 𝑆), declared observer model 𝑂 (Chapter 3 §2.3), declared context set 𝐾 (Chapter 3 §2.4), and
declared correspondence relation 𝑅 chosen from the correspondence-relation family of Chapter 3 §3, Axiom 2
requires that the consistency condition 𝑅(Surface(𝑆), Substrate(𝑆)) holds at the observability level that 𝑂
permits, within the operational conditions specified by 𝐾.
This is Axiom 2: surface-substrate consistency under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅).
The axiom is a single requirement with three declaration disciplines and one satisfaction predicate: §1.2
observer-model declaration, §1.3 context-set declaration, §1.4 correspondence-relation choice, and §1.5 the
satisfaction predicate evaluated under the three declarations. The axiom is not a claim of full truth or universal correspondence between Surface(𝑆) and Substrate(𝑆); consistency is claimed at the declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅)
resolution, not beyond it. When all three declarations are made and the satisfaction predicate holds under
them, Axiom 2 is satisfied; when the satisfaction predicate fails or the declarations themselves are misdeclared, the failure manifests in one of three primary failure patterns identified in §1.6.

5.1.2 Observer-model declaration discipline
The observer model 𝑂 is a typed observation calculus (Chapter 3 §2.3) specifying which behaviors of the
substrate are observable, with what precision, and under what conditions. Different observer models yield
different consistency claims: an observer with the full 𝐹 ⋆ (Swamy et al. 2016) or Liquid Haskell (Vazou et al.
2014) refinement-type calculus has access to a richer behavior space than an audit-style sampled observer;
a mass-transmission community of reciters with high aggregate coverage has different observability than a
single individual reciter; a static analyzer with bounded inspection depth has different observability than an
exhaustive symbolic-execution observer.
Axiom 2 requires 𝑂 to be declared explicitly as part of the consistency claim. The declaration is a publicsurface object: the observer model under which consistency is claimed appears on the surface, where downstream verifiers can read it. Without explicit 𝑂-declaration, the consistency claim is ambiguous between
different observer choices; with explicit 𝑂-declaration, the claim is specific and verifiable. The 𝑂-declaration
discipline operationalizes the principle that consistency claims must specify what is observable, not assert
observability simpliciter.

5.1.3 Context-set declaration discipline
The context set 𝐾 is a typed condition specification (Chapter 3 §2.4) declaring the operational conditions
under which the consistency claim applies. Different contexts yield different substrate behaviors: a software
substrate may behave differently under load, in different deployment environments, with different inputs,
under different sandboxing regimes; an audit substrate may yield different attestations under different engagement scopes, materiality thresholds, or compliance regimes; an AI-model substrate may produce different
outputs under different prompts, temperature settings, or fine-tuning configurations.
Axiom 2 requires 𝐾 to be declared explicitly. Like 𝑂, the context set is a public-surface object: the operational conditions under which consistency is claimed appear on the surface. Without explicit 𝐾-declaration,

CHAPTER 5. AXIOM 2 (SURFACE-SUBSTRATE CONSISTENCY UNDER (O, K, R))

65

the consistency claim is ambiguous between different contexts (consistency under what conditions, in what
deployment, for which inputs); with explicit 𝐾-declaration, the conditions are specific. The 𝐾-declaration
discipline operationalizes the principle that consistency claims must specify the operational regime, not assert
universal applicability.

5.1.4 Correspondence-relation choice from family
The correspondence relation 𝑅 is chosen from Chapter 3 §3’s correspondence-relation family, following the
relation-choice mechanism of Chapter 3 §3.6. The family is not assumed to satisfy uniform consistency
properties; members vary in strength, in symmetry, and in observer-sensitivity, and which member is the
appropriate 𝑅 for a given substrate depends on the substrate’s nature. Bisimulation (Park 1981; Milner
1980) is an appropriate 𝑅 when the declared claim requires symmetric finite-state behavioral equivalence
under the declared observer model and the relevant finite/image-finite assumptions. Simulation and refinement are appropriate choices when the declared claim is directional or implementation-refinement oriented.
Abstraction-preserving equivalence is the appropriate choice when extraction equality is the consistency
criterion.
Axiom 2 requires 𝑅 to be declared, with the substrate-appropriate choice from the family. Like 𝑂 and 𝐾,
𝑅 is a public-surface object: the correspondence relation under which consistency is claimed appears on
the surface, identifying which structural notion of correspondence the claim invokes. The 𝑅-declaration
discipline operationalizes the principle that consistency claims must specify the structural-correspondence
notion, not assert consistency simpliciter.

5.1.5 Surface-substrate satisfaction predicate
When 𝑂, 𝐾, and 𝑅 are all declared per §§1.2–1.4, the satisfaction predicate for Axiom 2 is:
𝑅(Surface(𝑆), Substrate(𝑆)) holds at the 𝑂-permitted observability level, within 𝐾-specified contexts.
The predicate is evaluated under the three declarations; the value of the predicate depends on (i) which
𝑂 is declared, (ii) which 𝐾 is declared, (iii) which 𝑅 is declared, and (iv) the actual substrate-surface
relationship at the 𝑂-observable level within 𝐾.
Axiom 2 consists of three declaration disciplines (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) plus the satisfaction predicate evaluated under
those declarations. The predicate is not a fourth declaration: producers declare 𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅; the satisfaction
predicate’s truth-value is computed from the declarations and the substrate-surface relationship. The producer commits to (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) and to the claim that the predicate holds under them; verifiers can evaluate
whether the predicate actually does hold under those declarations.

5.1.6 Three primary failure patterns
Within the Chapter 5 formalization, Axiom 2 has three primary failure patterns. Each pattern is a violation
of the consistency claim under the declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅); the patterns are not claims of full-truth failure but
of declaration-relative failure. The exhaustiveness of the three-pattern characterization across all possible
failure forms is deferred to Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy work; Chapter 5 §1.6 identifies these three as
the primary patterns the axiom treats as failures.
Observable inconsistency: 𝑅 fails at the declared (𝑂, 𝐾). The surface and substrate diverge at the observability level 𝑂 permits within 𝐾-contexts. The structural-honesty failure is that the producer’s consistency claim

CHAPTER 5. AXIOM 2 (SURFACE-SUBSTRATE CONSISTENCY UNDER (O, K, R))

66

does not hold even at the declared resolution: the surface claims one thing about the substrate’s 𝑂-observable
behavior in 𝐾-contexts, but the substrate’s actual 𝑂-observable behavior in 𝐾-contexts is something else.
Scope misdeclaration: the public surface presents or is used as if it supports a broader observer model or
context set than the declared (𝑂, 𝐾) actually covers. The Axiom 2 failure is the surface’s misstatement,
obscuring, or overextension of its own consistency claim. If the narrower scope is explicit and downstream
users rely on observations or contexts beyond it, the issue is caller-side or governance-side reliance and is not
by itself an Axiom 2 violation; Axiom 2 fails when the surface itself misstates the scope of its consistency
claim. This distinction preserves the consistency-not-truth discipline: Axiom 2 governs the surface’s honesty
about its own scope, not the downstream verifier’s reliance discipline (which is the territory of Axiom 3 in
Chapter 6).
𝑅-misdeclaration: the declared 𝑅 is the wrong choice from the family. Consistency may hold under some
𝑅 in the Chapter 3 §3 family, but not the 𝑅 that the surface’s claims actually rely on. For example, the
surface may claim correspondence under bisimulation when only a weaker simulation relation actually holds;
the failure is not that no correspondence exists, but that the declared 𝑅 does not hold.
In each case, the failure pattern is a structural violation of one or more of §§1.2–1.5 conditions. Whether the
three patterns exhaust the failure modes of Axiom 2 within the four-substrate scope is part of Chapter 8’s
definitional-adequacy proof obligation.

5.1.7 Examples across the four worked substrate instances
For each of the four worked substrate instances from Section 5 of the audit ledger, the consistency claim
under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) operationalizes differently. The following examples are illustrative; substantive
adequacy of these (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) choices for each substrate is the work of Chapter 8 and Chapters 13–16.
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner. The Bayyinah scanner (Arfeen 2026c) declares an observer 𝑂 comprising
the test-harness assertions over scanner outputs (file-kinds list, detection-mechanism list, zahir-layer/batinlayer classification, PDF parity, scan-incomplete primitive). 𝐾 is the scoped-input context set (declared file
types, specified probe categories, declared scanning regime such as production-mode vs developer-mode). 𝑅
is typically a refinement or simulation relation, depending on whether the surface claims the scanner returns
exactly the declared kinds (bisimulation appropriate) or at least the declared kinds (simulation appropriate).
Axiom 2 holds for Bayyinah when, under the test-harness observer’s assertions within the scoped-input
regime, the scanner’s actual behavior satisfies the declared 𝑅 with respect to the public file-kinds surface.
SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. The Furqan type-checker (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b, 2026a)

Axiom 2 holds for Furqan when, under the test-suite observer for programs in 𝐾, the type-checker’s behavior
refines the public type-system-feature surface under the declared 𝑅.
SI3 — Munafiq model-layer protocol. The Munafiq Protocol (Arfeen 2026d) declares an observer 𝑂 comprising the eval-prompt sampling (declared prompt categories, sampled outputs under specified prompting

5.1.8 Proof obligations and relationship to Chapter 8 definitional adequacy
Chapter 5 §1.8 closes the Axiom 2 development by identifying its proof obligations and the relationship to
Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy theorem.
The Axiom 2 proof obligations within Chapter 5 are three.
Well-formedness: Axiom 2 is well-formed as a structural condition over the Chapter 3 §2 typed objects
(Surface(𝑆), Substrate(𝑆), 𝑂, 𝐾) and the Chapter 3 §3 correspondence-relation family. This is verified by
the construction in §§1.1–1.5: each of the three declaration disciplines is defined over typed objects from
Chapter 3 §2; the satisfaction predicate is evaluated over the Chapter 3 §3 family member chosen by the
𝑅-declaration; the conjunction of the three declarations and the satisfaction predicate is itself well-typed.
Decidability scope: Axiom 2’s satisfaction predicate is a candidate for decidable treatment in the finitedefault fragment of Chapter 3 §7, assuming finite 𝑂, finite 𝐾, finite-state 𝑅 from the Chapter 3 §3 family,
and finite-state substrate. Chapter 10 carries the rigorous decidability burden; Chapter 8 §2’s finite-witness
construction (T82) operates within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. Outside the finitedefault fragment (infinite-state substrates, infinite 𝑂, infinite 𝐾), Axiom 2 remains structurally well-defined
but its decidability is not claimed for v1.0.
Exhaustiveness of the three primary failure patterns: whether the three patterns of §1.6 exhaust Axiom 2’s

failure modes within the four-substrate scope. This is a definitional-adequacy question—whether the three

The relationship to Chapter 8: Chapter 8 is assigned the definitional-adequacy proof—whether Axiom 2,

from Chapter 7), captures the operational SHV/Furqan/Munafiq vocabulary across the scoped substrate

§1.5 satisfaction predicate, and the §1.6 failure patterns are definitionally adequate for the scoped operational
vocabulary: whether behaviors classified as consistent under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) correspond to behaviors the
operational vocabulary treats as structurally honest, and whether behaviors classified as failure patterns
correspond to behaviors the operational vocabulary treats as structurally dishonest.
Chapter 5 supplies Axiom 2 statement, the three declaration disciplines, the satisfaction predicate, and the
