5.2 Axiom 2 edge cases and boundary cases
Section 2 explores Axiom 2’s behavior in edge cases that §1’s formal statement does not fully illuminate.
Each subsection identifies a structural edge case under one of the three declaration disciplines (§1.2 observermodel, §1.3 context-set, §1.4 correspondence-relation) or the joint Axiom-1/Axiom-2 interaction, and shows
how Axiom 2 applies or fails in that case. The edge cases are not a new failure taxonomy beyond §1.6’s three
primary patterns; they are structurally distinct cases of Axiom 2’s existing conditions, with their relationship
to the §1.6 taxonomy deferred to Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy work.

5.2.1 Observer-model edge cases
The observer-model declaration discipline of §1.2 requires that the consistency claim specify 𝑂 explicitly.
Three edge cases extend the discipline to scenarios §1.2 does not directly address.
Multiple declared observers. When a consistency claim is made under {𝑂1 , 𝑂2 , …}—for example, both a
test-suite observer and an audit-style sampled observer—the composition semantics matters. Intersection
(consistency holds at the intersection of observable behaviors), union (consistency holds across the union),
product (consistency holds for each observer separately combined into a joint observation), hierarchy (one
observer dominates), and weighted aggregation (consistency holds at some declared aggregation function)
are different constructions yielding different consistency claims. Axiom 2 does not commit Chapter 5 to a
single universal composition semantics; instead, the composition semantics must itself be declared as part
of the 𝑂-field for the relevant substrate. The producer who claims consistency under {𝑂1 , 𝑂2 } must also
declare which composition rule applies.
Composite observer models. A single observer model may be constructed from sub-observers—for example, a refinement-type observer composed of multiple type-system components. The composition operation
(Cartesian product of observation spaces, sequential composition, parallel composition) is itself part of the
𝑂-declaration. Axiom 2 treats the composite as a single declared 𝑂 once the composition is specified.
Observer mismatch. The declared 𝑂 differs from the actual verifier access. For example, the surface declares
a refinement-type observer with full 𝐹 ⋆ access, but a downstream verifier only has Liquid Haskell or static-

CHAPTER 5. AXIOM 2 (SURFACE-SUBSTRATE CONSISTENCY UNDER (O, K, R))

69

analysis-with-bounded-depth access. The mismatch is not an Axiom 2 failure (Axiom 2’s consistency claim
is under the declared 𝑂); it is a verifier-side scoping issue. Whether the verifier with restricted access can
still rely on the consistency claim is the territory of Axiom 3 (𝑅may handling of caller-side observation gaps).
Each of these edge cases is an application of A2.2’s declaration discipline in a structurally distinct scenario;
none introduces a new condition on the axiom.

5.2.2 Context-set edge cases
The context-set declaration discipline of §1.3 requires that the consistency claim specify 𝐾 explicitly. Three
context-set edge cases extend the discipline.
Context-set evolution. 𝐾 may change over time. A substrate’s declared context set in version 𝑣1 may differ
from its declared context set in version 𝑣2 —for example, a software API that initially supports only POSIX
deployment contexts is later extended to support Windows contexts, changing the declared 𝐾. Because 𝐾 is
part of the public consistency claim, changes to 𝐾 across versions are themselves public-surface changes and
are governed by Axiom 1’s append-only-provenance discipline (Chapter 4 §§1.2–1.4 apply): 𝐾-extensions
are compatible extensions when callers programmed against the prior 𝐾 can continue to rely on the same
consistency claim, and 𝐾-restrictions are corrigenda-tagged transitions when the prior 𝐾 is being withdrawn
or superseded.
Context-set narrowing. 𝐾 may be initially over-broad (claiming consistency in many contexts) and then
narrowed to handle resource constraints or to acknowledge unsupported contexts. The narrowing is a corrigenda event under Axiom 1: the producer is withdrawing or correcting the prior claim that consistency
holds in the broader 𝐾. The narrower 𝐾 must be tagged appropriately in the corrigenda register.
Context-set expansion. 𝐾 may be initially narrow (claiming consistency only in a small set of contexts)
and then expanded to cover additional contexts after verification. The expansion is a compatible extension
when the prior consistency claims remain valid in the original 𝐾 and additional consistency claims are
established for the new contexts. Like all surface-evolution events, 𝐾-expansion is governed by Axiom 1’s
compatible-extension discipline (Chapter 4 §1.2).
In each case, the edge case is an application of A2.3’s declaration discipline plus Axiom 1’s surface-evolution
governance for 𝐾-changes on the public surface.

The structural-honesty discipline routes 𝐾-evolution

through Axiom 1 so that downstream verifiers can navigate 𝐾-changes through the same corrigenda discipline that applies to other surface elements.

5.2.3 𝑅-family edge cases
The correspondence-relation-choice discipline of §1.4 requires 𝑅 to be chosen from Chapter 3 §3’s family and
declared. Three 𝑅-family edge cases extend the discipline.
𝑅 re-declaration. A previously-declared 𝑅 may be replaced by a different 𝑅 from the family—for example,
a surface initially claiming consistency under bisimulation may be re-declared to claim consistency under
simulation (weaker) or under abstraction-preserving equivalence (orthogonal). Because the declared 𝑅 is
part of the public consistency claim, 𝑅-redeclaration is itself a public-surface change governed by Axiom 1:
the prior 𝑅-claim is either superseded (replaced by a stronger or differently-scoped 𝑅) or corrected (the prior
𝑅 was the wrong choice) and must be tagged in the corrigenda register.

𝑅-family changes. The underlying correspondence-relation family of Chapter 3 §3 may itself be updated—for
example, a new member is added to the family in a subsequent version of Chapter 3 (a Chapter 3 patch). If
the new member becomes the declared 𝑅 for some substrate, the 𝑅-redeclaration discipline applies. If the
family update affects a previously-declared 𝑅 (e.g., a refinement of bisimulation’s definition under different
observer-model assumptions), the substrate’s 𝑅-declaration may need to be re-stated with the updated
𝑅-definition; the re-statement is itself a surface-evolution event under Axiom 1.
Declared-𝑅 becomes obsolete. A substrate may evolve such that, as observed through the declared 𝑂 within
the declared 𝐾, the declared 𝑅 is no longer satisfied, but a different 𝑅 in the family is. For example, a
software substrate initially supporting a bisimulation claim with respect to its surface may evolve such that
only a simulation claim now holds under the declared (𝑂, 𝐾). The structural-honesty options are: declare a
corrigendum identifying the bisimulation claim as no longer valid and supersede it with a simulation claim;
or correct the surface to match the substrate’s current behavior under the declared (𝑂, 𝐾). Either option is
governed by Axiom 1’s corrigenda discipline.
In each case, 𝑅-changes that affect the public surface are surface-evolution events governed by Axiom 1’s
versioning and corrigenda discipline (Chapter 4 §§1.2–1.4). The 𝑅-declaration discipline of A2.4 operates
within each version of the surface; transitions between versions are A1 territory.

5.2.4 Joint Axiom-1-Axiom-2 interaction
Axioms 1 and 2 interact along a single structural dimension: Axiom 1 governs how the public surface evolves
through time, including how the declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) evolves; Axiom 2 evaluates consistency at any given
surface version under that version’s declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅). The two axioms operate on different aspects of the
same surface, and their interaction is well-defined when each governs its respective aspect cleanly.
The structural relationship is as follows. At any given surface version 𝑆𝑖 , with declared (𝑂𝑖 , 𝐾𝑖 , 𝑅𝑖 ), Axiom 2
evaluates whether 𝑅𝑖 (𝑆𝑖 , Substrate(𝑆)) holds at the 𝑂𝑖 -permitted level within 𝐾𝑖 -contexts; this is a perversion consistency check. As the surface evolves through versions 𝑆0 , 𝑆1 , … , 𝑆𝑛 under Axiom 1, the declared
(𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) at each version may change. Each change is a surface-evolution event governed by Axiom 1’s
compatible-extension and corrigenda disciplines (Chapter 4 §§1.2–1.3): compatible-extension transitions
preserve the prior consistency claim while extending it; corrigenda-tagged transitions modify or withdraw
the prior consistency claim with explicit tagging.
§2.4 is not a re-statement of either axiom. Axiom 1 supplies the surface-evolution governance (covering
𝑂, 𝐾, and 𝑅 as they appear on the public surface); Axiom 2 supplies the per-version consistency claim
under whatever (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) is declared at that version. When both axioms hold, the surface evolves honestly
(Axiom 1) and the consistency claim at each version is satisfied under the declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) for that version
(Axiom 2). When Axiom 1 holds but Axiom 2 fails at some version, the surface is honest about its evolution
but the substrate has diverged from the claimed correspondence under the current (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅). When Axiom 2
holds but Axiom 1 fails (e.g., silent surface modification), the per-version consistency claim is meaningful
but the version history is unreliable for downstream verifiers.

Section 3 reviews how Axiom 2 operates across the four worked substrate instances introduced in Chapter 2

Axiom 2, and hands off to Chapter 6. The review in §3.1 is illustrative and preparatory rather than a

and Chapter 8.

5.3.1 Substrate-by-substrate operational surface practices for SI1–SI4 under
Axiom 2
Each of the four worked substrate instances has existing operational practices that can support some or
all of Axiom 2’s declaration disciplines. The review here identifies the support mechanisms and the places
where additional explicit surface support would be needed; substantive substrate adequacy is the work of
the case-study chapters (Chapters 13–16) and the definitional-adequacy theorem chapter (Chapter 8).
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner. Existing practices that can support Axiom 2 include the test-harness
specification (declaring 𝑂 as the assertions over scanner outputs), the scoped-input documentation (declaring 𝐾 as the file types and probe categories), and the README’s correspondence-criterion specification
(declaring 𝑅 as refinement or simulation depending on exactness vs at-least-ness claims). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for explicit (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) packaging—currently the three declarations
are spread across test-harness scripts, README documentation, and scanner output assertions rather than

SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. Existing practices that can support Axiom 2 include the testsuite results (the declared 𝑂 is implicitly the test-suite observer), the documented program kinds (declaring

is implicit in the test-suite-and-documentation combination) and for explicit composition-semantics if the
test-suite observer is composed with other observers (e.g., static-analysis observers in CI).
SI3 — Munafiq model-layer protocol. Existing practices that can support Axiom 2 include the eval-prompt

(cryptographic verification), context declaration (algorithm and time-validity windows), and 𝑅 declaration

5.3.2 How Axiom 2 prepares the caller-coverage analysis for Axiom 3
Axiom 2 supplies an input to the caller-coverage analysis that Axiom 3 (Chapter 6) will perform. When a
producer presents an Axiom 2 consistency claim under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), Chapter 6 can ask: which callers’
assumptions fall within that declared scope, and which possible outcomes must be handled under 𝑅may ?
The structural dependency operates as follows. Each caller has its own observation regime—what features
of the substrate the caller observes, in what contexts, under what correspondence assumptions. Chapter 6
will make this caller-side observation regime precise; Chapter 5 uses the phrase only to name the caller’s observed features, contexts, and correspondence assumptions for the purpose of the handoff. When a producer
publishes an Axiom 2 consistency claim under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), each caller’s observation regime can be
compared to the declared (𝑂, 𝐾): callers whose observation regime fits within (𝑂, 𝐾) are covered by the
Axiom 2 claim; callers whose observation regime extends beyond (𝑂, 𝐾) are not covered by the Axiom 2
claim but may still be supported under the conservative over-approximation 𝑅may (Chapter 3 §5).
Chapter 6 will state the Axiom 3 caller-side condition using 𝑅may to reason about callers whose observation
regimes extend beyond declared (𝑂, 𝐾). The specific 𝑅may discipline (whether through refinement-type
caller-side reasoning, substrate-side over-approximation, or per-substrate caller-coverage vocabulary) is the
work of Chapter 6.
This is a structural dependency about caller-scope, not a statement of Axiom 3’s content. Axiom 3 can be
stated whether or not Axiom 2 is satisfied; what changes when Axiom 2 fails or is absent is the input to
caller-coverage analysis. When Axiom 2 is satisfied under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), the consistency claim is an
input that Chapter 6 can use to identify covered callers and characterize 𝑅may -required handling of uncovered
callers. When Axiom 2 is unsatisfied, the failed or absent A2 claim is itself part of the caller’s verification
context, and Chapter 6’s caller-coverage check must account for the missing consistency foundation.

5.3.3 Chapter 6 handoff
Chapter 6 will state Axiom 3 using 𝑅may from Chapter 3 §5. When Axiom 2 is satisfied under declared
(𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), that consistency claim can serve as one input to the caller-coverage analysis: callers whose observation regimes fit within (𝑂, 𝐾) are covered, callers whose regimes extend beyond (𝑂, 𝐾) require 𝑅may
handling. When Axiom 2 is not satisfied, Chapter 6 can still state the caller-side coverage obligation, but
the failed or absent A2 claim must be visible as part of the caller’s verification context.
Chapter 6 will state how callers should reason about producer outcomes under 𝑅may ; Chapter 5 has stated
how the producer’s consistency claim is specified under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅). Together, the two axioms cover
the producer-side consistency claim and the caller-side coverage check. Axioms 1 and 4 (Chapters 4 and 7)
cover the temporal-evolution and substrate-projection-consistency dimensions, completing the four-axiom
synthesis AX-SH. This closes Chapter 5.

6.1 Axiom 3: Caller Exhaustiveness over 𝑅may Conservative OverApproximation
Section 1 states and develops Axiom 3, the third of AX-SH’s four axioms. Axiom 3 governs caller-side
coverage over the verifier’s conservative over-approximation of producer outcomes: it requires that every
𝑅may -identified outcome within a caller’s coverage scope be either handled, propagated-as-incomplete, or
proven-unreachable, following the three canonical discharge paths established in Chapter 3 §5.4. Axiom 3 is
a claim of caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may , not a claim that 𝑅may is complete in some absolute sense,
and not a claim about producer-side truth. The section is presented in seven subsections: §1.1 supplies
the formal statement; §1.2 reaﬀirms the 𝑅declared /𝑅may distinction from Chapter 3 §5.2; §1.3 formalizes the
caller-side observation regime as the precise Chapter 6 inheritance of the Chapter 5 §3.2 handoff vocabulary; §1.4 describes the three discharge paths inherited from Chapter 3 §5.4; §1.5 identifies three primary
failure patterns; §1.6 illustrates Axiom 3 across the four worked substrate instances; §1.7 closes with proof
obligations and the forward reference to Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy theorem.

6.1.1 Formal statement of Axiom 3
For every substrate 𝑆 with an Axiom-2-presented consistency claim under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) from Chapter 5
(whether the claim is satisfied or, per Chapter 5 §3.3, presented but failed/absent), and for every caller
of 𝑆 with its own observation regime (§1.3), Axiom 3 requires that the caller’s reasoning about producer
outcomes be exhaustive over the conservative over-approximation 𝑅may (Chapter 3 §5.1). The exhaustiveness
condition is that for every possible producer outcome identified by 𝑅may within the caller’s coverage scope,
the caller follows one of the three canonical discharge paths established in Chapter 3 §5.4: handled (the
caller provides an explicit case for the outcome), propagated-as-incomplete (the caller declares the outcome
as not-yet-handled and propagates the obligation to the caller’s own callers, with the propagation recorded
on the caller’s surface as a structural-honesty declaration), or proven-unreachable (the caller proves the
outcome cannot occur in the caller’s operational context, with the supporting invariant recorded on the
caller’s surface).
This is Axiom 3: caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may conservative over-approximation.
The axiom is about caller-side discipline, not producer-side truth. Producers state Axiom 2 consistency claims
under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅); callers must exhaustively address the 𝑅may -identified possible outcomes from those
producers, regardless of whether the Axiom 2 claim is satisfied. The exhaustiveness condition is not a claim
that 𝑅may is complete in some absolute sense: 𝑅may is the verifier’s conservative over-approximation as
established by Chapter 3 §§5.1–5.3, possibly including outcomes the producer does not actually exhibit. The
conservatism of 𝑅may is what makes the caller-side discipline tractable: the caller need only reason about an
over-approximation the verifier can construct, not about the actual outcome set, which the caller in general
cannot determine.

6.1.2 𝑅declared versus 𝑅may in the caller-side obligation
Chapter 3 §5.2 establishes the structural distinction between 𝑅declared (the producer’s declared correspondence relation, whose consistency Axiom 2 evaluates) and 𝑅may (the verifier’s conservative
over-approximation of possible producer outcomes). Axiom 3 quantifies over 𝑅may , not over 𝑅declared .
The structural reason for the distinction is the following. Even when the producer’s 𝑅declared correctly
identifies a narrow set of actual producer outcomes, the caller in general cannot verify that the producer’s
𝑅declared is exhaustive over the actual outcome set. The producer’s claim of 𝑅declared is the object Axiom 2
evaluates; the caller’s defensive reasoning operates against the conservative over-approximation 𝑅may , which
the verifier constructs, under the declared over-approximation discipline, to include outcomes the verifier
cannot rule out. The 𝑅may overhead—the gap between 𝑅declared and 𝑅may —is the structural-honesty cost
of caller-side reasoning under conservative producer-side claim-verification.
The distinction matters operationally. A caller that reasons only against 𝑅declared trusts the producer’s
exhaustiveness implicitly; a caller that reasons against 𝑅may does not. The dissertation’s caller-side discipline,
extending the producer-side refinement-type tradition (Swamy et al. 2016; Vazou et al. 2014) per Chapter 3
§5.5, is the latter: callers reason against 𝑅may and dispatch outcomes through the three discharge paths
regardless of the producer’s tighter 𝑅declared claim.

6.1.3 Caller-side observation regime
The caller-side observation regime is the Chapter 6 formalization of the Chapter 5 §3.2 handoff vocabulary.
It is a typed object recording the caller’s observed features, contexts, and correspondence assumptions for
purposes of evaluating the caller’s obligations over 𝑅may .
Concretely, each caller has: a typed observation calculus (its own observer model, analogous to but distinct from the producer’s declared 𝑂—what features of the substrate the caller observes); declared contexts
(analogous to but distinct from the producer’s declared 𝐾—under what operational conditions the caller
relies on producer outcomes); and correspondence assumptions about producer outcomes (analogous to but
distinct from the producer’s declared 𝑅). These three components are structurally analogous to the producer’s (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) declarations from Chapter 5 §§1.2–1.4, but they belong to the caller’s verification regime
rather than the producer’s consistency claim. These components are not a second producer-side (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅)
declaration; they are caller-side parameters used to determine which 𝑅may -identified outcomes fall within
the caller’s coverage scope.
The caller’s coverage scope is the set of 𝑅may -identified producer outcomes the caller must address. The
scope is determined by the intersection of the producer’s 𝑅may with the caller’s observation regime: a
possible producer outcome is in the caller’s coverage scope if the caller’s observation regime can detect or
rely on it. Outcomes outside the caller’s observation regime are not in the caller’s coverage scope, and
Axiom 3 imposes no obligation on the caller with respect to them. Whether a caller’s observation regime
appropriately captures the producer outcomes the caller actually relies on is a substrate-specific question
deferred to the case-study chapters.

6.1.4 Three discharge paths from Chapter 3 §5.4
For every 𝑅may -identified producer outcome within the caller’s coverage scope, the caller follows one of
the three canonical discharge paths established in Chapter 3 §5.4. The three paths together exhaust the
caller’s per-outcome obligation within the Chapter 6 formalization; whether the three-path vocabulary is
definitionally adequate across all scoped substrates is deferred to Chapter 8.
Handled. The caller provides an explicit case for the outcome. The specific form of the case is substratedependent: a code path for software callers; an audit response for audit callers; a model behavior specification
for AI-model callers; an attestation handling for supply-chain callers; or whatever substrate-appropriate
handling looks like in the caller’s operational context. The structural-honesty requirement is that the case
appear on the caller’s surface as a declared handling, so that downstream verifiers can determine which
outcomes the caller handles and how.
Propagated-as-incomplete. The caller declares the outcome as not-yet-handled and propagates the obligation
to the caller’s own callers. The propagation is recorded on the caller’s surface as a structural-honesty
declaration: the caller’s surface explicitly states that some 𝑅may outcomes are propagated rather than
handled, identifies which outcomes are propagated, and (when applicable) indicates whether the propagation
is to a specific successor caller or to all of the caller’s callers generically. Propagation is not the same as silent
failure: silent failure would be a hidden-propagation failure pattern per §1.5, while explicit propagation is a
structurally honest discharge of the obligation. The structural-honesty requirement is that the propagation
be visible and navigable.

CHAPTER 6. AXIOM 3 (CALLER-SIDE EXHAUSTIVENESS OVER R_MAY)

77

Proven-unreachable. The caller proves the outcome cannot occur in the caller’s operational context. The
proof rests on an invariant—a property of the caller’s operational context that is incompatible with the
outcome occurring. The supporting invariant is recorded on the caller’s surface as a structural-honesty
declaration: the caller’s surface explicitly states which outcomes are proven-unreachable and what invariant
supports each unreachability claim. Proven-unreachable is not the same as ignored: ignored outcomes are
unaddressed-outcome failures per §1.5, while proven-unreachable outcomes are explicitly justified by the
supporting invariant.
The discipline that every outcome must follow one of these three paths is what makes the caller’s surface
structurally honest about producer outcomes. The caller’s overall surface, considered as a public artifact,
declares which discharge path applies to each 𝑅may outcome within the caller’s coverage scope.

6.1.5 Three primary failure patterns
Within the Chapter 6 formalization, Axiom 3 has three primary failure patterns. Each pattern is a violation
of the caller-side exhaustiveness condition; the patterns are not claims of producer-side failure but of callerside discharge failure. The exhaustiveness of the three-pattern characterization across all possible failure
forms is deferred to Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy work; Chapter 6 §1.5 identifies these three as the
primary patterns the axiom treats as failures.
Unaddressed outcome. An 𝑅may -identified producer outcome within the caller’s coverage scope is not handled, not propagated-as-incomplete, and not proven-unreachable. The caller’s surface is silent about the
outcome—neither a case-handling nor an incompleteness declaration nor an unreachability invariant. The
structural-honesty failure is that the caller’s surface fails to declare any discharge path for the outcome,
leaving downstream verifiers unable to determine how the outcome is handled or whether it is handled at
all.
Hidden propagation. An outcome is implicitly propagated via runtime fault, exception bubble, silent failure,
or comparable substrate-specific mechanism, without the caller’s surface declaring the propagation. The
caller’s callers cannot determine, from the caller’s surface, whether the outcome is handled, propagated, or
proven-unreachable: the outcome appears to be discharged on the surface, but operationally the outcome
bubbles through. The structural-honesty failure is the gap between the caller’s declared handling and its
operational handling.
False unreachability claim. The caller declares an outcome as proven-unreachable, but the supporting invariant does not actually hold in the caller’s operational context. The structural-honesty failure is the false
invariant: the caller’s surface claims a proven-unreachable discharge, but the supporting proof is flawed, and
the outcome may occur despite the claim. The pattern is distinct from unaddressed-outcome (where no
claim is made) and hidden-propagation (where a discharge is implicit rather than declared).
In each case, the failure pattern is a structural violation of one or more of §§1.1–1.4 conditions. Whether the
three patterns exhaust the failure modes of Axiom 3 within the four-substrate scope is part of Chapter 8’s
definitional-adequacy proof obligation.

6.1.6 Examples across the four worked substrate instances
For each of the four worked substrate instances from Section 5 of the audit ledger, the caller-side exhaustiveness obligation operationalizes through illustrative candidate discharge of 𝑅may -identified outcomes. The
following examples are illustrative candidate discharge assignments; substantive adequacy of these candidates
is the work of Chapter 8 and Chapters 13–16.
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner. Callers of the Bayyinah scanner (Arfeen 2026c) are downstream tools
consuming scanner outputs (file-kind detection results, zahir/batin classifications, PDF parity checks, scanincomplete signals). Candidate discharge: each declared file kind is handled with an explicit case in the
caller’s processing logic; the scan-incomplete primitive is propagated-as-incomplete to the caller’s own callers
(passing through the incompleteness signal rather than silently treating an incomplete scan as complete); file
types outside the caller’s declared scope are proven-unreachable via scope restriction (the caller’s operational
context excludes those file types).
SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. Callers of the Furqan type-checker (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b,
2026a) include downstream compilers, CI pipelines, developer tools, and program authors consuming
Furqan’s diagnostics or type-checking results.

Candidate discharge:

typed-program cases that pass

type-checking are handled with the corresponding compilation path; type-check failures are propagatedas-incomplete to the caller’s diagnostic interface (the program-author receives the diagnostic rather
than the diagnostic being silently dropped); type-system features the caller’s program does not use are
proven-unreachable via program-context restriction.
SI3 — Munafiq model-layer protocol. Callers of the Munafiq protocol (Arfeen 2026d) are eval pipelines,
downstream judges, and other consumers of model-output markers. Candidate discharge: each declared
marker is handled with a specific evaluator path; marker-uncertainty (when the model’s output does not
clearly fall into one of the declared markers) is propagated-as-incomplete to the caller’s evaluation log; prompttypes excluded by the caller’s evaluation context are proven-unreachable via context restriction.
SI4 — Supply-chain four-substrate stack. Callers of the supply-chain stack are consumers of attestations

2026f) structural-honesty surfaces). Candidate discharge: declared attestation cases are handled with the
corresponding verification logic; attestation-uncertainty (when a layer’s attestation cannot be verified or
is missing) is propagated-as-incomplete to the caller’s verification log; substrate states the caller’s context
excludes (e.g., a release tier outside the caller’s deployment regime) are proven-unreachable via context
restriction.
In each case, the discharge assignments are illustrative candidates rather than adequacy findings. Whether
each substrate’s caller-side discipline is definitionally adequate for the structural-honesty needs of that substrate is the work of Chapter 8 and Chapters 13–16.

6.1.7 Proof obligations and relationship to Chapter 8 definitional adequacy
Chapter 6 §1.7 closes the Axiom 3 development by identifying its proof obligations and the relationship to
Chapter 8’s definitional-adequacy theorem.

6.2 Axiom 3: Edge Cases and Boundary Cases
Section 2 explores edge cases under the §1 conditions for Axiom 3, applying §§1.1–1.5 to four categories of
structurally compound or temporally evolving cases. The edge cases are not new conditions on Axiom 3;
they are applications of the existing conditions to compound scenarios. §2.1 covers caller-observation-regime
edges (multiple callers, hierarchical callers, observation-regime evolution); §2.2 covers 𝑅may edges, with
explicit distinction between public-surface 𝑅may updates (Axiom 1 events) and verifier-private refinements
(not automatically Axiom 1 events); §2.3 covers discharge-path combination edges (mixed-path, conditional,
partial-with-propagation), with adequacy deferred to Chapter 8; §2.4 articulates the joint Axiom-1–Axiom2–Axiom-3 structural interaction without re-stating any of the three axioms.

6.2.1 Caller-observation-regime edge cases
Section §1.3 establishes the caller-side observation regime as a typed object recording the caller’s observed
features, declared contexts, and correspondence assumptions for evaluating obligations over 𝑅may . Three
structurally distinct edge cases arise in operational practice.

CHAPTER 6. AXIOM 3 (CALLER-SIDE EXHAUSTIVENESS OVER R_MAY)

80

Multiple callers with different observation regimes. A single producer’s 𝑅may may be consumed by multiple
callers, each with its own observation regime. Each caller has its own coverage scope (the intersection of
the producer’s 𝑅may with that caller’s observation regime), and each caller’s exhaustiveness obligation is
evaluated against its own coverage scope. The same 𝑅may outcome may be in one caller’s coverage scope
and outside another caller’s coverage scope; the caller-side discipline is per-caller, not per-producer.
Hierarchical callers. When one caller’s outputs are inputs to another caller’s exhaustiveness check, the
upstream caller’s surface declarations (handled cases, propagated-as-incomplete annotations, provenunreachable invariants) become part of the downstream caller’s verification context.

The downstream

caller’s 𝑅may includes both the original producer’s 𝑅may outcomes (transitively, through the upstream
caller’s discharge) and any 𝑅may outcomes the upstream caller has explicitly propagated-as-incomplete.
The hierarchical structure does not introduce new conditions on Axiom 3; it applies the existing per-caller
conditions at each level.
Observation-regime evolution. A caller’s observation regime may change over time as the caller’s operational
context evolves. Changes to the caller’s observation regime that are published on the caller’s surface are
surface-evolution events governed by Axiom 1 applied to the caller’s surface. Changes to the caller’s observation regime that are not published—purely internal refinements of the caller’s verification configuration—are
not Axiom 1 events for the caller’s published surface, and the per-version Axiom 3 evaluation continues
against the published observation regime.

6.2.2 𝑅may edge cases
The 𝑅may machinery from Chapter 3 §5 admits several edge cases that bear on Axiom 3’s caller-side discipline.
Three are structurally important.
Public-surface 𝑅may updates versus verifier-private refinements. 𝑅may is the verifier’s conservative overapproximation of producer outcomes (Chapter 3 §5.1), but it may be published as part of a public surface—
in a producer’s specification, in a caller’s own surface, in an audit report, or in a verification artifact relied
on by downstream users—or it may remain private to the verifier. 𝑅may updates published as part of a
public surface are surface-evolution events governed by Axiom 1, requiring caller-side re-exhaustiveness as
the published 𝑅may evolves. 𝑅may updates that are verifier-private—refinements of the verifier’s internal
analysis that have not been published as part of a surface on which others rely—are not automatically
Axiom 1 events. They become Axiom 1 events at the moment the refined 𝑅may is published; until then, the
per-version Axiom 3 evaluation continues against the published 𝑅may .
𝑅may and 𝑅declared overlap. When the producer’s 𝑅declared converges with 𝑅may —for example, when the
producer’s 𝑅declared exhaustively enumerates the outcomes the verifier cannot rule out—the conservativeover-approximation overhead reduces, and the caller’s exhaustiveness obligation against 𝑅may also becomes
an exhaustiveness obligation against 𝑅declared . The convergence does not change the caller-side discipline; it
only narrows the gap between the producer’s claim and the caller’s defensive reasoning target.
𝑅may becoming obsolete. When the substrate evolves such that previously-identified 𝑅may outcomes can
no longer occur—for example, when a producer’s substrate is refactored to eliminate a class of possible
outcomes the prior 𝑅may included—the published-𝑅may update is itself an Axiom 1 surface-evolution event.
The caller’s exhaustiveness obligation against the prior 𝑅may is replaced by the obligation against the new
𝑅may ; outcomes the prior 𝑅may included but the new 𝑅may excludes may be removed from the caller’s

CHAPTER 6. AXIOM 3 (CALLER-SIDE EXHAUSTIVENESS OVER R_MAY)

81

coverage scope under the updated published surface, or classified as proven-unreachable only when the caller
records a supporting invariant.

6.2.3 Discharge-path combination edge cases
Section §1.4 establishes the three discharge paths from Chapter 3 §5.4 (handled, propagated-as-incomplete,
proven-unreachable) as the canonical vocabulary for caller-side discharge. Three edge cases involve structurally compound applications of the three paths.
Mixed-path callers. A single caller’s surface may discharge different 𝑅may outcomes through different paths:
some outcomes handled, others propagated-as-incomplete, others proven-unreachable. The caller’s surface
declares which path applies to each outcome. The mixed-path structure does not introduce a fourth discharge
path; it is a compound application of the three.
Conditional discharge. The caller’s discharge path for an outcome may depend on the caller’s operational
context. An outcome may be handled when the caller’s context includes certain features, propagated-asincomplete when the context lacks those features, and proven-unreachable when the context excludes the
outcome entirely. The conditional structure requires the caller’s surface to declare which discharge path
applies under which context condition. The conditional discharge does not introduce a new path category;
it is a context-parameterized application of the three.
Partial-handling-with-propagation. The caller may handle part of an outcome (executing some logic for the
outcome’s occurrence) and propagate-as-incomplete the remaining part (deferring full handling to the caller’s
own callers). The partial-with-propagation structure is a structurally compound application of handled and
propagated-as-incomplete; the caller’s surface declares both the handled portion and the propagated portion.
The combination does not introduce a new path category.
Each edge case is a structurally compound application of A3.4. Within Chapter 6’s formalization, each
outcome is assigned one or more discharge statuses drawn from the three canonical paths; whether this
three-path vocabulary is definitionally adequate across all scoped substrates is deferred to Chapter 8.

6.2.4 Joint Axiom-1, Axiom-2, Axiom-3 interaction
The three axioms operate on different aspects of the same substrate-caller relationship. Axiom 1 (Chapter 4)
governs how the producer’s public surface, including the producer’s declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) and any published
𝑅may , evolves over time across versions 𝑆0 , … , 𝑆𝑛 . Axiom 2 (Chapter 5) evaluates per-version consistency
under the declared (𝑂𝑖 , 𝐾𝑖 , 𝑅𝑖 ) at each version 𝑆𝑖 . Axiom 3 (Chapter 6) imposes caller-side exhaustiveness
over 𝑅may at each version, with caller obligations re-evaluated as 𝑅may evolves under Axiom 1’s surface
governance.
When all three axioms hold, the producer evolves the surface honestly (Axiom 1—compatible-extension
or corrigenda-tagged transitions), claims consistency under declared scope honestly (Axiom 2—surfacesubstrate consistency under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅)), and the caller addresses possible outcomes exhaustively
(Axiom 3—coverage over 𝑅may through the three discharge paths). The three axioms do not form a strict
linear dependency chain: each can be stated independently. Axiom 1 supplies the surface-evolution governance used by the other axiom analyses when surfaces change over time; Axioms 2–4 remain statable over
their relevant per-version surfaces, caller obligations, or projection families even when Axiom 1 is failed,

CHAPTER 6. AXIOM 3 (CALLER-SIDE EXHAUSTIVENESS OVER R_MAY)

82

absent, or not yet evaluated. Axiom 2 satisfaction supplies inputs to Axiom 3 (a presented consistency claim
that the caller’s coverage analysis uses) but is not a syntactic precondition for stating Axiom 3, per Chapter 5
§3.3. The structural interaction is therefore one of input-supply rather than precondition-stacking.
The joint structure has operational consequences. A substrate-caller relationship may satisfy Axiom 1 but
not Axiom 2 (the surface evolves honestly but a per-version consistency claim fails), or satisfy Axioms 1
and 2 but not Axiom 3 (the producer’s claims are honest but the caller fails to exhaustively discharge), or
satisfy Axioms 1 and 3 but not Axiom 2 (the surface evolves honestly and callers exhaustively discharge
over 𝑅may , but the producer’s 𝑅declared claim fails). Each combination corresponds to a structurally distinct
failure profile; the structural-honesty analysis must report which axioms hold and which do not, rather than
collapsing all failures into a single category.

Section 3 reviews the substrate-by-substrate operational practices that bear on Axiom 3’s caller-side discipline, articulates how Axiom 3’s caller-side artifacts may participate in later projection-consistency analysis

6.3.1 Substrate-by-substrate operational surface practices for SI1–SI4 under
Axiom 3
For each of the four worked substrate instances, existing operational practices can support some of Axiom 3’s
discharge paths, and additional explicit surface support would be needed to fully realize the caller-side
discipline. The review is illustrative and preparatory; detailed substrate adequacy remains deferred to
Chapters 13–16 and Chapter 8.
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner.

Existing operational practices supporting Axiom 3 for Bayyinah

callers (Arfeen 2026c): explicit case-handling in caller code (call-site dispatch on declared file kinds,
supporting the handled path); structured incompleteness signaling (the scan-incomplete primitive carries
a propagation semantics, supporting the propagated-as-incomplete path); scope-restriction declarations
in caller configuration (file-type filters and exclusions, supporting the proven-unreachable path through
scope invariants). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for: caller-surface declarations
explicitly enumerating which file kinds the caller handles versus which it propagates versus which it excludes;
structured propagation paths to the caller’s own callers.
SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. Existing operational practices for Furqan callers (Ashraf and
Arfeen 2026b, 2026a): compiler dispatch on typed-program cases (supporting the handled path); diagnostic
surfaces for type-check failures (supporting the propagated-as-incomplete path when diagnostics are surfaced
rather than silently dropped); type-system feature gating (supporting the proven-unreachable path when
callers exclude unused features). Additional explicit surface support would be needed for: explicit callersurface declarations of which type-check outcomes are handled, propagated, or proven-unreachable.

6.3.2 Axiom 3’s caller-side artifacts as possible projection inputs for Axiom 4
Axiom 3’s discharge vocabulary generates caller-side artifacts: handled-outcome records (which 𝑅may outcomes the caller handles, and how), propagated-incompleteness annotations (which 𝑅may outcomes the caller
declares as not-yet-handled), and proven-unreachable certificates (which 𝑅may outcomes the caller’s invariants exclude). These caller-side artifacts may, in later analyses, be treated as projections or projection inputs
under Chapter 3 §6’s Π𝑋 machinery.
This is not a claim that Axiom 4 depends on Axiom 3 for its statement, nor that caller exhaustiveness is a prerequisite for projection consistency. Axiom 4, to be developed in Chapter 7, will state projection consistency
over substrate-parameterized projection families Π𝑋 . The axiom is statable over Π𝑋 independently; satisfaction or failure of Axiom 3 supplies one class of inputs that may participate in the projection-consistency
analysis as projection-family members, but the axiom statement does not depend on Axiom 3 satisfaction.
When the caller-side artifacts of Axiom 3 are well-formed—handled cases, propagated-incompleteness annotations, and proven-unreachable certificates all explicitly declared on the caller’s surface—they can serve as
projection inputs in Π𝑋 -based analyses. When Axiom 3 is not satisfied—when the caller has unaddressed
outcomes, hidden propagations, or false unreachability claims—the caller-side artifacts are incomplete or
unreliable; this incompleteness remains visible as part of the projection-analysis context but does not block
Axiom 4’s statement.

7.1 Axiom 4: Substrate-Parameterized Projection Consistency
over Π𝑋
Section 1 states and develops Axiom 4, the fourth and final axiom of AX-SH. Axiom 4 governs projection
consistency: for every substrate 𝑋 and every projection family Π𝑋 declared over 𝑋 with substrate-specific
consistency relation ∼𝑋 , Axiom 4 requires that pairwise jointly-defined projections cohere under ∼𝑋 . The
axiom inherits its typed objects (projection families, projection domains, partiality structure, consistency
relations, sheaf-style vocabulary) from Chapter 3 §6 (MP6.1–MP6.6), with no new machinery introduced
in Chapter 7. The section is presented in seven subsections: §1.1 supplies the formal statement; §1.2
reaﬀirms the projection family Π𝑋 and projection-domain partiality from Chapter 3 §§6.1–6.2; §1.3 reaﬀirms
the substrate-specific consistency relation ∼𝑋 from Chapter 3 §6.3; §1.4 develops the joint-domain discipline
that distinguishes Axiom 4 from total reconstructibility (too strong) and from hand-picked-point consistency
(too weak); §1.5 identifies three primary A4-native failure patterns; §1.6 illustrates Axiom 4 across the four
worked substrate instances with candidate Π𝑋 and ∼𝑋 assignments; §1.7 closes with proof obligations and
85

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)86
the forward reference to Chapter 8’s integrative work (T81 mutual independence, T82 consistency, T83
definitional adequacy, plus adversarial-declaration / under-determination). Axiom 4 is about consistency
among declared projections within the family under the declared substrate-specific consistency relation: not
a claim of absolute substrate truth, not a claim of total reconstructibility of the substrate from the projections,
and not a claim of dependence on Axiom 3 satisfaction.

7.1.1 Formal statement of Axiom 4
For every substrate 𝑋 and every projection family Π𝑋 = {𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 } declared over 𝑋 (Chapter 3 §6.1,
MP6.1) with substrate-specific consistency relation ∼𝑋 (Chapter 3 §6.3, MP6.3), Axiom 4 requires that for
every pair of projections (𝜋𝑖 , 𝜋𝑗 ) in Π𝑋 and every substrate fact 𝑠 ∈ Substrate(𝑋) jointly defined under both
projections—that is, 𝑠 ∈ dom(𝜋𝑖 ) ∩ dom(𝜋𝑗 ) per Chapter 3 §6.2 (MP6.2)—the projection outputs satisfy
𝜋𝑖 (𝑠) ∼𝑋 𝜋𝑗 (𝑠). The condition extends to multi-way joint-domain regions: for any subset {𝜋𝑖1 , … , 𝜋𝑖𝑚 } of
the projection family and any 𝑠 in the multi-way intersection of their domains, the projection outputs are
required to pairwise satisfy ∼𝑋 .
This is Axiom 4: substrate-parameterized projection consistency over Π𝑋 under ∼𝑋 .
The axiom is about consistency among the projections within the declared family, not about absolute truth
of the substrate, not about total reconstructibility of the substrate from the projection family, and not
about dependence on Axiom 3 satisfaction. Projections that disagree about a jointly-projectable fact violate
Axiom 4; projections that simply have different domains do not. The relativization to declared ∼𝑋 parallels
the Axiom 2 relativization to declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) and the Axiom 3 quantification over the verifier’s 𝑅may :
Axiom 4 makes a claim about projection consistency under the substrate’s declared ∼𝑋 , not about absolute
substrate truth.
The elementary pairwise joint-domain formulation given above is the primary Chapter 7 statement of Axiom 4. The sheaf-style and commuting-diagram vocabulary from Chapter 3 §6.5 (MP6.5)—where each
projection plays the role of a local section over a local view, with restriction maps expressing comparison
across overlaps (Mac Lane and Moerdijk 1994)—supplies a compact notational rendering when restriction
maps and local-view overlaps are explicitly modeled. Chapter 7 does not require the full topos-theoretic
sheaf apparatus as part of the axiom statement: the elementary formulation suﬀices, with the categorical
vocabulary remaining available as a compact alternative presentation when the projection family’s structure
benefits from it.

7.1.2 Projection family Π𝑋 and projection-domain partiality
Following Chapter 3 §6.1 (MP6.1), the projection family Π𝑋 = {𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 } is a finite structured family of
projections from substrate states to typed views, indexed by the substrate 𝑋. The finiteness is the finitedefault convention from Chapter 3 §1.2 (MP1.2); the structuredness is that each 𝜋𝑖 is a typed object with
explicit domain and range. The family itself is not assumed to satisfy any consistency property; consistency
is precisely what Axiom 4 imposes.
Following Chapter 3 §6.2 (MP6.2), each projection 𝜋𝑖 has explicit domain dom(𝜋𝑖 ) ⊆ Substrate(𝑋) over
which it is defined; outside its domain, 𝜋𝑖 is partial. The partiality structure is what makes Axiom 4
statable: the consistency condition operates only on substrate states where the relevant projections are

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)87
jointly defined, not on substrate states where one or more projections is undefined. Different projections in
the family may have different domains; a substrate fact need not be projectable into every member of Π𝑋 .
The partiality structure is essential to avoiding spurious “inconsistency” claims. If Axiom 4 required 𝜋𝑖 (𝑠) ∼𝑋
𝜋𝑗 (𝑠) for all 𝑠 ∈ Substrate(𝑋) regardless of whether 𝜋𝑖 or 𝜋𝑗 is defined at 𝑠, the axiom would be either trivially
violated (whenever a projection is undefined somewhere) or would force a total-projection requirement that
the substrate may not satisfy. The joint-domain restriction is what makes the axiom both statable and
substantive.

7.1.3 Substrate-specific consistency relation ∼𝑋
Following Chapter 3 §6.3 (MP6.3), the substrate-specific consistency relation ∼𝑋 is the relation expressing
when two projection outputs are compatible. The relation varies by substrate.
For double-entry bookkeeping (Pacioli 1494), ∼𝑋 is arithmetic identity: the sum of debits projected from the
substrate equals the sum of credits projected from the substrate. For modern financial reporting (Previts
and Merino 1979), ∼𝑋 is the conjunction of accounting identities (assets = liabilities + equity, revenue
minus expenses equals net income, etc.) under the relevant jurisdiction’s accounting standard. For security
audit under multi-control regimes (International Organization for Standardization 2022; National Institute
of Standards and Technology 2020; American Institute of Certified Public Accountants 2017), ∼𝑋 is controlevidence-attestation consistency: control declarations, evidence records, and attestation outputs must cohere.
For textual-preservation philology (Timpanaro 2005; Reynolds and Wilson 2013; Tov 2012), ∼𝑋 is variantrecord comparison: witness lines projecting from the same archetype must cohere under stemmatic principles.
For recitation chains (Arfeen 2026h), ∼𝑋 is multi-substrate cross-coherence: hifz, manuscript, tajwid, riwayat,
and communal-verification projections must cohere. For software-release supply chains (Arfeen 2026f), ∼𝑋 is
supply-chain attestation consistency: sigstore identity, in-toto link, SLSA level, and SHV structural-honesty
surface projections must cohere.
Axiom 4 is parameterized by ∼𝑋 as part of the substrate’s declared structure; the axiom evaluates consistency relative to the declared ∼𝑋 , not in some context-free sense. This relativization parallels the Axiom 2
relativization to declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) and the Axiom 3 quantification over 𝑅may . As with the other relativizations, ∼𝑋 is itself part of the public surface for substrates where consistency claims are publicly made, and
changes to a published ∼𝑋 across substrate versions are surface-evolution events governed by Axiom 1. The
substantive content of ∼𝑋 is substrate-specific; the structural-honesty framework requires only that ∼𝑋 be
declared and that the projection family satisfy Axiom 4 under the declared relation.

7.1.4 Joint-domain discipline
Axiom 4’s consistency condition operates over joint-domain regions of the projection family. For two projections 𝜋𝑖 and 𝜋𝑗 in Π𝑋 , the joint-domain region is dom(𝜋𝑖 ) ∩ dom(𝜋𝑗 ); the consistency check 𝜋𝑖 (𝑠) ∼𝑋 𝜋𝑗 (𝑠)
is evaluated at substrate states 𝑠 in this region. For more than two projections, the joint-domain region is
the multi-way intersection.
The joint-domain discipline distinguishes Axiom 4 from two adjacent conditions, one stronger and one weaker.
The stronger condition would be total reconstructibility of the substrate from the projection family: that
every substrate fact is in dom(𝜋𝑖 ) for every 𝜋𝑖 , and that the projection outputs together fully determine

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)88
the substrate state. Total reconstructibility implies Axiom 4 (when projections are everywhere-defined,
joint-domain consistency reduces to pairwise consistency everywhere), but Axiom 4 does not imply total
reconstructibility. A substrate may have a projection family that satisfies Axiom 4 without the projections
being collectively faithful representations of the substrate; a substrate fact outside all joint domains is not
covered by Axiom 4. Whether such uncovered facts are problematic is a separate question about projectionfamily adequacy (deferred to Chapter 8 and Chapters 13–16).
The weaker condition would be pairwise consistency only at hand-picked sample points: that for some specific
substrate states 𝑠1 , … , 𝑠𝑚 , the projections cohere at those states, but elsewhere the consistency condition is
not evaluated. Pairwise sample consistency is weaker than Axiom 4 because Axiom 4 requires consistency
at every substrate state in every relevant joint-domain region, not just at sample points. Sample-point
consistency is what cursory audit reviews achieve; Axiom 4’s discipline is the structural-honesty requirement
that this be extended to the entire declared joint-domain region.
The sheaf-style vocabulary from Chapter 3 §6.5 (MP6.5) (Mac Lane and Moerdijk 1994) supplies the compact categorical apparatus for stating this condition when restriction maps and local-view overlaps are
explicitly modeled. In sheaf-style terms, the projection family forms a presheaf over a small finite category
whose objects are the projection domains and whose morphisms are domain-inclusion (or, more generally,
the substrate-specific overlap relation). Axiom 4 corresponds to the local-section-agreement-on-overlaps
condition under ∼𝑋 , which is the sheaf-style compatibility condition but does not assert the gluing axiom
(that compatible local sections extend uniquely to a global section). Whether ∼𝑋 additionally supports
a gluing condition is substrate-specific and is not part of the Axiom 4 statement, per Chapter 3 §6.5’s
explicit gluing/uniqueness deferral. The elementary pairwise joint-domain rendering and the sheaf-style
compatibility-condition rendering express the same Axiom 4 content; the full topos-theoretic sheaf condition
(compatibility plus gluing) is strictly stronger and is not asserted by Axiom 4. Chapter 7 uses the elementary
rendering as primary and the sheaf-style rendering as the compact alternative.

7.1.5 Three primary failure patterns
Within the Chapter 7 formalization, Axiom 4 has three primary failure patterns. Each pattern is a structural
violation of the conditions developed in §§1.1–1.4; the patterns are induced by Axiom 4’s own typed objects
(projections, joint domains, ∼𝑋 ) rather than imported from other axioms’ failure taxonomies. Exhaustiveness
of the three-pattern characterization across the four-substrate scope is deferred to Chapter 8’s definitionaladequacy work.
Projection inconsistency. Two or more projections in Π𝑋 are jointly defined at some substrate state 𝑠—that
is, 𝑠 ∈ dom(𝜋𝑖 ) ∩ dom(𝜋𝑗 )—but the projection outputs fail to satisfy ∼𝑋 at 𝑠. This is the canonical Axiom 4
violation: projections that should cohere at 𝑠 do not. The structural-honesty failure is that the substrate’s
declared projection family makes incompatible claims about the same substrate fact, with the incompatibility
detectable on the joint-domain region.
Hidden joint-domain use. The public surface or verifier practice relies on projections as mutually comparable
over a region not declared as part of the relevant joint domain. Operationally, the substrate’s verifier or
a downstream consumer treats two projections as comparable at a substrate state 𝑠 where at least one of
the projections is not declared as defined; the comparison either produces a meaningless result or implicitly
extends the projection’s domain beyond its declared scope. The structural-honesty failure is not a projection-

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)89
output mismatch but a domain-scope honesty failure: the gap between the projection’s declared scope and
its operational use scope.
False joint-domain declaration. The surface declares that a projection 𝜋𝑖 is defined at 𝑠, or that the jointdomain region dom(𝜋𝑖 ) ∩ dom(𝜋𝑗 ) covers a particular region of the substrate, but the declared domain
condition does not actually hold for the substrate state being projected. Operationally, the projection is
treated as defined at a substrate state where it does not actually produce a meaningful output (its underlying
computation fails, returns a default value silently, or relies on an invariant that does not hold). The structuralhonesty failure is the false domain claim: the surface promises a projection at 𝑠 that the substrate does not
actually support.
In each case, the failure pattern is a structural violation of one or more §§1.1–1.4 conditions, induced by
Axiom 4’s own typed objects. The three patterns are primary, not exhaustive: whether they cover every
Axiom 4 failure across SI1–SI4 is a Chapter 8 definitional-adequacy question.

and Chapters 13–16.
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner. Candidate Π𝑋 over file-system substrates (Arfeen 2026c): 𝜋kind (file-kind
detection result), 𝜋zb (zahir/batin manifest-vs-latent classification), 𝜋pdf (PDF-specific parity check), 𝜋scan
(scan-completeness signal). Candidate ∼𝑋 : file-kind agreement under the joint reading (kind, classification,
parity, completeness)—a PDF with a manifest zahir classification and a successful parity check must yield

SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. Candidate Π𝑋 over program substrates (Ashraf and Arfeen

𝜋dep (dependency-graph analysis). Candidate ∼𝑋 : type-system consistency under the joint reading—a program declared syntactically well-formed and successfully type-checked should not produce error diagnostics
inconsistent with that successful type-checking result, and its dependency graph must be consistent with the

7.1.7 Proof obligations and relationship to Chapter 8 integrative theorems
Chapter 7 §1.7 closes the Axiom 4 development by identifying its proof obligations and the relationship to
Chapter 8’s integrative theorems.
The Axiom 4 proof obligations within Chapter 7 are three.
Well-formedness: Axiom 4 is well-formed as a structural condition over Chapter 3 §6 projection-family
machinery (MP6.1–MP6.6) and the joint-domain discipline of §1.4. The construction in §§1.1–1.4 verifies
well-formedness: each component (Π𝑋 , projection-domain partiality, ∼𝑋 , joint-domain regions) is defined
over typed objects from Chapter 3, and the conjunction is well-typed.
Decidability scope: Axiom 4’s consistency check is a candidate for decidable treatment in the finite-default
fragment of Chapter 3 §7, assuming finite Π𝑋 , finite joint domains, and decidable ∼𝑋 . Chapter 10 carries
the rigorous decidability burden; Chapter 8 §2’s finite-witness construction (T82) operates within whatever
decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. Within the finite-default fragment, the decidability question is
well-posed but the rigorous result is not claimed for Chapter 7. Outside the finite-default fragment (infinite
projection families, infinite joint domains, undecidable ∼𝑋 ), Axiom 4 remains structurally well-defined but
its decidability is not claimed for v1.0.
Exhaustiveness of the three primary failure patterns of §1.5: whether the three patterns exhaust Axiom 4’s
failure modes within the four-substrate scope. This is a Chapter 8 definitional-adequacy question deferred
from Chapter 7.
The relationship to Chapter 8: Chapter 7 closes the statement-level development of AX-SH. At the close
of Chapter 7, the four axioms (A1 from Chapter 4, A2 from Chapter 5, A3 from Chapter 6, A4 from this
chapter) have been stated and their local machinery has been developed. Chapter 8 then evaluates the
complete A1–A4 system for four integrative obligations.
T81 (mutual independence) is the formal falsifiability theorem of AX-SH: each axiom is falsifiable while the
others hold. Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement that T81 needs to evaluate; the theorem itself is
Chapter 8’s burden.
T82 (consistency of AX-SH) requires that a finite witness system satisfies all four axioms simultaneously.
Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement that T82 needs to satisfy; the witness construction is Chapter 8’s
burden.
T83 (definitional adequacy) requires that A1–A4 satisfaction under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ) corre-

sponds to what operational practitioners call structural honesty across the four substrate instances. This
is an evaluation of finite judgment-set adequacy relative to the named set 𝐽 – principally author-selected
and author-labeled, with several constructed scenarios – and not a claim of broad independent practitioner
validation; independent annotation of 𝐽 is the registered successor test (the AX-SH Case Benchmark). Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement that T83 needs to evaluate; the adequacy argument is Chapter 8’s

The adversarial-declaration / under-determination evaluation asks whether adversarially weak declarations

Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement; Chapter 8 supplies the integrative evaluation. At the close of
Chapter 7, the dissertation’s four-axiom statement-level theory of structural honesty is fully stated; whether

7.2 Axiom 4: Edge Cases and Boundary Cases
Section 2 explores edge cases under the §1 conditions for Axiom 4, applying §§1.1–1.5 to four categories of
structurally compound or temporally evolving cases. The edge cases are not new conditions on Axiom 4; they
are applications of the existing conditions to compound scenarios. §2.1 covers projection-family evolution
edges; §2.2 covers consistency-relation ∼𝑋 edges, with explicit public-surface vs verifier-private distinction
paralleling Chapter 6 §2.2’s 𝑅may treatment; §2.3 covers joint-domain and projection-set compound edges
(stale projections, forked projection sets, empty and universal joint domains); §2.4 articulates the complete
four-axiom Axiom-1–Axiom-2–Axiom-3–Axiom-4 interaction.

7.2.1 Projection-family evolution edge cases
Section §1.2 establishes Π𝑋 as a finite structured family of projections with explicit domains. Three structurally distinct edge cases arise in operational practice as the projection family evolves over time.
New projections added. When a projection 𝜋𝑛+1 is added to the family—for example, a new audit dimension is introduced as part of a regulatory update—Π𝑋 grows from {𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 } to {𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 , 𝜋𝑛+1 }. The
joint-domain regions involving 𝜋𝑛+1 are new; previously-existing joint-domain regions among 𝜋1 , … , 𝜋𝑛 are
unchanged. Axiom 4 obligations for 𝜋𝑛+1 ’s joint-domain regions are introduced; obligations for the prior
joint-domain regions are preserved. Whether the added projection introduces a new ∼𝑋 requirement is
determined by the substrate’s declared consistency relation.
Projections removed. When a projection 𝜋𝑘 is removed from the family—for example, a deprecated audit
dimension is retired—Π𝑋 shrinks. The joint-domain regions involving 𝜋𝑘 are no longer covered by Axiom 4;
obligations narrow accordingly. Substrate data previously projected through 𝜋𝑘 may persist as historical
records but is no longer subject to the current Axiom 4 evaluation against the reduced Π𝑋 (the persistent
data becomes a candidate “stale projection” case per §2.3).

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)92
Projection-domain changes. When the domain of a projection changes—dom(𝜋𝑖 ) is expanded or restricted—
the joint-domain regions involving 𝜋𝑖 shift. Axiom 4 obligations are re-evaluated against the updated jointdomain regions: the old regions may no longer all be in scope, and new regions may come into scope.
Π𝑋 updates published as part of a public surface are surface-evolution events governed by Axiom 1, requiring
re-evaluation of Axiom 4 against the published Π𝑋 . Verifier-private refinements of Π𝑋 —internal analysis-tool
improvements that have not been published as part of a surface on which others rely—are not automatically
Axiom 1 events. They become Axiom 1 events at the moment the refined Π𝑋 is published; until then, the
per-version Axiom 4 evaluation continues against the published Π𝑋 . This parallels the Chapter 6 §2.2 𝑅may
public/private distinction.

7.2.2 Consistency-relation ∼𝑋 edge cases
Section §1.3 establishes ∼𝑋 as the substrate-specific consistency relation, parameterized as part of the
substrate’s declared structure. Three structurally distinct edge cases arise.
∼𝑋 evolution. The substrate-specific consistency relation may itself evolve as the substrate’s structural understanding evolves. New accounting standards may yield refined consistency relations for financial reporting;
new attestation schemes may yield refined consistency relations for supply-chain stacks; new philological
methods may yield refined consistency relations for textual-preservation. The substrate at version 𝑖 has its
declared ∼𝑖𝑋 , and Axiom 4 evaluates per-version consistency against ∼𝑖𝑋 .
∼𝑋 scope changes. The relation may apply to a narrower or broader class of substrate states than it previously
did—for example, a refined ∼𝑋 may handle a previously-out-of-scope substrate variant. Scope changes are
handled through the relativization to declared ∼𝑋 : each version’s Axiom 4 evaluation operates under that
version’s declared scope.
∼𝑋 obsolescence. When the substrate evolves such that the prior ∼𝑋 is no longer the right consistency
relation—for example, when a substrate is restructured in a way that makes the prior arithmetic-identity
relation irrelevant—the published ∼𝑋 update is itself an Axiom 1 surface-evolution event.
∼𝑋 refinements published as part of the substrate’s public surface are surface-evolution events governed
by Axiom 1; verifier-private refinements of ∼𝑋 —internal refinements of the verifier’s comparison logic that
have not been published as part of a surface on which others rely—are not automatically Axiom 1 events
unless and until they are published. This parallels the Π𝑋 public/private distinction from §2.1 and the 𝑅may
public/private distinction from Chapter 6 §2.2.

7.2.3 Joint-domain and projection-set edge cases
Section §1.4 establishes the joint-domain discipline as the arena where Axiom 4 lives. Four structurally
compound joint-domain situations arise.
Stale projection. A projection 𝜋𝑖 in Π𝑋 is computed from an outdated substrate state—for example, 𝜋𝑖
reflects Substrate(𝑋) at version 𝑡 − 1 while 𝜋𝑗 reflects Substrate(𝑋) at version 𝑡. The apparent inconsistency
between 𝜋𝑖 and 𝜋𝑗 is due to temporal misalignment rather than substantive disagreement. The structuralhonesty failure (if the discrepancy is not declared) is the failure of the projection family to declare which
version of the substrate each projection reflects. The remedy is explicit version-tagging on the projection
family’s surface, after which Axiom 4 evaluates within-version consistency rather than across-version.

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)93
Forked projection set. The projection family has been partitioned into mutually inconsistent subsets that the
substrate’s verifier treats as coexisting authoritative views—for example, an audit trail with two divergent
attestation chains that the substrate has not reconciled. The structural-honesty failure is the absence of a
single coherent projection family; the substrate has implicitly multiple Π𝑋 declarations without acknowledging the fork or supplying a unifying ∼𝑋 . The remedy is explicit declaration of the forked structure, after
which Axiom 4 evaluates each fork against its own ∼𝑋 .
Empty joint domain. Two projections in Π𝑋 nominally apply but have no shared substrate states—dom(𝜋𝑖 )∩
dom(𝜋𝑗 ) = ∅. No Axiom 4 obligation arises between this pair (the consistency condition is vacuously
satisfied), but the empty joint-domain region is a structurally honest observation: the substrate’s declared
projection family includes projections that do not meaningfully overlap. Whether the family should include
such projections is a substrate-design question, not an Axiom 4 violation.
Universal joint domain. All projections in Π𝑋 are defined on every substrate state—dom(𝜋𝑖 ) = Substrate(𝑋)
for all 𝑖. This is a special case where the consistency check is everywhere-applicable: Axiom 4 reduces
to pairwise consistency at every substrate state. Universal joint domain implies (but is not implied by)
total reconstructibility: even if every projection is everywhere-defined, the projections may not collectively
determine the substrate state.
Each edge case is a structurally compound application of §§1.1–1.4. Within Chapter 7’s formalization, these
compound applications are analyzed using the three failure-pattern vocabulary from §1.5; whether that
vocabulary is definitionally adequate across all scoped substrates is deferred to Chapter 8.

7.2.4 Joint Axiom-1, Axiom-2, Axiom-3, Axiom-4 interaction
The four axioms operate on different aspects of the same substrate-caller-projection relationship. Axiom 1
(Chapter 4) supplies surface-evolution governance: how the producer’s public surface (including declared
(𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), any published 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , and ∼𝑋 ) evolves over time across versions 𝑆0 , … , 𝑆𝑛 . Axiom 2 (Chapter 5) evaluates per-version consistency under declared (𝑂𝑖 , 𝐾𝑖 , 𝑅𝑖 ) at each version 𝑆𝑖 . Axiom 3 (Chapter 6)
imposes caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may at each version. Axiom 4 (Chapter 7) imposes projection
consistency over Π𝑋 under ∼𝑋 at each version.
When all four axioms hold, the producer evolves the surface honestly (Axiom 1), claims per-version consistency under declared scope honestly (Axiom 2), callers address possible outcomes exhaustively (Axiom 3),
and the projection family coheres on joint-domain regions under declared ∼𝑋 (Axiom 4). The four axioms
do not form a strict linear dependency chain: each can be stated independently. Axiom 1 supplies surfaceevolution governance used by the other axiom analyses when surfaces change over time; Axioms 2–4 remain
statable over their relevant per-version surfaces, caller obligations, or projection families even when Axiom 1
is failed, absent, or not yet evaluated. Axiom 2 satisfaction supplies inputs to Axiom 3 but is not a syntactic
precondition. Axiom 3 satisfaction supplies caller-side artifacts that may participate in Axiom 4’s projectionconsistency analysis but is not a syntactic precondition for stating Axiom 4. Each of Axioms 2, 3, and 4 is
statable without requiring satisfaction of the others, though each uses the shared Chapter 3 machinery and
may consume artifacts produced by the others’ analyses. The four-axiom structure is one of input-supply
rather than precondition-stacking.
The cross-axiom checking pattern operates as follows. Axiom 1 is designed to expose dishonest scopenarrowing through the corrigenda discipline: a producer cannot weaken declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), 𝑅may , Π𝑋 ,

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)94
or ∼𝑋 without an append-only corrigendum. Axiom 3 is designed to expose dishonest under-declaration
through caller-side exhaustiveness failures: callers cannot discharge 𝑅may obligations the producer has not
adequately published. Axiom 4 is designed to expose dishonest projection-restriction through joint-domain
failures: a projection family that restricts its joint-domain claims to avoid uncomfortable consistency checks
creates either hidden-joint-domain-use or false-joint-domain-declaration failures. Whether this cross-axiom
checking pattern is suﬀicient to prevent adversarial-declaration trivial satisfaction is a Chapter 8 obligation,
not a claim of Chapter 7.
The joint structure has operational consequences. A substrate-caller-projection relationship may satisfy any
subset of {𝐴1, 𝐴2, 𝐴3, 𝐴4} without satisfying the others; each combination corresponds to a structurally
distinct failure profile. The structural-honesty analysis must report which axioms hold and which do not,
rather than collapsing all failures into a single category.

7.3 Substrate-by-Substrate Operational Review and Chapter 8
Handoff
Section 3 reviews the substrate-by-substrate operational practices that bear on Axiom 4’s projectionconsistency discipline, articulates Axiom 4’s role as the closer of the four-axiom statement-level development
and the input-supply to Chapter 8’s integrative work, and hands off to Chapter 8. §3.1 reviews SI1–SI4
operational realities as illustrative support mechanisms for Axiom 4; §3.2 articulates Axiom 4’s role as
statement-level closer with input-supply to Chapter 8; §3.3 hands off to Chapter 8, closing the four-axiom
statement-level development of AX-SH.

7.3.1 Substrate-by-substrate operational surface practices for SI1–SI4 under
Axiom 4
For each of the four worked substrate instances, existing operational practices can support some of Axiom 4’s
projection-consistency discipline, and additional explicit surface support would be needed to fully realize the
discipline. The review is illustrative and preparatory; detailed substrate adequacy remains deferred to
Chapters 13–16 and Chapter 8.
SI1 — Bayyinah file-layer scanner. Existing operational practices supporting Axiom 4 for Bayyinah file
substrates (Arfeen 2026c): multi-stream scan output (file-kind, classification, parity, completeness streams
that can be cross-checked); the scan-incomplete primitive carries metadata enabling consistency checks
across streams; structured outputs in machine-readable form enable downstream parity audit. Additional
explicit surface support would be needed for: explicit declaration of Π𝑋 members and their domains; explicit
declaration of the substrate-specific ∼𝑋 that captures consistent file-kind detection across streams; explicit
joint-domain regions and their associated consistency obligations.
SI2 — Furqan language-layer type-checker. Existing operational practices for Furqan callers (downstream
compilers, CI pipelines, developer tools, program authors) (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b, 2026a): multi-stream
type-checker output (syntactic, typed, diagnostic, dependency streams); diagnostic emissions cross-referenced
with type-check outcomes; build-time gating on diagnostic streams. Additional explicit surface support would
be needed for: explicit declaration of which type-checker outputs constitute a projection family; explicit

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)95
declaration of ∼𝑋 (typically a refinement-type or static-analysis consistency relation); explicit joint-domain
regions where the projection-consistency claim holds.
SI3 — Munafiq model-layer protocol. Existing operational practices for Munafiq callers (eval pipelines,
downstream judges) (Arfeen 2026d): multi-stream model-output protocol (marker, calibration, diagnosis
streams); evaluation pipelines that cross-reference streams to detect inconsistencies. Additional explicit
surface support would be needed for: explicit declaration of Π𝑋 members (which streams constitute the
projection family); explicit declaration of ∼𝑋 (marker-calibration-diagnosis joint coherence); explicit jointdomain regions for prompt-types where the projection-consistency claim holds.
SI4 — Supply-chain four-substrate stack. Existing operational practices for supply-chain callers (consumers
of attestations across sigstore (Sigstore project (Open Source Security Foundation) 2021), in-toto (TorresArias et al. 2019), SLSA (Open Source Security Foundation 2023), SHV (Arfeen 2026f) layers): multi-layer
attestation streams that can be cross-checked for consistency; standardized formats enabling automated parity audit; trust-policy frameworks that gate downstream consumption on cross-layer consistency. Additional
explicit surface support would be needed for: explicit declaration that the four layers constitute a projection
family; explicit declaration of supply-chain ∼𝑋 (cross-layer attestation consistency); explicit joint-domain
regions for the release classes where the projection-consistency claim holds.
In each case, the review identifies operational practices that can support some of Axiom 4’s projectionconsistency discipline, and notes where additional explicit surface support would be needed. The review is
illustrative and preparatory; whether each substrate’s operational practices are definitionally adequate for
the structural-honesty needs of that substrate is the work of Chapter 8 and Chapters 13–16.

7.3.2 Axiom 4 as closer of the four-axiom statement-level development
Axiom 4 closes the statement-level development of AX-SH. At the close of Chapter 7, the four axioms have
been stated and their local machinery has been developed; the dissertation’s four-axiom statement-level
theory of structural honesty is fully stated. What Chapter 7 supplies is the complete statement-level system,
not the complete validated theory.
Chapter 8 is responsible for evaluating the complete A1–A4 system across four integrative obligations.
T81 (mutual independence) is the formal falsifiability theorem of AX-SH: each axiom is falsifiable while
the others hold. T81 directly addresses the disprovability surface of the axiom system—if any axiom were
implied by the conjunction of the others, T81 would fail and the axiom system would be over-determined.
Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement that T81 needs to evaluate.
T82 (consistency of AX-SH) requires that a finite witness system satisfies all four axioms simultaneously.
T82 directly addresses the question of whether AX-SH is satisfiable at all—if no finite witness could be
constructed, the axiom system would be inconsistent. Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement that T82’s
witness must satisfy.
T83 (definitional adequacy) requires that A1–A4 satisfaction under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ) corresponds to what operational practitioners call structural honesty across the four substrate instances. That
correspondence is likewise evaluated as finite judgment-set adequacy relative to the named set 𝐽 (principally
author-selected and author-labeled, with several constructed scenarios), not as broad independent practitioner validation. T83 directly addresses whether AX-SH is the right axiomatization—whether the formal

CHAPTER 7. AXIOM 4 (SUBSTRATE-PARAMETERIZED PROJECTION CONSISTENCY OVER PI_X)96
definitions match operational practice. Chapter 7 supplies the Axiom 4 statement that T83 needs to evaluate.
The adversarial-declaration / under-determination evaluation asks whether adversarially weak declarations
of the axiom-relativized objects yield trivial axiom satisfaction. The candidate mitigation discussed in §2.4—
cross-axiom checking through Axiom 1’s corrigenda discipline, Axiom 3’s caller-side failures, and Axiom 4’s
joint-domain failures—is to be evaluated in Chapter 8, not pre-endorsed in Chapter 7. Whether the crossaxiom checking pattern is suﬀicient is the methodological question Chapter 8 must answer.
Chapter 7 supplies the complete A1–A4 statement-level system; Chapter 8 supplies the integrative evaluation.
The relationship is input-supply, not theorem-by-Chapter-7.

7.3.3 Chapter 8 handoff
Chapter 8 will evaluate the complete four-axiom system A1–A4 for mutual independence (T81), consistency
(T82), definitional adequacy (T83), and adversarial-declaration / under-determination concerns. Chapter 7

patterns, illustrative candidate projection families for SI1–SI4—and the complete four-axiom statement-level

At the close of Chapter 7, the dissertation’s four-axiom statement-level theory of structural honesty is fully

Chapter 7 closes the axiom-statement development; Chapter 8 supplies the integrative evaluation. At the
