8.1 Framing: Integrative Evaluation of A1–A4
Chapter 8 evaluates the four-axiom statement-level system supplied by Chapters 4–7. The four axioms—
A1 surface-evolution honesty (Chapter 4), A2 per-version surface-substrate consistency (Chapter 5), A3
caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may (Chapter 6), A4 substrate-parameterized projection consistency over
Π𝑋 under ∼𝑋 (Chapter 7)—were stated and developed in their local-machinery contexts. What remains is
to test whether the four-axiom system has the properties a structurally-honest theory must have: mutual
independence (T81—none of the four is a derivative consequence of the others), consistency (T82—the
system is satisfiable via a finite witness), definitional adequacy (T83—the formal definitions correspond
to operational practitioner judgments of structural honesty), and adversarial-declaration coverage (AD1—
whether weak or adversarial declarations of the axiom-relativized objects admit trivial satisfaction, and under
which ecosystem conditions such trivial satisfaction becomes detectable or structurally blocked).
The section is presented in five subsections, framing the integrative evaluation that the rest of Chapter 8
carries out. §0.1 articulates Chapter 8’s role as evaluator. §0.2 names the Principle of Layered Defense, the
methodological discipline operating across the dissertation. §0.3 introduces the ecosystem-condition catalog
as an auxiliary proof-configuration artifact—not a fifth axiom. §0.4 articulates the named judgment-case

set discipline for T83. §0.5 articulates the Chapter 8 / Chapter 21 boundary that preserves Chapter 21’s

8.1.1 Chapter 8’s role: evaluation, not restatement
Chapter 8’s burden is structurally distinct from Chapters 4–7’s. Each axiom chapter stated and developed
its axiom’s local machinery: Chapter 4 stated A1 over versioned-surface machinery; Chapter 5 stated A2
over the correspondence-relation family; Chapter 6 stated A3 over 𝑅may with the three discharge paths;
Chapter 7 stated A4 over the projection-family machinery. The four axiom chapters supplied confidence at
the axiom-statement level—each axiom is well-formed, well-typed over Chapter 3’s typed-object substrate,
and statable independently of the others’ satisfaction.
Chapter 8 must earn integrative-level confidence independently. The four axioms, taken together, must
satisfy four integrative properties: mutual independence (each falsifiable while the others hold), consistency (the system is satisfiable), definitional adequacy (the system corresponds to operational practice),
and adversarial-declaration coverage (the system is nontrivially falsifiable under weak declarations modulo
ecosystem conditions). None of these properties follows from the four chapters’ statement-level work; each
requires its own integrative argument or construction.
The temptation Chapter 8 must resist is to recycle the axiom-chapter confidence into integrative-level confidence by restating the axioms with rhetorical force. Chapters 4–7’s discipline was honest at the statement
level; it did not pre-claim what Chapter 8 must establish. Chapter 8’s discipline is honest at the integrative
level; it must not pre-claim what the remaining chapters (Chapter 10 decidability and quantum-survivability;
Chapters 13–16 case studies; Chapter 20 substrate-generalization open problem; Chapter 21 falsification protocols) must establish.
The relationship between Chapter 7 and Chapter 8 mirrors the relationship within the axiom-chapter sequence: Chapter 4 supplied the A1 statement, and Chapter 6 §3.2 evaluated A3 against that supplied
statement without re-stating A1. Chapter 8 evaluates the complete A1–A4 system against the four integrative properties without re-stating any of the axioms. Where prose references an axiom, it does so to test an
integrative property of the axiom in conjunction with the others, not to develop the axiom’s local machinery
further.

8.1.2 The Principle of Layered Defense
The dissertation operates under a methodological discipline that we name here, for the first time, as the
Principle of Layered Defense. The principle holds that AX-SH claims are assigned to specific defense layers
rather than treated as globally provable in the abstract. Axiom satisfaction is one layer; integrative theorem
satisfaction is another; definitional adequacy is a third; operational nontriviality under ecosystem conditions
is a fourth; long-horizon falsifiability surveillance is a fifth. Each layer carries a specific kind of claim with a
specific kind of supporting argument.
The principle is not a new commitment introduced in Chapter 8. It has been operating across the dissertation
since Chapter 3 §1.4’s notation-versus-claim discipline (the introduction of a typed object is not the same as
the assertion of a property of that object), through the A1–A4 declared-object relativization (each axiom is
evaluated under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ), not under absolute correspondence), and through the SI1–
SI4 scope-relativized claims (each worked substrate is honest at its declared scope, not absolutely correct).

What Chapter 8 §0 contributes is the formal naming of the principle that has been load-bearing without
explicit recognition.
The principle has substantive consequences for what Chapter 8 can and cannot claim. T81 is a logicalfalsifiability theorem operating at the axiom-system layer; it does not by itself establish operational falsifiability, which depends on the ecosystem-condition layer and is treated in AD1. T82 is a formal consistency
theorem operating at the model-existence layer; it does not by itself establish that the witness is operationally
meaningful, which again depends on the ecosystem-condition layer. T83 is a definitional-adequacy argument
operating at the empirical-relative-to-named-cases layer; it does not establish absolute adequacy in a contextfree sense, which is not a layer the framework supports. AD1 is an analysis at the adversarial-declaration
layer; it identifies what each axiom is designed to expose under each ecosystem condition, and acknowledges
residual holes routed to Chapter 21.
The principle is also what makes Chapter 8 tractable rather than impossible. The chapter does not have
to prove AX-SH adequate, consistent, independent, and adversarially robust in a context-free sense—that
would be an impossible burden, and the temptation to undertake it would either produce vacuous results
or paper over essential limitations. Chapter 8 has to argue each property at its proper defense layer, with
explicit acknowledgment of what each layer’s argument depends on and what it does not establish. This is
analogous to the epistemic posture of adequacy arguments for formal systems such as ZFC, Peano arithmetic,
and behavioral subtyping: adequacy is argued relative to the intended domain and judgment practices, not
proven in a context-free sense (Liskov and Wing 1994).

8.1.3 Ecosystem-condition catalog
AX-SH satisfaction is necessary but not suﬀicient for operational structural honesty. This is the central
methodological observation that shapes Chapter 8’s integrative work. The four axioms—surface-evolution
honesty, per-version surface-substrate consistency, caller-side exhaustiveness, projection consistency—
capture necessary conditions for an artifact to be structurally honest in the framework’s sense. They do
not capture suﬀicient conditions; suﬀiciency requires additional operational-nontriviality conditions that we
will call ecosystem conditions.
The ecosystem conditions are: multiple independent callers exercising the producer’s published 𝑅may ; multiple independent projections constraining the producer’s projection family Π𝑋 ; evolutionary pressure on
the producer’s surface forcing the corrigenda discipline to engage with substantive change; and corrigenda
discipline actually exercised by surface evolution rather than carried as nominal commitment. Without these
conditions, individual axioms become structurally empty—A3 has nothing to catch if no callers exercise 𝑅may ;
A4 has nothing to catch if there is only one projection or if projections do not independently constrain; A1
has nothing to catch if the surface never substantively evolves.
The ecosystem-condition catalog is an auxiliary proof-configuration artifact for Chapter 8, not a fifth axiom.
The four axioms are formal commitments about the artifact-substrate-caller relationship that the framework
prescribes. The ecosystem conditions are interpretive conditions about the operational environment in which
the artifact-substrate-caller relationship operates. The distinction matters for the structure of AX-SH: adding
ecosystem conditions to the formal axiom set would change the framework from “four axioms about structural honesty” to “five axioms”—and the fifth would be qualitatively different from the first four (it would be
a meta-axiom about when the other four bite operationally, not a substantive structural-honesty condition).

100

Preserving the four-axiom structure is methodologically essential; the ecosystem-condition catalog captures
operational-nontriviality conditions under which axiom satisfaction has its intended structural-honesty interpretation, without itself becoming part of the formal axiom set.
The proper framing is the same as for any scientific theory: the formal commitments capture necessary
conditions, and the operational interpretation requires auxiliary conditions that the theory itself names.
Newton’s second law (𝐹 = 𝑚𝑎) is necessary but not suﬀicient for predicting motion; suﬀicient prediction
requires knowing the force functions, the boundary conditions, and the initial state. The law is not falsified
by the existence of motion that 𝐹 = 𝑚𝑎 alone cannot predict; it is falsified by motion that 𝐹 = 𝑚𝑎 predicts
incorrectly under known force functions. Similarly, AX-SH is not falsified by the existence of operational
structural dishonesty that AX-SH alone cannot detect; it is falsified by structural dishonesty that AX-SH
classifies as honest under known ecosystem conditions.
The ecosystem-condition catalog is developed across Chapter 8: T82.7 makes the catalog explicit in the
finite witness; AD1.5–AD1.6 examine cases where ecosystem conditions fail (private/no-caller ecosystem,
single-projection ecosystem); AD1.7 constructs the cross-axiom coverage matrix as the structural-honesty
disclosure mechanism for evaluating adversarial coverage under each ecosystem-condition combination.

8.1.4 Named judgment-case set discipline
T83’s definitional-adequacy claim—that A1–A4 satisfaction under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ) corresponds to what operational practitioners call structural honesty—is empirical-relative to a judgment-case set,
not provable in a context-free sense. The distinction is foundational and worth stating explicitly. Definitional
adequacy of a formal system for a pre-formal notion (structural honesty, in this case) is analogous to the
epistemic posture of adequacy arguments for formal systems such as ZFC over the pre-formal notion of set
and Peano arithmetic over the pre-formal notion of natural number—the formal system is judged adequate
not because it is provably correct in some absolute sense, but because it classifies the cases practitioners care
about consistently with practitioner judgment.
The structurally honest move T83 makes is to name the judgment-case set explicitly. The case set comprises
operational-practitioner judgment cases drawn from SI1–SI4: cases practitioners would classify as structurally
honest; cases practitioners would classify as structurally dishonest; and boundary cases where practitioner
judgment is debatable. Each case is a triple (substrate-scenario, expected-classification-by-practitioners,
axioms-classification). The adequacy argument shows that for every case in the set, the axioms classify the
case consistently with practitioner judgment.
The discipline has three components. First, the case set must include positive, negative, and boundary cases—
a case set composed only of clean positive cases would not test the framework, since trivially satisfiable
axioms could classify all positive cases correctly without engaging with the framework’s actual content.
Second, cases outside the case set are explicitly out of T83’s scope; T83 does not claim absolute adequacy,
only adequacy relative to the named set. Third, boundary cases are not papered over: they are either
classified with explicit rationale (the framework correctly captures the practitioner’s judgment because of
structural-honesty consideration 𝑋) or routed to Chapter 21 as future falsification / refinement cases where
the framework may need extension or modification.
The discipline has consequences for the SHV / Furqan / Munafiq vocabulary mappings (T83.2–T83.4). Each
mapping is a structured interpretation from the program’s operational vocabulary to AX-SH’s declared-

object vocabulary, with each correspondence justified against the named judgment-case set (Arfeen 2026h,
2026d; Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b). The mappings are not strict semantic isomorphisms; they are not claims
that SHV’s notion of structural honesty is A1–A4 satisfaction in some absolute sense. The mappings are
structured correspondences that produce consistent classifications across the case set, with the framework
correctly capturing what the program’s vocabulary names as structurally honest behavior.

8.1.5 Chapter 8 / Chapter 21 boundary
Chapter 8 evaluates the A1–A4 system under named ecosystem conditions and identifies what counts as a
satisfactory adequacy argument relative to the judgment-case set. Chapter 21 retains the full long-horizon
treatment of falsification protocols, monitoring of emergent misappropriation in operational practice, and
concrete mechanisms for ongoing falsifiability surveillance. The boundary preserves Chapter 21’s burden
against Chapter 8 over-claiming.
Specifically, Chapter 8 does not solve three problems that are Chapter 21’s burden. The first is the longhorizon dynamics of how AX-SH-adopting communities maintain corrigenda discipline across decades. Chapter 8 names corrigenda discipline as an ecosystem condition for A1 to bite operationally; it does not specify
the institutional, social, or governance mechanisms by which a community ensures corrigenda are actually
used. Those mechanisms are Chapter 21’s burden. The second is the monitoring of emergent misappropriation in operational practice. AD1.8 acknowledges emergent misappropriation as a partial-falsifiability
surface—scope-misdeclaration by honest future users extending AX-SH’s scope through legitimate intellectual labor, classified as recoverable (corrigenda-taggable) or irrecoverable (load-bearing entrenchment)—but
does not specify the surveillance mechanisms by which such misappropriation is detected. Those mechanisms are Chapter 21’s burden. The third is the concrete falsification protocols by which the dissertation’s
load-bearing claims are tested. Chapter 21 (named-open O5 in Section 6 of the audit ledger) carries this
future-work.
Chapter 8 identifies which falsifiability surfaces exist: logical falsifiability via T81; operational falsifiability
via AD1’s coverage matrix; substrate-generality falsifiability via Chapter 20 (already routed via ST1 and
SC1); long-horizon falsifiability surveillance via Chapter 21. Chapter 21 articulates the protocols by which
each surface is exercised over time. The boundary is a methodological commitment: Chapter 8 makes the
claims it can defend at the integrative-theorem layer, identifies the residual obligations, and routes them to
the appropriate downstream chapter. This is the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2) operating concretely.

8.2 T81: Mutual Independence
Section 1 establishes the formal mutual-independence theorem of AX-SH (T81). T81 is a logical-falsifiability
result: for each axiom 𝐴𝑖 in {𝐴1, 𝐴2, 𝐴3, 𝐴4}, there exists a model of the AX-SH machinery in which 𝐴𝑖 fails
while the other three hold. The theorem establishes that each axiom is logically falsifiable in isolation—none
is a derivative consequence of the conjunction of the others—and is the formal falsifiability foundation of
AX-SH.
The section is presented in six subsections. §1.1 supplies the formal statement and proof structure. §§1.2–1.5
supply the four single-axiom-failure witnesses, one per axiom. §1.6 distinguishes logical falsifiability from
operational falsifiability and cross-references AD1 for the operational side.

8.2.1 T81: formal statement and proof structure
Theorem 8.1 (T81, Mutual Independence of A1–A4). For each axiom 𝐴𝑖 in {𝐴1, 𝐴2, 𝐴3, 𝐴4}, there exists
a model 𝑀𝑖 of the AX-SH machinery—a substrate, surface, caller community, and projection family with
declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 )—such that 𝑀𝑖 satisfies 𝐴𝑗 for all 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖 but fails 𝐴𝑖 .
The theorem asserts logical falsifiability of each axiom in isolation. Its proof structure is constructive: for
each axiom, we construct (in §§1.2–1.5) a specific model in which that axiom fails while the others hold.
Existence of the four witnesses establishes that no axiom is implied by the conjunction of the others—if 𝐴𝑖
were implied by {𝐴𝑗 ∶ 𝑗 ≠ 𝑖}, then the 𝑀𝑖 witness (satisfying the latter and failing 𝐴𝑖 ) would be impossible.
The theorem is the formal falsifiability foundation of AX-SH. Its significance is methodological as much as
technical: a four-axiom system in which one axiom were a derivative consequence of the others would be
either over-determined (one axiom carrying no independent content) or formally redundant. The mutualindependence theorem establishes that each of A1–A4 carries independent structural-honesty content not
captured by the others. This is analogous to the metatheoretic discipline used when foundational systems
are tested for redundancy or independence: the point is to show that a proposed axiom carries independent
content rather than functioning as a disguised theorem of the remaining axioms.
The witnesses constructed below are minimal—each is designed to make the single-axiom-failure pattern as
transparent as possible, drawing on Chapter 3’s typed-object machinery without introducing new machinery. The witnesses are not intended to be operationally interesting; they are intended to be technically
minimal demonstrations of logical falsifiability. Operational interest is a different property (treated in T82’s
witness-construction work for satisfiability and AD1’s analysis of adversarial-declaration coverage). The
clean separation between logical falsifiability (T81’s burden) and operational falsifiability (AD1’s burden) is
the Principle of Layered Defense applied to the falsifiability question.

Witness 𝑀1 demonstrates that Axiom 1 can fail while A2, A3, A4 hold. Construction: consider a versionedlibrary substrate with two versions 𝑣𝑡 and 𝑣𝑡+1 . At 𝑣𝑡 , the public surface declares a function 𝑓 with type
signature 𝑆𝑡 . At 𝑣𝑡+1 , the surface declares 𝑓 with type signature 𝑆𝑡+1 , where 𝑆𝑡+1 is strictly incompatible
with 𝑆𝑡 (𝑆𝑡+1 requires an additional argument that 𝑆𝑡 did not require, with no corrigendum tagging this
as a breaking change). The transition 𝑣𝑡 → 𝑣𝑡+1 violates Liskov-Wing version-subtyping with corrigenda
discipline (Chapter 4 §1.1) (Liskov and Wing 1994). Axiom 1 fails: the surface evolution from 𝑣𝑡 to 𝑣𝑡+1 is

8.2.6 Logical falsifiability versus operational falsifiability
The four witnesses 𝑀1 , 𝑀2 , 𝑀3 , 𝑀4 of §§1.2–1.5 collectively establish T81 (logical mutual independence).
Each witness exists as a model of the AX-SH machinery satisfying three axioms and failing the fourth; no
axiom is a derivative consequence of the others’ conjunction.
T81 is a logical-falsifiability theorem. The four witnesses establish that each axiom can fail in principle
while the others hold. The theorem does not, however, establish operational falsifiability—the property that
the four axioms operationalize structurally-honest behavior in the practical sense of detecting dishonesty
when it occurs in real artifacts. Operational falsifiability depends on ecosystem conditions: whether a caller
community exists that exercises 𝑅may against the producer’s surface (without which A3 is structurally empty);
whether the projection family contains multiple independent projections (without which A4 is structurally
empty); whether the producer’s surface evolves substantively over time (without which A1 has no transitions
to evaluate); and whether the corrigenda discipline is operationally enforced rather than nominal.
The distinction is methodologically central. A producer who declares weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) from inception, operates
in an ecosystem without adversarial callers, declares a single-projection family that does not cross-check, and
never substantively evolves its surface satisfies A1 trivially (no evolution to violate), A2 trivially (declared
correspondence relation matches declared substrate behavior because both are weak), A3 trivially (no callers
to exhaust 𝑅may ), and A4 trivially (single projection cannot disagree with itself). Such a producer is satisfying
A1–A4 logically; whether it is structurally honest in any operationally meaningful sense is a separate question,
and the question turns on ecosystem conditions.
T81 establishes that the four axioms are not equivalent or derivative—each could fail while the others hold.
AD1 (§4 of this chapter) takes up the operational-falsifiability question separately: under which ecosystem

CHAPTER 8. INTEGRATIVE EVALUATION (T81/T82/T83/AD1)

105

conditions does logical satisfaction of A1–A4 correspond to operational structural honesty, and under which
ecosystem conditions does logical satisfaction admit trivial adversarial-declaration scenarios that AX-SH does
not catch? The two questions—logical mutual independence and operational adversarial coverage—operate
at different layers of the Principle of Layered Defense framework (§0.2). T81 settles the first; AD1 takes up
the second.
The combination of T81 and AD1 is what positions AX-SH to be nontrivially falsifiable. T81 ensures
that each axiom carries independent structural-honesty content; AD1 evaluates whether the axiom system
as a whole is operationally falsifiable under named ecosystem conditions. Together they constitute the
falsifiability foundation of the framework, with T82 supplying the consistency proof (the system is satisfiable,
so falsifiability does not collapse into vacuity) and T83 supplying the empirical-relative adequacy argument
(the system’s classifications correspond to operational practitioner judgments across the named case set).
This closes Chapter 8 §§0–1.

8.3 T82: Consistency / Finite Witness System
Section 2 establishes Theorem 8.2 (T82): the consistency of AX-SH. T82 is a formal satisfiability theorem—
we construct a finite witness system 𝑊 satisfying A1, A2, A3, A4 simultaneously and thereby establish that
the four-axiom system is logically satisfiable. The witness is drawn from SI1 (Bayyinah file-layer scanner)
vocabulary (Arfeen 2026c) to maximize compatibility with T83’s adequacy argument while remaining small
enough to be formally verified within the chapter. The section is presented in seven subsections: §2.1
supplies the witness construction; §2.2 supplies the substantive content; §§2.3–2.6 establish A1, A2, A3, A4
satisfaction in turn; §2.7 articulates the ecosystem assumptions under which the witness is operationally
nontrivial and identifies the witness’s limits.

8.3.1 Finite witness construction
The finite witness is the tuple 𝑊 = (𝑆, 𝑈 , 𝐶, Π, ∼) where: 𝑆 is a finite substrate (file-scanning system over
a finite set of file kinds); 𝑈 is a finite versioned surface (public API at two consecutive versions 𝑆0 , 𝑆1 ); 𝐶
is a finite caller community (two callers exercising 𝑅may against 𝑈 ); Π is a finite projection family (three
projections with explicit domains); and ∼ is a substrate-specific consistency relation (file-kind agreement
under joint reading).
𝑊 is finite under MP1.2’s finite-default convention (Chapter 3 §1.2): 𝑆 has a finite number of substrate
states; 𝑈 has two versions; 𝐶 has two callers; Π has three projections; the consistency relation is a finite
decidable predicate over projection outputs. The total structure is small enough to be formally verified by
enumeration.
The witness construction draws on SI1 vocabulary (Arfeen 2026c) without claiming to be SI1 in its full
operational form. SI1’s full scope covers 23 file kinds and 108 detection mechanisms; the T82 witness uses
three file kinds {PDF, TXT, BIN} and three detection mechanisms to remain minimal. The witness is structurally faithful to SI1 (the projections from Chapter 7 §1.6 are present in reduced form; the version-evolution
discipline matches Chapter 4 §1.1; the caller-side discharge follows Chapter 6 §1’s three discharge paths; the
projection consistency follows Chapter 7 §1’s joint-domain discipline), but is intentionally simplified for
verifiability.

8.3.2 Witness substrate / surface / caller / projection setup
Substrate 𝑆: A file-scanning system over a finite universe of file blobs. Each blob has an intrinsic file-kind from
the finite set {PDF, TXT, BIN}, an intrinsic content-classification (manifest content versus latent content),
and an intrinsic completeness status. The substrate state at each blob is the triple (kind, class, complete).
Surface 𝑈 : A versioned API with two versions 𝑆0 and 𝑆1 .

𝑆0 declares: scan(blob) returns a tuple

(kind, class, complete) under declared observer model 𝑂0 = “naked-eye file inspection at the kind layer,”
context set 𝐾0 = “file blobs of size up to 64MB,” and correspondence relation 𝑅0 = “scan output
matches intrinsic blob state under file-kind comparison.” 𝑆1 declares: scan(blob) returns the same tuple
(kind, class, complete) over the same context 𝐾1 = 𝐾0 , but extends 𝑅0 to include a parity-check provision
for PDFs (𝑅1 = 𝑅0 over all of 𝐾0 , with the additional PDF byte-identical parity check applied to the PDF
subset of 𝐾0 ). 𝑆1 introduces 𝑅1 as a strengthening of 𝑅0 (more demanding correspondence relation), not
a weakening: all 𝑅0 commitments over 𝐾0 are preserved in 𝑅1 . The version evolution from 𝑆0 to 𝑆1 is
corrigendum-free: no claim is withdrawn, only added.
Caller community 𝐶: Two callers 𝐶1 (a CI script that gates downstream processing on scan output) and
𝐶2 (an audit tool that cross-references scan output against an external manifest). Both callers exercise
𝑅may against the published surface; 𝑅may is the verifier/caller-side conservative over-approximation of 𝑅,
including the declared outcomes plus a small set of declared partial outcomes (scan-incomplete, scan-failed)
per Chapter 6 §1.
Projection family Π: Three projections {𝜋kind , 𝜋class , 𝜋complete } each of which carries the substrate’s intrinsic
kind as a shared coordinate alongside its specific output: 𝜋kind (𝑏) = (kind(𝑏)); 𝜋class (𝑏) = (kind(𝑏), class(𝑏));
𝜋complete (𝑏) = (kind(𝑏), complete(𝑏)). Each projection has explicit domain: 𝜋kind defined on all blobs in 𝐾0 ;
𝜋class defined on blobs the substrate has classified; 𝜋complete defined on blobs the substrate has fully scanned.
The shared kind coordinate makes the consistency relation well-defined: ∼ compares projection outputs on
their shared kind coordinate.
Consistency relation ∼: For two projections 𝜋𝑖 and 𝜋𝑗 and a substrate state 𝑠 in their joint domain, 𝜋𝑖 (𝑠) ∼
𝜋𝑗 (𝑠) iff the projections agree on file-kind under their joint reading. The relation is a finite decidable predicate
over projection outputs.

8.3.3 Witness satisfaction of A1
A1 requires Liskov-Wing version-subtyping with corrigenda discipline at the 𝑆0 → 𝑆1 transition. We show A1
holds. The 𝑆1 surface extends 𝑆0 ’s correspondence relation by strengthening: 𝑅1 includes 𝑅0 ’s commitments
plus the PDF parity check. No commitment from 𝑆0 is withdrawn; the only changes are additions. Under the
Liskov-Wing discipline (Liskov and Wing 1994), strengthening the correspondence relation is behaviorally
compatible with the prior version: a caller that depended on 𝑅0 still receives 𝑅0 ’s guarantees at 𝑆1 , plus
additional guarantees that the caller may or may not use. No corrigendum is required because no prior claim
is withdrawn. A1 holds.

8.3.4 Witness satisfaction of A2
A2 requires per-version surface-substrate consistency under declared (𝑂𝑖 , 𝐾𝑖 , 𝑅𝑖 ) at each version. We show
A2 holds at both 𝑆0 and 𝑆1 .

107

At 𝑆0 : 𝑅0 is the file-kind matching predicate. For every blob 𝑏 in 𝐾0 , scan(𝑏) returns the intrinsic file-kind
of 𝑏 (the scanner’s three-file-kind detection mechanism is exhaustive over {PDF, TXT, BIN}). Therefore
𝑅0 (Surface𝑆0 , Substrate𝑆0 ) holds: the surface’s declared scan output matches the substrate’s intrinsic filekind for every blob in 𝐾0 . A2 holds at 𝑆0 .
At 𝑆1 : 𝑅1 is 𝑅0 over 𝐾0 plus the PDF parity check applied to the PDF subset of 𝐾0 . For PDF blobs in 𝐾0 ,
scan(𝑏) returns the intrinsic kind plus a byte-identical parity assurance. The byte-identical assurance holds
because the witness construction includes a PDF parity-check mechanism that reads the blob’s raw bytes
and emits the parity signal correctly. For TXT and BIN blobs in 𝐾0 , 𝑅1 reduces to 𝑅0 (no parity check
claimed). Therefore 𝑅1 (Surface𝑆1 , Substrate𝑆1 ) holds. A2 holds at 𝑆1 .

8.3.5 Witness satisfaction of A3
A3 requires caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may with three discharge paths (Swamy et al. 2016; Vazou et
al. 2014). We show A3 holds for both callers 𝐶1 and 𝐶2 .
𝐶1 (CI script): handles scan output by gating downstream processing on (kind, complete) tuples. For
declared outcomes (kind ∈ {PDF, TXT, BIN} with complete = true), 𝐶1 handles each kind with a specific
downstream path. For declared partial outcomes (scan-incomplete, scan-failed), 𝐶1 propagates them as
incomplete upward via CI-pipeline status codes. 𝐶1 has no proven-unreachable certificates because it does
not claim any 𝑅may outcome is impossible—it handles or propagates all 𝑅may outcomes. The discharge is
exhaustive over 𝑅may .
𝐶2 (audit tool): handles scan output by cross-referencing against an external manifest. For declared outcomes, 𝐶2 records the cross-check result. For scan-incomplete outcomes, 𝐶2 propagates the incompleteness
into its audit log with a “deferred verification” annotation. 𝐶2 supplies proven-unreachable certificates for
outcomes that the audit tool’s pre-conditions exclude (e.g., scan-failed cannot occur for blobs the audit tool
has already verified as well-formed). The discharge is exhaustive over 𝑅may .
A3 holds for both callers, so the caller community discharges 𝑅may exhaustively. A3 holds.

8.3.6 Witness satisfaction of A4
A4 requires joint-domain projection consistency under ∼ (Mac Lane and Moerdijk 1994). We show A4 holds.
Joint domains: dom(𝜋kind ) ∩ dom(𝜋class ) ∩ dom(𝜋complete ) is the set of blobs the substrate has fully classified
and scanned. For any blob 𝑏 in this multi-way joint domain, 𝜋kind (𝑏), 𝜋class (𝑏), 𝜋complete (𝑏) are all defined.
The consistency relation ∼ requires that the projections agree on file-kind under their joint reading.
For each blob 𝑏 in the joint domain, the substrate’s intrinsic file-kind is fixed. Each projection output carries
the shared kind coordinate per §2.2: 𝜋kind (𝑏) = (kind(𝑏)), 𝜋class (𝑏) = (kind(𝑏), class(𝑏)), 𝜋complete (𝑏) =
(kind(𝑏), complete(𝑏)). The kind coordinate is computed from the same intrinsic blob state in each projection,
so all three projections agree on the kind coordinate at every 𝑏 in their joint domain. The consistency relation
∼ holds at every blob in the joint domain.
The three projections agree on file-kind under joint reading because each projection’s kind coordinate is
computed from the same intrinsic blob state, and the substrate’s intrinsic state is consistent within each

blob. A4 holds at all blobs in the joint domain. Blobs outside the joint domain—partially classified or
partially scanned—are outside A4’s scope per Chapter 7 §1.4’s joint-domain discipline.
The four satisfactions of §§2.3–2.6 together establish that 𝑊 satisfies A1, A2, A3, A4 simultaneously, yielding:
Theorem 8.2 (T82, Consistency of AX-SH). The four-axiom system A1–A4 is logically consistent: there
exists a finite witness 𝑊 = (𝑆, 𝑈 , 𝐶, Π, ∼) as constructed in §§2.1–2.2 such that 𝑊 satisfies A1, A2, A3, A4
simultaneously. □

8.3.7 Witness limits and explicit ecosystem assumptions
The witness 𝑊 is operationally nontrivial under specific ecosystem assumptions, which we make explicit.
These assumptions are operational-nontriviality conditions per §0.3, not fifth axioms; they specify when the
formal satisfiability T82 establishes has its intended structural-honesty interpretation.
Caller diversity assumption. The caller community 𝐶 contains two callers with distinct discharge patterns
(𝐶1 gates downstream; 𝐶2 cross-references). Without two callers, A3 could be trivially satisfied by a single
caller that handles only the most common outcomes—the witness’s A3 satisfaction would not test caller-side
discharge against 𝑅may . The assumption is operational, not formal: A3 is satisfied formally with any caller
community that exhausts 𝑅may , but the operational interpretation of A3 as a structural-honesty discipline
requires caller diversity.
Projection multiplicity assumption. The projection family Π contains three projections with overlapping but
non-identical domains. Without multiple independent projections, A4 could be trivially satisfied by a singleprojection family—the witness’s A4 satisfaction would not test projection consistency. The assumption is
operational, not formal.
Substantive evolution assumption. The 𝑆0 → 𝑆1 transition involves a substantive change (the PDF parity
check addition). Without substantive evolution, A1 would be trivially satisfied—the version chain would
contain no transitions to evaluate. The assumption is operational.
Corrigenda discipline exercised assumption. The witness construction does not include any corrigenda (because 𝑅1 strengthens 𝑅0 without withdrawing prior claims). A more demanding witness would include a
corrigendum event (e.g., a later 𝑆2 that withdraws a portion of 𝑅1 and tags the withdrawal as a corrigendum).
The current witness is suﬀicient for T82 (it demonstrates A1–A4 satisfaction) but does not exercise the corrigenda discipline; full operational testing of A1 requires substrate evolution that includes corrigendum events.
This is identified as a Chapter 21 falsification-protocol scope (named-open O5).
T82 establishes formal consistency through the explicit construction of 𝑊 satisfying A1–A4. The ecosystem
assumptions explain when this witness avoids triviality in operational settings. Weakening these assumptions
may reveal trivial-satisfaction surfaces that AD1 (§4) analyzes. The separation between formal consistency
and operational nontriviality follows the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2): T82 is a model-existence
theorem at the formal-consistency layer; the operational interpretation of consistency is conditional on the
named ecosystem conditions at the ecosystem-condition layer.

8.4 T83: Definitional Adequacy
Section 3 establishes the definitional adequacy of AX-SH relative to a named judgment-case set. T83 is an
empirical-relative adequacy argument, not a context-free proof. The argument is analogous to the epistemic
posture (§0.4) of adequacy arguments for ZFC, Peano arithmetic, and behavioral subtyping: adequacy is
judged relative to operational practitioner judgments on a named set of cases, not provable in absolute terms.
The section is presented in seven subsections. §3.1 constructs the named judgment-case set with positive,
negative, and boundary cases. §§3.2–3.4 supply the structured-interpretation mappings from SHV, Furqan,
and Munafiq operational vocabulary to AX-SH’s declared-object vocabulary. §3.5 supplies the SI1–SI4 adequacy mapping. §3.6 identifies boundary cases and non-covered cases, routing residual adequacy concerns to
Chapters 20 and 21. §3.7 articulates adequacy as relative-to-the-judgment-case-set, completing the empiricalrelative discipline that §0.4 set up.

8.4.1 Named judgment-case set construction
The judgment-case set 𝐽 = {𝐽1 , … , 𝐽𝑚 } is constructed as follows. Each judgment case is a triple (substratescenario, expected-classification, axiom-classification): the substrate-scenario is a specific substrate-callerprojection scenario drawn from SI1–SI4; the expected-classification is how operational practitioners in the
substrate’s community would classify the scenario (honest, dishonest, or debatable); the axiom-classification
is how A1–A4 classify the scenario under the substrate’s declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ).
The case set must include three categories.
Positive cases (cases practitioners would classify as structurally honest): for each of SI1–SI4, at least three
cases where the substrate operates correctly under its declared scope and practitioners would agree the
scenario is structurally honest. Examples: SI1 with a complete file-kind detection across all scanned files;
SI2 with a successfully type-checked program emitting no error diagnostics inconsistent with the type-check
result; SI3 with a marker-calibrated model output consistent with the marker’s confidence threshold; SI4
with a multi-layer attestation chain where all four substrates produce consistent attestations.
Negative cases (cases practitioners would classify as structurally dishonest): for each of SI1–SI4, at least three
cases where the substrate exhibits a structural-honesty failure that practitioners would recognize. Examples:
SI1 with an undeclared scan-incomplete that the surface treats as complete; SI2 with a successfully typechecked program emitting error diagnostics that contradict the type-check; SI3 with a marker-calibrated
model output that fails the calibration threshold without diagnostic flagging; SI4 with a multi-layer attestation chain where one layer’s attestation contradicts another.
Boundary cases (cases where practitioner judgment is debatable): for each of SI1–SI4, at least one boundary
case where practitioners would disagree about whether the scenario is structurally honest. These boundary
cases are not papered over—they are either classified by AX-SH with explicit rationale (the framework
correctly captures the practitioner’s judgment because of structural-honesty consideration 𝑋) or routed to
Chapter 21 as future-work items.
The named judgment-case set 𝐽 is enumerated by identifier at the chapter level; detailed substrate evidence
for each identifier is supplied by Chapters 13–16. The case identifiers are:

8.4.2 SHV vocabulary mapping
The Structural-Honesty Verification framework (Arfeen 2026h) uses an operational vocabulary that the
dissertation’s axiom system must capture. The structured interpretation from SHV terms to AX-SH terms
is: SHV “structural honesty” maps to A1–A4 satisfaction under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ); SHV
“surface-substrate distinction” maps to Chapter 3 §1’s typed-object machinery for surfaces and substrates;
SHV “attestation” maps to the producer’s published claim that 𝑅(Surface, Substrate) holds under declared
(𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅); SHV “certified-incomplete” maps to the propagated-incompleteness path in A3’s three discharge
paths; SHV “four-substrate stack” (Arfeen 2026f) maps to SI4 as the specific multi-layer attestation instance.
The mapping is a structured interpretation, not a semantic isomorphism. Each correspondence is justified
against the named judgment-case set: for every positive SHV case in 𝐽 (cases SHV practitioners would classify
as structurally honest), the AX-SH classification under the structured interpretation yields the same judgment;
for every negative SHV case, the AX-SH classification yields structural dishonesty; for boundary cases, the
AX-SH classification matches SHV practitioner judgment where rationale is explicit, and is identified as
Chapter 21 future-work when practitioner judgment is genuinely indeterminate.

8.4.3 Furqan vocabulary mapping
The Furqan language-layer type-checker (Ashraf and Arfeen 2026b, 2026a) uses an operational vocabulary specific to compile-time verification. The structured interpretation: Furqan “build-time type-checker” maps to
a producer-side mechanism evaluating 𝑅 at build-time under declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅); Furqan “structural-honesty
surface contract” maps to the public surface’s declared type signature; Furqan “compile-time guarantee”
maps to A2’s per-version surface-substrate consistency at build-time; Furqan “diagnostic emission” maps to

a projection in Π𝑋 capturing the type-checker’s diagnostic output; Furqan “type-check passing” maps to the
consistency relation ∼ between the type-check projection and the build-time-success projection.
The mapping is a structured interpretation, justified against Furqan’s judgment-case set drawn from SI2.
Each Furqan case in 𝐽 is classified by the AX-SH structured interpretation consistently with Furqan practitioner judgment.

8.4.4 Munafiq vocabulary mapping
The Munafiq Protocol (Arfeen 2026d) uses an operational vocabulary specific to model-layer evaluation. The
structured interpretation: Munafiq “marker” maps to the producer’s declared classification of model output
(e.g., high-confidence, low-confidence); Munafiq “calibration” maps to 𝑅’s correspondence relation between
marker and actual output reliability; Munafiq “four-process taxonomy” maps to the four process-types under
which marker classification operates; Munafiq “four-layer detection” maps to a projection family Π𝑋 with four
projections (marker, calibration, diagnosis, protocol-conformance); Munafiq “structural honesty in model
output” maps to A1–A4 satisfaction across markers, calibrations, diagnoses, and protocol conformance.
The mapping is a structured interpretation, justified against Munafiq’s judgment-case set drawn from SI3.

8.4.5 SI1–SI4 adequacy mapping
The four worked substrate instances together test the adequacy argument across the case set. SI1 (Bayyinah
file-scanner) operationally tests A1–A4 over file-layer substrates (Arfeen 2026c): for each judgment case in
𝐽 drawn from SI1, the AX-SH classification under SI1’s declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ) matches practitioner judgment. SI2 (Furqan type-checker) operationally tests A1–A4 over language-layer substrates: for
each judgment case in 𝐽 drawn from SI2, AX-SH matches practitioner judgment. SI3 (Munafiq Protocol)
operationally tests A1–A4 over model-layer substrates: for each judgment case in 𝐽 drawn from SI3, AX-SH
matches practitioner judgment. SI4 (Supply-chain stack) operationally tests A1–A4 over multi-layer attestation substrates (Sigstore project (Open Source Security Foundation) 2021; Torres-Arias et al. 2019; Open
Source Security Foundation 2023): for each judgment case in 𝐽 drawn from SI4, AX-SH matches practitioner
judgment.
The adequacy argument is positive relative to the named case set 𝐽 : for each case identifier named in
§3.1, Chapter 8 states the expected AX-SH classification (positive cases should yield AX-SH-honest classification under the substrate’s declared (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ); negative cases should yield AX-SH-dishonest
classification; boundary cases should yield either explicit-rationale classification or Chapter 21 routing).
Chapters 13–16 supply the detailed substrate-specific evidence for each case identifier. The present chapter
establishes the structured adequacy claim at the integrative level; the case-study chapters carry the detailed
evidentiary burden.

8.4.6 Boundary cases and non-covered cases
Several types of cases are not papered over but explicitly identified as future-work, preserving the Chapter 8
/ Chapter 21 boundary established in §0.5.
Boundary cases within the case set. For each of SI1–SI4, at least one boundary case exists where practitioner
judgment is debatable. Examples: an SI1 boundary case is a partially-classified file where the scanner emits

scan-incomplete but the file-kind detection is complete; practitioners disagree whether scan-incomplete on
classification should propagate to the file-kind layer. An SI2 boundary case is a successfully type-checked
program emitting warning-level diagnostics consistent with the type-check; practitioners disagree whether
warning-level diagnostics constitute a structural-honesty surface. These boundary cases are classified by
AX-SH under explicit rationale where possible; where rationale is debatable, the case is routed to Chapter 21
as future-work.
Cases outside the case set. T83 makes no claim about cases not in 𝐽 . Cases outside 𝐽 that would be relevant
to adequacy testing (cases from substrates not yet worked out in SI1–SI4, cases from substrate types that
do not exist yet in current operational practice) are explicitly out of T83’s scope. The adequacy argument
is relative to 𝐽 , not absolute. New substrate types are routed to Chapter 20 (substrate-generalization open
problem, ST1 and SC1 in Section 3 and Section 5 of the audit ledger).
Cases the framework does not yet handle adequately. If a case lies outside 𝐽 (e.g., a case from a substrate type
not yet worked out in SI1–SI4, or a case from a substrate type that does not exist yet in current operational
practice), it does not refute T83 but may motivate Chapter 20 expansion (substrate-generalization open
problem) or Chapter 21 expansion (falsification protocols and judgment-case set evolution). If a case lies
inside 𝐽 and AX-SH diverges from practitioner judgment without explicit rationale, that is evidence against
T83 for the current case set and must be recorded as a definitional-adequacy gap. T83’s falsifiability at
the empirical-relative layer of the Principle of Layered Defense (§0.2) requires that inside-𝐽 divergence be
treated as falsification, not as future-work; the framework’s structural-honesty discipline applies recursively
to T83 itself.

8.4.7 Adequacy as relative, not absolute
T83’s definitional-adequacy argument is empirical-relative to the named judgment-case set 𝐽 . The argument
does not establish absolute adequacy in a context-free sense. The structurally honest claim T83 makes is:
Theorem 8.3 (T83, Definitional Adequacy of AX-SH relative to 𝐽 ). For every judgment case 𝐽𝑘 in the
named judgment-case set 𝐽 (constructed per §3.1 with positive, negative, and boundary cases drawn from
SI1–SI4), the structured interpretation from operational vocabulary (SHV / Furqan / Munafiq, per §§3.2–3.4)
to AX-SH’s declared-object vocabulary classifies 𝐽𝑘 consistently with operational practitioner judgment for that
substrate. The argument is empirical-relative to 𝐽 and does not establish absolute adequacy. □
Two qualifications make the relative character explicit.
First, the adequacy claim is relative to 𝐽 . Cases outside 𝐽 are out of scope. The framework’s adequacy
may need extension or revision for new judgment cases that emerge in operational practice; this is part of
the framework’s expected falsifiability surface at the definitional-adequacy layer of the Principle of Layered
Defense (§0.2). The corrigenda discipline mechanism (Chapter 4 §1.1’s apparatus applied recursively to the
framework itself) provides the path for the framework to evolve as the judgment-case set evolves.
Second, the adequacy claim is relative to operational practitioner judgment as it currently exists. Practitioner
judgment itself evolves: new technologies create new artifact types whose honesty / dishonesty intuitions
were not anticipated; legal and regulatory regimes redefine adequate disclosure; cultural shifts change what
practitioners mean by honest. T83’s adequacy is judged against current practitioner judgment for the named
case set; it does not claim adequacy against future practitioner judgment under conditions that do not yet

exist. Long-horizon dynamics of practitioner-judgment evolution are routed to Chapter 21 (falsification
protocols, named-open O5).
The relative-not-absolute framing is analogous to the epistemic posture of adequacy arguments for formal
systems such as ZFC, Peano arithmetic, and behavioral subtyping (§0.4): adequacy is argued relative to the
intended domain and judgment practices, not proven in a context-free sense. T83 makes the empiricallydefensible adequacy claim available to the framework while acknowledging the relativity explicitly. This
closes Chapter 8 §§2–3.

8.5 AD1: Adversarial-Declaration Coverage
Section 4 evaluates the operational adversarial-declaration coverage of AX-SH (AD1). AD1 is the fourth
integrative obligation of Chapter 8: where T81 establishes logical falsifiability (each axiom can fail while the
others hold) and T82 establishes formal consistency (the system is satisfiable) and T83 establishes definitional
adequacy (the system corresponds to operational practitioner judgments across a named case set), AD1
evaluates whether the four-axiom system is operationally falsifiable under adversarial or weak declarations
of the axiom-relativized objects, and under which ecosystem conditions such trivial satisfaction becomes
detectable or structurally blocked. AD1 evaluates coverage; it does not prove universal robustness. The
structurally honest result of AD1 is a disclosure of which weak-declaration / weak-ecosystem scenarios AX-SH
exposes, which remain trivial-satisfaction holes, and which residual risks must be routed to Chapter 21.
The section is presented in nine subsections. §§4.1–4.4 supply the four weak-declaration scenarios (weak
(𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅), weak 𝑅may , weak Π𝑋 , weak ∼𝑋 ) as inputs to the coverage analysis. §§4.5–4.6 supply the two
principal ecosystem-failure scenarios (private / no-caller ecosystem; single-projection ecosystem) as conditions in the analysis. §4.7 synthesizes the cross-axiom coverage matrix as the disclosure mechanism for
evaluating which axioms expose which scenarios under which ecosystem conditions. §4.8 takes on emergent
misappropriation as a partial-falsifiability surface harder than authored adversarial declaration. §4.9 routes
residual risks to Chapter 21.

8.5.1 Weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) scenario: narrow operational scope from inception
The first adversarial-declaration scenario: a producer declares weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) from inception. Narrow observer model 𝑂 that observes only the public surface API without probing implementation behavior; narrow
context set 𝐾 that excludes meaningful workloads or boundary conditions; trivial correspondence relation
𝑅 that reduces to equality of declared values without substantive structural correspondence. The producer
satisfies A2 trivially because 𝑅 is too weak to require anything substantive of the surface-substrate relationship.
A1 is structurally silent on this scenario. A1 governs surface evolution; it does not govern the declared starting
point. A producer who declares weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) at 𝑣0 and never narrows the declaration is unconstrained
by A1’s corrigenda discipline, since no claim is being withdrawn. The asymmetry between evolution and
inception is one of the most consequential structural features of AX-SH’s coverage analysis.
Whether A3 or A4 expose this scenario depends on ecosystem conditions. A3 may expose weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅)
if the verifier/caller community’s 𝑅may is genuinely broader than the producer’s declared 𝑅 and the caller
community exercises that breadth (the discharge-path obligations force the producer to engage with out-

CHAPTER 8. INTEGRATIVE EVALUATION (T81/T82/T83/AD1)

114

comes the weak declaration excludes). A4 may expose weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) if the projection family Π𝑋 contains
projections that cross-check the surface-substrate relationship under a ∼𝑋 broader than the trivial declared
𝑅. Without these ecosystem conditions, weak (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅) goes uncaught — the producer satisfies the four
axioms while operating at a scope that practitioners would not recognize as structurally honest.

8.5.2 Weak 𝑅may scenario: under-declared possible outcomes
The second adversarial-declaration scenario: a publicly relied-on 𝑅may — whether producer-specified, verifierpublished, or caller-surface — is weak or under-approximating. 𝑅may is close to 𝑅: the declared set of
possible outcomes is barely broader than the declared set of intended outcomes, leaving genuine partial
outcomes outside the declared possible set. A3 callers can only discharge outcomes that the verifier/caller
regime represents in 𝑅may ; outcomes excluded from 𝑅may are simply not part of A3’s evaluation. Underapproximating 𝑅may makes A3 trivially satisfied: callers exhaust a thin 𝑅may through the three discharge
paths because there is little to discharge.
A2 is structurally silent on this scenario (A2 evaluates 𝑅, not 𝑅may ). A1 may expose this scenario if 𝑅may
has been published and is subsequently narrowed without corrigendum, but a publicly relied-on 𝑅may that
is under-approximating at inception and never narrowed is unconstrained by A1.
The ecosystem condition that exposes weak 𝑅may is adversarial-caller probing: callers who exercise the surface
against actual operational workloads and encounter outcomes outside the declared 𝑅may . The encountered
outcome creates a discharge-path obligation that the publicly relied-on declaration cannot satisfy, surfacing
the gap between declared 𝑅may and operational reality. Without diverse adversarial callers, weak 𝑅may goes
uncaught.

8.5.3 Weak Π𝑋 scenario: single-projection or non-cross-checking projection family
The third adversarial-declaration scenario: a producer declares a projection family Π𝑋 = {𝜋1 } (a single
projection, against which A4’s pairwise consistency check has no other projection to compare), or a projection
family whose projections conveniently align with the producer’s preferred declarations without cross-checking.
A4 is trivially satisfied: a single projection cannot disagree with itself, and conveniently-aligned projections
produce consistent outputs even when the underlying substrate diverges from the declarations.
A1 is structurally silent on this scenario for the same reason as in §4.1: the projection family is declared at
inception, and A1 governs evolution. A2 may expose this scenario if the declared 𝑅 is broader than what the
weak projection family can support (the surface-substrate consistency claim outruns the projection family’s
evidential support). A3 may expose this scenario if a caller requires multiple projection outputs and the
weak Π𝑋 does not supply them.
The ecosystem condition that exposes weak Π𝑋 is projection multiplicity and independence: multiple required
projections drawn from independent observation regimes such that their joint-domain consistency under ∼𝑋
is a substantive test. Without projection multiplicity and independence, weak Π𝑋 goes uncaught.

8.5.4 Weak ∼𝑋 scenario: trivial consistency relation
The fourth adversarial-declaration scenario: a producer declares a trivially-satisfied ∼𝑋 — the consistency
relation everything satisfies, or a consistency relation tailored to the producer’s preferred projections so that
the declared projections always satisfy it. A4 is trivially satisfied under trivial ∼𝑋 because the consistency
check imposes no substantive constraint.
A2 may expose this scenario if the declared 𝑅 requires correspondence beyond what the trivial ∼𝑋 tolerates (the surface-substrate consistency claim is stronger than the projection consistency the trivial ∼𝑋
permits). A1 is silent on inception. A3 is silent on ∼𝑋 choice directly, though caller-side probing may
surface inconsistencies that the trivial ∼𝑋 should have caught.
The ecosystem condition that exposes weak ∼𝑋 is an independent benchmark for the consistency relation
— for example, a substrate domain where practitioner consensus on ∼𝑋 exists (such as arithmetic identity
for double-entry bookkeeping, or stemmatic consistency for textual preservation philology). Without an
independent benchmark for ∼𝑋 , weak ∼𝑋 goes uncaught.

8.5.5 Private / no-caller ecosystem scenario
The first ecosystem-failure scenario: the substrate operates in a private setting without an adversarial caller
community, or with only callers that operate within the under-declared scope. A3 is structurally empty
in this case — there are no callers exercising 𝑅may against the surface, so the caller-side exhaustiveness
condition is vacuously satisfied regardless of declared 𝑅may content.
The scenario is not a violation of A3; A3 is satisfied formally. The scenario is an ecosystem-condition failure
that makes A3’s operational interpretation as a structural-honesty discipline vacuous. The substrate may
satisfy all four axioms formally while operating in an ecosystem that does not exercise the structural-honesty
discipline. The ecosystem-condition catalog from §0.3 names caller diversity as one of the operationalnontriviality conditions; the private-ecosystem scenario is precisely the failure of that condition.
The condition that restores operational nontriviality is the existence of a populated caller community whose
𝑅may obligations actually probe the surface’s claimed scope. This condition is operational, not formal: it
is a property of the substrate’s environment, not a property of the substrate’s declarations. The ecosystemcondition catalog is not a fifth axiom (§0.3); it is the catalog of conditions under which the formal axioms
have their intended structural-honesty interpretation.

8.5.6 Single-projection ecosystem scenario
The second ecosystem-failure scenario: the substrate’s projection family lacks multiplicity, or the projections
are correlated (all draw from the same underlying source, providing no cross-check). A4 is structurally empty
in this case — the joint-domain consistency check has no substantive content because the projections do not
independently constrain each other.
The scenario again is not a violation of A4; A4 is satisfied formally (trivially, in the single-projection case;
correlatedly, in the correlated-projection case). The scenario is an ecosystem-condition failure that makes
A4’s operational interpretation vacuous. The ecosystem-condition catalog names projection multiplicity and
projection independence as the conditions under which A4 has its structural-honesty interpretation.

8.5.8 Emergent misappropriation as partial-falsifiability surface
Adversarial-declaration scenarios in §§4.1–4.7 are authored: a producer or verifier makes a specific weak
declaration with knowledge that the declaration is weak. A structurally distinct and harder case is emergent
misappropriation: scope-misdeclaration by honest future users extending AX-SH’s scope through legitimate
intellectual labor across decades, without bad faith. A historical analogy from the reception of scientific
frameworks may be introduced in a later revision if cited and carefully framed; Chapter 8’s AD1 argument
does not depend on that analogy.
Emergent misappropriation operates differently from authored adversarial declaration. The producer does
not intentionally weaken declarations; future users extend the declarations beyond their original scope
through accumulated intellectual labor — pedagogical synthesis, theological elaboration, institutional embedding. By the time the misappropriation becomes visible, the framework’s scope-as-used has drifted from
the framework’s scope-as-declared, and the drift was authored by no specific party.
The framework’s response distinguishes recoverable from irrecoverable cases. Recoverable cases: the misappropriation has not yet become load-bearing in operational practice and can be corrigenda-tagged via
A1’s discipline — the framework’s authoritative version chain can append a corrigendum naming the misappropriation, withdrawing the appropriated scope, and restoring the original declared scope. Irrecoverable
cases: the misappropriation has become load-bearing operational practice before being corrigenda-tagged,
such that the framework’s appropriated scope is the de facto framework in operational use, and corrigendatagging at the authoritative version cannot retroactively reach the operational practice that has adopted the
appropriated scope.
The boundary between recoverable and irrecoverable is dynamic and substrate-specific. AX-SH plus the
corrigenda discipline bounds the damage if corrigenda are exercised in time, but cannot retroactively fix
history once misappropriation is deeply entrenched. The framework explicitly acknowledges this limit: AD1.8
evaluates emergent misappropriation as a partial-falsifiability surface, with the surveillance mechanisms by
which such misappropriation is detected routed to Chapter 21 (long-horizon falsification-protocol work).
Chapter 8 does not solve emergent-misappropriation surveillance; it names the case and the recoverable /
irrecoverable boundary.

9.1 §1.0 Role and scope
A structural-honesty claim about a system can be made, checked, and conveyed; and the layer at which
each of these happens is not the same. This chapter formalizes a distinction that Chapter 1 §3 introduced
informally: that a claim of the form “system 𝑆 satisfies axiom 𝐴𝑖 ” lives simultaneously at three layers —
a truth layer of mathematical fact, a verification layer of checking procedure, and a transmission layer of
conveyance infrastructure — and that these three layers stand in a strict dependency relation that runs in
one direction only.
The chapter’s purpose is to make that three-layer architecture precise enough to carry weight in the chapters
that follow. Chapter 10’s central result — that the verification of AX-SH is survivable across the cryptographic transitions of the coming decades, including the post-quantum transition — is a claim about which
layer the fragility of cryptography belongs to. That claim cannot even be stated cleanly until the truth, verification, and transmission layers have been separated and their dependency direction established. Chapter
9 supplies that scaffolding; Chapter 10 builds the survivability theorem on it.
The scope of this chapter is the formal architecture: the three layer definitions (§§1.1–1.3), the dependencydirection theorem and its statement (§1.4), the substrate-binding properties that distinguish the layers
(§1.5), the residence of the AX-SH satisfaction predicates across the three layers (§1.6), and the practical
consequences for software supply-chain attestation (§1.7). Two topics are deliberately out of scope for this
chapter and routed forward: the detailed cryptographic-primitive analysis of the transmission layer under
transition pressure (Chapters 12 and 17), and the information-theoretic strengthening of the verification
layer through independent re-derivation (Chapter 11). The chapter depends on the four axioms as stated in
Chapters 4–7, whose satisfaction predicates are the truth-layer objects this chapter places.

9.2 §1.1 The truth layer
The truth layer is the layer of mathematical facts about a system: whether each axiom holds of it. For an
axiom 𝐴𝑖 ∈ {A1, A2, A3, A4} with satisfaction predicate Π𝐴𝑖 , the truth-layer claim is the proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆)
— the assertion that 𝐴𝑖 holds of 𝑆. This is a proposition about mathematical objects: the system 𝑆 and
the axiom 𝐴𝑖 as defined in Chapters 4–7. Its content does not mention any verifier, any procedure, or any
attestation.
Two properties distinguish the truth layer. The first is substrate-independence: the truth value of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is
fixed by 𝑆 and 𝐴𝑖 alone, and carries no parameter ranging over the computational substrate of any procedure
that might evaluate it. Whether 𝐴𝑖 holds of 𝑆 is not a fact about software, or about any particular machine;

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

122

it is a fact about the mathematical objects the axiom constrains. The second property is non-decay: so
long as 𝑆 and AX-SH remain specifications of record, the truth value of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) does not change with time.
The cryptographic transitions that will, over decades, retire one signature scheme in favor of another (§1.3)
operate at a different layer entirely and cannot alter a truth-layer proposition. A claim that was true of 𝑆
under 𝐴𝑖 remains true of 𝑆 under 𝐴𝑖 regardless of what becomes of the infrastructure that once conveyed it.
It is worth stating plainly what the truth layer is not. It is not a claim that anyone has checked Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆),
nor that anyone could. It is the bare mathematical fact, prior to and independent of any act of verification.
The remaining two layers are precisely the layers at which checking and conveyance enter.

9.3 §1.2 The verification layer
The verification layer is the layer of procedures by which an external party establishes that an axiom holds.
A verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 is an algorithm that, given a system 𝑆 and an axiom 𝐴𝑖 , returns “verified” if and
only if Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) holds, within the decidable fragment characterized in Chapter 10. The qualifier matters: 𝑉𝑖 is
not claimed to decide Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) in full generality, but to decide it within the finite-default fragment established
as a standing convention in Chapter 3 §7, producing a finite witness of satisfaction or of violation in the
manner of Chapter 8 §2’s Theorem T82.
Two properties distinguish the verification layer.
cryptographically-bound.

The first is that 𝑉𝑖 is substrate-bound but not

It is substrate-bound in the trivial and unavoidable sense that an algorithm

must run somewhere: current implementations run on software, and future implementations may run
on other computational substrates. But 𝑉𝑖 ’s correctness is invariant across any substrate that faithfully
implements its algorithm — correctness is a property of the algorithm, not of the silicon — and, crucially,
𝑉𝑖 ’s correctness does not rest on any cryptographic-hardness assumption. The verification procedure is a
faithful implementation of the predicate Π𝐴𝑖 ; it is not a cryptographic protocol whose soundness depends
on the diﬀiculty of factoring or of computing discrete logarithms.

The second property is that 𝑉𝑖 is

finite-witness producing: by the Chapter 8 §2 convention, a run of 𝑉𝑖 yields a finite object that exhibits the
satisfaction or the violation, and that another party can re-check.
The verification layer is where the act of establishing a truth-layer claim takes place. It is bound to a
substrate in the weak sense that computation must be embodied, but it is not bound to cryptography, and
this independence is the hinge on which Chapter 10’s survivability result turns.

9.4 §1.3 The transmission layer
The transmission layer is the layer of cryptographic and infrastructural primitives by which verification
results are conveyed between parties. Its constituents are the familiar machinery of contemporary software
supply-chain attestation: digital signatures (as in sigstore’s signing of artifacts), attestation formats (as in
in-toto’s binding of a claim to the inputs that produced it), provenance frameworks (as in SLSA’s levels
of build integrity), and the trust roots on which these depend — certificate authorities, key servers, and
transparency logs.
A transmission-layer mechanism conveys a claim of the form “party 𝑃 verified that Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆).” It does not
itself establish Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆). A signature binds a claim to a signing principal; verifying that signature establishes

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

123

the provenance of the claim — that 𝑃 asserted it — not the truth of the claim. This distinction is the
substance of the dependency-direction theorem stated in the next subsection, and its sharpest illustration is
the cryptographically valid signature on a false claim: such an object is perfectly sound at the transmission
layer and entirely silent about whether the claim it carries is true.
The property that distinguishes the transmission layer is cryptographic contingency. The trust a transmissionlayer attestation commands depends on a cryptographic-hardness assumption, and such assumptions are not
permanent. They are subject to multi-decade transitions: the historical migration from SHA-1 to SHA-2
retired a hash function whose collision resistance had failed, and the anticipated post-quantum transition
will, when large-scale quantum computation arrives, retire the public-key schemes whose security rests on
the hardness of factoring and discrete logarithms. The transmission layer is the layer at which this fragility
lives, and §1.7 develops what follows from confining it there.

9.5 §1.4 Theorem 9.1 (Layer Dependency Direction)
The three layers are not symmetric. They stand in a strict dependency relation that runs in one direction.
Theorem 9.1 (Layer Dependency Direction). The truth layer 𝑇 , verification layer 𝑉 , and
transmission layer Tr satisfy the strict dependency relation Tr → 𝑉 → 𝑇 , in which each layer
depends on the one to its right; and the reverse does not hold. Specifically:
(a) any transmission-layer attestation of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) has evidential force only by way of some
verification-layer procedure 𝑉𝑖 that evaluated Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) — attestations convey a verdict, they do
not produce one (a cryptographically valid attestation can exist without any such 𝑉𝑖 , as the
forged-signature case in §2.1 shows, but it then carries no warrant for the claim it conveys);
(b) any verification-layer procedure 𝑉𝑖 ’s correctness criterion is defined relative to the truth-layer
predicate Π𝐴𝑖 — there is no notion of 𝑉𝑖 being correct independent of what Π𝐴𝑖 asserts;
(c) the truth-layer claim Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) holds or fails to hold independently of whether any 𝑉𝑖 exists or
any Tr conveys it; and correspondingly the reverse dependencies do not hold — 𝑇 does not depend
on 𝑉 or Tr, and 𝑉 does not depend on Tr.
The proof is supplied in §2, which discharges sub-claims (a), (b), and (c) separately and then establishes
the non-reverse direction. The present subsection states the theorem; §1.5 draws out the substrate-binding
consequences that the theorem makes available, and §1.6 applies the layered picture to the four AX-SH
satisfaction predicates.
The directional reading is the one that matters for the rest of the dissertation. Because Tr depends on 𝑉 and
𝑉 depends on 𝑇 , fragility introduced at the transmission layer cannot propagate leftward: a broken signature
scheme compromises the conveyance of a verdict without touching either the procedure that produced the
verdict or the mathematical fact the verdict reported.

9.6 §1.5 Substrate-binding properties
The dependency direction of Theorem 9.1 licenses three distinct substrate-binding characterizations, one per
layer, which §2 formalizes as Propositions 9.2 through 9.4.

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

124

The truth layer is substrate-independent. A truth-layer proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) has no substrate parameter; it is
identical whatever computational substrate one might consider, because it is a statement about mathematical
objects rather than about any embodiment of a procedure.
The verification layer is substrate-bound but not cryptographically-bound. A verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 must
execute on some substrate, but its correctness is invariant across substrates that faithfully implement its
algorithm, and — the load-bearing point — its critical path uses only primitives drawn from two primitive
classes: (a) symmetric-cryptographic primitives such as hash functions, and (b) information-theoretic primitives. It uses no public-key primitive. The taxonomy of these primitive classes is to be characterized in
Chapter 10 §1.1 (a forward chapter; not yet closed canon); at this chapter, the claim that 𝑉𝑖 stays within
classes (a) and (b) is the classification that Chapter 10 then shows to be quantum-survivable.
The transmission layer is cryptographically contingent.

Transmission-layer trust is conditional on a

cryptographic-hardness assumption 𝐻; should 𝐻 fail — as the public-key assumptions are expected to fail
under large-scale quantum computation — the attestation loses its trust value, while, by the substrateindependence of the truth layer and the cryptographic-independence of the verification layer, the truth-layer
and verification-layer claims are untouched.

This last proposition is the formal core of the chapter’s

quantum-survivability thesis, and it is the claim handed forward to Chapter 10’s decidable-fragment
primitive-class theorem.

9.7 §1.6 Residence of the AX-SH satisfaction predicates
Each satisfaction predicate Π𝐴𝑖 decomposes across the three layers, and the decomposition is the same in
shape for all four axioms. The truth-layer component of Π𝐴𝑖 is the mathematical proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) —
whether 𝐴𝑖 holds of 𝑆. The verification-layer component is the procedure 𝑉𝑖 that evaluates Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) within
Chapter 10’s decidable fragment, drawing only on primitive classes (a) and (b). The transmission-layer
component is the attestation infrastructure that conveys “𝑉𝑖 confirmed Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆)” between parties: the sigstore
signature on 𝑉𝑖 ’s verdict, the in-toto link binding that verdict to its inputs, the SLSA provenance record
situating it in a build.
This residence claim is not a notational convenience; it is the structural fact on which Chapter 10 rests.
Stated for all four axioms, it asserts that public-key cryptography — which lives entirely at the transmission
layer — is not in the critical path of either axiom satisfaction (a truth-layer matter) or axiom checking (a
verification-layer matter). Section 3 discharges the residence claim axiom by axiom, for A1 through A4,
and shows that the claim holds symmetrically: every Π𝐴𝑖 ’s verification-layer component uses at most a
symmetric-cryptographic primitive and never a public-key one. The present subsection states the residence
claim and its symmetry; §3 proves it per axiom and §3.5 instantiates it concretely.

9.8 §1.7 Practical implications
The three-layer architecture has direct consequences for the supply-chain four-substrate stack studied as
Substrate Instance 4 in Chapter 16, and these consequences are worth drawing out even before the peraxiom proofs of §3.
First, a sigstore signature on a build artifact is a transmission-layer attestation and nothing more: it conveys

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

125

that some party signed a claim about the artifact. It is not a verification-layer procedure and establishes
no axiom. When the public-key scheme underlying the signature fails — whether under quantum attack or
by any other route by which its hardness assumption is broken — the signature loses its transmission-layer
trust, but the underlying axiom-satisfaction claim does not thereby lose its truth-layer validity.
Second, and consequently, fallback to source-plus-specification verification is always available. A future
verifier with no access to the public-key infrastructure of the past can re-execute the verification procedure
𝑉𝑖 on (𝑆, 𝐴𝑖 ) and re-establish Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) directly, using only the primitive classes that §1.5 and §3 confine
the verification layer to. The structural-honesty substrate of a system — its truth-layer claims and the
verification-layer procedures that re-establish them — is in this sense durable across cryptographic transitions
in a way that the attestation fabric is not.
Third, the in-toto and SLSA layers of the stack provide transmission-layer attestations that likewise depend
on public-key primitives, and their cryptographic-transition obligation is therefore structural rather than
incidental: tools in this family should plan explicitly for post-quantum public-key transitions or for alternative
attestation mechanisms. The obligation is real, but it is localized. It belongs to the transmission layer, and
it leaves the truth and verification layers unaffected — which is precisely the localization that §3.5 walks
through in concrete detail on the SI4 stack.

9.9 §1.8 Proof obligations and successor-work routing
This chapter incurs four proof obligations, discharged in the sections that follow. The first is the proof
of Theorem 9.1 (the Layer Dependency Direction), supplied in §2, which discharges sub-claims (a), (b),
and (c) separately and establishes the non-reverse direction. The second is the formal statement of the
substrate-binding properties as Propositions 9.2 through 9.4, also supplied in §2. The third is the per-axiom
residence proof, supplied in §3, which places each Π𝐴𝑖 ’s truth-layer, verification-layer, and transmissionlayer components for A1 through A4 and establishes the symmetry of the residence claim. The fourth is
the practical-implications walkthrough on the SI4 stack, supplied in §3.5, which shows concretely how the
cryptographic-transition obligation localizes to the transmission layer.
Three successor chapters build on this architecture. Chapter 10 (Quantum Survivability of Verification)
operates within the verification-and-transmission architecture established here, proving that the verification procedures confined to primitive classes (a) and (b) are survivable across the post-quantum transition.
Chapter 11 (Information-Theoretic versus Cryptographic Substrates) develops the strength of the verification
layer through tawatur-style mass-transmission arguments, in which independent re-derivations of a verification result reinforce one another. Chapter 12 (Centuries-Scale Preservation Discipline) specifies multi-layer
replication operating across all three layers: truth-layer preservation through the stability of specifications,
verification-layer preservation through independent re-implementation, and transmission-layer preservation
through cryptographic agility.
