9.10 §2 Proof of Theorem 9.1 and the substrate-binding propositions
9.10.1 §2.0 The shape of the argument
Theorem 9.1 asserts a strict, directional dependency Tr → 𝑉 → 𝑇 with no reverse. The proof discharges the
three sub-claims of §1.4 in turn — (a) that the transmission layer depends on the verification layer, (b) that
the verification layer depends on the truth layer, and (c) that the truth layer depends on neither, together
with the two non-reverse facts that follow — and then formalizes the substrate-binding characterizations of
§1.5 as Propositions 9.2 through 9.4. Throughout, 𝑆 ranges over systems, 𝐴𝑖 over the four axioms of AX-SH,
Π𝐴𝑖 over their satisfaction predicates, and 𝑉𝑖 over verification procedures for Π𝐴𝑖 within the decidable
fragment that Chapter 10 characterizes.

9.10.2 §2.1 Sub-claim (a): the transmission layer depends on the verification
layer
We must show that any transmission-layer attestation of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) has evidential force only by way of some
verification-layer procedure 𝑉𝑖 that evaluated Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆). The argument turns on what an attestation is and
what it does.
A transmission-layer object — a sigstore signature, an in-toto link, an SLSA provenance record — is produced
by an attestation function that takes a claim and a signing key and returns a signed object: Att(claim, key) ↦
signature. This function does not take 𝑆, does not take Π𝐴𝑖 , and performs no evaluation of whether 𝐴𝑖 holds
of 𝑆. Its operation is purely cryptographic: it binds a claim to a principal. Verifying the resulting signature
establishes that the named principal asserted the claim — the claim’s provenance — and establishes nothing
about the claim’s truth.
The gap is exhibited sharply by the forged-but-valid signature on a false claim. Suppose a principal signs
the claim “Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆)” when in fact Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is false. The signature is cryptographically valid: it verifies against
the principal’s key, and the transmission layer reports no fault. Yet the claim it conveys is false. The
transmission layer is, by construction, silent on this difference; it certifies who said what, not whether what
was said is so.
It follows that an attestation’s evidential force — its capacity to count as warrant for believing Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) —
presupposes that some verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 actually established Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) upstream of the signing. This
is the precise sense of the dependency, and it is worth stating carefully to avoid a misreading. The claim is
not that a valid signature cannot exist without a prior 𝑉𝑖 run; the forged signature shows that it can. The
claim is that the signature’s evidential relation to the truth of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) exists only by way of an upstream
verification: the attestation conveys a verdict, and its trustworthiness as evidence for the verdict is exactly
the trustworthiness of the 𝑉𝑖 that produced the verdict. The transmission layer transports warrant; it does
not manufacture it. Hence Tr depends on 𝑉 .

■

9.10.3 §2.2 Sub-claim (b): the verification layer depends on the truth layer
We must show that the correctness of any verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 is defined relative to the truth-layer
predicate Π𝐴𝑖 . This is a definitional dependency, and the proof is correspondingly direct.

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

127

A verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 is correct exactly when, for the systems in its decidable fragment,
𝑉𝑖 (𝑆) = “verified” ⟺ Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) holds.
The right-hand side of this biconditional is a truth-layer proposition. The very statement of what it means for
𝑉𝑖 to be correct quantifies over Π𝐴𝑖 ’s content: there is no notion of “𝑉𝑖 is correct” that can be stated without
reference to the truth-layer fact the procedure is meant to track. A procedure that returned “verified” on
some other condition — one not coextensive with Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) within the fragment — would not be an incorrect
verifier of Π𝐴𝑖 ; it would be a verifier of something else. Correctness for 𝑉𝑖 is individuated by Π𝐴𝑖 .
The decidable-fragment qualifier does not weaken the dependency; it sharpens it. By the standing convention
of Chapter 3 §7 and the finite-witness construction of Chapter 8 §2 (Theorem T82), 𝑉𝑖 produces, within its
fragment, a finite witness exhibiting the satisfaction or the violation of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆). That witness is checkable
precisely because it is a witness for the truth-layer proposition: its adequacy is judged against Π𝐴𝑖 . Hence
𝑉 depends on 𝑇 .

■

9.10.4 §2.3 Sub-claim (c) and the non-reverse direction
We must show that Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) holds or fails independently of whether any 𝑉𝑖 exists or any attestation conveys
it, and that correspondingly the reverse dependencies fail: 𝑇 depends on neither 𝑉 nor Tr, and 𝑉 does not
depend on Tr.
For sub-claim (c) itself: Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is a proposition whose only free terms are the system 𝑆 and the axiom 𝐴𝑖 ,
both fixed mathematical objects under the definitions of Chapters 4–7. The proposition contains no variable
ranging over verifiers, procedures, or attestations. Its truth value is therefore determined by 𝑆 and 𝐴𝑖 alone,
and is what it is whether or not anyone ever checks it. This is sub-claim (c).
The non-reverse direction follows by two ablations (the third non-reverse fact, 𝑇 ⟂ Tr, is already subsumed
by sub-claim (c), since a truth-layer proposition independent of all verification is a fortiori independent of the
attestations that convey verification). First (𝑇 ⟂ 𝑉 ): remove every verification procedure from the world.
The proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) retains its truth value, because that value was never a function of any procedure
— it was fixed by 𝑆 and 𝐴𝑖 . So 𝑇 does not depend on 𝑉 . Second (𝑉 ⟂ Tr): remove every attestation
mechanism, every signing key, every transparency log. A verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 can still be run on (𝑆, 𝐴𝑖 ),
and by Chapter 8 §2 it still produces a finite witness of satisfaction or violation; nothing in 𝑉𝑖 ’s operation
consults a transmission-layer object. So 𝑉 does not depend on Tr.
Combining (a), (b), and (c): the dependency relation is the strict chain Tr → 𝑉 → 𝑇 , and the two ablations
show there are no reverse edges. This completes the proof of Theorem 9.1.

■

9.10.5 §2.4 The substrate-binding propositions
The dependency direction just established licenses three propositions, one per layer, formalizing the substratebinding characterizations stated informally in §1.5. Their statements are recorded in spec-canon at T9.13;
their proofs follow.
Proposition 9.2 (Truth-layer substrate-independence). For any computational substrates
𝜎, 𝜎′ , the proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is identical: it carries no substrate parameter.

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

128

Proof. Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is a statement about the mathematical objects 𝑆 and 𝐴𝑖 . A substrate 𝜎 enters the picture
only as a possible site of execution for a procedure, and Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) mentions no procedure. There is thus no
place in the proposition for a substrate parameter to occur, and the proposition one obtains “under 𝜎” is
■
syntactically and semantically the proposition one obtains under 𝜎′ .
Proposition 9.3 (Verification-layer substrate-boundedness without cryptographicboundedness). A verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 requires some substrate 𝜎 on which to execute;
its correctness is invariant across any 𝜎 that faithfully implements its algorithm; and its critical path uses only primitives from two primitive classes — (a) symmetric-cryptographic and (b)
information-theoretic — and no public-key primitive.
Proof. The first clause is the truism that an algorithm must be embodied to run. The second clause follows
from the definition of correctness in §2.2: correctness is the biconditional 𝑉𝑖 (𝑆) = “verified” ⟺ Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆), a
property of the algorithm’s input-output relation, and any substrate faithfully implementing the algorithm
realizes the same relation. The third clause — that the critical path stays within classes (a) and (b) and
uses no public-key primitive — is the per-axiom claim discharged in §3 below, where each of 𝑉𝐴1 , … , 𝑉𝐴4
is exhibited and its primitive usage classified. (The taxonomy of primitive classes (a) and (b) is to be
characterized in Chapter 10 §1.1, a forward chapter; at this chapter the third clause is the classification
result, established here per axiom, which Chapter 10 then takes as the hypothesis of its quantum-survivability
theorem.)

■

Proposition 9.4 (Transmission-layer cryptographic contingency). Transmission-layer
trust is contingent on a cryptographic-hardness assumption 𝐻; if 𝐻 fails, the attestation loses its
trust value, while the truth-layer and verification-layer claims are unaffected.
Proof. A transmission-layer attestation commands trust only insofar as its signature scheme is unforgeable,
which holds only under a hardness assumption 𝐻 (for current public-key schemes, the hardness of factoring
or of discrete logarithms). Should 𝐻 fail — as the public-key assumptions are expected to fail under largescale quantum computation — forgery becomes feasible and the attestation no longer warrants belief in its
conveyed claim. But by Proposition 9.2 the truth-layer proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is substrate- and assumptionindependent, and by Proposition 9.3 the verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 uses no public-key primitive in its critical
path; neither is touched by the failure of 𝐻. The loss is confined to the transmission layer.

■

Proposition 9.4 is the formal core of the chapter’s quantum-survivability thesis. It localizes cryptographic
fragility to the transmission layer and hands the verification layer’s primitive-class confinement (Proposition
9.3, discharged per axiom in §3) forward to Chapter 10, which proves that confinement to classes (a) and
(b) is survivable across the post-quantum transition.

9.11 §3 Residence of the satisfaction predicates and the SI4 walkthrough
9.11.1 §3.0 What §3 proves, and the division of labor with Chapter 10
Section 3 discharges the residence claim of §1.6: that each satisfaction predicate Π𝐴𝑖 decomposes across the
three layers, and that the decomposition is symmetric in the load-bearing respect — every 𝑉𝑖 ’s critical path
uses at most a symmetric-cryptographic primitive and never a public-key one. The section proceeds axiom
by axiom (§§3.1–3.4), concludes the symmetry (§3.4), and instantiates the whole picture on the supply-chain
stack of Substrate Instance 4 (§3.5).
One division of labor must be stated at the outset to forestall a circularity worry. Chapter 9 classifies: for
each axiom it exhibits the verification procedure and identifies which primitive classes its critical path uses.
Chapter 10 proves survivability: it takes “the critical path uses only classes (a) and (b)” as a hypothesis
and shows the procedure survives the post-quantum transition. The symmetry conclusion of §3.4 is the
classification result — “no public-key primitive in any 𝑉𝑖 ’s critical path” — not the survivability theorem.
Chapter 9 does not assume what Chapter 10 proves; it supplies the classified input that Chapter 10’s theorem
consumes.

9.11.2 §3.1 A1 (append-only provenance)
The truth-layer component of Π𝐴1 is the proposition that 𝑆’s provenance record is append-only and
corrigenda-disciplined, in the sense fixed by Axiom 1 in Chapter 4. The verification-layer component is the
procedure 𝑉𝐴1 that scans the provenance record for non-append mutations and checks the integrity of its
hash chain: each entry commits to its predecessor by hash, and a tampered or reordered history fails the
chain check. This is a finite-witness procedure — the witness is the offending entry, or the verified chain —
and its only cryptographic ingredient is the hash function, a primitive of class (a), symmetric-cryptographic.
No public-key primitive appears in 𝑉𝐴1 ’s critical path. The transmission-layer component is the attestation
that conveys “𝑉𝐴1 confirmed A1 for 𝑆” — typically a sigstore signature over the verdict, an in-toto link
binding it to the inputs, an SLSA record situating it.
That the A1 verification critical path uses only hash-chaining is the residence fact for A1, and it is the one
axiom whose verification touches cryptography at all. Even here the cryptography is symmetric, of the kind
transparency logs already rely on, and is the kind Chapter 10 is assigned to show survives the post-quantum
transition.

9.11.3 §3.2 A2 (surface-substrate consistency)
The truth-layer component of Π𝐴2 is the proposition that Surface(𝑆) is consistent with Substrate(𝑆) under
the declared correspondence relation 𝑅, in the sense fixed by Axiom 2 in Chapter 5. The verificationlayer component is the procedure 𝑉𝐴2 that checks the correspondence appropriate to the declared claim — a
bisimulation, simulation, or refinement check, drawn from the relation family of Chapter 5 §1.4 — within the
decidable fragment of Chapter 3 §7, producing a finite witness. This is a behavioral-equivalence computation
over typed objects; it consults no cryptographic primitive of any class. The transmission-layer component
is, as before, the attestation of the 𝑉𝐴2 verdict. The residence fact for A2 is therefore stronger than for A1:

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

130

𝑉𝐴2 ’s critical path contains no cryptographic primitive at all.

9.11.4 §3.3 A3 (caller-side exhaustiveness)
The truth-layer component of Π𝐴3 is the proposition that caller-side coverage over 𝑅may provides defensible exhaustiveness, in the sense fixed by Axiom 3 in Chapter 6. The verification-layer component is the
procedure 𝑉𝐴3 that checks caller coverage against the conservative over-approximation 𝑅may , confirming for
each outcome in the caller’s scope that it is handled, propagated-as-incomplete, or proven-unreachable —
the three discharge paths of Chapter 6 §§1.1–1.4, with 𝑅may itself constructed under the over-approximation
discipline of Chapter 3 §§5.1 and 5.4. This is a finite-witness set-coverage check; like 𝑉𝐴2 it consults no
cryptographic primitive. The transmission-layer component is the attestation of the verdict. The residence
fact for A3: no cryptographic primitive in 𝑉𝐴3 ’s critical path.

9.11.5 §3.4 A4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency), and the symmetry conclusion
The truth-layer component of Π𝐴4 is the proposition that the projection family is consistent across substrate
parameterization, in the sense fixed by Axiom 4 in Chapter 7. The verification-layer component is the
procedure 𝑉𝐴4 that checks projection consistency across the substrate-parameter family using the localsection and restriction-map machinery of Chapter 7 §1, within the decidable fragment, producing a finite
witness. This machinery is algebraic, not cryptographic; 𝑉𝐴4 ’s critical path contains no cryptographic
primitive. The transmission-layer component is the attestation of the verdict.
The four per-axiom results now combine.

For A1, the verification critical path uses a symmetric-

cryptographic primitive (hash-chaining) and no public-key primitive. For A2, A3, and A4, the verification
critical path uses no cryptographic primitive at all. In every case, then, the verification of an AX-SH
axiom uses at most a symmetric-cryptographic primitive and never a public-key one. This is the symmetry
conclusion: public-key cryptography is absent from the critical path of every 𝑉𝑖 . It is the residence claim
of §1.6 discharged, and — as the division of labor in §3.0 stressed — it is the classified hypothesis that
Chapter 10’s Quantum-Survivable Verification Theorem requires.

■

9.11.6 §3.5 The SI4 walkthrough
The supply-chain four-substrate stack of Substrate Instance 4 (Chapter 16) instantiates the three-layer
architecture concretely, and walking through it makes the localization of cryptographic fragility tangible.
Consider a build artifact moving through the stack. It carries a sigstore signature, an in-toto attestation
binding it to its build inputs, and an SLSA provenance record — three transmission-layer objects. The
structural-honesty claims about the artifact, that it satisfies A1 through A4, are truth-layer facts. The
procedures that re-establish those claims — 𝑉𝐴1 through 𝑉𝐴4 , with the primitive usage classified in §§3.1–
3.4 — are verification-layer activities. It is worth stating explicitly, since the stack’s most visible machinery
is its signing infrastructure, that structural-honesty verification itself lives at the verification layer, not the
transmission layer: running 𝑉𝐴𝑖 on the artifact is a verification act, and the signature that later conveys its
verdict is a separate, transmission-layer act.
Now suppose the public-key hardness assumption underlying the sigstore signature fails — under quantum

CHAPTER 9. THE TRUTH, VERIFICATION, AND TRANSMISSION LAYERS

131

attack, or by any other route by which the assumption is broken. By Proposition 9.4 the transmission-layer
attestations lose their trust value: the signatures can no longer be relied upon as unforgeable. But by
Propositions 9.2 and 9.3 the truth-layer claims remain valid and the verification-layer procedures remain
re-runnable: a verifier with no access to the compromised infrastructure can re-execute 𝑉𝐴1 through 𝑉𝐴4
on the artifact’s source and specification and re-establish A1 through A4 directly, using only the primitive
classes §§3.1–3.4 confine them to. The fallback to source-plus-specification verification, named in §1.7, is
exactly this re-execution.
The conclusion is the chapter’s thesis made concrete: when the cryptography of the attestation fabric ages
out, the obligation to migrate falls entirely on the transmission layer. The structural-honesty substrate —
the truth-layer claims and the verification-layer procedures that re-establish them — is untouched, and is
in this precise sense durable across the cryptographic transitions that the attestation fabric is not. The
general survivability of that durability across the post-quantum transition is the burden of Chapter 10; what
Chapter 9 has shown is that the burden falls where Chapter 10 can discharge it — on a verification layer
confined to symmetric and information-theoretic primitives.

10.1 §1.0 Role and scope
Chapter 10 carries two burdens, and it is worth saying at the outset that they are distinct burdens that
happen to be discharged in the same place. The first is the dissertation’s central long-horizon result: that
the verification of AX-SH survives the cryptographic transitions of the coming decades, the post-quantum
transition foremost among them. The second is a piece of formal housekeeping that five earlier chapters
deferred to this one: the characterization of the decidable fragment within which AX-SH verification actually
runs. The two are independent in principle — one could imagine a dissertation that proved survivability
without ever pinning down decidability, or vice versa — but they meet here because the survivability theorem
is most naturally stated relative to the very fragment the housekeeping defines.
The first role, quantum survivability, builds directly on Chapter 9. Chapter 9 separated the truth, verification,
and transmission layers and classified, axiom by axiom, which cryptographic primitives the verification
procedures actually use; its §3.4 reached the conclusion that no AX-SH verification procedure places a publickey primitive in any critical path. That conclusion is the load-bearing hypothesis of the present chapter.
Chapter 10 does not re-establish it. It takes Chapter 9 §3.4 as given and proves the consequence: that a
verification procedure built only from the surviving primitive classes remains sound and executable against
an adversary holding a large-scale quantum computer. The division of labor is the one Chapter 9 §3.0 set
down explicitly — Chapter 9 classifies; Chapter 10 proves survivability from that classification — and the
present chapter is written to honor it without slippage.
The second role, the decidability burden, is Chapter 10’s own contribution rather than an inheritance. Chapters 4 through 7 each close their decidability-scope subsection — §1.7 for A1, A3, and A4, and §1.8 for A2 —
with a forward-pointer to “Chapter 10’s decidable fragment,” and Chapter 8 §2’s finite-witness construction
(T82) operates, in its own words, within whatever decidable fragment Chapter 10 establishes. This chapter closes those pointers by characterizing, uniformly across the four axioms, what it means for an AX-SH
fragment to be decidable.
The scope of this opening section is the apparatus that the two roles require: the primitive-class taxonomy
by which survivability is judged (§1.1); the decidable-fragment framework (§1.2) and its per-axiom instantiation (§1.3); the quantum threat model and the definition of “quantum-survivable” (§1.4); the statement
of Theorem 10.1 (§1.5) and of its centuries-scale Corollary 10.2 (§1.6); and the practical consequences for
software supply-chain attestation (§1.7), before the proof obligations are routed forward (§1.8). Three topics
are deliberately out of scope and handed onward: the information-theoretic strengthening of the verification
layer through 𝑛-fold independent re-implementation (Chapter 11); the operational discipline of preserving
artifacts and specifications across long horizons (Chapter 12); and the genuinely undecidable fragments, together with settings in which the artifact or specification has not been preserved, which are routed to the

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

134

open-problems treatment (Chapter 17) and the falsification analysis (Chapter 21).

10.2 §1.1 The primitive-class taxonomy
Survivability is a claim about how a procedure fares against a particular adversary, and so it must be
indexed to the cryptographic primitives the procedure relies on. This section fixes a three-way classification
of primitives by their resilience to quantum attack. It is the same taxonomy Chapter 9 §1.5 and Proposition
9.3 invoked as a scoped forward-assumption, named there but characterized here; closing that forwardreference is part of this section’s work.
The first class, (a) symmetric-cryptographic primitives, comprises hash functions, symmetric ciphers,
and message-authentication codes. These are quantum-weakened but survivable. The sharpest general quantum attack against them is Grover’s algorithm, which accelerates unstructured search quadratically; against
a primitive offering 𝑛 bits of classical security, Grover reduces the effective security to roughly 𝑛/2 bits. The
mitigation is bounded and one-time: doubling the relevant parameter — moving from SHA-256 to SHA-512,
or from AES-128 to AES-256 — restores the original security margin. There is no unbounded escalation
here, a point that matters for the centuries-scale claim and is made precise in §1.4 and discharged in §2.
The second class, (b) information-theoretic and non-cryptographic primitives, comprises bitidentical equality checks, decidable graph- and type-system algorithms, mechanical extraction of structure
from an artifact, and the 𝑛-fold independent-re-implementation reference-parity that Chapter 11 will
develop.

These are quantum-unconditional.

The unifying property of the class is the absence of any

computational-hardness assumption, and it covers two superficially different things under one heading:
primitives that are information-theoretically secure in the cryptographic sense, and plain non-cryptographic
computation that has no “security” to break in the first place. A bit-identical comparison of two artifacts
does not become easier to subvert because an adversary has a quantum computer; there is nothing in it for
a quantum algorithm to attack. Because the class rests on no hardness assumption, no quantum algorithm
bears on it at all.
The third class, (c) public-key primitives, comprises RSA, Diﬀie–Hellman, and the elliptic-curve schemes
ECC and ECDSA. These are quantum-broken. Shor’s algorithm solves integer factorization and the discretelogarithm problem in polynomial time on a large fault-tolerant quantum computer, and the security of every
primitive in this class reduces to the hardness of one of those problems.
The taxonomy thus partitions into the survivable classes (a) and (b) and the broken class (c). The whole of
Chapter 10’s survivability argument turns on a single structural fact, established in Chapter 9 and consumed
here: that AX-SH verification lives entirely within classes (a) and (b).

10.3 §1.2 The decidable-fragment framework
The decidability burden is discharged by saying, once and uniformly, what a “decidable AX-SH fragment” is,
and then instantiating that definition per axiom in §1.3. The framework rests on the finite-default fragment
of Chapter 3 §7, the standing convention by which the dissertation treats state spaces as finite or otherwise
decidable unless a construction explicitly requires otherwise.
A fragment is decidable when three conditions hold together. First, the underlying state spaces over which the

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

135

axiom’s satisfaction predicate quantifies are finite or otherwise decidable. Second, the equality, consistency,
and subtyping checks that constitute the satisfaction predicate are themselves decidable relations. Third,
the finite-witness construction of Chapter 8 §2 (T82) succeeds: there is a finitary object that witnesses
satisfaction, or a finitary counterexample that witnesses violation. The third condition is what connects
decidability to verification in the operational sense, since it is the finite witness that a verification procedure
actually inspects.
The four-axiom decidable fragment is the conjunction of the four per-axiom decidable fragments characterized
in §1.3: a system lies within it when each of the four satisfaction predicates is decidable in the sense just
given. Theorem 10.1 is stated relative to this fragment, and its scope is exactly the fragment’s scope; systems
falling outside it are routed to Chapter 17, not silently assumed away.

10.4 §1.3 Per-axiom decidable-fragment scope
The general framework of §1.2 specializes to four concrete sets of conditions, one per axiom. In each case
the condition is a statement about decidability — Chapter 10’s own contribution — while the question of
which primitive classes the corresponding verification procedure uses is not settled here: it was settled in
Chapter 9 §§3.1–3.4 and is consumed below as a citation, not re-derived.
For A1 (append-only provenance), the satisfaction predicate is decidable under finite version histories, a finite
set of truth-status tags, and decidable behavioral-subtyping, as routed from Chapter 4 §1.7. For A2 (surface–
substrate consistency), it is decidable under finite observer-model and context-set data (𝑂, 𝐾), a finite-state
correspondence relation 𝑅 drawn from the family of Chapter 5 §1.4, and a finite-state substrate, with the
relevant decidability scope at Chapter 5 §1.8. For A3 (caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may ), it is decidable
under a finite 𝑅may , finite caller-discharge specifications, and decidable invariant-verification for the provenunreachable cases, as routed from Chapter 6 §1.7. For A4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency),
it is decidable under finite projection families Π𝑋 , finite joint domains, and a decidable consistency relation
∼𝑋 , as routed from Chapter 7 §1.7.
In every one of the four cases, the fact that the verification procedure carries no public-key primitive in its
critical path is established in Chapter 9 §§3.1–3.4 and consumed here. The reader who wishes to confirm that
no class-(c) primitive lurks in any of these procedures is directed to Chapter 9, which owns that classification;
the present section’s claim is only that, given that classification, the satisfaction predicates are decidable
under the stated finiteness conditions. Fragments that violate those conditions — unbounded histories,
undecidable consistency relations, and the like — are undecidable and route to Chapter 17.

10.5 §1.4 The quantum threat model
The adversary against which survivability is judged is one in possession of a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer: an adversary able to run Shor’s and Grover’s algorithms at the scales their asymptotic
analyses assume. This is the standard post-quantum threat model, and the taxonomy of §1.1 was built to
be read against it.
Against this adversary the three classes fare as §1.1 described. Class (c), public-key, is broken in polynomial
time by Shor. Class (a), symmetric, is preserved at a bounded parameter increase: Grover’s quadratic

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

136

speedup halves the effective security level, and a one-time doubling of the output or key size restores it.
Class (b), information-theoretic and non-cryptographic, is preserved unconditionally, because it rested on no
hardness assumption for the adversary to dissolve.
This licenses the chapter’s central definition. A procedure is quantum-survivable when it remains both
sound and executable under this adversary, subject to two conditions: it may rely on class-(a) primitives only
at bounded, one-time parameter increases, and it may not rely on any class-(c) primitive at all. The definition
is deliberately operational — “sound and executable,” not merely “not provably broken” — because the use
to which it is put in Corollary 10.2 is the concrete re-execution of a verification procedure by a future party,
not an abstract security reduction.

10.6 §1.5 Theorem 10.1 (Quantum-Survivable Verification) —
statement
The chapter’s principal result can now be stated.
Theorem 10.1 (Quantum-Survivable Verification). Within the four-axiom decidable fragment of §1.2–§1.3, for each AX-SH axiom 𝐴𝑖 the verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 is quantum-survivable.
Because, by Chapter 9 §3.4, the critical path of 𝑉𝑖 uses only primitives from classes (a) and
(b) and never a class-(c) public-key primitive, 𝑉𝑖 remains sound and executable under the §1.4
quantum adversary, with at most bounded parameter increases for any class-(a) primitive it employs. Equivalently: AX-SH verification places no public-key primitive in any critical path, and
therefore survives the post-quantum transition.
Two features of the statement deserve emphasis, both bearing on the discipline of the chapter. First, the
hypothesis is Chapter 9 §3.4’s conclusion, cited rather than re-derived; the theorem’s antecedent “the critical
path of 𝑉𝑖 uses only classes (a) and (b)” is precisely what Chapter 9 proved and what Chapter 10 is forbidden,
by Chapter 9 §3.0’s division of labor, from re-proving. Second, the statement is a statement only: the proof
is routed to §2, where the survivability of classes (a) and (b) established in §1.4 is applied to the Chapter
9–classified critical paths within the §1.2 decidable fragment. Stating the theorem here and proving it there
is the spec-then-prose boundary the dissertation has maintained since Chapter 3, not a deferral of diﬀiculty.

10.7 §1.6 Corollary 10.2 (centuries-scale re-verification) — statement
The post-quantum transition is the nearest of a family of cryptographic-infrastructure losses the dissertation
cares about, and Theorem 10.1 generalizes to the rest of that family in a single step.
Corollary 10.2 (centuries-scale re-verification). Any future verifier with no access to past
cryptographic infrastructure — no key servers, no transparency logs, no live public-key roots
of trust — can independently re-verify any prior structural-honesty claim from the preserved
artifact and specification alone, by re-executing 𝑉𝑖 within the decidable fragment. Confined to
classes (a) and (b), 𝑉𝑖 requires no surviving public-key infrastructure to run.
The corollary’s reach is wider than the post-quantum transition that motivates it. It speaks to durability

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

137

across arbitrary loss of cryptographic infrastructure — the disappearance of a certificate authority, the
abandonment of a transparency log, the obsolescence of an entire signature ecosystem — because the property
it relies on is not that any particular scheme survives but that the verification procedure never needed one.
Its proof, routed to §2, runs through Theorem 10.1 together with two results Chapter 9 hands forward: the
source-plus-specification fallback of Chapter 9 §1.7, which guarantees that re-verification consults only the
artifact and the specification, and Proposition 9.2’s truth-layer substrate-independence, which guarantees
that the proposition being re-verified has not itself decayed with time. The corollary is scoped, as the theorem
is, to preserved artifact–specification pairs within the decidable fragment; the discipline of achieving that
preservation is Chapter 12’s subject.

10.8 §1.7 Practical implications
The theorem and its corollary have concrete consequences for the software supply-chain stack that substrate
instance SI4 (Chapter 16) models, and stating them sharpens the contrast between what the surviving
verification layer guarantees and what the transmission layer must still manage.
The first consequence is that a signature — a sigstore signature, in SI4’s terms — is an eﬀiciency optimization
on verification rather than a precondition for it. A signature lets a party accept a verification verdict without
re-running 𝑉𝑖 itself, which is a real and worthwhile economy. But it is an economy, not a foundation: when
the signature’s public-key scheme breaks, the party can always fall back to re-running 𝑉𝑖 on the artifact and
specification, exactly as Chapter 9 §1.7 provides. The second consequence follows immediately: that fallback
path is permanent, not contingent on any cryptographic assumption, because 𝑉𝑖 itself depends on none. The
slow path is always open.
The third consequence concerns where the post-quantum obligation actually falls. Sigstore, in-toto, and
SLSA all depend on public-key signatures — class (c) — and therefore each carries a real cryptographictransition obligation: each must, over the coming years, migrate to post-quantum public-key schemes. But
that obligation is localized, by Chapter 9 Proposition 9.4, to the transmission layer. It never reaches the
truth layer, where the proposition Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) lives untouched, nor the verification layer, where 𝑉𝑖 runs without
any public-key primitive at all. The supply-chain stack has post-quantum work to do; the point of Theorem
10.1 is that the work is confined to the layer that conveys verdicts, and leaves the layer that establishes them
alone.

10.9 §1.8 Proof obligations and successor-work routing
This section closes by recording what the remainder of the chapter must discharge and what it routes
onward. Four obligations pass to §§2-3. The proof of Theorem 10.1 (§2) must apply the class-(a) and class(b) survivability of §1.4 to the Chapter 9–classified critical paths, within the §1.2 decidable fragment. The
proof of Corollary 10.2 (§2) must compose Theorem 10.1 with the Chapter 9 §1.7 fallback and Proposition 9.2.
The per-axiom application (§3) must instantiate the theorem on each of A1 through A4 and on the SI4 stack.
And the cryptographic-transition-obligation contrast (§3) must develop, against the sigstore/in-toto/SLSA
case, the localization of the post-quantum obligation to the transmission layer.
Two successor chapters are routed forward from here. Chapter 11 strengthens class (b) through the 𝑛-fold
independent re-implementation that yields reference-parity, a mass-transmission strengthening in the spirit

of tawatur: many independent witnesses to the same structural fact. Chapter 12 develops the operational
discipline of preserving artifacts and specifications across the centuries-scale horizon that Corollary 10.2
presupposes.
The boundary of §1 is the boundary the version status announced: this section has stated the taxonomy,
the decidable-fragment framework, the threat model, the theorem, and the corollary. It has not proved the

10.10 §2 Proof of Theorem 10.1 and Corollary 10.2
10.10.1 §2.0 The shape of the argument
Theorem 10.1 asserts that, within the four-axiom decidable fragment, each verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 is
quantum-survivable. The proof is a composition argument over the primitive classes of §1.1, and it rests
on a hypothesis it does not itself establish: that, by Chapter 9 §3.4, the critical path of every 𝑉𝑖 uses only
primitives of classes (a) and (b) and never a class-(c) public-key primitive. That classification is Chapter 9’s
result, consumed here; the present section proves only the survivability that follows from it.
The argument proceeds in four steps. Two lemmas treat the surviving classes in isolation: Lemma 10.1a
establishes that a class-(a) primitive remains sound and executable under the quantum adversary at a
bounded, one-time parameter increase (§2.1), and Lemma 10.1b establishes that a class-(b) primitive is
quantum-invariant (§2.2). The proof of Theorem 10.1 then composes these two facts over the Chapter 9–
classified critical path (§2.3). Corollary 10.2 follows by combining the theorem with two results Chapter
9 hands forward (§2.4). The section closes with the boundedness property that the centuries-scale reading
requires, and the scope conditions that bound the claim (§2.5). Throughout, 𝑆 ranges over systems, 𝐴𝑖 over
the four axioms of AX-SH, Π𝐴𝑖 over their satisfaction predicates, and 𝑉𝑖 over verification procedures for Π𝐴𝑖
within the decidable fragment of §1.2.

10.10.2 §2.1 Lemma 10.1a: survivability of class-(a) primitives
Lemma 10.1a (class-(a) survivability). Let 𝑃 be a symmetric-cryptographic primitive (a
hash function, symmetric cipher, or message-authentication code) whose security rests on the
infeasibility of an unstructured search over a space of size 2𝑛 . Under the quantum adversary of
§1.4, 𝑃 remains sound at the bounded, one-time parameter increase 𝑛 ↦ 2𝑛, and its executability
is unaffected.
Proof. The strongest general quantum attack against a primitive of this kind is Grover’s algorithm, which
√
finds a marked element in an unstructured search space of size 𝑁 using Θ( 𝑁 ) evaluations, a quadratic
speedup over the classical Θ(𝑁 ). Applied to the search problem on which 𝑃 ’s security rests — inverting the
primitive on a target, or finding a forgery — Grover reduces the adversary’s work from order 2𝑛 to order
2𝑛/2 . The effective security level is therefore at most halved, from 𝑛 bits to 𝑛/2 bits.
Two observations make this a bounded loss rather than the beginning of an erosion. First, Grover’s quadratic
speedup is optimal: the lower bound of Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard, and Vazirani establishes that no
√
quantum algorithm solves unstructured search in fewer than Ω( 𝑁 ) queries, so there is no further quantum

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

139

speedup beyond the quadratic for 𝑃 ’s security to lose. Second, the loss is recovered by a single doubling
of the size parameter: replacing 𝑃 at 𝑛-bit security with the corresponding primitive at 2𝑛-bit security (for
instance SHA-256 by SHA-512, or AES-128 by AES-256) restores the post-quantum effective security to
𝑛 bits, the pre-quantum margin. The increase is one-time — it answers a fixed quadratic speedup, not a
moving target — and it is bounded, in that no iteration of the mitigation is required.
Executability is unaffected because the doubled-parameter primitive is an ordinary symmetric primitive,
evaluated by the verifier exactly as the original was; the verification procedure that invoked 𝑃 now invokes
its doubled-parameter counterpart, at the same asymptotic cost up to the constant implied by the larger
parameter. Hence 𝑃 remains both sound and executable under the quantum adversary at the parameter
increase 𝑛 ↦ 2𝑛. □
A remark on collision resistance, which is the security property the provenance hash-chaining of §3.1 will
rely on. The generic quantum collision attack (the Brassard–Høyer–Tapp algorithm) is sometimes quoted
as reducing collision resistance from 2𝑛/2 to 2𝑛/3 ; under the realistic accounting that charges for quantum
memory, its advantage over classical collision search is smaller still. In either accounting the loss is bounded
and is covered, conservatively, by the same one-time output-size doubling, so the lemma’s mitigation applies
to collision resistance without modification.

10.10.3 §2.2 Lemma 10.1b: survivability of class-(b) primitives
Lemma 10.1b (class-(b) survivability).

Let 𝑄 be an information-theoretic or non-

cryptographic primitive — a bit-identical equality check, a decidable graph- or type-system
algorithm, a mechanical extraction, or an information-theoretically secure primitive. Under the
quantum adversary of §1.4, 𝑄 is quantum-invariant: it remains sound and executable without
any parameter change.
Proof. The defining property of class (b) is the absence of any computational-hardness assumption. The
proof splits on the two ways that absence can hold.
In the first case, 𝑄 is a non-cryptographic computation: it computes a total function 𝑓 on a decidable domain
— whether two artifacts are bit-identical, whether a graph has a property, whether an extraction yields a
given structure. The soundness of a verification step that invokes 𝑄 is the assertion that 𝑄 computes 𝑓
correctly, and this is a fact about the computation being carried out, not about any adversary’s inability
to solve a hard problem. A quantum computer can evaluate 𝑓 as well — quantum computation subsumes
classical computation — but there is no security property for it to subvert: 𝑄 has no secret, no hardness
assumption, and no adversarial game in which a quantum speedup could matter. The introduction of
quantum computational power cannot make a correct decidable computation incorrect.
In the second case, 𝑄 is information-theoretically secure: its security holds against a computationally unbounded adversary, by definition of the term. An adversary equipped with a quantum computer is in
particular a computationally bounded special case of an unbounded adversary, so 𝑄’s security holds against
it a fortiori.
In both cases the soundness of 𝑄 is independent of any hardness assumption, and is therefore invariant under
the introduction of quantum computational power. Executability is unaffected, since 𝑄 is computed by the
verifier identically regardless of the adversary’s resources. Hence 𝑄 is quantum-invariant. □

140

10.10.4 §2.3 Proof of Theorem 10.1
Theorem 10.1 (Quantum-Survivable Verification). Within the four-axiom decidable fragment of §1.2–§1.3, for each AX-SH axiom 𝐴𝑖 the verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 is quantum-survivable.
Proof. Fix an axiom 𝐴𝑖 and its verification procedure 𝑉𝑖 within the decidable fragment. By Chapter 9
§3.4 — the classification consumed as hypothesis, not re-derived here — the critical path of 𝑉𝑖 uses only
primitives of classes (a) and (b), and contains no primitive of class (c).
Within the decidable fragment, 𝑉𝑖 is a finite procedure, and each of its steps is of exactly one of three kinds:
a step that invokes a class-(a) primitive, a step that invokes a class-(b) primitive, or a step of decidable
control or data manipulation that invokes no cryptographic primitive at all. A step of the third kind is itself
a non-cryptographic computation, hence class (b) by the taxonomy of §1.1, so the three kinds reduce to two
for the purpose of the argument.
By Lemma 10.1a, every class-(a) step remains sound and executable under the quantum adversary at a
bounded, one-time parameter increase. By Lemma 10.1b, every class-(b) step is quantum-invariant, remaining sound and executable without change. It remains to show that the finite composition of these steps that
constitutes 𝑉𝑖 is itself sound and executable under the adversary.
Executability composes immediately: a finite sequence of individually executable steps is executable. For
soundness, recall that 𝑉𝑖 ’s verdict on Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is a decidable function of the verdict-relevant results of its
steps. Each step, by the two lemmas, contributes under the quantum adversary the same verdict-relevant
result it contributes classically — though what that preservation amounts to differs by class. A class-(b)
step is quantum-invariant: it returns the identical output, the underlying computation being unchanged. A
class-(a) step need not return an identical output — a doubled-parameter hash yields a different digest —
but its security property is restored at the doubled parameter, so it accepts and rejects exactly as it did
classically: a tampered provenance link still fails its collision check, a genuine one still passes. Either way
the verdict-relevant contribution of each step is preserved, so the decidable function composing them returns
a preserved value; hence 𝑉𝑖 ’s verdict under the quantum adversary equals its verdict in the absence of one,
and 𝑉𝑖 is sound under the adversary. No quantum attack on the composed procedure can succeed without
succeeding against some constituent step, and no constituent step is vulnerable; the decidable glue between
steps introduces no cryptographic assumption and so opens no new attack surface. There is therefore no
emergent vulnerability from composition.
Finally, because no class-(c) primitive appears anywhere in the critical path, Shor’s algorithm has no target
within 𝑉𝑖 : its polynomial-time solution of factoring and discrete logarithm bears only on public-key primitives,
of which 𝑉𝑖 uses none. The post-quantum break of class (c) thus does not touch 𝑉𝑖 at all.
Combining, 𝑉𝑖 remains sound and executable under the §1.4 quantum adversary, with at most bounded
parameter increases for its class-(a) primitives and no reliance on any class-(c) primitive — which is precisely
quantum-survivability in the sense of §1.4. As 𝐴𝑖 was an arbitrary one of the four axioms, the conclusion
holds for each. □

10.10.5 §2.4 Proof of Corollary 10.2
Corollary 10.2 (centuries-scale re-verification). Any future verifier with no access to past
cryptographic infrastructure can independently re-verify any prior structural-honesty claim from

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

141

the preserved artifact and specification alone, by re-executing 𝑉𝑖 within the decidable fragment.
Proof. Let (𝑆, 𝐴𝑖 ) be a preserved artifact–specification pair within the decidable fragment, and consider a
future verifier possessing 𝑆, the specification of 𝐴𝑖 , and ordinary computational resources (including, in the
strongest case, a quantum computer), but with no access to any past cryptographic infrastructure — no key
servers, no transparency logs, no live public-key roots of trust.
By Theorem 10.1, 𝑉𝑖 is quantum-survivable: it is sound and executable under the quantum adversary, using
only primitives of classes (a) and (b) and requiring no class-(c) primitive, hence no public-key infrastructure
of any kind. By Chapter 9 §1.7, the source-plus-specification fallback guarantees that an execution of 𝑉𝑖
consults only the artifact 𝑆 and the specification of 𝐴𝑖 — not any transmission-layer attestation, signature,
or log. The future verifier therefore has, in the preserved pair (𝑆, 𝐴𝑖 ), exactly the inputs 𝑉𝑖 requires, and by
quantum-survivability it can execute 𝑉𝑖 on those inputs to a sound verdict on Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆).
It remains only to confirm that the verdict so obtained concerns the same proposition the original verification
did. By Chapter 9 Proposition 9.2, the truth layer is substrate-independent and non-decaying: the truth
value of Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) is fixed by 𝑆 and 𝐴𝑖 alone and does not change with the passage of time or the loss of
any infrastructure. The proposition the future verifier re-establishes is thus identical to the one originally
established. Hence the future verifier independently re-verifies the prior structural-honesty claim from the
preserved artifact and specification alone. □
The corollary’s reach, noted in §1.6, is now visible in the proof: nothing in it is specific to the post-quantum
transition. The only properties used are that 𝑉𝑖 needs no public-key infrastructure (Theorem 10.1), that
its execution needs only the preserved pair (Chapter 9 §1.7), and that the proposition does not decay
(Proposition 9.2). Any loss of cryptographic infrastructure whatever — not merely the retirement of prequantum public-key schemes — leaves all three intact.

10.10.6 §2.5 The boundedness property and scope conditions
The centuries-scale reading of Corollary 10.2 depends on a property already established inside the proof
of Lemma 10.1a but worth isolating, because it is what distinguishes a survivable verification from one
that merely defers its failure. The class-(a) mitigation is a one-time, bounded parameter increase, not an
unbounded escalation. The reason is the optimality of Grover’s algorithm: because no quantum search
algorithm beats the quadratic speedup (§2.1), the security loss a class-(a) primitive can suffer to a quantum
adversary is capped at one halving, and a single doubling of the size parameter answers it permanently.
There is no sequence of ever-larger parameters to maintain, and so the verification’s resource requirements
do not grow without bound over the centuries-scale horizon. A verification whose cost escalated indefinitely
could not honestly be called survivable at that horizon; this one does not.
Two scope conditions bound the results of §2. First, Theorem 10.1 and Corollary 10.2 are stated and proved
within the decidable fragment of §1.2; an AX-SH instance whose satisfaction predicate falls outside that
fragment is not covered, and is routed to the open-problems treatment of Chapter 17. Second, Corollary
10.2 presupposes a preserved artifact–specification pair; the discipline by which such preservation is achieved
over long horizons is Chapter 12’s subject, and the analysis of settings in which preservation fails is Chapter
21’s.

contrast
10.11.1 §3.0 The shape of §3
Section 2 proved Theorem 10.1 in the form quantified over the axioms. Section 3 discharges the theorem’s
content axiom by axiom, citing for each the Chapter 9 classification it consumes, and then develops the practical contrast that the theorem draws between AX-SH verification and the public-key-dependent attestation
tooling of the software supply chain. As in §2, no axiom’s primitive-class membership is re-derived here;
Chapter 9 §§3.1–3.4 settled those memberships, and §3 applies Theorem 10.1 to each.

10.11.2 §3.1 A1: append-only provenance
By Chapter 9 §3.1, the verification procedure 𝑉𝐴1 for append-only provenance places in its critical path a
class-(a) primitive: the hash function that chains successive version records, by which each record commits
to its predecessor. No public-key primitive appears; the chaining is a symmetric construction. Applying
Theorem 10.1, 𝑉𝐴1 is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1a the survival is at a bounded, one-time
parameter increase: the provenance chain that hashed with, say, SHA-256 moves to SHA-512, after which the
append-only property is verified under the quantum adversary at full pre-quantum security. The provenance
structure itself is unchanged; only the size parameter of its hash is doubled, once.

10.11.3 §3.2 A2: surface–substrate consistency
By Chapter 9 §3.2, the verification procedure 𝑉𝐴2 for surface–substrate consistency consults no cryptographic
primitive of any class: it checks behavioral equivalence between the surface presentation and the substrate,
a class-(b) computation. Applying Theorem 10.1, 𝑉𝐴2 is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1b the
survival is unconditional — no parameter increase, no mitigation. The consistency check computes the same
verdict under a quantum adversary as without one, because its soundness rests on no hardness assumption.

10.11.4 §3.3 A3: caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may
By Chapter 9 §3.3, the verification procedure 𝑉𝐴3 for caller-side exhaustiveness consults no cryptographic
primitive: it checks coverage of the may-set 𝑅may by the caller’s discharge specifications, together with
decidable invariant-verification for the proven-unreachable cases — all class-(b) computation. Applying
Theorem 10.1, 𝑉𝐴3 is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1b unconditionally so.

10.11.5 §3.4 A4: substrate-parameterized projection consistency
By Chapter 9 §3.4, the verification procedure 𝑉𝐴4 for substrate-parameterized projection consistency consults
no cryptographic primitive: it checks the consistency relation ∼𝑋 over the projection families Π𝑋 on their
joint domains, the algebraic local-section and restriction-map checking that §3.4’s symmetry conclusion
identified as non-cryptographic. Applying Theorem 10.1, 𝑉𝐴4 is quantum-survivable, and by Lemma 10.1b
unconditionally so.
Taken together, the four applications give the chapter’s result in concrete form: AX-SH verification is
quantum-survivable across all four axioms — A1 at a bounded one-time parameter increase, A2 through A4

CHAPTER 10. QUANTUM SURVIVABILITY OF VERIFICATION

143

unconditionally — because not one of the four verification procedures places a public-key primitive in its
critical path.

10.11.6 §3.5 The cryptographic-transition contrast and the SI4 instantiation
The theorem’s practical force is sharpest where it is contrasted with tooling that does depend on the broken
class. On the SI4 software-supply-chain stack of Chapter 16, structural-honesty verification coexists with an
attestation fabric built from sigstore signatures, in-toto attestations, and SLSA provenance. Every one of
those attestation mechanisms depends on public-key signatures — class (c) — and each therefore carries a
genuine cryptographic-transition obligation: over the coming years, each must migrate to a post-quantum
public-key scheme, on pain of its signatures becoming forgeable once a large quantum computer exists.
The contrast Theorem 10.1 draws is that this obligation is confined to the attestation fabric and does not
reach the verification it attests. By Chapter 9 Proposition 9.4, the cryptographic fragility of the supply chain
is localized to the transmission layer; the truth layer, where Π𝐴𝑖 (𝑆) lives, and the verification layer, where
each 𝑉𝑖 runs without any public-key primitive, are untouched. Concretely, on SI4: when a sigstore key scheme
is retired, the signatures that conveyed past verification verdicts cease to be trustworthy, but the verdicts
themselves can be regenerated by re-running the 𝑉𝑖 on the preserved artifacts and specifications, exactly
as Corollary 10.2 provides. The signature was, as §1.7 put it, an eﬀiciency optimization on a verification
that never depended on it; its cryptographic-transition obligation is real but is the transmission layer’s to
bear, and bearing it changes nothing about whether the underlying structural-honesty claims are true or
re-verifiable. The supply chain has post-quantum work to do, and that work leaves the structural honesty
of its artifacts exactly where it found it.

11.1 §1 — Statement
11.1.1 §1.0 Role and scope
Chapter 11 takes up the comparator that Chapter 10 named but deliberately did not develop: the difference
between a verification guarantee that rests on a computational-hardness assumption and one that does not.
Chapter 10 proved that AX-SH verification survives the post-quantum transition because it lives entirely
within the survivable primitive classes, and class (b) — the information-theoretic and non-cryptographic
primitives — survives unconditionally, with no hardness assumption to break. The present chapter asks what
becomes possible once a verification substrate is built deliberately to exploit that unconditional character.
Its answer is a structural result about redundancy: that 𝑛 independent re-implementations of a single verifier,
checked against one another for bit-identical agreement, resist forgery in a way that is information-theoretic
rather than cryptographic, and that strengthens monotonically with 𝑛.
The chapter consumes two prior results as cited hypotheses and re-derives neither. From Chapter 9 it takes
the verification layer of §1.2 — the family of procedures 𝑉𝑖 that decide an axiom’s satisfaction predicate over
a substrate’s projections. From Chapter 10 it takes Lemma 10.1b, the placement of bit-identical equality and
parity checks in the quantum-unconditional class (b). The division of labor is linear and acyclic: Chapter
9 classifies which primitives the verification procedures use, Chapter 10 proves that each such procedure

CHAPTER 11. INFORMATION-THEORETIC VERSUS CRYPTOGRAPHIC SUBSTRATES

146

survives a quantum adversary, and Chapter 11 proves that 𝑛 independent copies of such a procedure resist
coordinated forgery. Chapter 11’s contribution — the 𝑛-fold redundancy-structure theorem — is orthogonal
to Chapter 10’s single-procedure survivability, and the chapter is written to keep it so.
The scope of this opening section is the apparatus the result requires and the statements it will establish:
the notion of 𝑛-fold independent re-implementation and the verification substrate of strength 𝑛 (§1.1); the
reference-parity check and the independence assumption it rests on (§1.2); the correspondence to the masstransmission (tawatur) epistemics of the textual-preservation tradition (§1.3); the forgery model and the
information-theoretic-versus-cryptographic contrast that gives the chapter its title (§1.4); the statement
of Theorem 11.1 (§1.5) and of its boundary, Proposition 11.2 (§1.6); and the practical implications for
the dissertation’s substrate instances (§1.7), before the proof obligations are routed forward (§1.8). Three
matters are out of scope and handed onward: the operational discipline by which the 𝑛 implementations
and their fixture corpora are preserved across long horizons (Chapter 12); the undecidable fragments and
the settings in which an artifact or specification has not been preserved (Chapter 17); and the empirical
falsification of the independence assumption on which the whole guarantee is conditional (Chapter 21).

11.1.2 §1.1 The 𝑛-fold independent re-implementation and the verification substrate of strength 𝑛
Fix a verification procedure in the sense of Chapter 9 §1.2: a procedure 𝑉 that, given an artifact and a
specification, decides the relevant AX-SH satisfaction predicate and returns a verdict. A single such procedure
is a single point of trust. The construction of this chapter replaces it with 𝑛 procedures 𝑉1 , … , 𝑉𝑛 , each an
independent re-implementation of the same verifier specification — the same input-output contract, realized
afresh by a distinct development effort. The collection {𝑉1 , … , 𝑉𝑛 }, together with a fixed fixture corpus on
which all 𝑛 implementations agree bit-for-bit — the admission criterion by which an implementation joins the
substrate, establishing that they realize the same specification — and the rule that compares their verdicts
on any later input, is a verification substrate of strength 𝑛.
The word independent is load-bearing and is made precise in §1.2; informally, the 𝑛 implementations are built
so that no single fault — no shared bug, no common misreading of the specification, no shared upstream
dependency — can corrupt more than one of them. The word strength is used throughout in a specific
sense: it denotes the coordinated-corruption burden, the number of implementations an adversary must
subvert simultaneously to forge a verdict undetected. It is not a key length and not a cryptographic security
parameter; it counts independent witnesses, not bits.

11.1.3 §1.2 The reference-parity check and the independence assumption
The rule that binds the 𝑛 implementations into a substrate is the reference-parity check: on a given
input, the substrate runs all 𝑛 implementations and tests whether their verdicts agree bit-for-bit. Write
𝑃 (𝑥) for the predicate that holds exactly when 𝑉1 (𝑥) = ⋯ = 𝑉𝑛 (𝑥) — unanimous, bit-identical agreement.
The substrate reports a verdict only when 𝑃 (𝑥) holds; any disagreement is a parity failure, surfaced rather
than resolved by majority or averaged away, and it localizes the fault to either an implementation defect or
a specification ambiguity — an Axiom-4-style projection divergence, in the sense of Chapter 7, made visible
across the implementations.
The guarantee the chapter will prove is conditional on an independence assumption: that the corruption

CHAPTER 11. INFORMATION-THEORETIC VERSUS CRYPTOGRAPHIC SUBSTRATES

147

of any one implementation is, as a fault event, independent of the corruption of the others. Concretely,
the implementations are to be authored by distinct groups, in distinct programming languages, on distinct
toolchains, so that the natural sources of common-mode failure are absent. The assumption is empirical — it
is a claim about the engineering and social provenance of the implementations, not a mathematical identity
— and it is therefore falsifiable. Chapter 21 owns its falsification; the present chapter states it plainly as the
hypothesis under which Theorem 11.1 holds, and Proposition 11.2 (§1.6) characterizes precisely what is lost
when it fails.

11.1.4 §1.3 The tawatur correspondence
The redundancy structure of a strength-𝑛 substrate has a long-studied analogue in the textual-preservation
tradition, where it is the basis of tawatur: the epistemic principle that a report transmitted by so many independent chains that their coordinated fabrication is implausible attains practical certainty. The correspondence is exact at the structural level. The 𝑛 independent implementations are 𝑛 independent transmission
chains; their bit-identical agreement is the parity evidence; and coordinated corruption of all 𝑛 is the sole
route to an undetected forgery, just as coordinated fabrication across all transmission chains is the sole route
to a corrupted mutawatir report. The chapter borrows this redundancy structure, and only the structure:
the correspondence is structural and epistemic, not scriptural, and asserts nothing about the content
or authority of any transmitted text.
It is worth being exact about which exemplars instantiate the structure, because the dissertation’s own substrate instances do not all sit where a first reading might place them. The genuine high-𝑛 exemplars are the
natural-language preservation traditions whose lineage Chapter 2 §4 traces: the Quranic tradition, in which
independent ḥāfiẓ memories and independent manuscript lines together form many independent witnesses to
one text, and the Vedic multi-pāṭha system, in which several partially-independent recitation patterns over
one source text serve mutually as the verification of transmission fidelity. The order-of-magnitude figures
sometimes attached to the Quranic case — on the order of 106 independent memorizers and 104 manuscript
traditions — come from the dissertation outline’s quantification; Chapter 2 §4 supplies the lineage and the
multi-substrate mechanism, not the counts. By contrast, the Bayyinah file-integrity scanner (SI1, Chapter
13) does not instantiate strength-𝑛 redundancy, and §1.7 is careful to say why.

11.1.5 §1.4 The forgery model, and the information-theoretic versus cryptographic contrast
A forgery against the substrate is an adversarial state in which the substrate’s reported verdict on some
input is wrong — it contradicts the satisfaction predicate the verifier is meant to decide. A forgery is
undetected exactly when the parity check passes while the verdict is wrong: when all 𝑛 implementations
have been made to agree on the same incorrect answer. This is the event the chapter’s theorem bounds.
The contrast that names the chapter is the contrast between two ways a forgery can be made hard. A
cryptographic guarantee makes forgery hard by reducing it to a computational problem assumed infeasible
— factoring, discrete logarithm — so that its security is conditional on that problem remaining hard, and
degrades if an adversary’s computational reach grows, as it does under the post-quantum transition of
Chapter 10. An information-theoretic guarantee makes forgery hard without any such assumption: the
diﬀiculty is in the structure of the situation, not in the cost of a computation. The reference-parity substrate

CHAPTER 11. INFORMATION-THEORETIC VERSUS CRYPTOGRAPHIC SUBSTRATES

148

is of the second kind. Subverting it requires corrupting implementations — a matter of compromising authors,
toolchains, or build pipelines — and no amount of adversarial computation substitutes for that. This is why
the guarantee composes with Chapter 10’s survivability rather than competing with it: a substrate whose
strength is information-theoretic carries nothing for a quantum algorithm to attack.

11.1.6 §1.5 Theorem 11.1 (Reference-Parity Forgery-Resistance) — statement
The central claim of the chapter is stated here and proved in §2.
Theorem

11.1

Let {𝑉1 , … , 𝑉𝑛 } be a verification substrate of strength 𝑛 for an AX-SH

axiom’s satisfaction predicate, satisfying the independence assumption of §1.2. Then:
(i) forging the substrate’s verdict on any (artifact, specification) input requires the simultaneous coordinated corruption of all 𝑛 implementations; equivalently, a single uncorrupted
independent implementation suﬀices to flag any forgery by parity-disagreement;
(ii) the resistance is information-theoretic — it rests on no computational-hardness assumption, and is therefore quantum-unconditional, the substrate’s comparison primitive lying in

(iii) the strength is monotone in 𝑛: the coordinated-corruption burden is non-decreasing as

Two points of reading govern the statement. First, clause (i) is a claim about detection, not impossibility:
it does not assert that a forgery cannot occur, but that any forgery is flagged — by a parity disagreement
— provided the check is run and at least one implementation remains honest. Second, clause (ii) reaches its
quantum-unconditional conclusion by citing Chapter 10’s Lemma 10.1b for the class-(b) placement of the
parity primitive, not by re-establishing it; the section that proves Theorem 11.1 inherits that lemma rather
than reproving it.

11.1.7 §1.6 The independence-failure boundary and strength calibration
The guarantee of Theorem 11.1 is conditional, and the condition is exactly the independence assumption.
Its failure is characterized by the chapter’s second statement.
Proposition 11.2 (Independence-failure boundary). When the independence assumption
fails — through a shared toolchain bug, a common misreading of the specification, or a shared
upstream dependency — a single fault can corrupt several implementations at once, reducing the
effective strength below 𝑛. In the limiting case of fully correlated implementations, the effective
strength collapses to 1.
The proposition has classical empirical support: Knight and Leveson (1986) demonstrated that twenty-seven
independently-written versions of one specification, produced by different author teams under controlled
conditions, still failed coincidentally far above the independence prediction. The result establishes that the
independence assumption is empirically at risk in engineered settings; the failure mode Proposition 11.2
characterizes is not hypothetical.

149

Proposition 11.2 is what makes “strength 𝑛” an honest quantity rather than a nominal one: the number
that matters is the count of genuinely independent fault sources, which the nominal implementation count
bounds from above but does not guarantee. The calibration of the chapter follows from this. The existing
high-strength instances are the natural-language traditions of §1.3 — the Quranic and Vedic cases, with the
outline’s order-of-magnitude figures and Chapter 2 §4’s lineage. The engineered target the dissertation sets
for itself is more modest and explicitly prospective: a substrate of perhaps ten independent implementations,
across at least three programming languages and at least three independent author groups. There is, at
this writing, no engineered substrate that instantiates strength greater than one; §1.7 states this without
softening it. Strength is to be read as a horizon a program moves toward, not a fixed security level a system
already possesses.

11.1.8 §1.7 Practical implications
Three consequences follow for the dissertation’s concrete substrates, and the first is a disclosure rather than
a claim. No engineered strength-𝑛 substrate with 𝑛 > 1 is yet operationally instantiated. The
dissertation outline’s framing of the Bayyinah scanner as a “𝑣0/𝑣0.1/𝑣1.1.0 chain” at strength three does
not survive scrutiny on two counts: a chain of versions of one scanner shares its authors, toolchain, and
language and so constitutes a single fault source, collapsing to effective strength one under Proposition
11.2; and the scanner’s much-cited 17-of-17 PDF parity check is, per Chapter 13 §§1.4, 2.5, and 8.2, a
single implementation’s 𝜋pdf projection-consistency check — 17 structural properties tested against 17 bytecomparison points, one projection within the Axiom-4 family Π𝑋 , with independence at the level of projection
roles rather than of implementations. It is related machinery, and it does provide redundant byte-level
evidence, but it is not an instance of the strength-𝑛 concept this chapter develops, and the chapter does not
present it as one.
The second consequence concerns software supply chains. The supply-chain substrate of Chapter 16 (SI4)
composes four verification substrates — sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, and the present framework — with uncorrelated failure modes. This is a related redundancy structure, but a distinct one: it places several different
verifiers over different verification dimensions, rather than several independent re-implementations of one
verifier, and it belongs alongside Proposition 11.2’s analysis of uncorrelated fault sources rather than as a
Theorem 11.1 instance. Its value for the present argument is that its class-(b) components remain intact
precisely when a public-key scheme such as sigstore’s breaks (Chapter 10 §1.7, class (c)), so the two kinds
of guarantee fail independently and reinforce one another.
The third consequence is programmatic. The engineered strength-𝑛 target — roughly ten independent
implementations, across at least three languages and three author groups — is a concrete milestone, crossreferenced to the falsification checkpoints of Chapter 21, where the multi-implementation reference-parity
goal sits at the year-ten horizon. It is named here as a research commitment, the engineered analogue of the
natural-language traditions’ existing strength, and not as a present achievement.
