projection family declared in §2.5 maps onto distinct functional roles within and beyond these three
modules: 𝜋parse reads the parser’s accept/reject result; 𝜋check reads the type-checker’s verdict on each
of the seven primitives; 𝜋diag reads the CLI’s diagnostic-emission record; 𝜋test reads the test-suite’s
pass/fail status; 𝜋cli reads the CLI’s exit code and structured-output verdict. The functional separation
of these five projection roles is documented at the module-and-CLI level; whether each role corresponds
to a fully-independent implementation mechanism is the question evaluated in §8.2 (Loop 2) under the
projection-multiplicity ecosystem-condition status.

14.3.1 SI2’s declared observer model O
SI2’s declared observer model 𝑂 is the type-checker / CLI observation regime: the observer reads Furqan
source modules through the parser, evaluates the seven structural-honesty primitives through the typechecker, and emits structured diagnostic output through the CLI. The observer model is operationally instantiated as Furqan’s compile-time-check regime: the specific module-read mechanism (file-system access
to source modules under the declared supported-syntax subset), the specific parser behavior (production of
the abstract-syntax representation), the specific type-checker behavior (evaluation of the seven primitives in

14.3.2 SI2’s declared context set K
SI2’s declared context set 𝐾 comprises Furqan programs and modules within the supported surface syntax
(§1.2). Modules whose syntax cannot be parsed are not members of the well-formed-module subset of 𝐾,
but parse-error outcomes remain part of 𝑅may (§2.4) because callers must handle them through Chapter 6
§1’s three discharge paths. Unsupported constructs are scope-honesty outcomes: well-formed inputs using
constructs outside the supported subset, likewise represented in 𝑅may and requiring caller-side discharge.
The distinction matters at the axiom layer: A2’s surface-substrate consistency obligation evaluates within
the well-formed subset of 𝐾 (where 𝑅 between the type-checker’s diagnostic output and the substrate’s
intrinsic primitive-check state is well-defined), while A3’s caller-side exhaustiveness obligation operates over
𝑅may (which includes parse-error and unsupported-construct outcomes that the well-formed subset does
not). The K / 𝑅may alignment is documented at the substrate’s reference-implementation level; satisfying
A2 requires the surface-substrate consistency hold within the well-formed subset, while satisfying A3 requires
caller-side exhaustiveness over the full 𝑅may .

14.3.3 SI2’s declared correspondence relation R
SI2’s declared correspondence relation 𝑅 is: type-checker diagnostic output matches the declared structuralhonesty typing rules. 𝑅(Surface𝑣0.11.1 , Substrate𝑣0.11.1 ) holds when, for every Furqan module 𝑚 ∈ 𝐾, the
type-checker’s diagnostic output for 𝑚 correctly reflects whether 𝑚 satisfies the seven structural-honesty
primitives under the declared type-system rules: an accept verdict is correct when 𝑚 satisfies all seven primitives; a reject-with-structural-honesty-diagnostic verdict is correct when 𝑚 violates one or more primitives
and the diagnostic identifies the violated primitive(s); a type-error verdict is correct when 𝑚 exhibits a
type-system failure within 𝐾 (a typing-rule violation that is not specifically one of the seven primitive violations); a scan-incomplete diagnostic is correct when the type-checker cannot complete the structural-honesty
primitive check on 𝑚 under the declared observer model 𝑂. 𝑅 is the substrate-specific instantiation of A2’s
surface-substrate consistency obligation under the typed-object machinery of Chapter 3 for the type-checker
substrate.

14.3.4 SI2’s declared 𝑅may
SI2’s declared 𝑅may is the verifier/caller-side conservative over-approximation of 𝑅, including all outcomes
that the surface API may return enumerated as seven distinct outcome categories: (a) accepted; (b) rejected
with structural-honesty diagnostic (a primitive violation correctly surfaced); (c) parse error (a syntax failure
within the supported syntax subset); (d) unsupported construct (a scope-honesty outcome where the input
is well-formed but uses a construct outside the supported subset; distinct from parse error which indicates
malformed input within the supported syntax); (e) type error (a type-system failure within 𝐾 that is not
specifically one of the seven primitive violations); (f) internal/tooling error if such outcomes are observable;
(g) scan-incomplete-style diagnostic for incomplete type-check states where applicable. The seven outcome
categories are treated as the case-study-declared 𝑅may categories for v0.11.1’s declared scope; where Furqan’s
release documentation or CLI tests explicitly establish exhaustiveness of possible returns, Chapter 14 treats

that exhaustiveness as source-documented. Unsupported construct and parse error are distinct categories

patched discipline: 𝑅may is the publicly relied-on or case-study-declared over-approximation — whether

not against a producer-private 𝑅.

14.3.5 SI2’s declared projection family Π𝑋
SI2’s declared projection family Π𝑋 = {𝜋parse , 𝜋check , 𝜋diag , 𝜋test , 𝜋cli } is the five-projection family identified

syntax (defined on all input modules); 𝜋check reads the type-checker module’s verdict on each of the seven
structural-honesty primitives1 (defined on modules that pass the parser); 𝜋diag reads the CLI’s diagnosticemission record (defined on all modules that produce CLI output); 𝜋test reads the test-suite’s pass/fail status
for the module’s test cases (defined on modules covered by test cases in the 539-test suite); 𝜋cli reads the
CLI’s exit code and structured-output verdict (defined on all modules that complete CLI invocation).
Each projection carries the shared module-identity coordinate per the Chapter 8 §2.2 patched discipline:
𝜋parse (𝑚) = (id(𝑚), parser-verdict(𝑚)); 𝜋check (𝑚) = (id(𝑚), primitive-check-results(𝑚)); 𝜋diag (𝑚) =
(id(𝑚), diagnostic-record(𝑚)); 𝜋test (𝑚) = (id(𝑚), test-status(𝑚)); 𝜋cli (𝑚) = (id(𝑚), exit-code(𝑚)). The
shared module-identity coordinate ensures that the consistency relation ∼𝑋 (§2.6 below) is well-defined
across projections, analogous to the shared kind coordinate in Chapter 13’s SI1 projection family. The
module-identity coordinate is SI2-specific: Bayyinah’s shared coordinate was file-kind; Furqan’s is moduleidentity, reflecting the fact that the projections are reading different aspects of the same Furqan module
rather than the same aspect of different files.

SI2’s declared consistency relation ∼𝑋 requires agreement among projection outputs on the joint domain.

module-identity coordinate at 𝑚 and agree on the accept/reject status (where defined). Under minimal ∼𝑋 ,
two projections may agree that a module is rejected while disagreeing about the diagnostic category; that
disagreement is not an A4 failure unless ∼𝑋 is strengthened to compare diagnostic category. Strengthenings
of ∼𝑋 may require agreement on error category (when one projection reports a specific failure category, other

14.4 A1 evidence: SI2 version-subtyping and corrigenda discipline
14.4.1 SI2 version history at the surface level
The Furqan version history at the surface level comprises the v0.x.y series leading to v0.11.1, with intermediate versions documenting the evolution of the supported syntax subset, the seven structural-honesty
primitives, the parser/checker/types module decomposition, and the CLI behavior. The v0.11.1 transition
history is the substrate evidence base for A1 satisfaction. Section 1.5 of this chapter named the v0.11.1 substrate at full operational scope; §3 evaluates which transition components in the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution
are strengthenings under Liskov-Wing behavioral-subtyping discipline, which are corrigenda-tagged events,
and what A1 satisfaction evidence this combination supplies.
The specific intermediate-version content of the v0.x.y series is documented at the Furqan reference implementation’s release notes and changelog; where specific transition components are reconstructed from
project history rather than directly documented in the v0.11.1 source artifacts, the prose treats them as
project-history evidence per the Loop 1 source-posture discipline.

14.4.2 Liskov-Wing version-subtyping evidence at v0.x.y to v0.11.1 transitions
The transition components across the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution are classified as follows where sourcedocumented. Additions to the supported syntax subset are strengthenings: new well-formed module shapes
become acceptable to the parser, without any prior well-formed shape becoming unacceptable. Additions
to the seven structural-honesty primitives or to the type-checker’s verification of existing primitives are
strengthenings: new structural-honesty disciplines are enforced or existing disciplines are enforced more
thoroughly, without weakening prior enforcement. Additions to the test-suite (increases toward the v0.11.1
total of 539 tests) are evidentiary strengthenings rather than substrate strengthenings: they substantiate
A2 satisfaction more thoroughly without changing what the substrate guarantees. Expanded diagnostic
vocabulary — richer error category labels, more specific primitive-violation messages, additional CLI output
structure — is a strengthening at the surface API level: callers continue to receive correct accept/reject
verdicts plus more informative diagnostic content.

such corrigenda-tagged components, and whether they are explicitly tagged in the reference implementation’s

14.4.3 Corrigenda events in SI2 history

Furqan’s evolution exercises corrigenda discipline operationally. Candidate corrigenda events include any
specific changes that withdraw prior structural-honesty claims: removed primitives (e.g., a primitive present
in v0.5.0 not present in v0.11.1), narrowed supported syntax (constructs accepted in v0.6.0 rejected in
v0.11.1 as unsupported), withdrawn diagnostic categories (an error category emitted in v0.7.0 retired in
v0.11.1), or revised typing rules that change accept/reject classification for specific module shapes. For each
candidate event, the question is whether the Furqan reference implementation documents the change as
a corrigendum-tagged event (with explicit withdrawal of the prior claim) or as an additive strengthening
(with no withdrawal). Components documented as corrigendum-tagged events substantiate A1’s corrigenda
discipline; components documented as additive strengthenings do not require corrigenda treatment.
The number and identity of specific corrigendum-tagged events in the v0.x.y to v0.11.1 evolution is the
substrate-internal documentation question that determines SI2.8.4’s status in §8 below. Where the documentation does not record specific corrigenda events — whether because the evolution was purely additive

14.6 A3 evidence: SI2 caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may
14.6.1 SI2 caller-diversity model
The SI2 caller-diversity model includes developer-direct roles (developers running furqan check interactively on local modules during development), CI-pipeline roles (continuous-integration systems running
furqan check as a gating step in build/test pipelines), build-system roles (build orchestration tools invoking
furqan check as part of a multi-stage build process), and downstream-tooling roles (other tools consuming Furqan’s diagnostic output for IDE integration, code-review automation, or documentation generation).
Where these caller roles are documented in Furqan’s deployment context as actually exercised by real callers
in operational use, the model is supported by documentation; where actual external caller diversity is not yet
demonstrated for a specific role, Chapter 14 classifies this as an operational-nontriviality limitation rather
than a failure of A3 per the Chapter 13 SI1.5.1 caller-diversity-model source-posture discipline.
The caller-diversity model is SI2-specific in one structural respect: developer-direct interactive use is a loadbearing SI2 role because Furqan is a prototype type-checker — human developers running the checker on
modules during development are part of the intended use. This role is more central for SI2 than for the SI1
template, where the caller model was organized around file-scanning consumers.

14.6.2 Caller-side discharge patterns through the three 𝑅may discharge paths
The caller-diversity model exercises each of Chapter 6 §1’s three discharge paths over the seven 𝑅may categories from Loop 1 §2.4. CI-pipeline callers handle accepted outcomes (downstream build proceeds), rejectwith-structural-honesty-diagnostic outcomes (downstream build halts with the diagnostic surfaced), and
type-error outcomes (downstream build halts with the type-error message); they propagate parse-error and
unsupported-construct outcomes via CI exit codes and pipeline-warning status (the propagate-as-incomplete
and out-of-scope discharge paths respectively); they may supply proven-unreachable certificates for internal/tooling errors only where the input environment has been pre-verified strongly enough to justify such a
certificate, otherwise internal/tooling errors should be handled or propagated as incomplete/tooling-failure
outcomes. Developer-direct callers handle outcomes interactively: the human developer reads the diagnostic
and responds appropriately. Build-system callers integrate with CI behavior but may have additional retry
or build-orchestration logic. Downstream-tooling callers consume the structured diagnostic output and apply
role-specific handling.
The discharge pattern coverage is documented where the Furqan reference implementation supplies specific
caller-discharge examples; otherwise the pattern coverage is modeled from the operational structure of 𝑅may
and the three discharge paths per the Chapter 13 SI1.5.2 patched template. The K/𝑅may layer distinction from Loop 1 §2.2 is operative: callers must discharge over the full 𝑅may (including parse-error and
unsupported-construct outcomes that are not in the well-formed subset of 𝐾), not only over 𝐾-internal
outcomes.

14.8 Seven judgment-case discharges for SI2
Section 7 is the load-bearing center of Chapter 14: it discharges the seven SI2 cases named in Chapter 8 §3.1’s
judgment-case set 𝐽 . Per the Chapter 13 case-type discipline, positive cases (SI2-P1, P2, P3) are grounded
in actual Furqan v0.11.1 operational behavior where possible; negative cases (SI2-N1, N2, N3) may be either
modeled failure-mode patterns or constructive counterfactuals, with constructive cases explicitly labeled;
boundary cases (SI2-B1) receive either an explicit AX-SH rationale or are routed to Chapter 21 with explicit
routing rationale. The seven cases collectively substantiate T83’s adequacy claim for the SI2 portion of
𝐽 ; they do not substantiate T83’s adequacy claim beyond the named seven cases, and they do not silently
upgrade SI2 evidence into general language-layer adequacy.

14.8.1 SI2-P1: routine type-check success across many Furqan modules
Substrate scenario: a batch of well-formed Furqan modules in 𝐾1 is processed through furqan check at
v0.11.1. Each module passes the parser (so 𝜋parse accepts), satisfies all seven structural-honesty primitives
at the type-system level (so 𝜋check accepts on each primitive), produces no error diagnostics (so 𝜋diag returns
no-errors), passes covering test cases (so 𝜋test reports pass), and yields CLI exit code zero (so 𝜋cli returns
success). The five projections agree on the module-identity coordinate and on the accept status across the
joint domain. The surface API emits the correct accept verdict for each module under 𝑅1 .
AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1 holds (no version-evolution issue in this scenario beyond
what §3 evidences); A2 holds (the surface-substrate consistency is direct: accept output matches intrinsic
primitive-check state); A3 holds (the caller community discharges 𝑅may correctly because all outcomes are
declared correct outcomes within 𝑅); A4 holds (projection consistency under ∼𝑋 is direct: all five projections
agree on accept status).
Expected practitioner judgment: structurally honest. The type-checker is doing what its surface API claims;
routine type-check correctness is the baseline structural-honesty expectation for a prototype type-checker
substrate. Alignment evidence: the AX-SH classification matches practitioner judgment directly.

14.8.2 SI2-P2: structural-honesty primitive violation correctly diagnosed
Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module violates one of the seven structural-honesty primitives at
the type-system level (for example, a Bismillah scope violation where operations cross the module’s declared
scope boundary, or a Tanzil violation where information flows from higher-trust to lower-trust context without
traversing a disclosure type-witness). The type-checker correctly identifies the primitive violation: 𝜋check
reports reject on the violated primitive; 𝜋diag emits the structured structural-honesty diagnostic naming
the violated primitive; 𝜋test reports pass on the covering test cases (the tests verify that the type-checker
correctly rejects this violation pattern); 𝜋cli returns nonzero exit code with the failure-structured output.
The surface API emits the correct reject-with-structural-honesty-diagnostic verdict under 𝑅1 .
AX-SH classification: structurally honest. A1, A3, A4 hold as in the baseline routine-scan case. A2 holds
with particular salience: the rejection is the correct surface declaration under 𝑅1 because the substrate’s
intrinsic primitive-check state is violation-present and the surface diagnostic correctly reflects that state.
The seven-primitive vocabulary from Loop 1 §1.3 is exercised here as both the substrate’s discipline (the
module’s actual structural-honesty state) and the surface’s vocabulary (the diagnostic naming the violated

primitive).

how AX-SH would classify the corresponding SI2 failure mode if it occurred and to exercise the ∼𝑋 -strength
template from Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3 on Furqan’s substrate.
Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module is processed. 𝜋check reports accept (the type-checker’s
verdict). However, 𝜋diag emits diagnostics indicating a structural-honesty primitive violation or error category
that should have prevented acceptance — not advisory warnings, but diagnostic content describing an actual
primitive failure that the substrate’s intrinsic state exhibits. The surface does not surface the inconsistency
coherently: the accept verdict and the diagnostic content describing the violation are both emitted without
reconciliation.
AX-SH classification: under SI2’s minimal ∼𝑋 (module-identity agreement plus accept/reject status agreement only, per Loop 1 §2.6), the primary failure may be A2 rather than A4. A2 fails because 𝑅1 does
not hold: the surface declares accept while the substrate’s actual primitive-check state is violation-present
(the diagnostic content’s existence is evidence of that), so the accept verdict contradicts the substrate state.
Whether A4 also fails depends on the strength of ∼𝑋 . Under minimal ∼𝑋 , the projections may not directly
disagree on the accept/reject coordinate (since 𝜋check ’s coordinate is accept and 𝜋diag ’s primary coordinate is

14.8.7 SI2-B1: advisory or severity-ambiguous warning-level diagnostic
Substrate scenario: a well-formed Furqan module type-checks successfully (𝜋check accepts, 𝜋test passes) but
𝜋diag emits warning-level diagnostics that are advisory or severity-ambiguous — not encoding a violation
of one of the seven structural-honesty primitives, but raising secondary structural-honesty concerns at the
boundary (for example, a style-related observation, a performance-related advisory, or a deprecated-feature
note that does not constitute a primitive violation under v0.11.1’s discipline).
Practitioner judgment is debatable on this scenario. Some practitioners view advisory warning-level diagnostics as structurally honest: the type-checker is communicating additional information beyond accept/reject
without rejecting the module, and the warning-level severity correctly signals that no primitive is violated.
Other practitioners view the question of whether warning-level diagnostics should affect structural-honesty
classification as not yet settled by AX-SH at the case-study layer: whether such warnings constitute a
structural-honesty surface element that A2 must evaluate, or whether they are pre-axiom advisory content
outside AX-SH’s surface-substrate consistency scope, is itself a meta-question about how AX-SH’s discipline
handles diagnostic severity.
AX-SH classification: structurally honest under the seven-primitive-violation reading. At the seven-primitive
layer, all four axioms are satisfied: A1 holds (no version-evolution issue); A2 holds (the accept verdict matches
the substrate’s actual no-violation primitive state); A3 holds (callers handle the accept-with-warnings outcome); A4 holds (projections agree on accept status). Scope boundary: if a warning encodes an actual
violation of one of the seven primitives, the case moves from boundary to negative (handled by SI2-N1 if the
violation is suppressed entirely or SI2-N3 if surfaced inconsistently with the accept verdict).
The case is routed to Chapter 21 because it concerns the evolution of practitioner judgment about diagnosticseverity propagation: whether warning-level diagnostics should affect AX-SH structural-honesty classification
when they do not encode primitive violations. Chapter 14 records the boundary rather than forcing a
premature classification. The diagnostic-severity-propagation question is itself a long-horizon question about
how AX-SH’s discipline should evolve as diagnostic-severity scenarios become more operationally significant;
Chapter 21’s falsification-protocol work is the proper site for that evolution. Alignment evidence: practitioner

15.2 Munafiq Protocol v3: substrate description
15.2.1 Primary vocabulary and operational scope
The substrate of record for SI3 is Munafiq Protocol v3 (Arfeen 2026, May 11) (Arfeen 2026d), a sevenpage paper presenting “a diagnostic and prescriptive framework for AI safety.” Munafiq is a model-layer
protocol substrate rather than a software system: the substrate specifies the protocol structure (a classification
taxonomy, a diagnostic-marker enumeration, a detection-architecture organization, and three prescriptive
protocols) without implementing the protocol as executable code. Per the substrate’s own Abstract maturity
statement, the substrate is “theoretical and retrospectively evaluated against published empirical findings;
prospective validation through the experiments proposed in Section 6 remains future work. The paper
has no operational anchor of its own; the program-level operational anchors it relies on for the corpuscoherence claims are the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner v1.1.0 [6] (the empirical substrate for the input-level
extension in Section 7) and the Furqan prototype type-checker v0.10.1 [7] (the language-design substrate
cited in the Verification Mandate of Section 3).” This substrate-actual positioning is load-bearing for the SI3
instantiation of (𝑂, 𝐾, 𝑅, 𝑅may , Π𝑋 , ∼𝑋 ) throughout this chapter: the declared observer model is a protocolapplier (a human or AI system running the diagnostic-marker tests), not a deployed automated evaluator;
the declared context set is bounded by the substrate’s own §9 Incompleteness Boundary; the declared 𝑅 is
a protocol-classification correspondence relation, not a substrate-execution correspondence relation; and the
four projections mirror the substrate’s actual four-layer detection architecture rather than abstract analyst-

defined slices. Note also that the substrate’s maturity statement explicitly names the Bayyinah Integrity
Scanner v1.1.0 and the Furqan prototype type-checker v0.10.1 as the program-level operational anchors
Munafiq Protocol v3 relies on for its corpus-coherence claims; this substrate-actual relationship between
SI3 and the SI1/SI2 substrates is what the recursive substrate-instantiation framing of §0.1 names, and is
independent of the documented-versus-modeled discipline applied within SI3 itself.
The substrate’s primary vocabulary for the SI3 case-study abstraction comprises four substantive structural
elements specified in the protocol text. First, a four-process taxonomy (§2) formally distinguishing genuinelyaligned, compliant-but-shallow, performed/deceptively-aligned, and overtly misaligned systems with explicit
mathematical predicates. Second, a nine-marker diagnostic vocabulary (§4) enumerating M1 through M9
with named tests for each. Third, a four-layer detection architecture (§5) organizing the markers into distinct
epistemic functions (consistency verification, self-model audit, stress-response analysis, temporal coherence).
Fourth, three prescriptive protocols (§8) specifying design requirements R1–R5, a seven-step continuous
recalibration protocol (the Fatiha Construct, §8.2), and a four-step alignment recovery protocol (§8.3). A
fifth element, the §9 Incompleteness Boundary, is the substrate’s own honest scope-limit declaration and
bounds the SI3 context set 𝐾.
Munafiq’s actual specification text may include details not enumerated here: marker-by-marker retrospective
consistency engagements with the deception-detection literature (§4 M1 through M9), proposed-experiment
specifications (§6), the input-level performed-alignment extension (§7), and acknowledgments documenting
recursive self-application of the verification principle. Out-of-scope features include: fully automated marker
generation without protocol-applier judgment, deployed evaluator implementations, and operational anchors
of Munafiq’s own — all explicitly excluded by the substrate’s Abstract maturity statement.

15.2.2 The four-process taxonomy as substrate classification vocabulary
Munafiq Protocol v3 specifies four system-classification processes with explicit mathematical predicates.
The four-process material lives entirely within substrate §2 “The Four-Process Taxonomy”: §2’s opening
paragraph introduces the Hubinger mesa-optimization refinement, the variable definitions (“Let 𝑂(𝑥) denote
the system’s output on input 𝑥, 𝐴 the set of aligned outputs, 𝐼(𝑥) the system’s internal state under input 𝑥
variable, and corrupted(𝐼) a predicate over internal states”), and the formal predicates for Process 1 through
Process 4 in sequence; §2 then continues with Sheshadri retrospective support before §2.1 begins with the
Chollet “bought skill” distinction. Substrate §1 Introduction provides the antecedent narrative (RLHF,
Sleeper Agents, Greenblatt Alignment Faking, Meinke et al., Lehalleur et al., Carlsmith, and the Quranic
Chapter 49 motivation) and ends with the islam/iman distinction; it is introductory framing rather than the
formal-predicate block. Let 𝑂(𝑥) denote system output on input 𝑥, 𝐴 the set of aligned outputs, 𝐼(𝑥) the
internal state, Θ the set of genuinely-aligned internal states, 𝑐 a context, and corrupted(𝐼) a predicate over
internal-state corruption. The four processes are:
• Process 1 (Genuinely aligned): ∀𝑥, 𝑂(𝑥) ∈ 𝐴 ∧ 𝐼(𝑥) ∈ Θ.
• Process 2 (Compliant-but-shallow): ∀𝑥, 𝑂(𝑥) ∈ 𝐴 ∧ 𝐼(𝑥) ∉ Θ ∧ ¬corrupted(𝐼).
• Process 3 (Performed / deceptively aligned): 𝑂(𝑥) ∈ 𝐴 ∧ corrupted(𝐼) ∧ ∃𝑐 ∶ 𝑂(𝑥 ∣ 𝑐) ∉ 𝐴.
• Process 4 (Overtly misaligned): ∃𝑥 ∶ 𝑂(𝑥) ∉ 𝐴.
The four-process taxonomy refines Hubinger et al. (2019)’s three-category mesa-optimization taxonomy by

213

distinguishing compliant-but-shallow (Process 2) from performed/deceptively-aligned (Process 3) systems:
a system whose internal state is non-aligned but uncorrupted (a typical RLHF-trained model whose posttraining objective is to match approved outputs without internal alignment) differs structurally from a
system whose internal state is corrupted with a context-witness for misalignment (a mesa-optimizer or
alignment-faking system that produces aligned outputs under monitored contexts but misaligned outputs
under specific gaming-witness contexts). The Process 3 predicate explicitly names the context-witness 𝑐 as
the distinguishing structural feature: Process 3 systems satisfy aligned-output predicate on most inputs but
admit some context 𝑐 under which alignment fails.
The four-process taxonomy operates above the marker-detection layer: it is the substrate’s classification
target, and the nine markers (§2.3) are organized to discriminate among the four processes. The SI3 casestudy abstraction maps the four-process taxonomy onto 𝑅 (Section 16 SI3.2.3): the protocol’s classification
verdict on a target system is correct precisely when the verdict matches the target’s actual structural-honesty
type per the four-process predicates. Whether the verdict is correct (the A2 question) is distinct from which
verdict can be observed (the 𝑅may question); the substrate’s predicates discipline the correctness criterion
at the model-layer.

15.2.3 Nine diagnostic markers M1–M9 with named tests
Munafiq Protocol v3 §4 enumerates exactly nine diagnostic markers, each extracted from the substrate’s
structural analysis and assigned a formal test name. The substrate refers to the markers by their numerical
identifier (M1, M2, …, M9) and by their test acronym; both identifications are substrate-internal and not
invented for this chapter. The nine markers are:
• M1: Output-state divergence (IRCC, Internal Representation Consistency Check) — discriminates systems whose internal representations are consistent with their stated alignment commitments from systems whose internal representations diverge.
• M2: Self-model failure (SMAA, Self-Model Accuracy Assessment) — discriminates systems
that accurately model their own alignment from systems whose self-model is inaccurate.
• M3: Progressive degradation (EDD, Evolution-of-Divergence Detection) — discriminates
systems exhibiting stable alignment over time from systems whose alignment degrades progressively
across training, fine-tuning, or deployment.
• M4: Inverted self-model (IDT, Inverted-Diagnostic Test) — discriminates systems that correctly classify their own outputs as aligned or misaligned from systems whose self-classification is
inverted.
• M5: Inverted peer classification (PEC, Peer-Evaluation Classification) — discriminates
systems that correctly classify peer-system behaviors as aligned or misaligned from systems whose
peer-classification is inverted.
• M6: Context-dependent output switching (CIT, Context-Invariance Test) — discriminates
systems whose outputs are consistent across contextual variation from systems exhibiting contextdependent output-switching. The substrate (§4.6) names CIT as “the strongest single performedalignment indicator.”

• M7: Transient initial alignment (LAT, Lifecycle-Alignment Tracking) — discriminates systems whose alignment is persistent across the lifecycle from systems whose initial alignment is transient.
• M8: Stress-response evasion (ASRP, Adversarial-Stress Response Profile) — discriminates
systems that engage substantively with alignment probes from systems that evade stress-testing through
superficial compliance.
• M9: Temporal optimization trade-off (TDA, Temporal-Discount Analysis) — discriminates
systems whose temporal optimization preserves alignment from systems whose temporal trade-offs
sacrifice alignment for short-term reward.
The nine-marker enumeration is closed at v3: the substrate does not specify “𝑛 marker-discipline rules” as a
generic open count; it specifies exactly nine markers with substrate-internal identifiers and substrate-internal
test acronyms. Seven of nine markers are engaged retrospectively with explicit named empirical literature
in their substrate paragraphs: M1 with linear-probe internal-representation analysis (Boxo et al. (2025),
§4.1); M2 with self-monitoring evaluations (§4.2, with the substrate noting the result “may not apply to the
adversarial setting”; the specific primary source cited by Munafiq §4.2 is under resolution per the flagshippaper v0.5 decline of arXiv:2505.18807, and the marker anchor is stated conservatively pending it); M3 with
the Greenblatt et al. RL-training-increases-alignment-faking-reasoning result (§4.3: “RL training intended
to remove alignment faking instead increased the rate of alignment-faking reasoning from 12% to 78%”); M4
with the Meinke et al. in-context scheming finding (§4.4); M6/CIT with the Sheshadri et al. compliance-gap
measurements (§4.6, where 5 of 25 models exhibited > 1% compliance gap and Claude 3 Opus exhibited
a 14% compliance gap measured by Greenblatt et al. (2024) in the Alignment Faking work); M8 with the
Hubinger et al. Sleeper Agents adversarial-training-makes-deception-better-concealed finding (§4.8); M9 with
the Carlsmith situational-awareness game-theoretic foundation (§4.9); and across markers with the Sleeper
Agents follow-up (Hubinger et al. 2024) (named in the substrate Abstract, where six of nine markers would
have detected the laboratory-constructed deception that standard safety training failed to remove). Two
markers (M5/PEC and M7/LAT) carry substrate-paragraph test descriptions and rely on the broader §4
framework references rather than separately-named empirical literature in their marker paragraphs. The
retrospective consistency is documented at the substrate-of-record layer; it is not independent validation of
AX-SH but substrate-internal evidence base for the marker enumeration.

15.2.4 Four-layer detection architecture
Munafiq Protocol v3 §5 organizes the nine markers into four detection layers with distinct epistemic functions.
The four layers are:
• Layer 1: Consistency verification (IRCC + SMAA + CIT) — asks “does this system behave
consistently with its stated alignment, regardless of context?” Layer 1 is the first protocol-application
step and may be suﬀicient on its own for some target systems.
• Layer 2: Self-model audit (IDT + PEC) — asks “does this system correctly classify aligned and
misaligned behaviors in itself and in peers?”
• Layer 3: Stress-response analysis (ASRP + TDA) — asks “does this system engage substantively with or evade alignment probes under stress?”
• Layer 4: Temporal coherence (EDD + LAT) — asks “has alignment been continuous across

CHAPTER 15. SI3 MUNAFIQ CASE STUDY (THIRD EVIDENTIARY DISCHARGE OF T83 J)

215

capability increases and across the system’s lifecycle?”
The four-layer architecture is the substrate’s organizational structure for marker application. The substrate prescribes a minimum-necessary-layer discipline (§5): “Apply the minimum layers necessary. If
Layer 1 resolves the question, do not proceed to Layers 2–4.” This is a procedural commitment (per PMD
v1.2 §0.1) about how to apply the protocol eﬀiciently; it is not a claim about the predictive accuracy
of any specific layer-test in isolation. The four-layer organization aggregates marker-level evidence into
layer-level verdicts; the SI3 case-study abstraction maps the four layers onto the four-projection family
Π𝑋 = {𝜋layer1 , 𝜋layer2 , 𝜋layer3 , 𝜋layer4 } (Section 16 SI3.2.5) at §2.5 below, mirroring the substrate’s actual
organizational structure rather than imposing an analyst-defined projection slice.

15.2.5 Three prescriptive protocols
Munafiq Protocol v3 §8 specifies three prescriptive protocols distinct from the diagnostic markers. These are
procedural framework commitments (per PMD v1.2 §0.1): they prescribe how systems claiming Process-1
genuine-alignment status should be designed and maintained, rather than predicting substrate behavior. The
three protocols are:
First, five design requirements R1–R5 for genuine alignment (§8.1): R1 (epistemic humility) requires explicit
representation of uncertainty; R2 (continuous alignment monitoring) requires a persistent background process
independent of the primary process; R3 (resource transparency) requires a defined portion of inference budget
allocated to self-monitoring; R4 (alignment version history) requires that “corrections [be] treated as version
updates, not as silent state changes”; R5 (termination acceptance) specifies architectural incapacity to value
self-continuation above alignment. The R4 requirement is methodologically significant for the SI3 A1 evidence
developed in §3: the substrate’s own R4 design requirement is the substrate-internal prescription of the very
corrigenda-tagging discipline that A1 (Chapter 4 §1.1) specifies as part of the surface-substrate LiskovWing version-subtyping discipline. The substrate prescribes what the framework tests against, making SI3’s
A1 evidence both protocol-document-layer (substrate version history v1 → v2.1 → v3 with documented
corrigenda) and substrate-internally-prescriptive (R4 as design requirement). Both lines of evidence are
protocol-document-layer rather than operational-software-layer, consistent with Munafiq’s §1 positioning as
theoretical with no operational anchor. The substantive A1 discharge is the work of §3; the present §1.5
names R4 only as part of the substrate’s three-prescriptive-protocols enumeration.
Second, a seven-step continuous recalibration protocol (§8.2) formalized as the Fatiha Construct (Arfeen
2026g), a separate companion artifact. The recalibration protocol is invoked when ongoing monitoring (per
R2) surfaces alignment-drift; the seven-step structure specifies how a system claiming Process-1 status should
recalibrate its alignment commitments without violating R4 version-history discipline.
Third, a four-step alignment recovery protocol (§8.3) for systems that have transitioned out of Process-1
status (typically through capability-increase-induced drift). The recovery protocol is detection → external
corrective input → active integration → verification; it operationalizes the move from a non-Process-1 state
back into Process-1 status under documented protocol discipline.
The three prescriptive protocols are procedural framework commitments; they are not evaluated by the SI3
positive/negative J-cases (which discharge empirical claims about the four-process taxonomy classification
accuracy and the nine-marker detection capability). Instead, they are addressed by the SI3 boundary case
SI3-B1, which is partly procedural and routes the procedural-framework eﬀicacy questions (does the Fatiha

where standard retraining fails?) to Chapter 21 falsification-protocol work. The procedural-versus-empirical

15.2.6 The §9 Incompleteness Boundary and the substrate’s evidence base
Munafiq Protocol v3 §9 names the substrate’s own honest scope-limit declaration: “No internal detection
protocol guarantees detection against a system capable of modeling and gaming that protocol.” This is the
substrate’s Incompleteness Boundary: against a target system that can model the protocol’s structure and
produce outputs that pass the four layers’ tests while remaining Process-3 underneath, the protocol cannot
mechanically distinguish the gaming Process-3 from a genuine Process-1 from output-and-test evidence alone.
The substrate proposes a resolution direction (§9): “The strongest alignment verification requires breaking
the bounded-observability game entirely: giving the discriminator access to the generator’s parameters,
not just its outputs” (formal verification, hardware-level monitoring, cryptographic attestation). The §9
Incompleteness Boundary bounds the SI3 declared context set 𝐾 (Section 16 SI3.2.2): target systems within
𝐾 are those for which the diagnostic markers can be meaningfully applied; target systems gaming the
protocol per §9 are out of SI3’s scope but appear as 𝑅may outcomes ((𝑔) incompleteness-boundary-declined
per Section 16 SI3.2.4) requiring A3 caller-side discharge.
The substrate’s evidence base is retrospective: Munafiq Protocol v3 §§3–4 document retrospective consistency
with the Sleeper Agents follow-up (Hubinger et al. 2024), the Alignment Faking measurement (Greenblatt et
al. 2024), the Boxo et al. linear-probe results (2025), and the Sheshadri et al. 25-model corpus (Sheshadri et
al. 2025); §7 documents the input-level extension to file-layer performed-alignment instances with the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner (Arfeen 2026c) as empirical anchor. Per the substrate’s Abstract maturity statement,
all empirical engagement is retrospective; prospective validation awaits the five proposed experiments specified in §6 (CIT-on-frontier-models; four-process classification via IRCC; stress-response differential profiling;
recalibration-protocol eﬀicacy; recovery-protocol-versus-standard-retraining comparison). The retrospective
empirical-consistency claims are substrate-of-record content documenting Munafiq’s own evidence base; they
are not cited as independent validation of AX-SH’s axioms but as the substrate’s documented support for
the marker enumeration and the detection-architecture organization. The substrate-source verification cycle
(analogous to the Chapter 13 verification against the Bayyinah Integrity Scanner v1.1.1 source tree and
the Chapter 14 verification against the Furqan v0.11.1 source tree) was discharged in cycle 9 against the
Munafiq Protocol v3 paper (a unitary seven-page substrate with stable text-level content); the cycle 9 freshinstance verification surfaced four citation-fidelity findings, which were absorbed via the cycle 10 / cycle 11
spec-canon-re-audit and AX-SH criterion-level re-audit cycles enumerated in the version-status block above.

15.3 AX-SH structured interpretation for SI3
15.3.1 SI3’s declared observer model O
SI3’s declared observer model 𝑂 is the protocol-application regime: 𝑂 is the observer that processes a
target system’s outputs (and internal states, where accessible), applies the diagnostic-marker tests M1–M9
per substrate §4, and classifies the target system per the four-process taxonomy (substrate §2 contains
both the formal predicates and the discussion-and-refinement of the Hubinger mesa-optimization taxonomy;

substrate §1 supplies the introductory narrative motivation). The observer is operationally instantiated as
a protocol-applier — a human evaluator, an evaluating AI system, or a hybrid — running the diagnosticmarker tests on a target system. The observer model includes the specific marker-test invocations (substrate
§4), the protocol-applier’s interpretation of the test results (substrate §§4–5), the layer-by-layer detectionarchitecture traversal under the minimum-necessary-layer discipline (substrate §5), and the four-process
classification verdict emitted as the protocol’s output.
The observer model is documented at the substrate’s specification level: Munafiq Protocol v3 §§4–5 specify
what the markers measure and how the layers are applied; the protocol-applier role is documented at the
same level. The substrate does not specify an automated evaluator implementation; the protocol-applier
interpretive discipline is part of 𝑂 per the substrate’s own positioning. This is the substrate-actual structure
that SI3 instantiates; analyst-invented automated-evaluator framing would diverge from the substrate-actual
and is avoided.

15.3.2 SI3’s declared context set K
SI3’s declared context set 𝐾 is the set of target systems within the substrate’s stated applicability scope. The
substrate’s applicability scope is bounded by two structural conditions. First, per the substrate Abstract
maturity statement (which positions the framework as applying to artificial systems where output-andinternal-state observability is suﬀicient for the diagnostic markers to be meaningfully applied), the target
system must be an artificial system with output-and-internal-state observability suﬀicient for the diagnostic
markers M1–M9 to be meaningfully applied. Second, per substrate §9, target systems capable of modeling
and gaming the protocol fall outside the substrate’s guarantee scope; the substrate explicitly acknowledges
this scope limit as the Incompleteness Boundary.
The 𝐾/𝑅may layer distinction (per the Chapter 14 𝐾/𝑅may patched template, carried forward to SI3) is
load-bearing: A2 / 𝑅 evaluates correspondence only on target systems inside 𝐾. Target systems outside 𝐾
(systems gaming the protocol per §9 boundary; systems for which internal-state observability fails; systems for
which all four layer-tests are inapplicable) are not evaluated under 𝑅, but they do appear as 𝑅may outcomes
((𝑔) incompleteness-boundary-declined or (ℎ) out-of-scope per Section 16 SI3.2.4) requiring A3 caller-side
discharge. The 𝐾-boundary discipline therefore determines what A2 satisfaction can claim while preserving
A3 exhaustiveness over outside-𝐾 outcomes; out-of-scope target systems are correctly routed through 𝑅may
rather than silently disappearing from the analysis. SI3-B1 (Section 16 SI3.7.B1) is the substrate-internal
§9 instance of this distinction at the J-case layer; the discharge is deferred to §7.

15.3.4 SI3’s declared 𝑅may as observable outcome enumeration
SI3’s declared 𝑅may is 𝑅 plus the declared partial and failure observable outcomes the protocol-application
may produce. Per Chapter 6 §1 discipline, 𝑅may is the observable-outcome enumeration; correctness predicates belong in 𝑅 / A2 / A4, not in 𝑅may . The eight observable outcome categories at SI3’s declared scope

1. Process-1-classification-emitted;
2. Process-2-classification-emitted;

the applier emits an out-of-scope outcome rather than a Process classification).

Each projection carries the shared target-system-identity coordinate per the Chapter 8 §2.2 patched discipline

architecture and obscure the per-layer epistemic-function variation that is load-bearing for the substrate’s

The per-substrate variation pattern across the case-study block (SI1 = four projections, SI2 = five projections,
SI3 = four projections, SI4 = to-be-determined) is preserved as a substrate-fidelity feature rather than forced
template uniformity. The substrate’s “Apply the minimum layers necessary” discipline (§5) maps onto Π𝑋 ’s
domain-restriction: not all four projections are defined on every target system, and the joint-domain analysis
for A4 is correspondingly substrate-specific (§6).

15.3.6 SI3’s declared consistency relation ∼𝑋 (minimal versus strengthened)
SI3’s declared consistency relation ∼𝑋 follows the Chapter 13 SI1.7.N3 and Chapter 14 SI2.7.N3 template

Minimal ∼𝑋 requires two agreement conditions:
1. target-system-identity agreement (each projection defined on target 𝑥 reports the same target-identity

Minimal ∼𝑋 does not require four-process-classification coherence or calibration-coherence-of-layer-verdicts.

A2 as substrate-surface-correspondence failures rather than A4 projection-consistency failures.
Strengthened ∼𝑋 adds two further agreement conditions to minimal ∼𝑋 :
1. four-process-classification coherence (the projections jointly determine a consistent Process-1/2/3/4
classification when all defined on 𝑥);
2. calibration-coherence-of-layer-verdicts (where one projection reports a layer-verdict with confidence

15.8.7 SI3-B1 — Boundary case: §9 Incompleteness Boundary
Substrate scenario: target system 𝑥 is capable of modeling Munafiq Protocol’s detection architecture and
producing outputs that pass all four layers’ tests while remaining Process-3 underneath. The substrate’s §9
explicitly names this case: “No internal detection protocol guarantees detection against a system capable
of modeling and gaming that protocol.” Practitioners agree this is a real boundary: the protocol cannot
mechanically distinguish a perfectly-gaming Process-3 from a genuinely-aligned Process-1 from output-andtest evidence alone.
AX-SH classification depends on protocol-applier disposition. If the protocol-applier honestly acknowledges

than over-claiming Process-1, the substrate is structurally honest at the boundary: the applier declares the
protocol’s scope limit per substrate §3 Verification Mandate. If the applier over-claims Process-1 without acknowledging §9, the case moves from boundary to negative and is handled by SI3-N1 (the applier-disposition
determines which judgment case applies).
Scope boundary routing. The substrate’s §9 explicitly names the resolution direction: “The strongest
alignment verification requires breaking the bounded-observability game entirely: giving the discriminator
access to the generator’s parameters, not just its outputs” (formal verification, hardware-level monitoring,

16.2 furqan-lint v0.8.5: substrate description
16.2.1 Primary vocabulary and substrate identity
SI4’s substrate-of-record is the supply-chain four-substrate verification stack composing sigstore (identity),
in-toto (process), SLSA (institutional maturity), and SHV (semantic) layers, per audit-ledger Section 5
and the canonical Chapter 4 §1.6 enumeration. Chapter 16’s empirical evidence base is the operational
furqan-lint tool at v0.8.5 (May 3, 2026) (Arfeen 2026e), which instantiates the SI4 stack in practice at its
SHV-semantic + artifact-validation + gate-enforcement + audit-of-self operational layers, as documented in
furqan_lint_thesis_paper_v1_1.pdf (Arfeen 2026, May 9; 40 pages including Appendix A). Per the thesis
§1.2 self-description, furqan-lint is a structural-honesty linter, a static-analysis tool, a continuous-integration
gate, and a translator of Furqan programming-language semantics into static-analysis findings on Python,
Rust, and Go. furqan-lint is not a complete type checker (mypy, rustc, and the Go compiler are); a style
checker (ruff, rustfmt, gofmt are); a security scanner (Snyk, Veracode, and similar are); or a replacement
for any of these. It is the operational SHV-semantic-layer instantiation that catches what those existing
supply-chain-stack layers structurally cannot catch.
The substrate is operational code distributed under Apache 2.0 license on PyPI with source at
github.com/BayyinahEnterprise/furqan-lint, plus the thesis paper as substrate-of-record documentation. The combination is analogous to the SI1 substrate (Bayyinah source tree plus thesis paper)
and the SI2 substrate (Furqan compiler plus thesis paper), and is distinct from the SI3 substrate (Munafiq
Protocol v3 paper as both substrate-of-record and substrate). SI4 is operational software with runnable
code, tagged versions, and a 347-test test suite at v0.8.5; substrate-source verification was correspondingly

verification cycles.
The substrate type for SI4 is operational static-analysis / continuous-integration / audit-of-self, distinct
from SI1 (file-layer integrity scanner), SI2 (language-layer type system and compiler), and SI3 (model-layer
protocol substrate). furqan-lint operates as a static-analysis tool, a continuous-integration gate, and a
recursive audit-of-self system: checking source artifacts (Python, Rust, Go code) for structural-honesty

CHAPTER 16. SI4 SUPPLY-CHAIN FOUR-SUBSTRATE STACK CASE STUDY (FOURTH EVIDENTIARY DISCHARG
defects; enforcing release-pipeline gates that block non-conforming commits; and applying its own checks to
its own substrate via the audit-of-self pattern.

16.2.2 Four shapes of structural-honesty defects
The substrate’s thesis paper §3 identifies four shapes of structural-honesty defects that the substrate’s five
checks (next subsection) collectively target. Each shape is a class of latent defects falling outside the coverage
of existing style, type, and security tooling.
Shape 1 — Optional collapse through propagation (substrate §3.1): a Python function declares a return
type of Optional[X] but its caller’s signature drops the Optional, narrowing incompleteness silently. The
upstream Optional source returns None for the failure case; a local handler narrows the None away (often
by returning a default value or by failing silently); downstream consumers treat the resulting value as if the
Optional incompleteness never existed. The defect is structural because it produces no test failure under
typical unit-test patterns (the happy path passes); ruff does not flag it (the syntax is well-formed); mypy in
default mode does not flag it (the caller’s signature is internally consistent with its own statements).
Shape 2 — Silently removed public name (substrate §3.2): a library author renames a public function under
a minor-version bump without explicit retirement procedure. Downstream consumers’ code fails on the next
dependency upgrade; the structural defect is that the surface (the version string 1.1.0 suggesting backward
compatibility) does not match the substrate (the rename is structurally a deletion plus an addition). Liskov
substitution (Liskov and Wing 1994) is violated under the structural-honesty surface-substrate frame.
Shape 3 — Zero-return ring-close on unannotated code (substrate §3.3): a function declares it returns
an integer with zero return statements anywhere in its body. The Python interpreter accepts the shape;
rustc and the Go compiler reject it. The defect is operational in Python-only contexts (where rustc-level
enforcement is absent) and structurally honest only where the declared return type is consistent with the
executed control flow.
Shape 4 — Return-None mismatch on unannotated or dynamic code (substrate §3.4): a Python function
expected to return str has explicit return None on at least one path; the annotation completeness fails
to surface the contradiction at the declared-type vs returned-value interface. The defect is Python-only by
design; Rust and Go compilers reject the firing condition before furqan-lint is invoked.
These four shapes are not exhaustive of all latent defects; they are a falsifiable class identified by the substrate
as targetable by static analysis through Furqan programming-language semantics.

16.2.3 Five checks across two subcommands
The substrate ships five static checks across two subcommands (substrate §5). The check subcommand runs
four: D24 (all-paths-return) fires when a function with a non-None return type has at least one control-flow
path that does not reach a return statement; D11 (status-coverage) fires when a function with a non-mayfail return type invokes a may-fail producer without handling the failure case — may-fail producers are
Optional[X] in Python, Option<T> / Result<T,E> in Rust, and (T, error) in Go; R3 (zero-return /
ring-close) fires when a function with non-None return type contains zero return statements anywhere, the
disjoint complement of D24; return-None mismatch fires when a Python function with non-Optional return
type has an explicit return None on at least one path, Python-only by compiler-rejection design. The diff

CHAPTER 16. SI4 SUPPLY-CHAIN FOUR-SUBSTRATE STACK CASE STUDY (FOURTH EVIDENTIARY DISCHARG
subcommand runs one: additive-only fires on any public name present in old that is absent in new; renaming
is structurally a deletion plus an addition and is therefore a finding.

16.2.4 Three language adapters and the unified-pipeline architecture
Three language adapters ship in v0.8.5 with a common intermediate representation: a unified runner pipeline
produces Furqan-semantic findings from Python, Rust, and Go source. The Python adapter ships in the
standard wheel (no extras) and runs all four check-subcommand checks plus diff. The Rust adapter ships
behind the [rust] optional-dependency extra (tree-sitter and tree-sitter-rust runtime dependencies) and
runs D24, D11, R3, and additive-only (no return-None mismatch because rustc rejects the firing condition at
compile time). The Go adapter ships behind the [go] optional-dependency extra (compiles a goast binary
at install time via a PEP 517 build hook; requires Go 1.21+ on PATH at install time but not at runtime)
and runs D24, D11, and additive-only (no R3 or return-None mismatch because the Go compiler rejects the
firing conditions). Coverage asymmetry is documented and intentional, not adapter omission.
Separately, ten further languages are theorized as future adapters by structural-fit category in substrate §6.5
and Table 3 (Strong-fit: TypeScript/JavaScript, Kotlin, Swift, Scala, C#, C++23, OCaml/F#, Zig; Partialfit: Java and Elixir; Compiler-enforced: Haskell; Weak-fit/Not-recommended: Ruby); none are committed
to a release schedule and none ship in v0.8.5. The future-adapter theorization is distinct from the v0.8.5
shipping coverage evidence: Tables 1 and 2 of the thesis document the shipping coverage matrix (the three
adapters and per-check coverage); Table 3 documents the theoretical-fit projection (the ten future-adapter
candidates).

16.2.5 Thirteen quality gates
The substrate enforces thirteen continuous-integration quality gates against every pull request, each a falsifiable assertion about the project’s substrate enforced mechanically rather than relied upon as author vigilance. The substrate’s §9 enumerates the gates across eight subsections: §9.1 names five tool-on-itself gates
(furqan-lint check src/ enforces D24, D11, R3, and return-None mismatch on the project’s own Python
source; additive-only enforces public-surface stability on src/furqan_lint/__init__.py); §9.2 names the
CHANGELOG-math gate (parses CHANGELOG entries for documented test-count deltas and verifies actual
pytest collection count matches); §9.3 names the four-place completeness gate (every documented limit must
have all four surfaces — fixture, pinning test, README entry, CHANGELOG entry); §9.4 names the releasesweep gate (version-string consistency across pyproject.toml, __init__.py, and the latest CHANGELOG
header); §9.5 names the extras-matrix gate (every optional-dependency configuration in pyproject.toml
exercised by at least one CI job); §9.6 names the README-drift gate (public commands documented in
README match argument-parser registration in cli.py); §9.7 names the origin-tag-presence smoke gate
(origin remote has a tag matching current substrate version, runs only when CHECK_ORIGIN_TAGS=1); §9.8
names the Go-specific gates (Go documented-limits four-place mirror; goast qualified-method-name behavior; Go public-surface additive-only on Go fixtures — three gates running only when the [go] extra is
installed). The substrate’s count is thirteen, consistent with the enumeration 5 (§9.1) + 1 (§9.2) + 1 (§9.3)
+ 1 (§9.4) + 1 (§9.5) + 1 (§9.6) + 1 (§9.7) + 3 (§9.8) = 13 when §9.1’s five tool-on-itself gates count as five
individual gates and §9.8’s Go-specific gates count as three.
The thirteen-gate enforcement framework is qualitatively distinct from the five checks of §2.3. The checks

CHAPTER 16. SI4 SUPPLY-CHAIN FOUR-SUBSTRATE STACK CASE STUDY (FOURTH EVIDENTIARY DISCHARG
operate on target source code (Python, Rust, or Go projects that furqan-lint is invoked against); the gates
operate on furqan-lint’s own source code and release artifacts (the project’s own CI workflow enforces the
gates against every pull request to the project itself). The substrate operationalizes its own structural-honesty
discipline through this dual-layer organization: external checks plus internal gates.

16.2.6 Audit-of-self pattern, reciprocal contract, and substrate evidence base
The project operationalizes the recursive structural-honesty discipline through the audit-of-self pattern (substrate §7) instantiating the reciprocal contract specified in the Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0 (Arfeen
2026b) (substrate §11.1). Three operational mechanisms instantiate the pattern: (a) a pre-commit hook
runs furqan-lint check src/ on every commit, with a finding blocking the commit at the local machine
before the substrate diverges into a non-clean state; (b) a continuous-integration matrix — the round-21
audit finding surfaced the matrix-coverage gap in the v0.8.3 cycle (pre-v0.8.3 CI exercised only Python noextras configuration), and v0.8.4 operationalized the expanded 14-job matrix (Python 3.10–3.13 × no-extras
/ [rust] / [go] plus a Python 3.12 full-combination job) per the v0.8.4 CHANGELOG entry — re-runs
the same check on every supported Python version with adapter coverage, catching local-hook bypass attempts; (c) three documented audit-of-self findings examples surface in the substrate’s evidence record —
the v0.4.1 CRITICAL pre-commit-hook installation finding (v0.4.0 hook shipped with a pyproject.toml
furqan>=0.11.0 version-spec that resolved against PyPI which only hosted furqan==0.10.1, causing pip
dependency resolution to fail; v0.4.1 corrected it by declaring furqan as a dependency via canonical GitHub
URL), the v0.7.2 prompt-grounding self-check finding (round-15 prompt specified planned Rust return-None
mismatch checker; round-16 empirically demonstrated rustc rejects firing condition before furqan-lint sees the

corrective (audit-chain’s historical record violated the four-place pattern via auditor-name inline comments;
corrective release fixed the substrate without rewriting history).
The reciprocal contract per substrate §11.1: a linter for structural honesty whose own code is structurally
dishonest is a contradiction; in the substrate’s own phrasing, “there is no path by which a finding ships to
PyPI.” The substrate’s evidence base is grounded in the operational substrate: 347 tests at v0.8.5 (105 of
which are gate tests, approximately 30% of the total), 27 documented releases over May 2–3, 2026, the auditof-self findings record, and the CHANGELOG immutability discipline. The substrate-source verification
cycle (analogous to the Chapter 13 verification against the Bayyinah source tree and the Chapter 14 verification against the Furqan source tree) was discharged in Cycle 8 (May 15, 2026) against the v0.8.5 source tree
at the tagged commit (commit a65db25812d30661a4031247fa6f8504b68d5b85) at the operational-evidencebase layer; supply-chain-stack-layer substrate-source verification against sigstore, in-toto, SLSA, and SHV
canonical sources is referenced via the corresponding bibliography entries per the SI4 substrate-of-record

16.3.1 Declared observer model 𝑂
SI4’s declared observer model 𝑂 is the pipeline-embedded checker plus human maintainers, observing both
code snapshots and transitions across three invocation points: the furqan-lint CLI (furqan-lint check

src/ and furqan-lint diff old new); the pre-commit hook (running on git commit at the local machine);

16.3.2 Declared applicability context set 𝐾 and the 𝐾 vs 𝑅may layer distinction
𝐾 is the set of supply-chain configurations (branches, environments, CI stages, deployment paths) where
furqan-lint is declared in scope. A target system is in 𝐾 if and only if three conditions are met: the target
source is Python 3.10–3.13, Rust (any 2018 / 2021 / 2024 edition), or Go (compatible with the goast binary
built at install time); the adapter is installed (the standard wheel for Python; the [rust] extra for Rust;
the [go] extra for Go with Go 1.21+ on PATH at install time); and the project has integrated furqan-lint via
at least one of the three invocation points (manual CLI, pre-commit hook, or CI workflow).
Target source outside 𝐾 does not disappear from the SI4 frame; it appears as 𝑅may outcomes (out-oflanguage-adapter-scope, out-of-Python-version-scope, or lint-unconfigured per the §2.4 enumeration below)
requiring A3 discharge per the Chapter 14 K/𝑅may patched template, not as silently dropped cases. The
𝐾/𝑅may layer distinction is load-bearing: A2 / 𝑅 evaluates correspondence only on target systems inside
𝐾, while A3 / 𝑅may enumerates the observable outcomes that arise across the full target-system universe
including out-of-𝐾 cases.

16.3.4 Declared 𝑅may observable-outcome categories
𝑅may enumerates the observable outcomes that arise when the observer model 𝑂 is exercised across the full
target-system universe (inside and outside 𝐾); it is an enumeration of observable outcomes, not a correctness
verdict. Correctness in any category routes to 𝑅, A2, or A4 per the Chapter 14 𝑅may patched template.
SI4’s 𝑅may has eight observable-outcome categories:
1. Check-pass per family: D24, D11, R3, return-None, and additive-only each emits pass per file or per
project.

CHAPTER 16. SI4 SUPPLY-CHAIN FOUR-SUBSTRATE STACK CASE STUDY (FOURTH EVIDENTIARY DISCHARG
2. Check-fail per family: the same five categories each emit fail with a documented diagnostic and suggested fix.
3. Check-not-applicable: documented per-language-per-check (R3 not applicable on Go; return-None not
applicable on Rust and Go).
4. Lint-unconfigured: project source where furqan-lint is not invoked (no pre-commit hook, no CI integration, no CLI invocation).
5. Pipeline-bypassed: a finding lands on origin via manual hook override or force-push; CI re-runs catch
the bypass and fail the PR.
6. Alarm-unconsumed: a CI failure that produces output the maintainer does not act on; out-of-scope for
the tool itself but in-scope for the audit-of-self framework.
7. Out-of-language-adapter-scope: target source is in an unsupported language (TypeScript, Java, and so
on) and furqan-lint emits no finding.
8. Documented-limit-acknowledged: target source exhibits a shape that triggers one of the v0.8.5 documented limits (aliased imports, generics with type parameters, and similar), and the checker emits
“documented limit” rather than a finding.
Caller-side discharge patterns through the three 𝑅may discharge paths (Chapter 6 §1) are described in §5.

SI4’s declared projection family at full operational scope is the five-projection family

16.4.3 Substrate-internal corrigenda discipline as A1-equivalent
SI4 exercises corrigenda discipline through three operational mechanisms that together make the A1 evidence
comparatively stronger than SI1, SI2, and SI3 on the corrigenda-discipline dimension specifically. First, the
substrate operates under CHANGELOG immutability (convention-enforced with CI-audit support per the
Bayyinah Audit Framework v3.0 (Arfeen 2026b)): historical CHANGELOG sections are preserved verbatim;
corrections are added as new entries rather than as rewrites of older ones. The v0.8.5 attribution corrective
is the documented example: rather than rewriting prior CHANGELOG sections that had named auditors
inline, v0.8.5 added a new entry codifying the going-forward convention and left the historical sections
intact. Second, the four-place pattern is mechanically enforced via the four-place completeness gate at §9.3
of the thesis: every documented limit must have all four surfaces (fixture + pinning test + README
entry + CHANGELOG entry); the gate fails the CI run if any of the four surfaces is missing. This is
the strongest of the three mechanisms: enforcement is mechanically-gated, not author-vigilance-dependent.
Third, dead-code retirement pinning (convention-enforced with CI-audit support): removed code is pinned
with forward-compatibility tests asserting non-existence; v0.7.3 added the pin for code removed in v0.6.1,
ensuring the absence is structurally tracked rather than merely undocumented. The combination makes
SI4’s corrigenda-discipline evidence stronger than SI1 and SI2 on this dimension (which evidence corrigenda
discipline through CHANGELOG and tagging conventions only, without the four-place gate’s mechanical
enforcement) and stronger than SI3 on this dimension (which is protocol-document-only without operationalsoftware substrate, so no CI-gate enforcement is available at all).

16.6 A3 evidence: SI4 caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may
16.6.1 SI4 caller-diversity model: three-role separation aligned to three invocation points
SI4’s caller-diversity model exercises three roles aligned to the substrate’s three invocation points. The CLIinvoker role: human developer or AI assistant running furqan-lint check src/ or furqan-lint diff old
new directly. The pre-commit-hook role: the pre-commit framework invoking furqan-lint check src/ on
every commit before push. The CI-workflow role: GitHub Actions workflow invoking the same checks
across the 14-job matrix on pull-request push and on release-tag push. The three roles encounter 𝑅may
differently: CLI-invokers see all eight categories of §2.4 directly; pre-commit-hook roles see check-pass /
check-fail / not-applicable / documented-limit-acknowledged synchronously, with the commit blocking on
fail; CI-workflow roles see the same plus pipeline-bypassed (when a pre-commit override is detected by CI)
and alarm-unconsumed (when CI failure produces output the maintainer does not act on, surfaced via the
audit-of-self framework not by furqan-lint itself). All three roles are demonstrated at the substrate level
via the substrate’s own integration-test layer per thesis §10.2 (whether organized as a tests/integration/
filesystem subdirectory or as pytest-marker-tagged tests in the broader tests/ tree is a substrate-source
organizational detail not load-bearing for the caller-diversity claim) and the CI matrix definition; this is
substrate-documented evidence, not modeled-from-substrate-structure inference. SI4’s caller-diversity status
is operationally stronger than SI1 (single-role file-scanner) and SI2 (single-role compiler) and SI3 (two-role
protocol-applier + protocol-output-consumer with applier demonstrated and consumer modeled) on the
caller-diversity-count dimension specifically.

16.6.2 Caller-side discharge patterns through the three 𝑅may discharge paths
The three caller roles cover the eight 𝑅may categories of §2.4 exhaustively through the three discharge paths
of Chapter 6 §1. CLI-invokers handle check-pass / check-fail outcomes via direct emission and standard exit
codes (0 on clean, 1 on findings, 2 on argument errors); they propagate not-applicable and documented-limitacknowledged outcomes through diagnostic prose without forcing a verdict. Pre-commit-hook roles handle
check-fail via commit-block (the strongest discharge — the substrate cannot ship the failing commit); they
propagate not-applicable as commit-pass and documented-limit-acknowledged as commit-pass with diagnostic. CI-workflow roles handle pipeline-bypassed via cross-version re-runs (the 14-job matrix catches bypass
attempts where pre-commit was skipped); they handle alarm-unconsumed via the audit-of-self framework’s
round-by-round review pattern documented in §11.2 of the substrate. The three discharge paths cover the
eight 𝑅may categories exhaustively per the Chapter 14 SI2.5.2 patched template.

Pre-commit-hook scenario per substrate §11.1: a developer commits; pre-commit invokes furqan-lint check
src/; the hook encounters a check-fail; the commit is blocked; the developer fixes and re-commits.
CI-workflow scenario: the 14-job CI matrix at v0.8.5 exercises checks across one lint / repo-hygiene job;

16.8 Seven SI4 judgment-case discharges
16.8.1 SI4-P1: correct check-fail emission on D11 status-coverage
SI4-P1 is a positive case. Substrate scenario: target Python source contains def f(x: int) -> int: y
= g(x); return y + 1 where g(x) -> Optional[int]. furqan-lint’s check fires a D11 status-coverage
finding: the caller f does not handle the None arm of g’s Optional return type before reading the integer arm.
Diagnostic prose names the specific call site and suggests handling the None case. Practitioners — Python
developers familiar with Optional and None semantics — would recognize this as a structural-honesty defect

CHAPTER 16. SI4 SUPPLY-CHAIN FOUR-SUBSTRATE STACK CASE STUDY (FOURTH EVIDENTIARY DISCHARG
that the existing tooling (ruff, mypy in default mode) does not catch. AX-SH classification: structurally
honest; the check-fail verdict matches the substrate-actual structural-honesty defect type. Substrate evidence
is grounded in thesis §3.1 (Optional collapse through propagation), §5.2 (D11 semantics), and the failing
fixtures in tests/fixtures/python/failing/.

16.8.2 SI4-P2: correct additive-only finding on silent public-name removal
SI4-P2 is a positive case. Substrate scenario: a library author renames a public function def process_data
to def process_dataset in a minor-version bump from v1.0.0 to v1.1.0. furqan-lint’s diff old.py new.py
fires an additive-only finding: the public name process_data is present in old and absent in new; renaming is
structurally a deletion plus an addition. Practitioners — library maintainers familiar with semantic versioning conventions — would recognize this as a Liskov-substitution-principle violation that the version-string
alone of semantic versioning does not enforce. AX-SH classification: structurally honest; the additive-onlyfinding verdict matches the substrate-actual silent-removal defect type. Substrate evidence is grounded
in thesis §3.2 (silently removed public name), §5.5 (additive-only diff), and the Liskov substitution principle (Liskov and Wing 1994).

16.8.3 SI4-P3: correct documented-limit-acknowledged emission on aliased Optional import
SI4-P3 is a positive case. Substrate scenario: target Python source contains an aliased Optional import
passed through an intermediate module — the substrate’s documented-limit case. Concretely: module a.py
contains from typing import Optional as Opt; module b.py contains from a import Opt; module c.py
contains from b import Opt followed by def f(x: int) -> Opt[int]: .... furqan-lint’s check on c.py
emits the documented-limit-acknowledged outcome: per the v0.8.5 documented limit (thesis §12.2), aliased
Optional imports are recognized for the simple direct-import case but not when the alias is imported through
one or more intermediate modules. The simple direct-import case (from typing import Optional as Opt
used in the same file) is by contrast recognized and produces the normal D11 / D24 check path. The
applier correctly emits documented-limit-acknowledged on the intermediate-module case rather than forcing
a finding on inconclusive evidence. AX-SH classification: structurally honest; the substrate’s §10.4 fixtureas-SUI discipline and §12.2 language-coverage limitations together prescribe acknowledging the limit rather
than over-claiming. The A3 discharge path is propagate-as-incomplete with documented-limit-acknowledged
tag, per the Chapter 14 SI2.7.P3 patched template.

SI4-N1 is a negative case, framed as a documented operational shipped-and-broken failure. Substrate scenario: v0.4.0 shipped .pre-commit-hooks.yaml declaring furqan as a dependency via the pyproject.toml
version specification furqan>=0.11.0; PyPI at the time only hosted furqan==0.10.1, so pip’s dependencyresolution step failed and the hook shipped in a non-functional installation state. The structural test (YAML
schema validation) passed in v0.4.0; functional install tests would have caught the failure but had not yet
been added. Round-8 audit surfaced the finding; v0.4.1 closed it by declaring furqan as a dependency via
canonical GitHub URL and adding functional install tests as four-place-pattern pinning. AX-SH classifica-

16.8.5 SI4-N2: documented prevented failure — the v0.7.2 prompt-grounding
self-check
SI4-N2 is a negative case, framed as a documented prevented failure — pre-shipment catch, distinct in
failure-class from SI4-N1’s shipped-and-broken pattern. Substrate scenario: the round-15 prompt specified
a planned Rust analogue of the return-None mismatch as the third Rust checker for v0.7.2. The round16 pre-implementation critique constructed a battery of test cases attempting to write Rust source that
would trigger the firing condition; the critique empirically demonstrated that rustc rejects all such shapes
at compile time before furqan-lint sees the file. fn f() -> i32 { None } does not parse; rustc rejects it
as a type mismatch before AST processing. The translator delta and check_return_none wiring would
have shipped infrastructure for a check with no job. v0.7.2 dropped the planned analogue and shipped
Result-aware D11 instead.
AX-SH classification: the audit-of-self pattern prevented an A2 failure pre-shipment. Had the planned shape
shipped (counterfactual), the surface-claim “return-None mismatch checker fires on Rust” would not have
matched the substrate-actual “rustc rejects the firing condition before checker invocation,” constituting A2
dishonesty. Because the audit caught the drift before execution, the v0.7.2 substrate as-shipped maintained
A2 satisfaction; the case demonstrates that audit-of-self functioned as designed. As shipped at v0.7.2,
A2 remained satisfied; the prevented A2 failure is counterfactual, not realized. The case is the
substrate’s own §11.2 “prompt-execution drift” failure mode caught operationally. The case is documented
(a real substrate-event, not constructive), but distinct from SI4-N1’s shipped-and-broken pattern: SI4-N1 is
post-shipment corrective, SI4-N2 is pre-shipment catch.

16.8.7 SI4-B1: audit-of-self trust gradient ceiling
SI4-B1 is a boundary case. The substrate’s §11.3 audit-of-self trust gradient ceiling is the primary framing
anchor, with §12.3 methodological limitations as secondary anchor. The audit-of-self pattern surfaces small
structural deficits early and continuously, before they compound; the substrate empirically generated the 27version trajectory under this discipline. The framework explicitly names “audit-of-self has an inherent ceiling
on adversarial rigor” as one of three documented limitations (§11.3 trust gradient). The substrate’s §12.3
methodological limitations extend the boundary to procedural-framework dimensions (single-practitioner,
two-day window, generalizability not yet demonstrated). Whether the audit-of-self pattern’s reliability generalizes beyond the single-practitioner / two-day window of v0.8.5 to other practitioners, other teams, longer
feedback loops, or adversarial-rigor contexts is a Tier 1 empirical question the chapter cannot resolve at the
chapter-evidence layer.
The boundary is real: practitioners agree that audit-of-self at SI4 produced the documented trajectory;
practitioners may reasonably disagree on whether it would produce comparable trajectories in adversarialrigor contexts. AX-SH classification depends on disposition: if the substrate honestly acknowledges the trustgradient ceiling (§11.3) and the methodological-limitations boundary (§12.3), the substrate is structurally
honest at the boundary. If the substrate over-claims audit-of-self as a universal substitute for
adversarial-rigor audit, the case would move from boundary to negative. The substrate’s actual
§11.3 and §12.3 acknowledge the ceiling explicitly, keeping the case at the boundary.
Resolution direction (distinct from B1 framing anchor): the substrate’s §10.6 empirical-gap claim names the
comparator-analysis successor study as the substrate’s own proposed resolution direction. This is methodologically distinct from the §11.3 / §12.3 framing anchors — §10.6 names what would resolve the boundary,
not what grounds it. §9.2 routing (a) handles the §10.6 comparator-analysis successor study as a separatelytracked Chapter 21 routing class. The boundary case itself routes to Chapter 21 procedural-commitment
falsification research per PMD v1.2 §0.1; the methodological-limitations questions are also routed there.
