17.1 §17.0 Role and scope
This chapter names two boundaries of the dissertation’s central results, and it names them as open problems
rather than closing them. The first is a boundary of decidability: the verification of AX-SH is decidable
only within a specific fragment, characterized in Chapter 10, and outside that fragment the question of
axiom satisfaction is undecidable. The second is a boundary of preservation: the long-horizon guarantees
of Chapters 11 and 12 hold for artifacts, specifications, and implementations that are in fact preserved, and
they fall silent where preservation has not occurred. Four earlier passages route these two matters here
explicitly — Chapter 10 §1.3 (“systems falling outside it are routed to Chapter 17, not silently assumed
away”), Chapter 11 §1.0, Chapter 12’s scope statement, and Chapter 21 §21.3 — and the present chapter
exists to receive them.
The discipline of the chapter is inherited, not invented. The scan-incomplete primitive of the Furqan
structural-honesty discipline (Chapter 14), instantiated operationally in the Bayyinah file scanner (Chapter 13) and the Munafiq protocol (Chapter 15), prescribes that a verifier which cannot fully extract the
substrate it is meant to judge clamps its confidence and names the gap, rather than asserting a consistency
claim it has not earned. Chapter 17 applies that same primitive reflexively, to the dissertation’s own theorems. Where the theory cannot decide, it says so; where it cannot reach a preserved substrate, it says so.
Naming the boundary is not a concession appended to the framework; it is the framework behaving as it
requires its objects to behave.
Two limits on the chapter’s ambition should be stated at the outset. First, it does not re-derive the apparatus
it works from: the decidable-fragment framework is Chapter 10’s, the preservation-adequacy result is Chapter
12’s, and both are consumed here as cited boundaries, not reproved. Second, it does not solve the problems
it names. In the manner the outline sets for the open-problems part, it states each problem precisely, locates
it against the established results, and identifies the preliminary work that would constitute progress, leaving
the problems open for future researchers. The claim ledger records the decidability limit as E1, a scopeexclusion held to be bounded-complete by design; this chapter is the prose discharge of that exclusion’s
forward-reference, not its resolution.

17.2 §17.1 The undecidable fragments
17.2.1 §17.1.1 Where decidability ends
Chapter 10 §1.3 fixes, axiom by axiom, the conditions under which the satisfaction predicate of AX-SH is
decidable. For Axiom 1 (append-only provenance), decidability holds under finite version histories, a finite

CHAPTER 17. UNDECIDABLE FRAGMENTS AND NON-PRESERVED SETTINGS

257

set of truth-status tags, and decidable behavioral subtyping. For Axiom 2 (surface–substrate consistency), it
holds under a finite observer-model and context-set (𝑂, 𝐾), a finite-state correspondence relation 𝑅 drawn
from the Chapter 5 family, and a finite-state substrate. For Axiom 3 (caller-side exhaustiveness over 𝑅may ),
it holds under a finite 𝑅may , finite caller-discharge specifications, and decidable invariant-verification for
the proven-unreachable cases. For Axiom 4 (substrate-parameterized projection consistency), it holds under
finite projection families Π𝑋 , finite joint domains, and a decidable consistency relation ∼𝑋 . The decidable
fragment is precisely the conjunction of these four finiteness conditions.
A fragment that violates them lies outside. Unbounded version histories, infinite-state substrates, an undecidable correspondence or consistency relation, an infinite 𝑅may or projection family — any of these places
the corresponding satisfaction predicate beyond the reach of a decision procedure. This is not a defect
in the proofs of Part III. Those proofs are stated relative to the fragment, and within it they are sound;
Theorem 10.1, Theorem 11.1, and Theorem 12.1 each carry the decidable-fragment scope as a stated hypothesis. The undecidability is a limit on the reach of those results, marked here so that no reader mistakes a
fragment-relative theorem for an unconditional one.
The undecidability is also not exotic. It is inherited from the underlying relations once their finiteness is
dropped, and those relations are classically understood. The bisimulation relation that underwrites Axiom
2 is decidable on finite-state systems in 𝑂(𝑚 log 𝑛) time but undecidable on general Turing machines; the
refinement relation that underwrites the Axiom 3 typing direction is decidable on finite algebraic types but
undecidable on infinite types in general. The dissertation’s introductory matter already names this in its
statement of what the work does not do. Chapter 17 simply takes the statement seriously as a research
boundary: the fragment is exactly as large as decidable bisimulation and decidable refinement allow it to be,
and the interesting question is what happens at its edge.

17.2.2 §17.1.2 The open problem
Inside the decidable fragment, a verifier can answer the question “does this system satisfy the axiom?” with
a terminating procedure. Outside it, no such procedure exists, and the dissertation’s downstream guarantees
inherit the conditionality directly: the 𝑛-fold independence of Chapter 11, the quantum survivability of
Chapter 10, and the preservation adequacy of Chapter 12 are all stated over the decidable fragment and say
nothing beyond it. The open problem is therefore not the satisfaction question itself, which is settled to be
undecidable, but its honest successor: what verifier behavior is available, and what can be claimed, when
the satisfaction question cannot be decided?
The survivability question of Chapter 10 illustrates how the problem changes character at the boundary, a
point Chapter 21 §21.3 makes precisely. Within the fragment, Theorem 10.1 shows that verification survives
the quantum transition because no public-key primitive sits in its critical path; the procedure exists, and
the theorem shows it endures. In the undecidable fragment there is no terminating verification procedure to
begin with, so the question “does the procedure survive the transition?” is replaced by the prior question
“is there a procedure at all?” — and the answer is no. A guarantee about the durability of a verification
capability is vacuous where the capability does not exist. The open problem inherits this: it asks not how to
preserve a decision procedure beyond the fragment, but what honest partial capability can stand in for one.

CHAPTER 17. UNDECIDABLE FRAGMENTS AND NON-PRESERVED SETTINGS

258

17.2.3 §17.1.3 Preliminary directions
Three directions would constitute progress, and the chapter names them without claiming any of them is
reached.
The first is sound one-sided semi-decision. Several of the underlying relations, while undecidable, are semidecidable in the direction of violation: a counterexample to consistency, once exhibited, is checkable even
when the search for it may not terminate. A verifier built on this asymmetry returns “violation found”
soundly, returns “no violation found within the bound” honestly, and never returns “consistent” without
a proof; on non-termination it clamps its confidence rather than defaulting to a positive claim. This is
the scan-incomplete primitive lifted from the file substrate to the undecidable fragment. Progress would
consist of characterizing, per axiom, which satisfaction predicates admit sound semi-decision in the violation
direction, and stating the resulting honest-verifier contract as a theorem rather than a design preference.
The second is sound finite abstraction. An infinite system can be replaced by a finite abstraction whose
satisfaction is decidable, after which the honesty question becomes whether the abstraction is sound: does
satisfaction on the abstraction imply satisfaction on the concrete system, or only the converse, and which
one-sidedness does each axiom require? Progress would consist of abstraction families, one per axiom, with a
proven direction of soundness and a calibration that ties the verifier’s reported confidence to the abstraction’s
precision, so that a coarse abstraction yields a correspondingly clamped claim.
The third treats the fragment boundary as a design constraint rather than only an analysis result. A system
can be engineered to remain inside the decidable fragment — bounded histories, finite-state correspondence
relations, finite projection families — and the Furqan type-checker of Chapter 14 already does exactly this,
declaring its scope as a decidable fragment of AX-SH and type-checking only within it. Progress here is
a characterization of the expressiveness cost: how much of the operationally interesting structural-honesty
discipline can be kept inside the fragment by construction, and which properties genuinely require the
undecidable reach and so can only ever be approached by the first two directions. This is named as a
dissertation-scale problem for future researchers; the present work establishes only that the boundary is real,
located, and not silently crossed.

17.3 §17.2 The non-preserved settings
17.3.1 §17.2.1 Where preservation’s guarantee ends
Theorem 12.1 proves that a system observing the six elements of the preservation discipline — multi-substrate
replication, cryptographic agility, format stability, institutional anchoring, translation discipline, and the
designated-continuation protocol — secures retrievability, integrity-checkability, and re-executability across
the long horizon. The theorem is an adequacy result conditioned on observance. It does not speak to the
settings it explicitly hands onward: those in which the discipline was not observed, and those in which it was
observed but preservation failed nonetheless, through catastrophic loss exceeding the replication redundancy,
institutional collapse outlasting the anchoring, or format obsolescence outrunning the migration cadence. In
each of these the artifact, specification, or implementations have not been preserved, and Theorem 12.1 is
silent by construction.
The forgery-resistance guarantee of Chapter 11 meets the same boundary from a different side. Theorem

CHAPTER 17. UNDECIDABLE FRAGMENTS AND NON-PRESERVED SETTINGS

259

11.1 makes undetected forgery require the coordinated corruption of all 𝑛 independent re-implementations,
and Proposition 11.2 fixes the effective strength of the guarantee as the count of surviving independent
fault sources. A setting in which implementations have been lost is a setting in which 𝑛 has fallen, and the
guarantee falls with it: below the threshold at which enough independent witnesses survive, the resistance the
theorem promises is no longer present. Non-preservation is thus not a single failure mode but a continuum
along which the Part III and Part IV guarantees lose their hypotheses.

17.3.2 §17.2.2 The open problem
The open problem is what structural-honesty guarantee, if any, survives when the substrate is not preserved,
and it has two faces. The first is reconstruction: from what partial remains can a verification capability
be recovered, and with what residual confidence? The second is graceful degradation: as preservation is
progressively lost — implementations dropping below 𝑛, fixture corpora decaying, reference parity eroding
— how does the guarantee degrade, is the degradation monotone, and, the structurally decisive question,
does the system know that it has degraded? A guarantee that silently continues to assert full strength while
its substrate erodes is precisely the surface–substrate divergence that Axiom 2 exists to detect; the honest
requirement is that reported confidence track surviving redundancy.

17.3.3 §17.2.3 Preliminary directions
Three directions again mark what progress would look like.
The first is degradation as a clamp rather than a cliff. The honest response to partial preservation loss is the
scan-incomplete clamp once more: a verifier that has lost some of its independent re-implementations should
report the reduced effective strength of Proposition 11.2, not a maintained guarantee. Progress would be a
formal degradation curve for each Part III and Part IV guarantee as a function of surviving preservation,
carrying the honesty constraint that the system’s reported confidence is a sound lower bound on its actual
surviving redundancy — never an over-claim.
The second is reconstruction bounds. Because the specification is itself a preserved artifact under the discipline, a lost implementation can in principle be re-implemented from it. But a reconstructed implementation
is an independent witness only if the re-implementer does not consult the survivors; otherwise reconstruction
restores count without restoring independence, and the effective strength of Proposition 11.2 does not rise.
Progress would be a characterization of the conditions under which reconstruction restores genuine independence, connecting directly to the independence assumption that Chapter 21 §21.2 names as the empirically
falsifiable hinge of the whole forgery-resistance guarantee.
The third observes that the non-preserved setting is the dual of the undecidable fragment, and names the
duality as itself a research direction. In the undecidable fragment the verifier lacks a terminating procedure;
in the non-preserved setting it lacks the substrate on which to run a procedure it has. Both are settings in
which the verifier cannot obtain what a positive consistency claim would require, and in both the honest
response is the same primitive: name the gap, clamp the claim. A unified account of partial verification
under missing capability and missing substrate — one theory covering both faces — is named here as a
multi-decade target, of a piece with the substrate-generalization program that Chapter 20 takes up.

CHAPTER 17. UNDECIDABLE FRAGMENTS AND NON-PRESERVED SETTINGS

260

17.4 §17.3 The unifying principle
The two boundaries are not independent caveats. They are one discipline applied in two places, and the
discipline is the scan-incomplete primitive turned upon the dissertation itself. In every operational instance
the framework already insists on it: the Bayyinah scanner clamps confidence when it cannot extract the
bytes (Chapter 13); the Furqan type-checker confines itself to a declared decidable fragment (Chapter 14);
the Munafiq protocol operates under bounded observability and reports accordingly (Chapter 15). The
structurally honest move, whenever a verifier cannot fully see, is to name the limit and clamp the claim
rather than assert a guarantee it has not earned.
Chapter 17 makes that move for the theory. AX-SH does not claim to decide structural honesty on arbitrary
systems; to claim it would be to assert a decision for an undecidable question, which is the very species of
surface–substrate divergence the framework is built to catch. It does not claim to preserve what has not been
preserved. Stating these two boundaries is therefore not an apology for the theory’s reach but an exercise
of the theory: a surface claim — “AX-SH verification is decidable,” “the preservation guarantee holds” — is
held to exactly its substrate warrant, the decidable fragment and the observed discipline, and not extended
past it. The recursive Incompleteness Boundary that Chapter 22 develops applies here in its simplest form:
no framework certifies its own complete reach from the inside, and the honest response is the append-only
naming of the boundary, left open to future work, in place of a claim of completeness.

17.5 §17.4 Synthesis and routing
This chapter discharges the forward-references that Chapter 10 (§1.0, §1.3, §1.8), Chapter 11 (§1.0), Chapter
12 (scope), and Chapter 21 (§21.3) route to Chapter 17. The undecidable fragments and the non-preserved
settings are named-open here, each located precisely against the established result it bounds — the decidable
fragment of Chapter 10, the preservation adequacy of Chapter 12, the effective-strength count of Proposition
11.2 — and each accompanied by the preliminary directions whose completion would constitute progress.
Consistent with claim-ledger E1, the decidability limit is recorded as a scope-exclusion, bounded-complete
by design; naming it here is the discharge of its forward-reference obligation, not its solution.
Three forward routings remain. The empirical falsification of the independence assumption, on which the
non-preservation degradation of §17.2 depends, is Chapter 21’s (§21.2). The self-application of the naming
discipline this chapter uses — the framework holding its own surface claims to their substrate — is Chapter
22’s. The designated-continuation protocol on which the reconstruction question of §17.2.3 ultimately leans,
since reconstruction presupposes a preserved specification and an institution to maintain it, is Chapter 23’s.
The chapter solves neither problem, and that is its function. It marks, as exactly as the established results
allow, where the dissertation’s guarantees stop: at the edge of the decidable fragment, and at the edge
of what has been preserved. A reader who carries that boundary forward will not mistake the conditional
theorems of Part III and Part IV for unconditional ones, which is the whole of what an honest open-problems
chapter is asked to secure.

18.1 §18.0 Role and scope
The preceding open-problems chapters named boundaries of the dissertation’s theory: Chapter 17 the points
at which axiom satisfaction becomes undecidable or the substrate is not preserved, Chapter 20 the substrates
to which the schema may not instantiate. This chapter and the next turn from the theory to the method.
The audit methodology by which this dissertation was built and verified makes, on every finding, a decision
among a small set of response shapes; and that decision, made hundreds of times across the audit chain, has
never been formalized. Naming its formalization as an open problem is this chapter’s whole task.
The decision is concrete. The six-element findings format requires every finding to carry a disposition, and
the disposition is one of three shapes: accept the finding and fix the artifact (Shape A); accept the finding
but defer the fix (Shape B); or decline the finding with a justification (Shape C). The choice among the three
is currently made by judgment. An auditor weighs how severe the finding is, how much of the artifact it
touches, what the fix would cost, and what the risks are of fixing or of not fixing – and selects a shape. The
weighing is real and largely consistent across the audit chain, but its criteria are implicit: there is no stated
function from a finding’s properties to its shape, only an exercised one. The open problem is to make that
function explicit, principled, and checkable.
The chapter owns the two ledger items that record this problem, O2 and E3, and it treats them as namedopen rather than solved. In the manner of the open-problems part, it states the problem precisely, sketches
the shape a formalization would take, identifies the existing theory it would build on, and says what progress
would consist of – and it stops there. It does not supply the decision algebra; it argues that one is constructible
and names its construction as a tractable medium-term research target, in the ledger’s own words. Two
scoping notes. First, the chapter takes the response-shape classification as given from the methodology;
it does not revise the shapes. Second, one of the four decision inputs – severity – is itself only partially
formalized, carrying its own named-open problem, and §18.2 marks that dependency rather than resolving
it.

18.2 §18.1 The response shapes and the implicit decision
A finding, in the six-element format, is an attack on an artifact: it asserts that some element of the artifact
fails a standard the artifact claims to meet. The disposition is the artifact’s answer to that attack, and it
takes one of three shapes. Shape A, accept-and-fix, concedes the attack and repairs the artifact, after which
a re-verification confirms the repair. Shape B, defer, concedes the attack but routes the repair to a later
cycle, recording the deferral so that the obligation is not lost; the publication-form items carried through this

CHAPTER 18. A DECISION ALGEBRA FOR RESPONSE SHAPES

263

dissertation’s punch list are Shape B dispositions. Shape C, decline-with-justification, contests the attack,
supplying a reason the asserted failure is not in fact a failure – a misreading of the substrate, a convention
the finding did not account for, a scope the finding overstepped.
The three shapes are a discrete space, and selection among them is a function in the mathematical sense:
the same finding, with the same properties, before the same standards, should receive the same shape. But
the function is exercised, not written. What an auditor actually consults, in choosing, is a small cluster of
considerations: the severity of the finding, on the CRITICAL / HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW scale; the scope
of what it affects, from a single locus to a cross-cutting structural concern; the cost of the fix, in effort and
in the risk of disturbing what already verifies; and the risk attached to each shape, the residual exposure
of deferring or declining weighed against the exposure of an unnecessary or destabilizing fix. These four
considerations are weighed, and a shape falls out. That the weighing is consistent enough to run an audit
chain on is evidence that an implicit function exists; that no one has written it down is the open problem.
The cost of leaving it implicit is the cost of any unstated standard: it cannot be checked, it cannot be taught
except by apprenticeship, and it cannot be shown to be free of the inconsistencies an explicit standard
would expose. An implicit shape-selection function might, on two findings that are identical in their four
considerations, return different shapes, and nothing in the method would catch the divergence. Making the
function explicit is what would make it auditable – which is precisely the discipline the dissertation argues
for, turned upon the dissertation’s own process.

18.3 §18.2 The shape of a decision algebra
A formalization would have the structure of a decision algebra: a set of decision inputs, a structure on those
inputs, and a selection rule that maps an input tuple to a shape, subject to constraints. The inputs are the
four considerations of §18.1 – severity, scope, cost, and risk. The selection rule would render shape-selection
as a constrained optimization: among the shapes admissible for a given input tuple, choose the one that
minimizes residual risk together with fix cost, subject to hard constraints that encode the non-negotiable
parts of the method. A CRITICAL finding, for instance, is not deferrable, which is a constraint forbidding
Shape B in the high-severity region; a Shape C decline is admissible only when its justification clears a stated
bar, which is a constraint on the conditions under which declining is in the admissible set at all. The algebra
is the pairing of this input structure with this constrained selection rule.
Two features of the inputs make the algebra non-trivial, and both are why the problem is open rather than
closed. The first is that the inputs do not collapse to a single scalar. Severity, scope, cost, and risk are distinct
dimensions, and a finding that is low-severity but cross-cutting is not comparable on a single axis to one that
is high-severity but local; the input is a vector, and selection over a vector input is a multi-criteria decision,
a partial order rather than a threshold on a number. The second, and sharper, is that one of the four inputs
is not itself fully formalized. Severity is operated as a total preorder over the four bands CRITICAL / HIGH
/ MEDIUM / LOW, but the criteria beneath the bands – user impact, data loss, frequency, recoverability –
do not themselves collapse to a scalar, so severity is more faithfully a partial order on impact vectors than a
four-point scale. That severity rubric carries its own named-open formalization problem; it is the item the
cycle-66+P reconciliation re-homed from a dedicated chapter to a named-open mention placed where the
rubric is used, and this is that placement. A decision algebra over severity therefore inherits an unformalized
input: until the severity rubric is itself a defined partial order, the algebra’s severity dimension is only as

CHAPTER 18. A DECISION ALGEBRA FOR RESPONSE SHAPES

264

precise as the band scale. The algebra can be built atop the band scale as an approximation, but its exactness
is bounded by the severity problem it sits on.

18.4 §18.3 The connection to argumentation frameworks
The natural theory to build the algebra on is the theory of argumentation frameworks. A finding is an
attack and a disposition is a response to it, and the formal study of which attacks survive which responses
is exactly what abstract argumentation frameworks were introduced to model (Dung 1995). In that setting
one has a set of arguments and an attack relation between them, and the question is which sets of arguments
are collectively acceptable – which survive all attacks from within an acceptable set. An audit chain has
the same shape: findings attack an artifact, dispositions respond, re-verifications attack the repairs, and the
question of whether the artifact closes clean is the question of whether a stable, acceptable configuration
has been reached. The response shapes map onto resolution moves in such a framework, and shape-selection
onto the computation of an acceptable extension.
The connection is more than an analogy, because the audit process is already, informally, a structured dispute:
a finding and its disposition, a re-bind that may attack the disposition, a lone flag checked against the source
rather than outvoted. The literature on formal-dispute mediation studies precisely such structured, multiparty resolution processes, and a decision algebra for response shapes would sit at the meeting of that
literature with Dung’s frameworks. Formalizing the audit chain as an argumentation framework, the shapes
as resolution moves, and shape-selection as extension computation is the route this chapter names. It does
not walk the route; it identifies the framework the walking would use.

18.5 §18.4 Tractability and preliminary directions
The ledger calls this a tractable medium-term target, and the qualifier is earned rather than hopeful, for
three reasons. The decision space is small: three shapes and four inputs, not an open-ended space. The
supporting theory is mature: argumentation frameworks have three decades of development behind them and
formal-dispute mediation a substantial literature. And, distinctively, the problem comes with data. Every
cycle of this dissertation’s audit chain is a recorded instance of the implicit function in action – a finding
with its four properties, and the shape it received – so the audit ledger is itself a corpus of input-to-shape
decisions against which a candidate algebra can be fit and tested. The problem is not to invent a decision
rule in the abstract but to recover one that already operates and to check it for the consistency an explicit
rule can be held to.
Three directions would constitute progress, and the chapter names them without claiming any is reached.
The first is empirical recovery: extract the implicit shape-selection function from the audit-ledger corpus, by
reading each finding’s recorded severity, scope, cost, and risk against the shape it received, and ask whether
a consistent rule fits and where it fails. The second is the formal dependency: resolve, or at least bound,
the severity input’s own partial-order problem, since the algebra’s exactness is capped by it; progress on the
severity rubric is progress on the algebra. The third is the framework mapping: cast the shapes as resolution
moves in an argumentation framework after Dung, define shape-selection as extension computation, and
check the resulting algebra for the two properties an explicit decision rule must have – consistency, that it
never prescribes two incompatible shapes for one finding, and coverage, that it prescribes some shape for

CHAPTER 18. A DECISION ALGEBRA FOR RESPONSE SHAPES

265

every finding the method admits. Each is a self-contained piece of work; together they are the medium-term
program the chapter proposes.

18.6 §18.5 Synthesis and routing
This chapter names the open problem recorded as O2 and E3: the response-shape decision – Shape A acceptand-fix, Shape B defer, Shape C decline-with-justification – is a discrete space selected by an implicit function
of severity, scope, cost, and risk, and its formalization as a decision algebra over those inputs, with shapeselection as a constrained optimization grounded in argumentation frameworks, is a tractable medium-term
research target. No earlier chapter routed this problem here; the chapter names a question the method raises
about itself, and naming it discharges nothing in the ledger beyond recording O2 and E3 as named-open,
which they remain.
Two routings connect this chapter outward. The severity input carries the re-homed severity-rubric problem
(the E2 item), and this chapter is where the cycle-66+P reconciliation places its mention; the rubric’s
formalization as a partial order is a dependency of the algebra, named here and owned nowhere as a dedicated
chapter. And the empirical corpus the formalization would be fit against is the dissertation’s own audit chain,
which is the subject of Chapter 19’s audit-chain dynamics and of Chapter 22’s self-application; the decision
algebra and the audit-chain regularities are two formalizations of the same recorded process, and progress
on either informs the other.
The chapter supplies no algebra, and that restraint is the discipline. It shows that the response-shape decision
is a real function exercised consistently enough to run an audit chain on, that the function is currently implicit
and therefore unauditable, and that the materials for making it explicit – a small decision space, a mature
supporting theory, and a corpus of recorded decisions – are at hand. Naming the construction of the algebra
as the open problem, rather than presenting a half-built one as a result, is what an honest open-problems
chapter is asked to do.

19.1 §19.0 Role and scope
Chapter 18 turned from the dissertation’s theory to its method and named the response-shape decision as
an unformalized object. This chapter stays with the method and takes up a larger object: the behavior
of an audit chain as a whole, over its cycles. The Bayyinah Audit Framework predictive paper records
eleven empirical regularities, R1 through R11, that audit chains exhibit – patterns observed to recur across
chains, strong enough that the framework treats them as predictive. The open problem this chapter names is
whether those eleven regularities can be promoted from observed patterns to the axioms of a formal theory:
a theory of audit-chain dynamics from which the observed behavior would follow as consequence rather than
coincidence.
The move is the familiar one by which an empirical science becomes a formal one. Regularities are noticed;
they are catalogued; and at some point one asks whether they can be taken as primitives from which the rest
is derived, whether those primitives are mutually consistent, and whether they are complete. This chapter
asks those questions of R1–R11 and answers none of them. It states the formalization program, identifies
its two principal checks – consistency and completeness – and names the construction of the formal model
as the open target, in keeping with the open-problems discipline of this part. It does not build the model,
prove the consistency, or settle the completeness.
Two scoping notes govern what follows. First, the eleven regularities are the cited paper’s (Arfeen 2026b), and
this chapter does not restate them: their content belongs to that source, and the survey of each regularity
against its evidence is itself the first task of the program named here, not a thing this chapter performs.
Naming a regularity-set one has not reproduced is the honest posture when the set lives in a cited work;
inventing eleven statements to fill the slot would be the opposite of the discipline this dissertation argues
for. Second, the chapter owns O3 and E4 as named-open, and it treats the dissertation’s own audit chain –
recorded in full in the append-only ledger – as the nearest available instance of the dynamics in question, a
data source rather than a proof.

19.2 §19.1 Regularities as candidate axioms
An empirical regularity and an axiom are different kinds of statement. A regularity is observed: across
many audit chains, a pattern holds often enough to be worth recording and, in the predictive paper’s use, to
forecast. An axiom is posited: it is taken as true at the base of a theory, and the theory’s other statements
are derived from it. The proposal O3 records is to attempt the promotion – to take R1–R11, observed

CHAPTER 19. AUDIT-CHAIN DYNAMICS: R1–R11 AS CANDIDATE AXIOMS

268

regularities of audit-chain behavior, and treat them as the axioms of a formal model in which audit-chain
behavior is the derived consequence.
The promotion is not automatic, and the gap between the two kinds of statement is exactly where the open
problem lives. Regularities are observed one at a time and need not cohere as a set; two patterns each
reliable on its own may, taken as simultaneous axioms, over-determine some configuration or contradict on
some edge case. Regularities are also observed within the range of the chains that produced them and need
not extend; a set complete for the observed chains may be silent on chains of a kind not yet seen. So the first
task of the program is the survey the cited paper’s regularities invite: for each of R1–R11, state precisely
what it claims, identify the evidence that supports it, and judge whether its form is fit to serve as an axiom
rather than a summary statistic. That survey is named here as work to be done against (Arfeen 2026b), not
work this chapter discharges.
The dissertation’s own audit chain illustrates the kind of regularity at issue without standing in for the
cited set. This chain is multi-cycle and multi-vendor, and its ledger records patterns that recur: that a
producer-correlated error is most reliably caught by a vendor of a different family than the producer; that
a lone fidelity flag checked against the source is more often right than the majority that missed it; that a
chain converges toward clean as corrections are bound rather than diverging. These are observed regularities
of one chain, and they are the texture of what a theory of audit-chain dynamics would have to predict.
Whether they are among R1–R11, instances of them, or regularities the eleven do not yet name is precisely
the completeness question of §19.3.

19.3 §19.2 The consistency check
The first formal question, once R1–R11 are taken as candidate axioms, is whether they are mutually consistent: whether there is any audit-chain scenario in which two of them prescribe incompatible outcomes.
Consistency is not given by the regularities’ individual reliability. Each may hold on its own and still conflict
with another at the boundary – one regularity predicting that findings concentrate early in a chain, say,
and another predicting a late surge under some condition, with a scenario satisfying the condition forcing
both at once. Empirical regularities are observed in the aggregate, where such conflicts average out and go
unnoticed; as axioms, evaluated pointwise, the conflicts become visible.
The consistency check is therefore the demand that the candidate axiom set have a model: that some formal
structure of audit-chain dynamics satisfies all eleven regularities simultaneously, with no scenario in which the
set entails a contradiction. Discharging it requires the formal model first – one cannot check the consistency
of axioms without a semantics in which to interpret them – which is why the model’s construction (§19.4)
is prior to both checks. The consistency check is named here as the first thing the constructed model must
establish, and it is left open.

19.4 §19.3 The completeness check
The second formal question is completeness: whether R1–R11 characterize all observable audit-chain patterns,
or whether there are behaviors that occur but that the eleven do not predict. A regularity set can be perfectly
consistent and still incomplete, covering the chains it was drawn from while missing patterns that appear

CHAPTER 19. AUDIT-CHAIN DYNAMICS: R1–R11 AS CANDIDATE AXIOMS

269

in chains of a different shape – a different vendor mix, a different artifact class, a longer horizon than the
observed chains ran.
The completeness check has two possible outcomes, and naming both is the honest form of the question.
Either the eleven regularities are demonstrated to generate every observed audit-chain pattern, in which
case the theory is complete on the available evidence; or specific patterns are exhibited that R1–R11 do not
predict, in which case the missing regularities are identified and the set is extended – an R12, an R13 – and
the check is run again. The dissertation’s own chain is a natural first test corpus: its recorded patterns
can be put to the candidate axiom set to ask whether each is predicted, and the producer-correlated-miss
pattern of §19.1 is exactly the kind of recorded behavior against which completeness would be probed. The
completeness check, like the consistency check, presupposes the model and is left open.

19.5 §19.4 Constructing the model, and preliminary directions
The two checks share a prerequisite: a formal model of audit-chain dynamics in which R1–R11 can be
interpreted as axioms and audit-chain behavior derived as consequence. The natural form is a dynamical
one – audit-chain states, with the cycle as the transition, and the regularities as constraints on the transition
relation – but the form is itself part of what the open problem must settle, and this chapter does not fix
it. What it can say is that the materials are unusually favorable: the regularities are already catalogued
and cited (Arfeen 2026b), and recorded audit chains, including this dissertation’s own fully documented one,
supply transition data of exactly the kind a dynamical model is fit and tested against.
Three directions would constitute progress, matching the program O3 and the v0.1 outline name. The first
is construction: build the formal model – a state space of audit-chain configurations, a cycle transition, and
R1–R11 expressed as constraints on it. The second is the consistency proof: exhibit a structure satisfying
all eleven regularities at once, establishing that the candidate axioms are jointly satisfiable and entail no
contradiction. The third is the completeness determination: test the model against recorded chains, and
either demonstrate that R1–R11 generate every observed pattern or identify the regularities they miss and
extend the set. Each is a self-contained piece of work, each presupposes the construction before it, and
together they are the program this chapter names and leaves open.

19.6 §19.5 Synthesis and routing
This chapter names the open problem recorded as O3 and E4: the eleven empirical regularities R1–R11 of
the Bayyinah Audit Framework predictive paper (Arfeen 2026b) are candidate axioms for a formal theory of
audit-chain dynamics, and the construction of that theory, its consistency check, and its completeness check
are an open research target. No earlier chapter routed this problem here; the chapter names a question the
method raises about its own behavior, and naming it records O3 and E4 as named-open, which they remain.
The eleven regularities are cited, not restated, and the survey of each against its evidence is the program’s
first task, not this chapter’s act.
The chapter’s routings are two, and both point at the same place. The audit chain whose dynamics are in
question is recorded in the dissertation’s own append-only ledger, which is also the empirical corpus Chapter
18 would fit its decision algebra against: the response-shape decision and the audit-chain dynamics are two
formalizations of one recorded process, and a model of the chain’s transitions would carry the shape-selection

CHAPTER 19. AUDIT-CHAIN DYNAMICS: R1–R11 AS CANDIDATE AXIOMS

270

of each finding as part of its state. And the reading of the dissertation’s own chain as data – a structurally
honest object turning its method’s record upon itself – is the self-application Chapter 22 takes up. The
decision algebra of the previous chapter and the dynamics theory of this one are the method becoming, in
two complementary ways, an object of its own study.
The chapter constructs no model and proves no check, and that restraint is the point. It shows that audit
chains exhibit catalogued regularities, that promoting those regularities to axioms is a definite and well-posed
program with consistency and completeness as its principal questions, and that the data for the program
– catalogued regularities and recorded chains – are at hand. Naming the construction of the theory as the
open problem, rather than presenting a sketch of one as a result, is what an honest open-problems chapter
is asked to do.

20.1 §20.0 Role and scope
The dissertation makes a substrate-independence claim, and it makes it carefully. Chapter 1 §3 states that
the formalization is substrate-independent in a scoped sense: the same axiom schema can be interpreted
across files, programming languages, machine-learning models, supply-chain artifacts, and candidate further
substrates, once the substrate-specific extraction is specified. The claim is not that AX-SH applies to every
substrate without modification; it is that AX-SH is a schema, and that the schema instantiates on a substrate
once one supplies that substrate’s surface and substrate definitions and its projection families. Part IV made
the claim concrete four times, instantiating the schema on four substrates. This chapter takes up what those
four instances do not settle: whether, and on which further substrates, the schema instantiates at all.
The question is genuinely open, and the chapter treats it as open. In the manner of the open-problems
part — and of Chapter 17, which named the decidability and preservation boundaries of the dissertation’s
core results — this chapter names a boundary of the substrate-independence claim and does not pretend
to have walked it. It owns three ledger items as named-open problems: ST1, the substrate-independence
claim itself, drafted in Chapter 1 and carrying its proof obligation here; SC1, the catalog of candidate future
substrates whose schema-applicability is a research question rather than a foregone conclusion; and O4,
the generalization-beyond-the-four problem itself. It also owns one falsification path: the path on which a
substrate is exhibited to which the schema does not instantiate at all, recorded as ST1’s falsification route
and cross-referenced from Chapter 21 §21.2. The scope of the chapter is to state the generalization question
precisely, to distinguish its three possible outcomes for any candidate substrate, to catalog the candidates
and identify what progress on each would look like, and to fix the boundary with Chapter 21. It does not
generalize the schema to any fifth substrate; that is the multi-decade research program the chapter names.

20.2 §20.1 The schema-instantiation claim and what the four instances establish
The substrate-independence claim has a precise form, and the form matters to everything that follows.
AX-SH is parameterized by substrate. Axiom 4, developed in Chapter 7, is already a substrate-parameterized
projection consistency over a family Π𝑋 of projections indexed to the substrate 𝑋; the other three axioms
acquire their substrate content the same way, through the substrate’s surface and substrate definitions and
the correspondence relation between them. To instantiate the schema on a substrate 𝑋 is to supply four

CHAPTER 20. SUBSTRATE GENERALIZATION BEYOND THE CURRENT FOUR

273

things: an append-only history structure for Axiom 1, a surface-substrate distinction with a correspondence
relation for Axiom 2, a caller boundary with a conservative outcome approximation for Axiom 3, and a
projection family Π𝑋 with a consistency relation ∼𝑋 for Axiom 4. Where those four can be supplied and the
resulting predicates are operationally checkable, the schema instantiates; where they cannot, it does not.
Part IV supplied them four times. Chapter 13 instantiated the schema at the file-integrity layer, the Bayyinah
substrate, with its surface as rendered content and its substrate as raw bytes and embedded payloads.
Chapter 14 instantiated it at the programming-language layer, the Furqan substrate, mapping the language’s
structural-honesty primitives onto the axioms. Chapter 15 instantiated it at the model layer, the Munafiq
protocol, restating its four-process taxonomy in AX-SH terms. Chapter 16 instantiated it at the software
supply-chain layer, composing four independent verification substrates. Each of these is an existence proof:
it shows that on this substrate, the four components can be supplied and the axioms become operationally
checkable. Four existence proofs are exactly four existence proofs.
What the four do not establish is generalization, and the case-study chapters are scrupulous about saying
so. Each carries a permissive Chapter 20 routing note that surfaces substrate-specific observations while
explicitly declining to assert that they transfer. Chapter 13’s note is representative: the four-projection
family it uses — kind, zahir-batin, pdf, scan — is SI1-specific to file-layer scanning, and whether that
projection-family structure carries to any other substrate is left to this chapter, not claimed there. The same
restraint governs Chapters 14 through 16. The four instances therefore establish that the schema instantiates
on these four substrates; they are silent, by their own declaration, on whether it instantiates on a fifth. The
gap between “instantiates on these four” and “instantiates generally” is the whole of this chapter’s subject.

20.3 §20.2 The generalization question
For a candidate substrate 𝑋 not among the four, the schema-instantiation question has three possible
outcomes, and naming them sharply is most of what the open problem needs at this stage.
The first outcome is clean instantiation: the four components can be supplied for 𝑋 with the existing four
axioms, the substrate’s surface and substrate admit a correspondence relation and a projection family Π𝑋 ,
and the resulting predicates are operationally checkable. This is the hoped-for case and the one the four
existing instances make plausible, but plausibility across four substrates is not a proof across all of them.
The second outcome is instantiation requiring a new axiom. It is possible that some substrate exhibits
a structural-honesty property that none of the four axioms captures, so that faithful instantiation would
require extending the schema. The corpus already contains a candidate for exactly this: the Mizan primitive
of the Furqan substrate (Chapter 14) is a calibration condition that sits orthogonal to the four axioms, and
it has been carried as a candidate fifth axiom rather than folded into the existing four. The framework’s
posture toward new axioms is deliberately conservative — the Chapter 8 §0.3 ecosystem-condition catalog, for
instance, was held explicitly to be an auxiliary proof-configuration artifact and NOT a fifth axiom, precisely
to prevent the axiom set from absorbing every interpretive condition that arises. Whether any substrate
genuinely forces a new axiom, as opposed to surfacing a condition expressible within the four, is open; the
Mizan calibration question is the concrete form the open problem currently takes.
The third outcome is non-instantiation: a substrate for which the four components cannot be supplied at
all, so that the axioms are operationally inapplicable rather than merely demanding. This outcome is not

CHAPTER 20. SUBSTRATE GENERALIZATION BEYOND THE CURRENT FOUR

274

a defect to be avoided in the framing; it is a falsification. The substrate-independence claim is scoped, but
it is not empty, and a substrate to which the schema demonstrably does not instantiate would falsify the
claim that the schema is general in the asserted sense. This is the falsification path the chapter owns, and
§20.4 fixes its boundary with the different falsification Chapter 21 owns. Determining, for a given candidate
substrate, which of the three outcomes obtains is the substrate-generalization problem.

20.4 §20.3 Candidate substrates and preliminary directions
The claim ledger’s SC1 names a catalog of candidate substrates whose schema-applicability is a research
question: natural-language and broadcast or journalistic information, the direction the BayyinahEnterprise
al-Khabir line points toward; agent-behavior monitoring; scientific-publication integrity; financial-disclosure
integrity; and legal-document integrity. These are not chosen at random. They span a useful range of
structural distance from the four existing instances: financial filings and legal documents have appendonly and surface-substrate structure not far from the file and supply-chain substrates, while broadcast and
journalistic information is markedly less formal than files or code, with a surface-substrate distinction that
is harder to define and a correspondence relation that may not be finite-state. The catalog is therefore a
graded test of the generalization claim, from substrates where instantiation looks near at hand to substrates
where it is genuinely in doubt.
Three directions would constitute progress, and the chapter names them without claiming any is reached.
The first is a fifth worked instantiation on a substrate structurally unlike the four — broadcast or journalistic
information being the most informative, precisely because it strains the surface-substrate distinction; a clean
instantiation there would extend the evidence far more than a fifth instance close to the existing four, and a
failure there would locate the boundary. The second is a structural-feature characterization: a statement of
exactly which features a substrate must possess for the schema to instantiate — an append-only history for
Axiom 1, a definable surface-substrate distinction with a tractable correspondence relation for Axiom 2, a
caller boundary with a conservative outcome approximation for Axiom 3, and a projectable family of views
with a decidable consistency relation for Axiom 4 — so that instantiability could be predicted a priori from a
substrate’s structure rather than discovered case by case. The third is the resolution of the Mizan calibration
question: a determination of whether the calibration condition is expressible within the four axioms on the
substrates that exhibit it, or whether it is a genuinely new axiom, which would settle whether the schema
is four-axiom-complete or open-ended. Each is named as a dissertation-scale problem; together they are the
multi-decade substrate-generalization research program the chapter proposes.

20.5 §20.4 The boundary with Chapter 21
Two distinct falsifications travel under the word “independence,” and the dissertation keeps them in separate chapters on purpose. Chapter 21 §21.2 owns the falsification of the independence assumption: the
𝑛-fold independent re-implementation guarantee of Chapter 11 is conditional on the fault sources of the
independent implementations being genuinely independent, and that conditional is falsified by exhibiting
common-mode faults that drive the implementations wrong together, collapsing the effective strength below
𝑛. That falsification concerns whether the implementations are independent.
This chapter owns a different falsification entirely: whether there exists a substrate to which the AX-SH

CHAPTER 20. SUBSTRATE GENERALIZATION BEYOND THE CURRENT FOUR

275

schema does not instantiate at all, so that the axioms are operationally inapplicable on it. That concerns
whether the substrate admits the schema, not whether implementations on it are independent. The two are
unrelated in content and meet only in the shared word; Chapter 21 §21.2 cross-references the substrate-noninstantiation path to this chapter and does not restate it, in keeping with substrate-of-record uniqueness, and
this section is the reciprocal statement of that boundary. The substrate-non-instantiation path is recorded
as ST1’s falsification route in the claim ledger. Stating the boundary explicitly is itself a small act of the
discipline the dissertation argues for: two claims that share a surface term are held to their distinct substrates
rather than allowed to blur.

20.6 §20.5 Synthesis and routing
This chapter discharges the substrate-generalization forward-references that Chapter 13, Chapter 14, Chapter 15, and Chapter 16 route to Chapter 20 through their permissive surfacing notes, and the falsification
cross-reference that Chapter 21 §21.2 routes here. The four case studies surfaced substrate-specific observations relevant to generalization while declining to assert it; this chapter receives those observations, states
the generalization question they raise, and leaves it open. It records ST1 (the substrate-independence claim,
drafted in Chapter 1, carrying its proof obligation here as a named-open problem), SC1 (the candidate
substrates, each a research question), and O4 (substrate generalization beyond the four, named-open), consistent with their ledger status; naming the problem discharges the forward-reference obligation, it does not
discharge ST1, SC1, or O4.
Three forward routings remain. The schema-instantiation mechanism this chapter reasons about is Axiom
4’s substrate-parameterized projection consistency, owned by Chapter 7; any new instantiation is an application of that machinery, not a new one. The preservation of any further substrate instance, should one be
constructed, falls under the discipline of Chapter 12 and the continuation protocol of Chapter 23. And the
question of whether the dissertation is itself a substrate instance — whether the document submits to the
schema it proposes — is Chapter 22’s, the reflexive self-application.
The chapter generalizes the schema to no fifth substrate, and that restraint is the point. The substrateindependence claim is strong enough to be falsifiable and scoped enough to be honest: it asserts schemainstantiation, demonstrated four times, and it names the question of further instantiation as open rather
than assuming the four instances settle it. A reader who carries that distinction forward will not mistake four
existence proofs for a universal theorem, which is exactly what an honest substrate-generalization chapter is
asked to secure.
